title: Numbers - Introduction
content:
Introduction to Numbers

Part 1: General Introduction

Outline of Numbers

  1. Preparing to leave Sinai (1:1–10:10)
    1. Counting and assembling the tribes (1:1–4:49)
    2. Regulations (5:1–6:27)
    3. Dedicating the altar (7:1–89)
    4. Setting up the lampstand (8:1–4)
    5. Setting apart the Levites (8:5–29)
    6. Second Passover; the cloud to lead them; trumpets (9:1–10:10)
  2. Sinai to Moab, through the wilderness (10:11–17:13)
    1. Complaining and murmuring (10:11–11:15)
    2. The quails (11:16–35)
    3. Miriam’s leprosy (12:1–16)
    4. The spies selected and sent (13:1–14:45)
    5. Commands (15:1–41)
    6. Korah’s rebellion (16:1–17:13)
  3. The Priests and purifying (18:1–19:22)
    1. Priests and Levites (18:1–32)
    2. The law about purifying (19:1–22)
  4. Conflicts (20:1–21:35)
    1. Miriam’s death (20:1–13)
    2. Edom’s refusal and Aaron’s death (20:14–29)
    3. Journey to Moab (21:1–35)
  5. The Plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    1. Balaam (22:1–24:25)
    2. Baal Peor (25:1–18)
    3. The second counting (26:1–65)
    4. Inheritance rights for daughters (27:1–11)
    5. Joshua succeeds Moses (27:12–23)
    6. Offerings and women’s vows (28:1–30:16)
    7. Midianite war (31:1–54)
    8. Across the Jordan (32:1–42)
    9. The people set up camp (33:1–56)
    10. Land west of the Jordan; cities for Levites and cities of refuge (34:1–35:34)
    11. Female heirs marry (36:1–13)

What is the book of Numbers about?

The book of Numbers tells about the people of Israel as they traveled from Mount Sinai in the wilderness to the Jordan River. While traveling, the Israelites became discouraged. So they rebelled against the leaders whom God had given them. At the Jordan River, the people of Israel refused to enter the Promised Land. Because the Israelites were afraid and did not trust God, he delayed their entry into the Promised Land for 40 years (13:1–14:45).

How should the title of this book be translated?

The title of this book, “Numbers,” refers to when the number of the Israelites was counted. The people of the project language may already be familiar with the name “Numbers” from other Bible versions. If not, the translator could consider a clearer name for the book, such as “The Counting of the People of Israel.”

Who wrote the book of Numbers?

The writers of both the Old and New Testaments present Moses as being very involved with writing the book of Numbers. Since ancient times, both Jews and Christians have thought that Moses wrote Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

How does Numbers present the idea of the whole community being responsible when only a few people sinned?

The people understood and assumed that God would punish the whole community of Israel if some of the people rebelled against him. God did often punish the entire nation when some of them sinned. All of the people in the ancient Near East would have understood and expected this. However, Moses and Aaron prayed for God to punish only those who were guilty.

Part 3: Important Translation Issues

Why does Moses speak using third-person pronouns about himself?

When an author wrote about something he was involved in, it was common for him to use the pronoun “he” instead of “I,” or “they” instead of “we.” The translator may decide to use the project’s normal pronouns instead.

“Shall” and “Shall not”

In this book, “shall” is used to give a command and “shall not” is used to give a prohibition. While the form itself is not a command or prohibition, it can be interpreted and translated as such. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words using a command or instruction form.

Sons of Israel and Israel

Throughout this book, “sons of Israel” and “Israel” usually refer to the Israelite nation or people group as if all of them were the sons of their ancestor Israel, who is also called Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language.

title: Numbers - Chapter 1 Introduction
content:
Numbers 1 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter is intended to form a smooth transition from the last chapter of the book of Leviticus. It describes the counting of Israelite men who are able to fight in the army.

  1. Yahweh commands Moses to take a census of Israel’s fighting men (1–46)
  2. Yahweh sets apart the Levites for service of the tabernacle (47–53)
  3. Israel obeys Yahweh’s commands concerning the census (54)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Census

In this chapter, Yahweh commands Moses and Aaron to count how many men of military age were in each tribe of Israel. Some of these men were also called to lead their family groups.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

“Fathers”

Throughout this chapter, the author uses “fathers” to refer more generally to ancestors. The UST translates this word with “ancestor” or “ancestral.” Consider how you would most naturally refer to male ancestors in your language.

“A son of 20 years and upward”

Throughout the chapter, this phrase refers to a man who is at least 20 years old. The man could be significantly older than 20 years old. Consider how you would naturally refer to an age limitation of this kind in your language.

Possession with tribal names in 1:5–16

In 1:5–16, the author consistently uses the word “of” followed by the name of a tribe. In these cases, the possessive form indicates that the named person is a member of that specific tribe. Consider how you would indicate that someone belongs to a specific group.

“One who goes out to war”

Throughout the chapter, this phrase refers to a man who is able to fight in a war. It indicates that the man is fit and able, not that he is already a soldier. Be sure that your translation indicates the ability to fight.

Does Yahweh also speak 1:16?

The words in 1:16 could be a summary provided by the narrator, or they could be the final words spoken by Yahweh to Moses in this section. If these are words spoken by Yahweh to Moses, they should be translated in the present tense (“are”) instead of the past tense (“were”). The ULT and UST indicate that Yahweh’s words end in 1:15, since it is common for the narrator to include a conclusion of this type.

The list of the tribes in 1:20–43

The list of tribes in 1:20–43 includes the exact same wording for most of the tribes. The exceptions are Reuben (which includes “the firstborn of Israel” and “according to their skulls”), Simeon (which includes “his counted ones” and “according to their skulls”), and Naphtali (which omits the opening “Of” to indicate that the list is ending). Notes on these variations are included at the verses where they appear. Notes on the repeated elements are listed here. It can be helpful to decide how to translate the consistently repeated phrases first and then translate the variations with Reuben, Simeon, and Naphtali.

  • Sequence. Some languages would naturally arrange the data about each tribe in a different sequence. The UST models this by creating verse bridges in order to include the number earlier. Consider what would be a natural order in your language.
  • Metaphor: “sons of.” The word “sons” refers to male descendants in general. Consider how you would naturally refer to male descendants in your language.
  • Metaphor: “house of their fathers.” Here, the word “house” refers to a group of people who are related to each other. It does not refer to a building. The word “fathers” refers to male ancestors, not just male parents. So, the phrase “house of their fathers” refers to a group of people who are related to each other because they have the same male ancestors. Consider how you might refer to a group of related people like this in your language.
  • Metaphor: “a son of 20 years and upward.” See the discussion of this phrase above.
  • Implicit: “everyone who goes out to war.” See the discussion of this phrase above.
  • Passive: “their counted ones.” The expression “counted ones” is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Moses and Aaron with the help of the 12 leaders.
  • Possession: “of the tribe of.” The possessive form indicates that “the counted ones” belong to “the tribe,” and the following phrase “of [tribe name]” defines which tribe. Consider how you would indicate that people belong to a specific, named tribe.
  • Large numbers. The numbers in this section are all over 10,000. Consider how you would express large numbers in your language and use that form consistently in this chapter.

title: Numbers 1:1 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠מִדְבַּ֥ר סִינַ֖י

"in the wilderness of Sinai"

A wilderness is a kind of dry, remote, uncultivated area. If your readers would not be familiar with what a wilderness is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in the barren region of Sinai] or [in the remote desert of Sinai]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 1:1 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠אֶחָד֩

"on one"

The implication is that one means “the first day” of the second month. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on the first day]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:1 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠אֶחָד֩

"on one"

The word one here means “first.” Hebrew sometimes uses cardinal numbers (1, 2, 3) where other languages would use ordinal numbers (first, second, third). If your language does not use cardinal numbers this way, you can use an ordinal number instead.

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 1:1 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠חֹ֨דֶשׁ הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֜י

"of the second month"

The second month of the Hebrew calendar includes the last half of April and the first half of May on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar, which is “Iyar” here, then say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

See: Hebrew Months

title: Numbers 1:1 (#5)
content:
לַ⁠חֹ֨דֶשׁ הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֜י בַּ⁠שָּׁנָ֣ה הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֗ית

"of the second month in the second year"

The words second month and second year use ordinal numbers (first, second, third). Some languages use cardinal numbers (1, 2, 3) in these situations. If your language does not use ordinal numbers this way, you can use cardinal numbers instead.

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 1:1 (#6)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"saying"

Here and throughout this chapter, the term saying introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly. For more information, see the book introduction.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 1:2 (#1)
content:
שְׂא֗וּ אֶת־רֹאשׁ֙

"Lift up the head of"

The phrase Lift up the head of is a common expression of this culture to mean “count” or “take a census of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [count the number of] or [record the total of]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 1:2 (#2)
content:
שְׂא֗וּ

"Lift up"

The command Lift up is plural here because God is speaking to both Moses and Aaron. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 1:2 (#3)
content:
כָּל

"all"

The implication is that all refers specifically to the men, as shown later in the verse by “every male.” You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the men of]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:2 (#4)
content:
עֲדַ֣ת בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"the congregation of the sons of Israel"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a congregation that is characterized by being the sons of Israel. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the congregation that consists of the sons of Israel]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 1:2 (#5)
content:
בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"of the sons of Israel"

This is the first of many times in this book that sons of Israel refers to the Israelite nation or people group who descended from Israel. See the discussion of how to translate this phrase in the Introduction to Numbers.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:2 (#6)
content:
לְ⁠מִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֖⁠ם לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם

"according to their clans, according to the house of their fathers"

Here and throughout this chapter, the phrase house of their fathers refers to largest divisions within a single tribe. The word clans refers to the largest divisions of each house of their fathers. Alternate translation: [according to their clans, according to the house of their fathers made up of those clans]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:2 (#7)
content:
לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם

"according to the house of their fathers"

Here, house refers to people who are related. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to the family groups of]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:2 (#8)
content:
אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם

"their fathers"

Yahweh is using the term fathers to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their ancestors]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:2 (#9)
content:
בְּ⁠מִסְפַּ֣ר שֵׁמ֔וֹת

"by the number of the names"

The implication is that Moses was to write down the name of each man as he counted them, creating a list or record. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [by listing the names of each one counted]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:2 (#10)
content:
לְ⁠גֻלְגְּלֹתָֽ⁠ם

"according to their skulls"

Yahweh is using skulls to represent whole persons. He means that each person should be counted only one time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [counting each person] or [one by one]

See: Synecdoche

title: Numbers 1:3 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠בֶּ֨ן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ וָ⁠מַ֔עְלָ⁠ה

"from a son of 20 years and upward"

Yahweh is using from a son of 20 years and upward as a common expression of his culture to mean “any male who is at least 20 years old.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who are twenty years old or older] or [aged twenty and above]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 1:3 (#2)
content:
יֹצֵ֥א צָבָ֖א

"who goes out to war"

The implication is that these men are able to serve as soldiers and fight in battle. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who is able to serve in the army] or [who is fit for military service]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:3 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"in Israel"

Here, Israel refers to the Israelite nation or people group. See the discussion of how to translate Israel in the Introduction to Numbers.

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 1:3 (#4)
content:
אַתָּ֥ה

"you"

The word you is singular here because Yahweh is speaking to Moses. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 1:3 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֖⁠ם

"according to their armies"

The implication is that each tribe was organized and arranged into military units or divisions. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [by their military divisions]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:4 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אִתְּ⁠כֶ֣ם

"And with you"

The implication is that these men will be helping Moses and Aaron with the task of counting the people. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [To assist you in this task] or [Working together with you]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:4 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אִתְּ⁠כֶ֣ם

"And with you"

Since Yahweh is speaking to both Moses and Aaron, the form of you would be dual here, if your language uses that form. Otherwise, the word would be plural.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Dual/Plural

title: Numbers 1:4 (#3)
content:
יִהְי֔וּ אִ֥ישׁ

"will be a man"

Here, the phrase will be is plural, but man is singular. The implication is that one man from each tribe will assist Moses and Aaron. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [must each be represented by one man] or [will each send one man]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:4 (#4)
content:
אִ֖ישׁ לַ⁠מַּטֶּ֑ה

"a man of the tribe"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a man who belongs to each tribe. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a man who represents each tribe] or [a man who belongs to each tribe]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 1:4 (#5)
content:
אִ֛ישׁ רֹ֥אשׁ

"the head man"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the tribal leader were the head of a body. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the chief leader] or [the principal leader]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:4 (#6)
content:
לְ⁠בֵית

"of the house"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of the ancestors figuratively means all the people descended from the tribal patriarchs. Alternate translation: [from the clan] or [from the extended family]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:4 (#7)
content:
אֲבֹתָ֖י⁠ו

"of his fathers"

Yahweh is using the term fathers to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of his ancestors] or [of his forefathers]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:5 (#1)
content:
יַֽעַמְד֖וּ אִתְּ⁠כֶ֑ם

"will stand with you"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if helping with the census were actually standing with Moses and Aaron. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will help you count the people] or [will assist you with the census]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:5 (#2)
content:
אִתְּ⁠כֶ֑ם

"with you"

Since Yahweh is speaking to two people, Moses and Aaron, the form of you would be dual here, if your language uses that form. Otherwise, the word would be plural.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Dual/Plural

title: Numbers 1:5 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠רְאוּבֵ֕ן

"of Reuben"

Here and in 1:6–15, of indicates that the named person (here Elizur) is a member of the tribe (in this case, Reuben). See the chapter introduction for more information. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different expression. Alternate translation: [from the tribe of Reuben]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 1:5–15 (#1)
content:
In this list, the name after son of is always the name of a man.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 1:15 (#1)
content:
עֵינָֽן

"of Enan"

The direct speech that began in 1:2 could: (1) end at the end of this verse. (2) end at the end of 1:16.

See: Quote Markings

title: Numbers 1:16 (#1)
content:
קריאי הָ⁠עֵדָ֔ה

"were} the called ones of the congregation"

The expression called ones is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, it could be: (1) God. Alternate translation: [were the ones whom God called from the congregation]; or (2) the congregation. Alternate translation: [were the ones whom the congregation called]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 1:16 (#2)
content:
קריאי

"were} the called ones of"

The implication is that these men were appointed or chosen by God for leadership in Israel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [were the chosen ones of]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:16 (#3)
content:
אֲבוֹתָ֑⁠ם

"their fathers"

See how you translated the same use of this phrase in 1:2.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:16 (#4)
content:
רָאשֵׁ֛י אַלְפֵ֥י & הֵֽם

"They {were} the heads of the thousands of"

See how you translated the same use of “head” in 1:4.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:16 (#5)
content:
אַלְפֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל

"the thousands of Israel"

Here, the author is speaking as if Israel’s tribal divisions were actually thousands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the divisions within Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:17 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקַּ֥ח מֹשֶׁ֖ה וְ⁠אַהֲרֹ֑ן אֵ֚ת הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֣ים הָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה

"And Moses and Aaron took these men"

Here, the author is speaking as if these men were objects that Moses and Aaron physically took. He means that Moses and Aaron gathered these men together. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then Moses and Aaron summoned these men] or [Then Moses and Aaron gathered these men together]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:17 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִקְּב֖וּ

"who were designated"

The expression were designated is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [whom Yahweh had designated]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 1:17 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠שֵׁמֽוֹת

"by names"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [by their names]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 1:18 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠אֶחָד֙ לַ⁠חֹ֣דֶשׁ הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֔י

"on one of the second month"

See how you translated this phrase in 1:1.

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 1:18 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּתְיַֽלְד֥וּ

"And they recorded their ancestry"

Here, they could refer to: (1) all the Israelite men who were 20 years old or older. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites recorded their ancestry]; or (2) Moses and Aaron, while their refers to all the Israelites. Alternate translation: [And Moses and Aaron recorded the Israelites’ ancestry]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 1:18 (#3)
content:
עַל־מִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֖⁠ם לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם בְּ⁠מִסְפַּ֣ר שֵׁמ֗וֹת

"in accordance with their clans, according to the house of their fathers, by the number of the names"

See how you translated the similar phrases in 1:2.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:18 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠גֻלְגְּלֹתָֽ⁠ם

"according to their skulls"

See how you translated this phrase in 1:2.

See: Synecdoche

title: Numbers 1:20 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּהְי֤וּ

"And they were"

The phrase and they were introduces the whole list of names and numbers that follows. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Here is what Moses recorded:]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:20 (#2)
content:
יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"of Israel"

The word Israel is the name of a man, the son of Isaac. The word Israel does not refer to the Israelites here. Alternate translation: [Isaac’s son Israel]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 1:20 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠גֻלְגְּלֹתָ֔⁠ם

"according to their skulls"

The author is using skulls to represent whole persons. He means that each person should be counted only one time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [individually]

See: Synecdoche

title: Numbers 1:20–43 (#1)
content:
These verses list the number Israelites from each tribe who were above 20 years old and able to fight. See the chapter introduction for information on how to translate these repetitive verses. The following notes give information on verses that include unique elements.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:22 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠גֻלְגְּלֹתָ֔⁠ם

"according to their skulls"

See how you translated this phrase in 1:20.

See: Synecdoche

title: Numbers 1:22 (#2)
content:
פְּקֻדָ֗י⁠ו

"his counted ones"

It might seem that the expression his counted ones contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, especially since a similar phrase appears in the next verse. If so, you can omit it.

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 1:22 (#3)
content:
פְּקֻדָ֗י⁠ו

"his counted ones"

The expression counted ones is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [those whom Moses and Aaron counted]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 1:22 (#4)
content:
פְּקֻדָ֗י⁠ו

"his counted ones"

The author is using the possessive form to mean the counted ones who came from Simeon’s tribe. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the counted ones from Simeon]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 1:34 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה

"Of the sons of Manasseh"

The implication is that Manasseh, along with Ephraim, was one of Joseph’s sons. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Also of the sons of Joseph: of the sons of Manasseh]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:42 (#1)
content:
בְּנֵ֣י נַפְתָּלִ֔י

"Of} the sons of Naphtali"

Here, the preposition translated Of is omitted to indicate that this is the last tribe in the list. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Lastly, of the sons of Naphtali]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:44 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠פְּקֻדִ֡ים אֲשֶׁר֩ פָּקַ֨ד מֹשֶׁ֤ה וְ⁠אַהֲרֹן֙

"were} the counted ones, whom Moses and Aaron had counted"

It might seem that the expression counted ones whom Moses and Aaron had counted contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [were the people whom Moses and Aaron had counted]

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 1:44 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠נְשִׂיאֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל שְׁנֵ֥ים עָשָׂ֖ר אִ֑ישׁ

"and the leaders of Israel, 12 men"

Here Moses implies that these 12 men helped Moses and Aaron count the people, as stated in 1:5. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [with the 12 leaders of Israel helping them]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:44 (#3)
content:
אִישׁ־אֶחָ֥ד לְ⁠בֵית־אֲבֹתָ֖י⁠ו הָיֽוּ

"They were one man for the house of his fathers"

The author is using one man for the house of his fathers as a common expression of his culture to mean “each person represented his ancestral house.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Each one of them was from the house of his fathers]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 1:44 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠בֵית

"for the house"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. Alternate translation: [of the household]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:44 (#5)
content:
אֲבֹתָ֖י⁠ו

"of his fathers"

The author is using the term fathers to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of his ancestors] or [of his family line]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:45 (#1)
content:
פְּקוּדֵ֥י בְנֵֽי

"the counted ones of the sons"

The expression counted ones is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones whom Moses, Aaron, and the 12 leaders counted]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 1:45 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם

"according to the house of their fathers"

See how you translated the similar phrase in 1:44.

title: Numbers 1:45 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠בֶּ֨ן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ וָ⁠מַ֔עְלָ⁠ה כָּל־יֹצֵ֥א צָבָ֖א

"from a son of 20 years and upward, everyone who goes out to war"

title: Numbers 1:46 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠פְּקֻדִ֔ים

"the counted ones"

The expression counted ones is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones whom Moses, Aaron, and the 12 leaders counted]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 1:46 (#2)
content:
שֵׁשׁ־מֵא֥וֹת אֶ֖לֶף וּ⁠שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֑ים וַ⁠חֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת וַ⁠חֲמִשִּֽׁים

See how you translated the large numbers in 1:20–43.

title: Numbers 1:47 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֖ם

"And the Levites"

The author uses the word And here to indicate a contrast between what was expected (that the Levites would be counted along with the other tribes) and what actually happened (they were not counted). In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But the Levites]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Numbers 1:47 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠מַטֵּ֣ה אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם

"according to the tribe of their fathers"

See how you translated the similar phrase “tribes of their fathers” in 1:16.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:47 (#3)
content:
לֹ֥א הָתְפָּקְד֖וּ

"were not counted"

The expression were not counted is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [were those whom Moses, Aaron, and the 12 leaders did not count]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 1:47 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠תוֹכָֽ⁠ם

"in the midst of them"

Here, the author is speaking as if including the Levites in the census count meant counting the Levites in the midst of the other tribes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [together with them]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:48 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה

"And Yahweh spoke"

The word And indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [The reason for this is that Yahweh spoke]

title: Numbers 1:48 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה

"And Yahweh spoke"

The previous verse describes how the Levites were not included in the census. If it is helpful in your language, you might want to make it clear that the account that starts in this verse happened before the census was taken. The UST does that by using the phrase “had told.” Alternate translation: [And Yahweh previously spoke]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 1:49 (#1)
content:
לֹ֣א תִפְקֹ֔ד & לֹ֣א תִשָּׂ֑א

"you shall not count & you shall not lift up"

The word you is singular here because God is speaking directly to Moses. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

title: Numbers 1:49 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אֶת־רֹאשָׁ֖⁠ם לֹ֣א תִשָּׂ֑א

בְּ⁠ת֖וֹךְ בְּנֵ֥י

"in the midst of the sons"

title: Numbers 1:50 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אַתָּ֡ה

"And you"

The word you is singular here because God is speaking directly to Moses. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 1:50 (#2)
content:
מִשְׁכַּ֨ן הָ⁠עֵדֻ֜ת

"the Dwelling of the Testimony"

The implication is that the Testimony refers to the Ten Commandments that were kept in the ark inside this tent. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the tent holding the ark containing the Ten Commandments]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:50 (#3)
content:
ל⁠וֹ֒

"belongs to it"

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean “the items that are used in the Dwelling.” If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is used in it]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 1:50 (#4)
content:
הֵ֜מָּה יִשְׂא֤וּ & וְ⁠הֵ֖ם יְשָׁרְתֻ֑⁠הוּ

"They themselves shall carry & and they themselves shall minister to it"

The intensive pronouns themselves represent emphasis in what Yahweh is saying. If your language uses explicit pronouns for emphasis, you may want to use that construction in your translation. Other languages may have other ways of bringing out this emphasis. Alternate translation: [It is they who shall carry … and it is they who shall minister to it]

See: Reflexive Pronouns

title: Numbers 1:51 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בִ⁠נְסֹ֣עַ הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּ֗ן & וּ⁠בַ⁠חֲנֹת֙ הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּ֔ן

"And when the Dwelling sets out & and when the Dwelling camps"

Yahweh is speaking of the Dwelling as if it were a living thing that sets out and camps. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And when the Israelites set out with the Dwelling … and when the Israelites camp with the Dwelling]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 1:51 (#2)
content:
יוֹרִ֤ידוּ אֹת⁠וֹ֙ & יָקִ֥ימוּ אֹת֖⁠וֹ

"shall take it down & shall raise it up"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if disassembling and assembling the Dwelling were lowering and raising it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [must take it apart … must put it back together]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:51 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠זָּ֥ר

"And the stranger"

The implication is that a stranger refers to anyone who is not a Levite, even another Israelite. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And anyone other than a Levite]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:51 (#4)
content:
יוּמָֽת

"shall be put to death"

The expression shall be put to death is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is one or several Israelites. Alternate translation: [the Israelites must put that person to death]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 1:52 (#1)
content:
אִ֧ישׁ עַֽל־מַחֲנֵ֛⁠הוּ וְ⁠אִ֥ישׁ עַל־דִּגְל֖⁠וֹ

"a man at his camp and a man at his banner"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [each person at his or her camp and each person at his or her banner]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 1:52 (#2)
content:
אִ֧ישׁ & וְ⁠אִ֥ישׁ

"a man & and a man"

Yahweh is not referring to a specific man. He means each person in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [each man … each man]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 1:52 (#3)
content:
דִּגְל֖⁠וֹ

"his banner"

A banner is a kind of flag made of cloth attached to a pole that identifies a group. If your readers would not be familiar with what a banner is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [his flag]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 1:52 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָֽ⁠ם

"according to their armies"

The implication is that armies refers to the organized military divisions of Israel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated this phrase in 1:3. Alternate translation: [by their military divisions]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:53 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠מִשְׁכַּ֣ן הָ⁠עֵדֻ֔ת & מִשְׁכַּ֥ן הָ⁠עֵדֽוּת

"the Dwelling of the Testimony & of the Dwelling of the Testimony"

See how you translated this phrase in 1:50.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:53 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֣ה קֶ֔צֶף עַל־עֲדַ֖ת בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"and wrath will not be on the congregation of the sons of Israel"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if wrath were actually an object that could be placed on people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the congregation of the sons of Israel will not experience wrath]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 1:53 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֣ה קֶ֔צֶף

"and wrath will not be"

The word and introduces the result of obeying the instructions stated in the previous clause. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [which will result in wrath not being]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 1:53 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֣ה קֶ֔צֶף

"and wrath will not be"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of wrath, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will not be wrathful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 1:53 (#5)
content:
עֲדַ֖ת בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"the congregation of the sons of Israel"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a congregation that is characterized by being the sons of Israel. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 1:2. Alternate translation: [the congregation, that is, the sons of Israel]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 1:53 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁמְרוּ֙ הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֔ם אֶת־מִשְׁמֶ֖רֶת

"And the Levites shall keep the keeping"

God is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [The Levites shall carefully keep] or [The Levites must be fully responsible for keeping]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 1:54 (#1)
content:
וַֽ⁠יַּעֲשׂ֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כְּ֠⁠כֹל אֲשֶׁ֨ר צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־מֹשֶׁ֖ה כֵּ֥ן עָשֽׂוּ

"And the sons of Israel did according to all that Yahweh commanded Moses, so they did"

The expressions the sons of Israel did according to all that Yahweh commanded Moses and so they did mean similar things. The author is using them together to emphasize that the Israelites did exactly what Yahweh had commanded. If it would be clearer in your language, you could combine these into a single phrase.

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 1:54 (#2)
content:
צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־מֹשֶׁ֖ה

"Yahweh commanded Moses"

The implication is that Yahweh commanded Moses to command the people to do these things. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh commanded Moses to command them to do]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 1:54 (#3)
content:
כֵּ֥ן עָשֽׂוּ

"so they did"

Here, so they did is a comment about what happened after the story as a result of the events within the story itself. This signals the end of a story. Use the natural form in your language for expressing the conclusion of a story. Alternate translation: [and that is exactly what they did]

See: End of Story

title: Numbers - Chapter 2 Introduction
content:
Numbers 2 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes how the tribes are to camp around the tabernacle. It also establishes the order in which they are to travel.

  1. Yahweh assigns the tribes their camp positions and order of travel (1–31)
  2. Israel camps and travels according to Yahweh’s commands (32–34)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Cardinal directions

Yahweh explains how the Israelites will camp in relation to the sacred tent and does so using cardinal directions: north, east, south, and west. These terms describe a person’s orientation in relation to the sunrise. The sun rises in the east and sets in the west. If one faces the direction of the sunrise and then turns to his right, he is facing south. If, when facing the sunrise, he turns left, he is facing north.

Banners

Each of the four camps (each made up of three tribes) would have its own “banner.” A banner is a type of flag that has images and sometimes words on it. In this case, the specific images and possibly words would indicate which tribes would camp near that banner. The banner was most closely connected with the tribe that was the leader of the camp: Judah, Reuben, Ephraim, and Dan.

The order of the tribes

Here is a diagram of the tribes around the tent of meeting. Note the groups of three on each of the four cardinal directions.

``` Asher Dan Naphtali

Benjamin Levites Issachar

Ephraim Tent of Meeting Judah

Manasseh Zebulun

      Gad Reuben Simeon

```

Translation Issues in This Chapter

“The sons of [tribe]”

Throughout this chapter, Yahweh uses the phrase “the sons of [tribe name].” He speaks of the people who belong to the tribe as if they were the direct “sons” of the man whom the tribe was named after. Consider how you would naturally refer to the members of a tribe. The UST uses the phrase “the descendants of [tribe name].”

“According to their armies”

The phrase “according to their armies” indicates that each tribe and camp was organized and arranged into military units or divisions. The people in each military unit would camp together, and their names were listed together when the census was recorded. The UST expresses this idea with the phrase “by their army divisions.”

Names repeated from chapter 1

In this chapter, the leaders of the tribes are the same as the leaders listed in 1:5–15. The only difference is that the name Reuel in 2:14 is spelled Deuel in 1:14. See the note on 2:14 for more information. For the rest of the names, translate them in this chapter as you did in chapter 1.

Verses with total numbers

The description of each tribe’s army ends with a phrase that is almost identical in each case. The only variation is whether “his” or “their” goes with the phrase “counted ones.” Translate these verses in the same way, changing only the numbers. Notes on the first instance of this phrase 2:4 provide guidance for several translation issues that it presents.

Repeated structure for the sides of the tent of meeting

This chapter repeats the same basic structure for each of the four sides of the tent of meeting. For the first occurrence of each structure, there are notes that give guidance on specific issues. For the following verses that use the same structure, there is just a single note that points back to a previous verse and that lists any major differences from that verse. Besides those differences, translate the verses with the same structure in the same way.

title: Numbers 2:1 (#1)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"saying"

Here and throughout the chapter, the word saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 2:2 (#1)
content:
אִ֣ישׁ עַל־דִּגְל֤⁠וֹ

"a man at his banner"

See how you translated this phrase in 1:52.

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 2:2 (#2)
content:
בְ⁠אֹתֹת֙

"with the sign"

A sign is a kind of identifying mark or symbol. It is different from the “banner” referred to elsewhere in the chapter. The “banner” seems to represent each camp, while the sign identifies just one tribe or a portion of a tribe. If your readers would not be familiar with what a sign is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [with the symbol]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 2:2 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אֲבֹתָ֔⁠ם

"of the house of their fathers"

See how you translated the house of their fathers in 1:2.

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 2:2 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠נֶּ֕גֶד סָבִ֥יב לְ⁠אֹֽהֶל־מוֹעֵ֖ד

"from the front, around the tent of meeting"

Yahweh is using from the front as a common expression of his culture to mean “at a distance from.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [around but far away from the tent of meeting]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 2:3 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠חֹנִים֙

"And the ones camping"

The implication is that these are the tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, as shown in verses 3–9. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the three tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, who are camping]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 2:3 (#2)
content:
קֵ֣דְמָ⁠ה מִזְרָ֔חָ⁠ה

"to the east, from the sunrise"

It might seem that the expression to the east to the sunrise contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [to the east]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 2:3 (#3)
content:
קֵ֣דְמָ⁠ה

"to the east"

This implies that this direction is in relation to the tent of meeting. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to the east of the tent of meeting]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 2:3 (#4)
content:
דֶּ֛גֶל מַחֲנֵ֥ה יְהוּדָ֖ה

"will be} the banner of the camp of Judah"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the tribes that will camp to the east were actually the banner of the camp of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will be located near the banner of the camp of Judah]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 2:3 (#5)
content:
דֶּ֛גֶל מַחֲנֵ֥ה

"will be} the banner of the camp of"

See how you translated banner in 1:52.

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 2:3 (#6)
content:
מַחֲנֵ֥ה יְהוּדָ֖ה

"the camp of Judah"

Here, the camp of Judah represents the combined tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun who camp together under Judah’s leadership. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the camp of Judah, which includes Issachar and Zebulun]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 2:3 (#7)
content:
לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֑⁠ם

"according to their armies"

This is the first of many times in this chapter that Yahweh uses the phrase according to their armies. See the chapter introduction for more information.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 2:3 (#8)
content:
לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה

"of the sons of Judah"

This is the first of many times in this chapter that Yahweh uses the phrase the sons of followed by a tribe name to refer to the men who belong to that tribe. See the chapter introduction for more information.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 2:3 (#9)
content:
נַחְשׁ֖וֹן בֶּן־עַמִּינָדָֽב

"is} Nahshon, the son of Amminadab"

For these and the other names in this chapter, translate them as you did in chapter 1. See the chapter introduction for more information.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 2:4 (#1)
content:

title: Numbers - Chapter 3 Introduction
content:
Numbers 3 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes the counting of Levite men and their assignments for taking care of the tent of meeting. It also describes how the Levites and their animals act as ransoms for the firstborn Israelites and the Israelites’ firstborn animals.

  1. Aaron’s sons serve as priests (1–4)
  2. Yahweh sets apart the Levites to serve the priests and care for the tabernacle (5–13)
  3. Yahweh commands Moses to count the Levite clans and assigns their duties (14–39)
  4. The Levites replace Israel’s firstborn, and the remaining firstborn are redeemed (40–51)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The tribe of Levi

The Levites had a special role in Israel, which is why they were not included in the census in chapters 1 and 2. They were specially dedicated to serve Yahweh and to keep and serve the sacred tent. They also functioned as a ransom for the firstborn Israelites and the firstborn animals of the Israelites. See the following entries for more information on the specific roles the Levites fulfilled.

Keep

One of the primary duties of the Levites was to “keep” various things, including Aaron, the Israelites, and the parts of the sacred tent. In this context, “keep” refers specifically to keeping watch or guarding. No one besides the Levites was supposed to approach the sacred tent or do any priestly duties. So, the Levites guarded the sacred tent and the Israelites to prevent any non-Levite from approaching. Consider how to refer to this type of guard duty.

Serve

One of the primary duties of the Levites was to “serve.” In this context, “serve” refers specifically to physical labor, including carrying, setting up, and tearing down the sacred tent and its equipment. There is more information about the physical labor required of the Levites in Numbers 4. Consider how to refer to this type of physical labor.

Ransom

In 3:45–51, Yahweh requires the Israelites to pay a ransom to him for the firstborn males that he did not kill during the tenth plague in Egypt, as described in Exodus 12:29 and 13:15. Because Yahweh did not kill the firstborn male people and animals among the Israelites, he considered them to owe him their lives. Instead of taking their lives, Yahweh chose the Levite men to be his special servants in their place. However, the number of Levites was 273 people less than the number of firstborn males, so Yahweh required the people to pay money to him to redeem those additional people.

“House of the father” and “clan”

The phrase “house of the father” and the word “clan” refer to divisions of an Israelite tribe. In Numbers, the “house of the father” was the larger division, and each “house of the father” contained several “clans.” For example, one “house of the father” within the tribe of Levi was named after Levi’s son, Gershon. Within the “house of the father” of the Gershonites were two clans named after Gershon’s sons (Levi’s grandsons): Libni and Shimei. Consider how you might refer to tribal divisions within other tribal divisions.

Firstborn

Throughout this chapter, the word “firstborn” always refers to the oldest male child or offspring of a human or animal. Sometimes the word “male” is explicitly included, and other times it is implied. Use a word or phrase that clearly refers to the oldest male child or offspring.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

“From a son of a month and upward”

Many instructions in this chapter apply only to the Levites who qualify as “from a son of a month and upward.” This phrase refers to people who are at least one month old. They could be young or old, but they must have lived for at least one month after their birth. Consider how you might refer to anyone who is one month old or older.

“Keep the keeping” and “serve the service”

Multiple times in this chapter, Yahweh or the narrator uses a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. They do this for emphasis. The two specific phrases are “keep the keeping” and “serve the service.” You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of showing the emphasis. Consider how you might emphasize the completeness of the “keeping” and “serving.”

title: Numbers 3:1 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֛לֶּה

"And these"

The author is using the word And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event. Alternate translation: [Now these]

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 3:1 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠י֗וֹם

"on the day"

The phrase on the day is a common expression of this culture to mean “when.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 3:3 (#1)
content:
אֵ֗לֶּה שְׁמוֹת֙ בְּנֵ֣י אַהֲרֹ֔ן הַ⁠כֹּהֲנִ֖ים

"These {are} the names of the sons of Aaron, the priests"

It might seem that the expression These are the names of the sons of Aaron contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, since the same words are in the previous verse. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [They are the priests]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 3:3 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠מְּשֻׁחִ֑ים אֲשֶׁר־מִלֵּ֥א יָדָ֖⁠ם

"the ones who were anointed, whose hand he filled"

The expressions the ones who were anointed and whose hand he filled are describing the same priests, not distinguishing between different priests. They are not making a distinction between the priests and the ones who were anointed or whose hand he filled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this relationship between these phrases clearer. Alternate translation: [that is, the ones who were anointed and whose hand he filled]

See: Distinguishing Versus Informing or Reminding

title: Numbers 3:3 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠מְּשֻׁחִ֑ים

"the ones who were anointed"

The expression who were anointed is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Moses. Alternate translation: [the ones whom Moses anointed]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 3:3 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־מִלֵּ֥א יָדָ֖⁠ם לְ⁠כַהֵֽן

"whose hand he filled to serve as priest"

In this verse, the words hand and priest are singular in form, but they refer to all the priests as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms of “hand” and “priest.” Alternate translation: [whose hands he filled to serve as priests]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 3:3 (#5)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־מִלֵּ֥א יָדָ֖⁠ם

"whose hand he filled"

The author is using whose hand he filled as a common expression of his culture to mean “whom he dedicated as priests.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whom he dedicated]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 3:4 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֣מָת נָדָ֣ב וַ⁠אֲבִיה֣וּא

"But Nadab died and Abihu"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the words “and Abihu” before the word “died.” Alternate translation: [But Nadab and Abihu died]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 3:4 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֡ה & לִ⁠פְנֵ֤י יְהוָה֙

"to the face of Yahweh & to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of … in the presence of]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 3:4 (#3)
content:
אֵ֨שׁ זָרָ֜ה

"strange fire"

Here, strange fire represents burning coals that were not authorized for use in worship, as indicated in the account of this event in Leviticus 10:1. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [strange coals that were on fire]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 3:4 (#4)
content:
אֵ֨שׁ זָרָ֜ה

"strange fire"

Here, the author is speaking of fire that was not authorized as if it were strange or foreign. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [unauthorized fire]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 3:4 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠בָנִ֖ים לֹא־הָי֣וּ לָ⁠הֶ֑ם

"and sons were not to them"

The author is using sons were not to them as a common expression of his culture to mean “they had no sons.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they had no sons]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 3:4 (#6)
content:
וַ⁠יְכַהֵ֤ן אֶלְעָזָר֙ וְ⁠אִ֣יתָמָ֔ר

"And Eleazar served as priest and Ithamar"

The word And here indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [As a result, only Eleazar served as priest and Ithamar]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 3:4 (#7)
content:
וַ⁠יְכַהֵ֤ן אֶלְעָזָר֙ וְ⁠אִ֣יתָמָ֔ר

"And Eleazar served as priest and Ithamar"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Eleazar and Ithamar together by saying that they both served as priests. Alternate translation: [And Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 3:4 (#8)
content:
עַל־פְּנֵ֖י אַהֲרֹ֥ן

"against the face of Aaron"

The author is using against the face of as a common expression of his culture to mean “under the supervision of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [under the supervision of Aaron]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 3:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה

"And Yahweh spoke"

The author is using the word translated And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event. Alternate translation: [Now Yahweh spoke]

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 3:5 (#2)
content:
לֵּ⁠אמֹֽר

"saying"

Here and throughout the chapter, the word saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 3:6 (#1)
content:
אֶת־מַטֵּ֣ה לֵוִ֔י

"the tribe of Levi"

Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean the tribe that has the name Levi. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. See how you translated this phrase in 1:21. Alternate translation: [Levi tribe] or [the tribe that is named Levi]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 3:6 (#2)
content:
אֹת֔⁠וֹ

"it"

Here, it refers to all the men of the tribe of Levi. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [the men from the tribe]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 3:6 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י אַהֲרֹ֣ן

"to the face of Aaron"

See how you translated the same use of this phrase in 3:4.

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 3:7 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁמְר֣וּ אֶת־מִשְׁמַרְתּ֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־מִשְׁמֶ֨רֶת֙ כָּל־הָ֣⁠עֵדָ֔ה

"And they shall keep his keeping and the keeping of all the congregation"

For emphasis, people in this culture used a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. Here and throughout this chapter, this happens with the words keep and keeping. See the chapter introduction for more information. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of showing the emphasis. Alternate translation: [And they shall carefully keep him and all the congregation]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 3:7 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֑ד

"to the face of the tent of meeting"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of the tent of meeting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of the tent of meeting]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 3:7 (#3)
content:
לַ⁠עֲבֹ֖ד אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֥ת הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּֽן

"to serve the service of the Dwelling"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to serve what needs to be served for the Dwelling]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 3:7 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠עֲבֹ֖ד

"to serve"

Here, the phrase to serve could introduce: (1) something that happens at the same time as the “keeping” earlier in the verse. Alternate translation: [while serving]; or (2) the means by which they do the “keeping” earlier in the verse. Alternate translation: [by serving]

See: Connect — Simultaneous Time Relationship

title: Numbers 3:8 (#1)
content:
כְּלֵי֙ אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֔ד

"the vessels of the tent of meeting"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe vessels that are characterized by being used in the tent of meeting. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the vessels that are used in the tent of meeting]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 3:8 (#2)
content:
לַ⁠עֲבֹ֖ד אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֥ת הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּֽן

"to serve the service of the Dwelling"

See how you translated this phrase in 3:7.

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 3:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נָתַתָּה֙ אֶת־הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֔ם לְ⁠אַהֲרֹ֖ן וּ⁠לְ⁠בָנָ֑י⁠ו נְתוּנִ֨ם נְתוּנִ֥ם הֵ֨מָּה֙ ל֔⁠וֹ

"And you shall give the Levites to Aaron and to his sons. They {are} given, given to him"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the Levites were actually objects that could be given to Aaron and his sons. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you shall assign the Levites to Aaron and to his sons. They are assigned, assigned to him]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 3:9 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נָתַתָּה֙

"And you shall give"

The word you is singular here because Yahweh is speaking to Moses. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 3:9 (#3)
content:
נְתוּנִ֨ם נְתוּנִ֥ם הֵ֨מָּה֙

"They {are} given, given"

The expression are given, given is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [I have given them, given them]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 3:9 (#4)
content:
נְתוּנִ֨ם נְתוּנִ֥ם הֵ֨מָּה֙

"They {are} given, given"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb given in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [They are wholly given]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 3:9 (#5)
content:
ל֔⁠וֹ

"to him"

The implication is that him refers to Aaron and his sons, who were just mentioned. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to Aaron and his sons]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 3:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֶת & תִּפְקֹ֔ד

"And you shall count"

The implication is that count means to appoint or assign Aaron and his sons as priests. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And you shall appoint as priests]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 3:10 (#2)
content:
אֶת־כְּהֻנָּתָ֑⁠ם

"their priesthood"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of priesthood, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what they do as priests]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 3:10 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠זָּ֥ר הַ⁠קָּרֵ֖ב יוּמָֽת

"And the stranger who comes near shall be put to death"

See how you translated this sentence in 1:51.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 3:12 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִ֞י הִנֵּ֧ה לָקַ֣חְתִּי

"And I, behold, I have taken"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I have taken already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is the one who has chosen the Levites. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [And behold, I am the one who has taken]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 3:12 (#2)
content:
הִנֵּ֧ה

"behold"

Yahweh is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [listen]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 3:12 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִ֞י & לָקַ֣חְתִּי אֶת־הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֗ם מִ⁠תּוֹךְ֙ בְּנֵ֣י

"And I & I have taken the Levites from the midst of the sons"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if choosing the Levites were actually taking them from the midst of the sons of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I … have selected the Levites from]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 3:12 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִ֞י & לָקַ֣חְתִּי אֶת־הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֗ם

"And I & I have taken the Levites"

The implication is that Yahweh has taken the Levites to serve him at the tent of meeting. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I … have taken the Levites to minister to me in the tent of meeting]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 3:12 (#5)
content:
בְּכ֛וֹר פֶּ֥טֶר רֶ֖חֶם

"firstborn, the opener of the womb"

It might seem that the expression firstborn, the opener of the womb contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [firstborn]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 3:12 (#6)
content:
בְּכ֛וֹר

"firstborn"

Here and throughout the chapter, the implication is that firstborn refers specifically to firstborn males. See the chapter introduction for more information. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [firstborn male]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 3:12 (#7)
content:
פֶּ֥טֶר רֶ֖חֶם

"the opener of the womb"

Yahweh is using the opener of the womb as a common expression of the culture to mean “first child to be born to a woman.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the first child of every woman]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 3:12 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠הָ֥יוּ לִ֖⁠י הַ⁠לְוִיִּֽם

"and the Levites shall be for me"

The word and indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and as a result, the Levites shall be for me]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 3:13 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠יוֹם֩ הַכֹּתִ֨⁠י

"On the day of my striking down"

See how you translated this phrase in 3:1.

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 3:13 (#2)
content:
הַכֹּתִ֨⁠י

"my striking down"

By striking down, Yahweh means that he killed the firstborn Egyptians. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to Numbers. Alternate translation: [my slaying]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 3:13 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"in Israel"

Here, Israel refers to the people who descended from Israel. See the discussion in the Introduction to Numbers.

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 3:13 (#4)
content:
מֵ⁠אָדָ֖ם עַד־בְּהֵמָ֑ה

"from man up to animal"

The expression from man up to animal is a common expression of this culture to mean “both humans and animals.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [both men and animals]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 3:13 (#5)
content:
מֵ⁠אָדָ֖ם

"from man"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [from human]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 3:15 (#1)
content:
אֶת־בְּנֵ֣י לֵוִ֔י

"the sons of Levi"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of the sons of Levi as if they were Levi’s direct children, but he is actually referring to all men who were descended from Levi. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the men descended from Levi]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 3:15 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠בֵ֥ית אֲבֹתָ֖⁠ם לְ⁠מִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֑⁠ם

"according to the house of their fathers, according to their clans"

Here and throughout this chapter, the phrase house of their fathers refers to largest divisions within a single tribe. The word clans refers to the largest divisions of each house of their fathers. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [according to the house of their fathers, according to the clans that make up each house of their fathers]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 3:15 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠בֵ֥ית אֲבֹתָ֖⁠ם

"according to the house of their fathers"

See how you translated this phrase in 1:2.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 3:15 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠מִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֑⁠ם כָּל־זָכָ֛ר & תִּפְקְדֵֽ⁠ם

"according to their clans. You shall count them, every male"

It might seem that the expression You shall count them contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language since it repeats the command from the first part of the verse. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [according to their clans, every male]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 3:15 (#5)
content:
כָּל־זָכָ֛ר מִ⁠בֶּן־חֹ֥דֶשׁ וָ⁠מַ֖עְלָ⁠ה

"every male from a son of a month and upward"

Here and throughout this chapter, the phrase from a son of a month and upward is a common expression of this culture to mean “someone who is at least one month old.” See the chapter introduction for more information. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [every male who is one month old or older]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 3:16 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּפְקֹ֥ד אֹתָ֛⁠ם מֹשֶׁ֖ה

"And Moses counted them"

The word And indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [As a result, Moses counted them]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 3:16 (#2)
content:
עַל־פִּ֣י יְהוָ֑ה כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֖ר צֻוָּֽה

"upon the mouth of Yahweh, just as he was commanded"

It might seem that the expression upon the mouth of Yahweh, just as he was commanded contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [exactly as he was commanded by Yahweh]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 3:16 (#3)
content:
עַל־פִּ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"upon the mouth of Yahweh"

The author is using upon the mouth of Yahweh as a common expression of his culture to mean “according to what Yahweh said.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as Yahweh had said]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 3:25 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּ֖ן וְ⁠הָ⁠אֹ֑הֶל

"was} the Dwelling and the tent"

Here, the word Dwelling refers specifically to the inner part of the sacred tent, made out of ten curtains. The word tent refers specifically to the outer part of the sacred tent, made out of eleven curtains. See Exodus 26:1–13 for details. You could indicate these details explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the inner curtains and the outer curtains of the Dwelling]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 3:25 (#3)
content:
מִכְסֵ֕⁠הוּ

"its covering"

The implication is that this was the covering that went over the entire tent. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the covering over the tent]

title: Numbers 3:26 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠קַלְעֵ֣י הֶֽ⁠חָצֵ֗ר

"and the hangings of the courtyard"

The implication is that these were the curtains that marked off and formed a fence around the courtyard, as described in Exodus 27:9–15. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the curtains that marked off the courtyard]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 3:26 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֧ר עַל־הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּ֛ן וְ⁠עַל־הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֖חַ סָבִ֑יב

"that {is} on the Dwelling and on the altar all around"

The author is using on the Dwelling and on the altar all around as a common expression of his culture to mean “that contains the sacred tent and the altar.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that contains the Dwelling and the altar]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 3:26 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אֵת֙ מֵֽיתָרָ֔י⁠ו לְ⁠כֹ֖ל עֲבֹדָתֽ⁠וֹ

"and its ropes for all its service"

Here, the pronoun its could refer to: (1) the curtains mentioned in this and the previous verse. Alternate translation: [and the ropes for the curtains for all their service]; or (2) the Dwelling. Alternate translation: [and the ropes for the Dwelling for all its service]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 3:26 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠כֹ֖ל עֲבֹדָתֽ⁠וֹ

title: Numbers 3:27 (#2)
content:
הַֽ⁠עַמְרָמִי֙ & הַ⁠יִּצְהָרִ֔י & הַֽ⁠חֶבְרֹנִ֔י & הָֽ⁠עָזִּיאֵלִ֑י & הַ⁠קְּהָתִֽי

"the Amramite & the Izharite & the Hebronite & the Uzzielite & the Kohathite"

Amramite refers to a descendant of Amram, Izharite refers to a descendant of Izhar, Hebronite refers to a descendant of Hebron, Uzzielite refers to a descendant of Uzziel, and Kohathite refers to a descendant of Kohath.

title: Numbers 3:27 (#3)
content:
הַֽ⁠עַמְרָמִי֙ & הַ⁠יִּצְהָרִ֔י & הַֽ⁠חֶבְרֹנִ֔י & הָֽ⁠עָזִּיאֵלִ֑י & הַ⁠קְּהָתִֽי

"the Amramite & the Izharite & the Hebronite & the Uzzielite & the Kohathite"

The author is not referring to a specific Amramite, Izharite, Hebronite, Uzzielite, or Kohathite. He means all the people in each of these clans. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Amramites … the Izharites … the Hebronites … the Uzzielites … the Kohathites]

"and its bases"

These bases were silver blocks that had a slot in them to keep the pillars in place and off the ground. If a translation is available in your language, see how it translates this term in Exodus 26:19. Alternate translation: [and its metal foundations]

title: Numbers 3:36 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠כֹ֖ל עֲבֹדָתֽ⁠וֹ
