Here, the pronoun him refers to the Nazirite. The pronoun he could refer to: (1) any person who could accompany the Nazirite. Alternate translation: [a person shall bring the Nazirite] or [the Nazirite shall be brought]; or (2) the Nazirite, who brings himself. Alternate translation: [the Nazirite shall bring himself]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 6:14 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִקְרִ֣יב אֶת־קָרְבָּנ֣⁠וֹ

"and he shall present his offering"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb (present) and its object (offering) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [and he shall give his offering]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 6:14 (#2)
content:
בֶּן־שְׁנָת֨⁠וֹ

"a son of his year"

Yahweh is using the common expression of his culture a son of his year to mean “one year old.” See how you translated this phrase in 6:12. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a year old]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 6:14 (#3)
content:
בַּת־שְׁנָתָ֛⁠הּ

"a daughter of her year"

The phrase a daughter of her year is a common expression of the culture that means “a year old.” See how you translated the similar phrase “a son of his year” earlier in the verse. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a year old]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 6:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠סַ֣ל מַצּ֗וֹת סֹ֤לֶת חַלֹּת֙ בְּלוּלֹ֣ת בַּ⁠שֶּׁ֔מֶן וּ⁠רְקִיקֵ֥י מַצּ֖וֹת מְשֻׁחִ֣ים בַּ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶן וּ⁠מִנְחָתָ֖⁠ם וְ⁠נִסְכֵּי⁠הֶֽם

"and a basket of unleavened bread, flour of loaves mixed with the oil and wafers of unleavened bread anointed with the oil; and their grain offering and their drink offerings"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about their grain offering and their drink offerings immediately after the sacrifices mentioned in verse 14, since these offerings accompany those sacrifices. Alternate translation: [and their grain offering and their drink offerings; and a basket of unleavened bread, flour of loaves mixed with the oil and wafers of unleavened bread anointed with the oil]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 6:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠סַ֣ל מַצּ֗וֹת

"and a basket of unleavened bread"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a basket that is characterized by having unleavened bread in it. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and a basket full of unleavened bread]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 6:15 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠סַ֣ל

"and a basket"

A basket is a kind of container used to hold and carry things. If your readers would not be familiar with what a basket is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and a box]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 6:15 (#4)
content:
מַצּ֗וֹת סֹ֤לֶת חַלֹּת֙ בְּלוּלֹ֣ת בַּ⁠שֶּׁ֔מֶן וּ⁠רְקִיקֵ֥י מַצּ֖וֹת מְשֻׁחִ֣ים בַּ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶן

"of unleavened bread, flour of loaves mixed with the oil and wafers of unleavened bread anointed with the oil"

The implication is that there were two distinct types of unleavened bread in the basket: loaves mixed with oil and wafers anointed with oil. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [unleavened bread of two types, both flour of loaves mixed with the oil and wafers of unleavened bread anointed with the oil]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 6:15 (#5)
content:
סֹ֤לֶת חַלֹּת֙ בְּלוּלֹ֣ת בַּ⁠שֶּׁ֔מֶן וּ⁠רְקִיקֵ֥י מַצּ֖וֹת מְשֻׁחִ֣ים בַּ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶן

"flour of loaves mixed with the oil and wafers of unleavened bread anointed with the oil"

The phrase flour of loaves mixed with the oil refers to thick loaves of bread in which oil was mixed before cooking. The phrase wafers of unleavened bread anointed with the oil refers to thin loaves of bread on which oil was spread after cooking. If your readers would not be familiar with these kinds of bread, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [thick loaves made from flour and oil and thin loaves spread with oil]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 6:15 (#6)
content:
סֹ֤לֶת חַלֹּת֙

"flour of loaves"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe loaves that are characterized by flour. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [loaves made of flour]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 6:15 (#7)
content:
בְּלוּלֹ֣ת

"mixed"

The expression mixed is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is whoever cooked the bread. Alternate translation: [that someone has mixed]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 6:15 (#8)
content:
בַּ⁠שֶּׁ֔מֶן & בַּ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶן

"with the oil & with the oil"

Yahweh is not referring to specific portions of oil. He means oil in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with oil … with oil]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 6:15 (#9)
content:
מְשֻׁחִ֣ים

"anointed"

The expression anointed is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is whoever cooked the bread. Alternate translation: [that someone has anointed]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 6:15 (#10)
content:
וּ⁠מִנְחָתָ֖⁠ם וְ⁠נִסְכֵּי⁠הֶֽם

"and their grain offering and their drink offerings"

The pronoun their refers to the grain offerings and drink offerings that go with the sacrificial animals mentioned in verse 14. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the grain offering and drink offerings for each of those sacrifices]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 6:15 (#11)
content:
וּ⁠מִנְחָתָ֖⁠ם

"and their grain offering"

In this verse, the word grain offering is singular in form, but it refers to all the grain offerings as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “grain offering.” Alternate translation: [and their grain offerings]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 6:16 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִקְרִ֥יב הַ⁠כֹּהֵ֖ן

"And the priest shall present"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply the offerings from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And the priest shall present the offerings]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 6:16 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 6:16 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠עָשָׂ֥ה אֶת־חַטָּאת֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־עֹלָתֽ⁠וֹ

"and he shall make his sin offering and his burnt offering"

The pronoun his refers to the Nazirite, while the pronoun he refers to the priest. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the priest shall make the Nazirite’s sin offering and his burnt offering]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 6:17 (#1)
content:
זֶ֤בַח שְׁלָמִים֙

"a sacrifice of peace offering"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a sacrifice that is characterized by being part of the peace offering. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sacrifice that is part of the peace offering]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 6:17 (#2)
content:
עַ֖ל סַ֣ל

"upon the basket of"

Yahweh is using upon the basket as a common expression of this culture to mean “along with the basket.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [along with the basket]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 6:17 (#3)
content:
עַ֖ל סַ֣ל

"upon the basket of"

A basket is a kind of container made from woven material. If your readers would not be familiar with what a basket is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. See how you translated basket in 6:15. Alternate translation: [upon the box]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 6:17 (#4)
content:
סַ֣ל הַ⁠מַּצּ֑וֹת

"the basket of the unleavened bread"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a basket that is characterized by the unleavened bread. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 6:15. Alternate translation: [the basket full of unleavened bread]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 6:17 (#5)
content:
אֶת־מִנְחָת֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־נִסְכּֽ⁠וֹ

"his grain offering and his drink offering"

Here, the pronoun his could refer to: (1) the Nazirite who brought the grain offering and drink offering. Alternate translation: [the Nazirite’s grain offering and his drink offering]; or (2) the peace offering. Alternate translation: [its grain offering and its drink offering]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 6:18 (#1)
content:
אֶת־רֹ֣אשׁ נִזְר֑⁠וֹ & אֶת־שְׂעַר֙ רֹ֣אשׁ נִזְר֔⁠וֹ

"the head of his separation & the hair of the head of his separation"

See how you translated the similar phrase in 6:9. The only difference here is that the second phrase makes hair explicit. Alternate translation: [the hair on his head that represents how he made himself separate … the hair on his head that represents how he made himself separate]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 6:18 (#2)
content:
עַל־הָ⁠אֵ֔שׁ אֲשֶׁר־תַּ֖חַת

"on the fire that {is} under"

Yahweh assumes that readers will know that the fire was burning on the altar and that the peace offering was being sacrificed on that altar. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the fire that burns on the altar under]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 6:18 (#3)
content:
זֶ֥בַח הַ⁠שְּׁלָמִֽים

"the sacrifice of peace offering"

See how you translated this phrase in 6:17.

See: Possession

title: Numbers 6:19 (#1)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠זְּרֹ֣עַ בְּשֵׁלָה֮ מִן־הָ⁠אַיִל֒

"the boiled shoulder from the ram"

This means that he had boiled the ram’s shoulder. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the shoulder of the ram that he boiled]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 6:19 (#2)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠זְּרֹ֣עַ בְּשֵׁלָה֮ מִן־הָ⁠אַיִל֒

"the boiled shoulder from the ram"

Here, the word shoulder refers to one of the front legs of the ram. The word boiled indicates that it has been cooked in hot water. If your readers would not be familiar with what a boiled shoulder is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the front leg of the ram that has been cooked]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 6:19 (#3)
content:
וְֽ⁠חַלַּ֨ת מַצָּ֤ה אַחַת֙ מִן־הַ⁠סַּ֔ל וּ⁠רְקִ֥יק מַצָּ֖ה אֶחָ֑ד

"and one loaf of unleavened bread from the basket and one wafer of unleavened bread"

The phrase one loaf of unleavened bread refers to a thick loaf of bread in which oil was mixed before cooking. The phrase one wafer of unleavened bread refers to a thin loaf of bread on which oil was spread after cooking. See how you referred to these kinds of bread in 6:15. Alternate translation: [one thick unleavened loaf from the basket and one thin unleavened loaf]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 6:19 (#4)
content:
מִן־הַ⁠סַּ֔ל

"from the basket"

A basket is a kind of container made from woven materials. If your readers would not be familiar with what a basket is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. See how you translated basket in 6:15. Alternate translation: [from the box]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 6:19 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠נָתַן֙ עַל־כַּפֵּ֣י הַ⁠נָּזִ֔יר

"and he shall put {them} on the palms of the Nazirite"

Yahweh is using on the palms of the Nazirite as a common expression of this culture to mean “to give to the Nazirite to hold.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he shall give them to the Nazirite to hold]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 6:19 (#6)
content:
אֶת־נִזְרֽ⁠וֹ

"his separation"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of separation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how he made himself separate]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 6:19 (#7)
content:
אֶת־נִזְרֽ⁠וֹ

"his separation"

Here, separation represents the hair that showed that this person was separated to God as a Nazirite. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the hair that represents his separation]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 6:20 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֵנִיף֩ אוֹתָ֨⁠ם הַ⁠כֹּהֵ֥ן

"And the priest shall raise them"

The implication is that the Nazirite first gives these items to the priest, who then lifts them up as an offering. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Nazirite shall hand them back to the priest, and the priest shall raise them]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 6:20 (#2)
content:
תְּנוּפָה֮ & הַ⁠תְּנוּפָ֔ה

"as} a raised offering & of the raised offering"

The expression raised offering is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [as an offering that the priests raise … the offering that the priests raise]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 6:20 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָה֒

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 6:20 (#4)
content:
קֹ֤דֶשׁ הוּא֙

"It {is} a holy thing"

The pronoun It refers to the portions of the sacrifice that the priest has raised up to Yahweh (the meat and bread). Yahweh is referring to those things as a group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [They are holy things]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 6:20 (#5)
content:
עַ֚ל חֲזֵ֣ה הַ⁠תְּנוּפָ֔ה וְ⁠עַ֖ל שׁ֣וֹק הַ⁠תְּרוּמָ֑ה

"upon the breast of the raised offering and upon the thigh of the contribution"

Yahweh assumes that readers will know that the breast and thigh portions of peace offerings were always given to the priests as their share of the offering. See Leviticus 7:28–34 for more information on this. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [upon the breast of the raised offering and upon the thigh of the contribution that are always given to the priest from any peace offering]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 6:20 (#6)
content:
עַ֚ל חֲזֵ֣ה הַ⁠תְּנוּפָ֔ה וְ⁠עַ֖ל שׁ֣וֹק הַ⁠תְּרוּמָ֑ה

"upon the breast of the raised offering and upon the thigh of the contribution"

The phrase upon the breast … and upon the thigh is a common expression of this culture that means “in addition to the breast and thigh.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [along with the breast of … and along with the thigh of]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 6:20 (#7)
content:
חֲזֵ֣ה הַ⁠תְּנוּפָ֔ה

"the breast of the raised offering"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a breast that is offered as the raised offering. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the breast that is presented as a raised offering]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 6:20 (#8)
content:
שׁ֣וֹק הַ⁠תְּרוּמָ֑ה

"the thigh of the contribution"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a thigh that is a contribution. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the thigh that is contributed]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 6:20 (#9)
content:
יִשְׁתֶּ֥ה הַ⁠נָּזִ֖יר יָֽיִן

"the Nazirite will drink wine"

Yahweh is using a future statement to give an instruction or command in the Nazirite will drink wine. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words using a command or instruction form. Alternate translation: [the Nazirite is allowed to drink wine]

See: Statements — Other Uses

title: Numbers 6:21 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠נָּזִיר֮

"the Nazirite"

Yahweh is not referring to a specific Nazirite. He means Nazirites in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. See how you translated the similar phrase in 6:13. Alternate translation: [the Nazirites]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 6:21 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִדֹּר֒ קָרְבָּנ֤⁠וֹ לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ עַל־נִזְר֔⁠וֹ

"who vows his offering to Yahweh upon his separation"

By upon his separation, Yahweh means after the time of being a Nazirite is completed. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who vows to present this offering to Yahweh after his separation]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 6:21 (#3)
content:
עַל־נִזְר֔⁠וֹ

"upon his separation"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of separation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [after he has been separate]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 6:21 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־תַּשִּׂ֣יג יָד֑⁠וֹ

"what his hand reaches"

Yahweh is using what his hand reaches as a common expression of this culture to mean “whatever else he can give” or “whatever more he can afford.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whatever else he can give]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 6:21 (#5)
content:
כְּ⁠פִ֤י נִדְר⁠וֹ֙

"According to the mouth of his vow"

Yahweh is speaking of his vow as if it were a living thing that had a mouth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [According to the words of his vow]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 6:21 (#6)
content:
נִדְר⁠וֹ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִדֹּ֔ר

"his vow that he vowed"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [what he vowed]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 6:21 (#7)
content:
תּוֹרַ֥ת נִזְרֽ⁠וֹ

"the law of his separation"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of separation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the law concerning when people make themselves separate]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 6:23 (#1)
content:
דַּבֵּ֤ר אֶֽל־אַהֲרֹן֙ וְ⁠אֶל־בָּנָ֣י⁠ו לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר כֹּ֥ה תְבָרֲכ֖וּ

"Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying, ‘Thus you shall bless"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Speak to Aaron and to his sons. Tell them that this is how they shall bless]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 6:23–26 (#1)
content:
אָמ֖וֹר לָ⁠הֶֽם & יְבָרֶכְ⁠ךָ֥ יְהוָ֖ה וְ⁠יִשְׁמְרֶֽ⁠ךָ & יָאֵ֨ר יְהוָ֧ה ׀ פָּנָ֛י⁠ו אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ וִֽ⁠יחֻנֶּֽ⁠ךָּ & יִשָּׂ֨א יְהוָ֤ה ׀ פָּנָי⁠ו֙ אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ וְ⁠יָשֵׂ֥ם לְ⁠ךָ֖ שָׁלֽוֹם

"saying to them,“May Yahweh bless you, and may he keep you.May Yahweh make his face shine to you, and may he be gracious to you.May Yahweh lift up his face to you and may he put peace to you"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [telling them that they pray that Yahweh may bless them and keep them, that they pray that Yahweh may make his face shine to them and be gracious to them, and that they pray that Yahweh may lift up his face to them and put peace to them.]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 6:24 (#1)
content:
יְבָרֶכְ⁠ךָ֥ יְהוָ֖ה וְ⁠יִשְׁמְרֶֽ⁠ךָ

"May Yahweh bless you, and may he keep you"

The word you is singular here because God is telling Aaron and his sons to bless each individual Israelite. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh bless each one of you, and may he keep each one of you]

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 6:24–26 (#1)
content:
יְבָרֶכְ⁠ךָ֥ יְהוָ֖ה וְ⁠יִשְׁמְרֶֽ⁠ךָ & יָאֵ֨ר יְהוָ֧ה ׀ פָּנָ֛י⁠ו אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ וִֽ⁠יחֻנֶּֽ⁠ךָּ & יִשָּׂ֨א יְהוָ֤ה ׀ פָּנָי⁠ו֙ אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ וְ⁠יָשֵׂ֥ם לְ⁠ךָ֖ שָׁלֽוֹם

"May Yahweh bless you, and may he keep you.May Yahweh make his face shine to you, and may he be gracious to you.May Yahweh lift up his face to you and may he put peace to you"

The priests are asking God to bless the Israelites. In your translation, use a form that people would recognize as a blessing in your language. You might express this as a prayer, if that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [We pray that Yahweh will bless you and keep you. We pray that Yahweh will make his face shine to you and be gracious to you. We pray that Yahweh will lift up his face to you and put peace to you.]

See: Blessings

title: Numbers 6:25 (#1)
content:
יָאֵ֨ר יְהוָ֧ה ׀ פָּנָ֛י⁠ו אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ

"May Yahweh make his face shine to you"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if his face were actually shining on someone with light. This refers to him acting favorably toward them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh favor you]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 6:25 (#2)
content:
אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ וִֽ⁠יחֻנֶּֽ⁠ךָּ

"to you, and may he be gracious to you"

The word you is singular here because this blessing was originally spoken to each individual Israelite. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [to each of you, and may he be gracious to each of you]

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 6:26 (#1)
content:
יִשָּׂ֨א יְהוָ֤ה ׀ פָּנָי⁠ו֙ אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ

"May Yahweh lift up his face to you"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if Yahweh had a physical face that he could lift up toward someone. This expression means that Yahweh would pay attention to someone in order to help them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh pay attention to you for your good]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 6:26 (#2)
content:
אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ & לְ⁠ךָ֖

"to you & to you"

The word you is singular here because Aaron and his sons are speaking this blessing to each individual Israelite. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [to each of you … to each of you]

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 6:26 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יָשֵׂ֥ם לְ⁠ךָ֖ שָׁלֽוֹם

"and may he put peace to you"

Yahweh is using put peace to you as a common expression of this culture to mean “give you peace” or “cause you to have peace.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he give you peace]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 6:26 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יָשֵׂ֥ם לְ⁠ךָ֖ שָׁלֽוֹם

"and may he put peace to you"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of peace, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and may he make you live peacefully]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 6:27 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שָׂמ֥וּ אֶת־שְׁמִ֖⁠י עַל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"And they shall put my name on the sons of Israel"

Here, God is speaking of Aaron and his sons putting his name on the Israelites as if his name were a physical object that could be placed on them. This means that the priests will declare that the Israelites belong to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they shall call the sons of Israel mine] or [And they shall link the sons of Israel with me through the use of my name]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 6:27 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִ֖י אֲבָרֲכֵֽ⁠ם

"and I, I will bless them"

The word and here indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and as a result I, I will bless them]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 6:27 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִ֖י אֲבָרֲכֵֽ⁠ם

"and I, I will bless them"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I will bless already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is the one who will do the blessing. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [and it is I who will bless them]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers - Chapter 7 Introduction
content:
Numbers 7 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter lists the offerings that each leader of the 12 Israelite tribes gave to Yahweh after Moses dedicated the altar.

  1. The tribal leaders provide wagons and oxen for the Levites’ work (1–9)
  2. Each tribal leader brings offerings for the dedication of the altar (10–88)
  3. Moses hears Yahweh speaking from above the atonement lid (89)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Anointing and dedicating the altar

To set the altar apart for Yahweh, Moses poured olive oil on it. This was the “dedication” of the altar. After Moses did this, the leaders of the 12 tribes presented offerings to Yahweh, which Yahweh told Moses to give to the Levites. These offerings were called a “dedication,” since they were presented at the dedication of the altar.

The offerings

The leaders of the 12 Israelite tribes together presented six wagons and 12 oxen. The Levites would use these wagons and oxen as they set up, took down, and transported the sacred tent. Then, on successive days, each of the 12 leaders presented an offering to Yahweh. Each offering was identical to the others and included a silver dish and basin with flour and oil filling them, a small bowl or ladle with incense filling it, and animals for a burnt offering (a bull, a ram, and a male lamb), for a sin offering (a male goat), and for a peace offering (two cattle, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs). The priests would use the animals, flour, and incense to make sacrifices to Yahweh. The priests would use the dishes, basins, and ladles regularly during their work at the sacred tent.

The shekel of the holy place

A “shekel” is a standard of weight. There were several different definitions of the weight of a “shekel.” The phrase “the shekel of the holy place” identifies a specific definition: the one used by the priests at the sacred tent. This shekel weighed about 11 grams. Throughout this chapter, the author makes it clear that it is this weight for “shekel” that the leaders used to weigh the gold and silver dishes that they presented to Yahweh.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Sequence with the previous chapters

This chapter begins with a specific date: the day that Moses set up and consecrated the sacred tent and the altar. According to Exodus 40:17, that day was the first day of the first month of the second year. However, Numbers 1:1 indicates that the census and the instructions for the Levites in chapters 1–4 began on the first day of the second month of the second year. So, the events narrated in this chapter took place before the events of Numbers 1–4. You may need to make this explicit for your readers. See the notes on 7:1–2 for specific issues and translation options.

“Sons of [tribe or clan]”

Throughout this chapter, the phrase “sons of [tribe or clan name]” appears. This phrase refers to the people who belong to the tribe or clan as if they were the direct “sons” of the man whom the tribe or clan was named after. Consider how you would naturally refer to the members of a tribe or clan. The UST uses the phrase “descendants of [tribe name].”

Names from earlier in Numbers

In this chapter, the author includes twice the name of each leader and the name of each leader’s father. These names already appeared in Numbers 1 in identical form. Be sure that you translate them in exactly the same way in this chapter.

Repetition

The list of items offered by each of the leaders is very repetitive. In fact, words that indicate what items the leader gave are exactly identical in each of the twelve sections. Most likely, this kind of repetition represents a list or table in sentence form. The author thought that listing each item for each leader was important, perhaps to indicate that each tribe shared equally in this task or to reenact with words how the Israelites dedicated the altar with these offerings. Because of this, it is recommended that you do not shorten the repetition. Instead, be sure that the repeated verses are translated in the same way. You could also use formatting to make these verses look more like a list and enable readers to follow the repetition better. See the UST for an example of one way to do this.

title: Numbers 7:1 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְהִ֡י בְּ⁠יוֹם֩ כַּלּ֨וֹת מֹשֶׁ֜ה

"And it happened on the day of Moses finishing"

This day is the day that Exodus 40:17 refers to, which is the first day of the first month of the second year. That means that this day occurred before the day that 1:1 refers to, which is the first day of the second month of the second year. If it is helpful in your language, you might want to make it clear that the account that starts in this verse happened before the events in chapters 1–6. Alternate translation: [Now previously, on the day of Moses finishing]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 7:1 (#2)
content:
כַּלּ֨וֹת מֹשֶׁ֜ה

"Moses finishing"

The implication is that Moses and the Levites did all the work of setting up the sacred tent, though the text only mentions Moses finishing. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Moses and the Levites finishing]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 7:1 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּמְשַׁ֨ח אֹת֜⁠וֹ וַ⁠יְקַדֵּ֤שׁ אֹת⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠אֶת־כָּל־כֵּלָ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֖חַ וְ⁠אֶת־כָּל־כֵּלָ֑י⁠ו וַ⁠יִּמְשָׁחֵ֖⁠ם וַ⁠יְקַדֵּ֥שׁ אֹתָֽ⁠ם

"that he anointed it and consecrated it and all its vessels and the altar and all its vessels. And he anointed them, and he consecrated them"

It might seem that the expression And he anointed them, and he consecrated them contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [that he anointed and consecrated it and all its vessels and the altar and all its vessels]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 7:2 (#1)
content:
רָאשֵׁ֖י בֵּ֣ית

"the heads of the houses of"

Here, the author is speaking of the leaders or rulers of the houses of their fathers as if they were the heads of those families. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the rulers of the houses]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 7:2 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠עֹמְדִ֖ים עַל

"the ones standing over"

Here, the author is speaking of the leaders as if they were standing over the people they supervised. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones who oversaw]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 7:2 (#3)
content:
בֵּ֣ית אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם

"the houses of their fathers"

See how you translated the similar phrase in 1:2. Alternate translation: [the family groups of their ancestors]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 7:2 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יַּקְרִ֨יבוּ֙

"And & presented"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The verb presented needs an object to make clear what they presented. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [presented an offering]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 7:2 (#5)
content:
הַ⁠פְּקֻדִֽים

"the counted ones"

As the first note to 7:1 makes clear, the events in this chapter happened before the census in chapters 1–2. So, these people have not yet been counted. If it is helpful in your language, you might want to make it clear that the counting happened after the events in this chapter. Alternate translation: [the ones who would be counted]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 7:2 (#6)
content:
הַ⁠פְּקֻדִֽים

"the counted ones"

The expression the counted ones is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4. Alternate translation: [the ones whom they, Moses, and Aaron counted]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 7:3 (#1)
content:
אֶת־קָרְבָּנָ֜⁠ם

"their offering"

In this verse, the word offering is singular in form, but it refers to all the gifts from the leaders as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “offering.” Alternate translation: [their offerings]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 7:3 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֗ה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 7:3 (#3)
content:
עֶגְלֹ֥ת צָב֙ & עֲגָלָ֛ה

"covered wagons & a wagon"

A covered wagon is a kind of cart with a protective covering over it. If your readers would not be familiar with what a covered wagon is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [carts with coverings … a cart]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 7:3 (#4)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּֽן

"to the face of the Dwelling"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of the Dwelling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before the Dwelling]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 7:4 (#1)
content:
לֵּ⁠אמֹֽר

"saying"

Here, the word saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 7:5 (#1)
content:
קַ֚ח מֵֽ⁠אִתָּ֔⁠ם

"Take from with them"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Take the wagons and cattle from with them]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 7:5 (#2)
content:
לַ⁠עֲבֹ֕ד אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֖ת

"to serve the service of"

Here, just as in Numbers 4, the words serve and service refer to tasks of setting up, taking down, and carrying the sacred tent. See how you translated these words in 4:30. Alternate translation: [for the physical labor required to move]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 7:5 (#3)
content:
לַ⁠עֲבֹ֕ד אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֖ת

"to serve the service of"

The phrase to serve the service is poetic language in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [to serve]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 7:5 (#4)
content:
אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֖ת אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֑ד

"the service of the tent of meeting"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as the tent of meeting needs to be served]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 7:5 (#5)
content:
אִ֖ישׁ

"a man"

In some languages it is more natural to express a man with a distributive form meaning “each man” or “each one.” This refers to how Moses was to distribute the carts and oxen to each of the groups of Levites according to their needs. If your language has a distributive form, you may want to use it here. Alternate translation: [each man]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 7:5 (#6)
content:
כְּ⁠פִ֥י עֲבֹדָתֽ⁠וֹ

"according to the mouth of his service"

Yahweh is using the expression according to the mouth of his service as a common expression of his culture to mean “according to how he was required to serve.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to how he was required to serve]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 7:5 (#7)
content:
עֲבֹדָתֽ⁠וֹ

"his service"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how he serves]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 7:6 (#1)
content:
אֶת־הָ⁠עֲגָלֹ֖ת

"the wagons"

See how you translated wagons in 7:3.

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 7:7 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י גֵרְשׁ֑וֹן

"to the sons of Gershon"

This is the first of many times in this chapter that the author uses the phrase the sons of followed by a tribe or clan name to refer to the men who belong to that tribe or clan. See the chapter introduction for more information.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 7:7 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠פִ֖י עֲבֹדָתָֽ⁠ם

"according to the mouth of their service"

The author is using according to the mouth of their service as a common expression of his culture to mean “according to how they were required to serve.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 7:5. Alternate translation: [according to how they were required to serve]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 7:7 (#3)
content:
עֲבֹדָתָֽ⁠ם

"their service"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how they serve]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 7:8 (#1)
content:
כְּ⁠פִי֙ עֲבֹ֣דָתָ֔⁠ם

"according to the mouth of their service"

See how you translated this phrase in 7:7.

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 7:8 (#2)
content:
עֲבֹ֣דָתָ֔⁠ם בְּ⁠יַד֙ אִֽיתָמָ֔ר

"their service, in the hand of Ithamar"

Here, the author means that both the sons of Merari and the “sons of Gershon” (7:7) are in the hand of Ithamar. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [their service. The service of the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari was in the hand of Ithamar]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 7:8 (#3)
content:
עֲבֹ֣דָתָ֔⁠ם

"their service"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how they serve]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 7:8 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠יַד֙ אִֽיתָמָ֔ר

"in the hand of Ithamar"

The author is using in the hand of as a common expression of his culture to mean “under the control of” or “under the supervision of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 4:28. Alternate translation: [under the control of Ithamar]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 7:9 (#1)
content:
עֲלֵ⁠הֶ֔ם

"was} upon them"

Here, the author is speaking of the responsibility of caring for the holy items as if it were a physical burden that was upon the Kohathites. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was their duty]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 7:9 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י קְהָ֖ת לֹ֣א נָתָ֑ן כִּֽי־עֲבֹדַ֤ת הַ⁠קֹּ֨דֶשׁ֙ עֲלֵ⁠הֶ֔ם

"But to the sons of Kohath he did not give, for the service of the holy place {was} upon them"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [But the service of the holy place was upon the sons of Kohath, so he did not give to them]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 7:9 (#3)
content:
לֹ֣א נָתָ֑ן

"he did not give"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. In he did not give, he does not say what Moses did not give to the Kohathites. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he did not give any wagons or cattle]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 7:9 (#4)
content:
עֲבֹדַ֤ת

"the service of"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [serving]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 7:9 (#5)
content:
הַ⁠קֹּ֨דֶשׁ֙

"the holy place"

Here, the holy place represents the sacred items that were kept in the holy place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the things in the holy place]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 7:9 (#6)
content:
יִשָּֽׂאוּ

"They carried"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [They carried the holy things]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 7:9 (#7)
content:
בַּ⁠כָּתֵ֖ף

"on the shoulder"

The author is not referring to a specific shoulder. He means their shoulders in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [on their shoulders]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 7:10 (#1)
content:
אֵ֚ת חֲנֻכַּ֣ת הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֔חַ

"the dedication of the altar"

Here, dedication represents the gifts and offerings that were given to dedicate the altar. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the dedication offerings for the altar]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 7:10 (#2)
content:
אֵ֚ת חֲנֻכַּ֣ת הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֔חַ

"the dedication of the altar"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of dedication, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what they offered for when the altar was dedicated]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 7:10 (#3)
content:
הִמָּשַׁ֣ח אֹת֑⁠וֹ

"its being anointed"

The expression its being anointed is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Moses. Alternate translation: [Moses anointing it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 7:10 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יַּקְרִ֧יבוּ הַ⁠נְּשִׂיאִ֛ם אֶת־קָרְבָּנָ֖⁠ם

"And the leaders presented their offering"

The author is using a construction in which a verb (presented) and its object (offering) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And the leaders gave their offering]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 7:10 (#5)
content:
אֶת־קָרְבָּנָ֖⁠ם

"their offering"

The term their offering refers to the combined gifts from all the leaders, even though each leader brought his own individual offering. The author describes it as a single collective offering, though the next verse clarifies that the leaders presented their offerings one at a time over several days. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the plural form to emphasize that there were multiple individual offerings. Alternate translation: [their offerings]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 7:10 (#6)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּֽחַ

"to the face of the altar"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of the altar. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of the altar]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 7:11 (#1)
content:
נָשִׂ֨יא אֶחָ֜ד לַ⁠יּ֗וֹם נָשִׂ֤יא אֶחָד֙ לַ⁠יּ֔וֹם

"One leader for the day, one leader for the day"

Yahweh is using One leader for the day, one leader for the day as a common expression of his culture to mean “one leader on each separate day in sequence.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [One leader on each day for 12 days]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 7:11 (#2)
content:
יַקְרִ֨יבוּ֙ אֶת־קָרְבָּנָ֔⁠ם

"they shall present their offering"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb (present) and its object (offering) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [they shall give their offering]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 7:11 (#3)
content:
אֶת־קָרְבָּנָ֔⁠ם

"their offering"

In this verse, the word offering is singular in form, but it refers to the offerings of all the leaders of Israel as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “offering.” Alternate translation: [their offerings]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 7:11 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠חֲנֻכַּ֖ת הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּֽחַ

"for the dedication of the altar"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of dedication, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for when the altar is dedicated]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 7:12 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְהִ֗י הַ⁠מַּקְרִ֛יב & אֶת־קָרְבָּנ֑⁠וֹ

"And the one presenting his offering"

The author is using a construction in which a verb (presenting) and its object (offering) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And the one giving his offering]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 7:12 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֥וֹם הָ⁠רִאשׁ֖וֹן

"on the first day"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as on the first day, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [on day one]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 7:12 (#3)
content:
נַחְשׁ֥וֹן בֶּן־עַמִּינָדָ֖ב

"was Nahshon, the son of Amminadab"

For these and the other names in this chapter, translate them as you did in chapter 1. See the chapter introduction for more information.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 7:13 (#1)
content:
קַֽעֲרַת־כֶּ֣סֶף אַחַ֗ת

"one silver dish"

A silver dish is a kind of large bowl made out of silver, although its exact shape is uncertain. If your readers would not be familiar with what a silver dish is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [one deep silver bowl]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 7:13 (#2)
content:
שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים וּ⁠מֵאָה֮ מִשְׁקָלָ⁠הּ֒

"its weight 130"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply “shekels” from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [its weight was 130 shekels]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 7:13 (#3)
content:
שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים וּ⁠מֵאָה֮ מִשְׁקָלָ⁠הּ֒

"its weight 130"

These 130 shekels came to about one and one-half kilograms or about three and one-third pounds of silver. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “shekel” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

See: Biblical Weight

title: Numbers 7:13 (#4)
content:
מִזְרָ֤ק אֶחָד֙ כֶּ֔סֶף

"one silver basin"

A silver basin is a kind of jug or deep bowl used to store liquids, although its exact shape is uncertain. If your readers would not be familiar with what a silver basin is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [one silver pitcher]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 7:13 (#5)
content:
שִׁבְעִ֥ים שֶׁ֖קֶל

"70 shekels"

These 70 shekels came to about 800 grams or about 1.75 pounds of silver. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “shekel” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

See: Biblical Weight

title: Numbers 7:13 (#6)
content:
בְּ⁠שֶׁ֣קֶל הַ⁠קֹּ֑דֶשׁ

"in the shekel of the holy place"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a shekel that was used in the holy place. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See the chapter introduction for more information about this shekel. Alternate translation: [in the shekel that is used in the holy place]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 7:13 (#7)
content:
שְׁנֵי⁠הֶ֣ם ׀ מְלֵאִ֗ים סֹ֛לֶת בְּלוּלָ֥ה בַ⁠שֶּׁ֖מֶן

"the two of them full of flour mixed with the oil"

The expression full of flour mixed with the oil is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the two of which he had filled with flour that he had mixed with the oil]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 7:13 (#8)
content:
בַ⁠שֶּׁ֖מֶן

"with the oil"

The author is not referring to a specific oil. He means oil in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with oil]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 7:14 (#1)
content:
כַּ֥ף אַחַ֛ת

"one palm-sized bowl"

A palm-sized bowl is a kind of small ceremonial dish about the size of a person’s palm, although its exact shape is uncertain. If your readers would not be familiar with what a palm-sized bowl is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [one large spoon]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 7:14 (#2)
content:
עֲשָׂרָ֥ה זָהָ֖ב

"ten gold"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. Here ten gold means “ten shekels of gold,” which the author has shortened. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [ten gold shekels]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 7:14 (#3)
content:
עֲשָׂרָ֥ה זָהָ֖ב

"ten gold"

These ten gold shekels came to about 114 grams or a quarter pound of gold. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “shekel” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

See: Biblical Weight

title: Numbers 7:14 (#4)
content:
מְלֵאָ֥ה קְטֹֽרֶת

"full of incense"

The expression full of incense is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that he had filled with incense]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 7:15 (#1)
content:
בֶּן־בָּקָ֗ר

"a son of cattle"

Here, the author uses the phrase son of cattle to indicate that the bull was young. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a young one]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 7:15 (#2)
content:
בֶּן־שְׁנָת֖⁠וֹ

"a son of his year"

Here, the author is speaking of a male lamb as if it were a son of his year, meaning it was one year old. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 6:12. Alternate translation: [a year old]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 7:15 (#3)
content:
שְׁנָת֖⁠וֹ לְ⁠עֹלָֽה

"his year) for a burnt offering"

The author implies that all three animals were used for the burnt offering. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [his year), all three for a burnt offering]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 7:16 (#1)
content:
שְׂעִיר־עִזִּ֥ים אֶחָ֖ד

"one buck of the goats"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a buck that is characterized by being of the goats. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a goat that is a buck] or [an adult male goat]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 7:17 (#1)
content:
בְּנֵֽי־שָׁנָ֖ה

"sons of a year"

Here, the author is speaking as if the lambs were actually sons of a year. This expression means that they were one year old. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 7:15. Alternate translation: [each a year old]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 7:17 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠זֶ֣בַח הַ⁠שְּׁלָמִים֮

"and for the sacrifice of the peace offering"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a sacrifice that is part of the peace offering. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and for the animal sacrifices that are part of the peace offering]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 7:18 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠יּוֹם֙ הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֔י

"On the second day"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as the second day, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [On day two]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 7:18 (#2)
content:
הִקְרִ֖יב

"presented"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [presented his offering]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 7:19 (#1)
content:
הִקְרִ֨ב אֶת־קָרְבָּנ֜⁠וֹ

"He presented his offering"

It might seem that the expression He presented his offering contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language since 7:18 already states that Nethanel presented. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [This was his offering]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 7:19 (#2)
content:
הִקְרִ֨ב אֶת־קָרְבָּנ֜⁠וֹ

"He presented his offering"

Here the author is using a construction in which a verb (presented) and its object (offering) come from the same root. title: Numbers 7:85 (#2)
content:
שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים וּ⁠מֵאָ֗ה

"130"

These 130 shekels came to about one and one-half kilograms or about three and one-third pounds of silver. See how you translated this weight in 7:13. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “shekel” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

See: Biblical Weight

title: Numbers 7:85 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠קְּעָרָ֤ה הָֽ⁠אַחַת֙ כֶּ֔סֶף & הַ⁠מִּזְרָ֣ק הָ⁠אֶחָ֑ד

"was} the one silver bowl & was} the one basin"

Here, the one silver bowl and the one basin represent each of the silver bowls and basins in general, not just two of them. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [each silver bowl … each basin]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “shekel” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

See: Biblical Weight

אַלְפַּ֥יִם וְ⁠אַרְבַּע־מֵא֖וֹת

"was} 2,400"

These 2,400 shekels came to about 27 kilograms or 60 pounds of silver. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “shekel” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

See: Biblical Weight

If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 7:17. title: Numbers 7:89 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠בֹ֨א מֹשֶׁ֜ה אֶל־אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵד֮ לְ⁠דַבֵּ֣ר אִתּ⁠וֹ֒ וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֨ע & וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֖ר אֵלָֽי⁠ו

"And when Moses went to the tent of meeting to speak with him, then he heard & And he spoke to him"

Here, the author could be describing: (1) a specific event that happened after the altar was anointed and the offerings were given. Alternate translation: [And then Moses went to the tent of meeting to speak with him, and he heard … And he spoke to him]; or (2) what Moses and Yahweh normally did once the altar was anointed and the offerings were given. Alternate translation: [And whenever Moses went to the tent of meeting to speak with him, he would hear … And he would speak to him]

content:
אִתּ⁠וֹ֒

The pronoun him refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [with God]

title: Numbers 7:89 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֨ע אֶת־הַ⁠קּ֜וֹל מִדַּבֵּ֣ר

"then he heard the voice speaking"

The author is using the voice to represent God himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. title: Numbers 7:89 (#4)
content:
מֵ⁠עַ֤ל הַ⁠כַּפֹּ֨רֶת֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ עַל־אֲרֹ֣ן הָ⁠עֵדֻ֔ת מִ⁠בֵּ֖ין שְׁנֵ֣י הַ⁠כְּרֻבִ֑ים

"from upon the atonement lid that {is} on the Box of the Testimony, from between the two cherubs"

The implication is that Yahweh’s voice came not only from above the atonement lid, but also specifically from the space between the two cherubs that were on top of it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from the area above the atonement lid that is on the Box of the Testimony, which is between the two cherubs that are above the Box of the Testimony]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 7:89 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֖ר אֵלָֽי⁠ו

"And he spoke to him"

The pronoun he refers to Yahweh, while the pronoun him refers to Moses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh spoke to Moses]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 7:89 (#6)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֖ר אֵלָֽי⁠ו

"And he spoke to him"

By And he spoke to him, the author means that what he describes in this verse is the way that Yahweh spoke to Moses. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He spoke to him in that way] or [Thus he spoke to him]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers - Chapter 8 Introduction
content:
Numbers 8 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter details the cleansing and consecration of the Levites so that they could serve at the sacred tent. It also provides brief instructions on the orientation of the lamps on the lampstand and on the age requirements for service at the tent.

  1. Yahweh gives instructions for arranging the seven lamps (1–4)
  2. The Levites are purified and presented to Yahweh for service (5–22)
  3. Yahweh establishes the ages for the Levites’ service (23–26)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Cleansing and consecrating the Levites

In this chapter, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to cleanse and consecrate the Levites. 8:6–7 gives instructions for cleansing them: they must be sprinkled with water, shave off their hair, and wash their clothing. 8:8–14 gives instructions for consecrating them after they have been cleansed: they must offer two bulls, and they must be presented like a raised offering to Yahweh. 8:15 gives a clear summary: in order to serve at the sacred tent, the Levites need to be cleansed and consecrated like a raised offering.

“Service” and “keeping”

As in Numbers 3–4, the word “keeping” refers to keeping watch or guarding. No one else was supposed to approach the sacred items, so the Levites were required to guard these items, especially when they were transporting them. 8:26 includes an unusual plural form: “keepings.” It probably refers to all the kinds of guard duty the Levites might need to perform. The word “service” refers to physical labor, particularly taking down and setting up the sacred tent and the items that were in it. The Levites were also responsible for these tasks. See how you translated “keeping” and “service” in Numbers 3–4.

The Levites and the firstborn Israelites

As outlined in chapter 3, Yahweh required the Israelites to pay a ransom to him for the firstborn males that he did not kill during the tenth plague in Egypt, as described in Exodus 12:29 and 13:15. Because Yahweh did not kill the firstborn male people and animals among the Israelites, he considered them to owe him their lives. Instead of taking their lives, Yahweh chose the Levite men to be his special servants in their place. Yahweh repeats some of that information in 8:17–18. See how you translated the similar statements in Numbers 3.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Starting service at 25 or 30 years old?

In 8:24, Yahweh states that Levites who are 25 years old can begin serving at the sacred tent. However, in 4:3, the age at which Levites begin serving at the sacred tent is 30 years old. This chapter is chronologically prior to chapter 4 (see the Introduction to Numbers 7), so it is possible that the lower age requirement was updated from 25 to 30 years old. It is also possible that the census in Numbers 4 only included men who were 30–50 years old, but men as young as 25 were able to serve at the sacred tent. There is not enough information to know for sure. In the end, do not harmonize this chapter with Numbers 4; this chapter should say 25 years and Numbers 4 should say 30 years.

The “army”

In 8:24–25, as in Numbers 4, serving at the sacred tent is sometimes described as if it were being part of an army and fighting. The rest of the Israelite men had to serve in the army when necessary, but the Levites were exempt from serving in the army. Instead, they served at the tent of meeting. Because of this, their duties as Levites can be described as if they were serving in the army. The ULT preserves the army metaphor, and the UST models how to express the idea without this metaphor.

title: Numbers 8:1 (#1)
content:
לֵּ⁠אמֹֽר

"saying"

Here, the word saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 8:2 (#1)
content:
דַּבֵּר֙ אֶֽל־אַהֲרֹ֔ן וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֖ אֵלָ֑י⁠ו

"Speak to Aaron and say to him"

The term Speak to Aaron and say to him introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly. Alternate translation: [Say to Aaron]

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 8:2 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֖ אֵלָ֑י⁠ו בְּ⁠הַעֲלֹֽתְ⁠ךָ֙

"and say to him, ‘When you lift up"

The text includes quotations within quotations. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and say to him that when he lifts up]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 8:2 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠הַעֲלֹֽתְ⁠ךָ֙ אֶת־הַ⁠נֵּרֹ֔ת

"When you lift up the lamps"

The implication is that Aaron would lift up the lamps to put them in their proper places on the lampstand. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you lift up the lamps and put them on the lampstand]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:2 (#4)
content:
יָאִ֖ירוּ שִׁבְעַ֥ת הַ⁠נֵּרֽוֹת

"the seven lamps shall shine"

The implication is that the lampstand should be set up in such a way that the seven lamps illuminate the area in front of it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the seven lamps must be oriented so that they shine]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:2 (#5)
content:
אֶל־מוּל֙ פְּנֵ֣י הַ⁠מְּנוֹרָ֔ה

"to the front of the face of the lampstand"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of the lampstand. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [on the place before the lampstand]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 8:3 (#1)
content:
אֶל־מוּל֙ פְּנֵ֣י הַ⁠מְּנוֹרָ֔ה הֶעֱלָ֖ה נֵרֹתֶ֑י⁠הָ

"To the front of the face of the lampstand he lifted up its lamps"

The implication is that the lamps were positioned so they would shine forward from the lampstand. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [To shine to the front of the face of the lampstand he lifted up its lamps]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:3 (#2)
content:
אֶל־מוּל֙ פְּנֵ֣י הַ⁠מְּנוֹרָ֔ה

"To the front of the face of the lampstand"

See how you translated this phrase in 8:2. Alternate translation: [Facing the place before the lampstand]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 8:3 (#3)
content:
הֶעֱלָ֖ה נֵרֹתֶ֑י⁠הָ

"he lifted up its lamps"

The implication is that someone needed to put the lamps in their places on the lampstand to get them ready to burn. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar phrase in 8:2. Alternate translation: [he lifted up the lamps and put them on the lampstand]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:4 (#1)
content:
מַעֲשֵׂ֤ה הַ⁠מְּנֹרָה֙

"the work of the lampstand"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a lampstand that was made by a specific kind of work. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how the lampstand was made]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 8:4 (#2)
content:
מִקְשָׁ֣ה זָהָ֔ב & מִקְשָׁ֣ה הִ֑וא

"a hammered work of gold; it {was} a hammered work"

A hammered work is a kind of metal object that is formed by repeatedly striking a sheet of metal to shape it. If your readers would not be familiar with what a hammered work is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [constructed from a sheet of gold that was hammered into shape, it was constructed this way]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 8:4 (#3)
content:
עַד־יְרֵכָ֥⁠הּ עַד־פִּרְחָ֖⁠הּ

"up to its side, up to its blossom"

The author is referring to all of the lampstand by naming two major components, its side and its blossom. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in its entirety] or [completely, including its side and its blossom]

See: Merism

title: Numbers 8:4 (#4)
content:
פִּרְחָ֖⁠הּ

"its blossom"

A blossom is a kind of flower that decorated the golden lampstand. If your readers would not be familiar with what a blossom is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. See the description of the lampstand in Exodus 25:33–36. Alternate translation: [the blossom that decorated it]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 8:4 (#5)
content:
פִּרְחָ֖⁠הּ

"its blossom"

In this verse, the word blossom is singular in form, but it refers to all the flower decorations on the lampstand as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “blossom.” Alternate translation: [its blossoms]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 8:4 (#6)
content:
כַּ⁠מַּרְאֶ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֶרְאָ֤ה יְהוָה֙ אֶת־מֹשֶׁ֔ה

"According to the appearance that Yahweh showed Moses"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of appearance, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [According to what Yahweh showed Moses about how the lampstand should look]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 8:4 (#7)
content:
כֵּ֥ן עָשָׂ֖ה אֶת־הַ⁠מְּנֹרָֽה

"so he made the lampstand"

The implication is that someone made the lampstand at Moses’s direction rather than Moses making it himself. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [so he had the workers make the lampstand]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:6 (#1)
content:
קַ֚ח אֶת־הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֔ם מִ⁠תּ֖וֹךְ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"Take the Levites from the midst of the sons of Israel"

Here, Moses is speaking as if the Levites were an object that could be physically taken from among the Israelites. He means that they should be selected and set apart from the rest of the people. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Select the Levites from among the sons of Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:7 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כֹֽה־תַעֲשֶׂ֤ה לָ⁠הֶם֙

"And thus you shall do to them"

The implication is that some of these instructions will be carried out by Moses and others will be carried out by the Levites themselves. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And here is how]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:7 (#2)
content:
הַזֵּ֥ה עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֖ם מֵ֣י חַטָּ֑את

"Sprinkle on them the water of the sin offering"

Sprinkling the water of the sin offering was a symbolic action by which the priests showed that the Levites were being purified and made clean for their service. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Sprinkle on them the water of the sin offering to purify them]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Numbers 8:7 (#3)
content:
חַטָּ֑את

"the sin offering"

Here, sin offering represents the purification from sin that occurs when a sin offering is offered. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [purification]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 8:7 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הֶעֱבִ֤ירוּ תַ֨עַר֙ עַל־כָּל־בְּשָׂרָ֔⁠ם

"And they shall pass a razor over all their flesh"

The phrase pass a razor over all their flesh is a common expression of his culture to mean “cut off the hair from their entire body.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they shall use a razor to cut off the hair on their entire body]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 8:7 (#5)
content:
תַ֨עַר֙

"a razor"

A razor is a kind of cutting tool used for shaving hair. If your readers would not be familiar with what a razor is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. See how you translated razor in 6:5. Alternate translation: [a shaving tool]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 8:7 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠הִטֶּהָֽרוּ

"and they shall cleanse themselves"

Here, the word and introduces a summary or conclusion for this section. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this more explicit. Alternate translation: [and thus they shall cleanse themselves]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 8:8 (#1)
content:
בֶּן־בָּקָ֔ר & בֶן־בָּקָ֖ר

"a son of cattle & a son of cattle"

Here, Yahweh uses the phrase son of cattle to indicate that the bull was young. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 7:15. Alternate translation: [a young one … a young one]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:8 (#2)
content:
סֹ֖לֶת בְּלוּלָ֣ה בַ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶן

"flour mixed with the oil"

The expression mixed with the oil is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. See how you translated this phrase in 6:15. Alternate translation: [flour that they had mixed with the oil]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 8:8 (#3)
content:
בַ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶן

"with the oil"

Yahweh is not referring to a specific oil. He means oil in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. See how you translated this phrase in 6:15. Alternate translation: [with oil]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 8:8 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠פַר־שֵׁנִ֥י בֶן־בָּקָ֖ר תִּקַּ֥ח

"And you shall take a second bull, a son of cattle"

Here, Yahweh could be telling Moses that: (1) he must be the one who offers the second bull. Alternate translation: [And you yourself shall take]; or (2) he must instruct the Levites to offer the second bull. Alternate translation: [And you shall have them take]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:8 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠פַר־שֵׁנִ֥י

"And & a second bull"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as a second bull, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [another bull] or [bull two]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 8:9 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֑ד

"to the face of the tent of meeting"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of the tent of meeting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before the tent of meeting]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 8:9 (#2)
content:
אֶֽת־כָּל־עֲדַ֖ת בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"all the congregation of the sons of Israel"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a congregation that is made up of the sons of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the congregation that consists of all the sons of Israel]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 8:10 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 8:10 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"to the face of Yahweh"
