Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [to my face]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 8:10 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠סָמְכ֧וּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל אֶת־יְדֵי⁠הֶ֖ם עַל־הַ⁠לְוִיִּֽם

"and the sons of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites"

To lay hands on the Levites was a symbolic action by which the Israelites could have shown: (1) that the Levites were substitutes for them. Alternate translation: [and the sons of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites to designate the Levites as their substitutes]; or (2) that the Levites were being dedicated to God. Alternate translation: [and the sons of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites to dedicate them to God]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Numbers 8:10 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠סָמְכ֧וּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל

"and the sons of Israel shall lay"

By the sons of Israel, Yahweh means the leaders of Israel who were representing all of Israel in this ceremony. It would not be possible for all the Israelites to lay their hands on the Levites. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the leaders of the sons of Israel]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:11 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֵנִיף֩ אַהֲרֹ֨ן אֶת־הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֤ם תְּנוּפָה֙ לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה

"And Aaron shall raise the Levites {as} a raised offering to the face of Yahweh"

Here, Moses is speaking of presenting the Levites to Yahweh as if they were a raised offering. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Aaron shall dedicate the Levites to Yahweh as he does when he raises a raised offering]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:11 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הֵנִיף֩ אַהֲרֹ֨ן אֶת־הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֤ם תְּנוּפָה֙

"And Aaron shall raise the Levites {as} a raised offering"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And Aaron shall offer the Levites as a raised offering]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 8:11 (#3)
content:
תְּנוּפָה֙

"as} a raised offering"

The expression raised offering is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is a priest. Alternate translation: [as an offering that the priests raise]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 8:11 (#4)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה & אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֥ת יְהוָֽה

"to the face of Yahweh & the service of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [to my face … my service]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 8:11 (#5)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 8:11 (#6)
content:
לַ⁠עֲבֹ֖ד אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֥ת

"to serve the service of"

Here, just as in Numbers 4, the words serve and service refer to tasks of setting up, taking down, and carrying the sacred tent. See how you translated these words in 4:30. Alternate translation: [for the physical labor required to move]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:11 (#7)
content:
לַ⁠עֲבֹ֖ד אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֥ת

"to serve the service of"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [to serve]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 8:11 (#8)
content:
אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֥ת יְהוָֽה

"the service of Yahweh"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a service that is done for Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the service they do for Yahweh]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 8:11 (#9)
content:
אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֥ת יְהוָֽה

"the service of Yahweh"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as Yahweh needs to be served]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 8:12 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠לְוִיִּם֙ יִסְמְכ֣וּ אֶת־יְדֵי⁠הֶ֔ם עַ֖ל רֹ֣אשׁ הַ⁠פָּרִ֑ים

"And the Levites shall lay their hands on the head of the bulls"

To lay hands on the bulls was a symbolic action by which the Levites could have shown: (1) that the bulls were substitutes for the Levites. Alternate translation: [And the Levites shall lay their hands on the head of the bulls to designate the bulls as their substitutes]; or (2) that the bulls were being dedicated to God. Alternate translation: [And the Levites shall lay their hands on the head of the bulls to dedicate them to God]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Numbers 8:12 (#2)
content:
וַ֠⁠עֲשֵׂה

"and make"

This is a command addressed to Moses. Yahweh could be indicating that: (1) Moses should have the priest make the offerings. Alternate translation: [and have a priest make]; or (2) Moses should make the offerings himself. Alternate translation: [and you must make]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:12 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠כַפֵּ֖ר עַל־הַ⁠לְוִיִּֽם

"to make atonement for the Levites"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of atonement, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to redeem the Levites and restore them to Yahweh]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 8:13 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֵנַפְתָּ֥ אֹתָ֛⁠ם תְּנוּפָ֖ה לַֽ⁠יהוָֽה

"and you shall raise them {as} a raised offering to Yahweh"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of dedicating the Levites to Yahweh as if their dedication were a raised offering that was lifted up to him. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 8:11. Alternate translation: [and you shall dedicate the Levites to Yahweh as you do when you raise a raised offering]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:13 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י אַהֲרֹ֖ן וְ⁠לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י בָנָ֑י⁠ו

"to the face of Aaron and to the face of his sons"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Aaron and his sons. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Aaron and before his sons]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 8:13 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הֵנַפְתָּ֥ אֹתָ֛⁠ם תְּנוּפָ֖ה לַֽ⁠יהוָֽה

"and you shall raise them {as} a raised offering to Yahweh"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [and you shall offer them as a raised offering to Yahweh]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 8:13 (#4)
content:
תְּנוּפָ֖ה

"as} a raised offering"

The expression raised offering is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is a priest. Alternate translation: [as an offering that the priests raise]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 8:13 (#5)
content:
לַֽ⁠יהוָֽה

"to Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [to me]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 8:14 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִבְדַּלְתָּ֙ אֶת־הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֔ם

"And you shall separate the Levites"

Here, the word And introduces a summary or conclusion for this section. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this more explicit. Alternate translation: [And thus you shall separate the Levites]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 8:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אַֽחֲרֵי־כֵן֙ יָבֹ֣אוּ הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֔ם לַ⁠עֲבֹ֖ד אֶת־אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֑ד וְ⁠טִֽהַרְתָּ֣ אֹתָ֔⁠ם וְ⁠הֵנַפְתָּ֥ אֹתָ֖⁠ם תְּנוּפָֽה

"And after that the Levites shall go to serve the tent of meeting, and you shall cleanse them and you shall raise them {as} a raised offering"

The event in the second clauses (you shall cleanse them and you shall raise them as a raised offering) will happen before the events in the first clause (the Levites shall go to serve the tent of meeting). If having the clauses in this order would make the sequence unclear, you can change the order. Alternate translation: [And you shall cleanse the Levites and you shall raise them as a raised offering, and after that the Levites shall go to serve the tent of meeting]

See: Connect — Sequential Time Relationship

title: Numbers 8:15 (#2)
content:
יָבֹ֣אוּ & לַ⁠עֲבֹ֖ד

"shall go to serve"

Yahweh is using shall go to serve as a common expression of his culture to mean “shall be capable of serving.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [shall be capable of serving]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 8:15 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הֵנַפְתָּ֥ אֹתָ֖⁠ם תְּנוּפָֽה

"and you shall raise them {as} a raised offering"

See how you translated this clause in 8:13.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:16 (#1)
content:
נְתֻנִ֨ים נְתֻנִ֥ים הֵ֨מָּה֙ לִ֔⁠י מִ⁠תּ֖וֹךְ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"they {are} given, given to me from the midst of the sons of Israel"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the Israelites were actually given to Yahweh like objects that could be handed over. This represents the formal dedication and appointment of people for service to Yahweh. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are appointed, appointed to me out of all the sons of Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:16 (#2)
content:
נְתֻנִ֨ים נְתֻנִ֥ים הֵ֨מָּה֙ לִ֔⁠י

"they {are} given, given to me"

The expression are given, given is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [I have given them, given them to myself]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 8:16 (#3)
content:
נְתֻנִ֨ים נְתֻנִ֥ים הֵ֨מָּה֙

"they {are} given, given"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb given in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [they are wholly given]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 8:16 (#4)
content:
פִּטְרַ֨ת כָּל־רֶ֜חֶם בְּכ֥וֹר

"the opener of every womb, the firstborn of"

It might seem that the expression the opener of every womb, the firstborn of contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [the firstborn of]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 8:16 (#5)
content:
פִּטְרַ֨ת כָּל־רֶ֜חֶם

"the opener of every womb"

Yahweh is using the opener of every womb as a common expression of his culture to mean “the first child of every woman.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 3:12. Alternate translation: [the first child of every woman]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 8:16 (#6)
content:
בְּכ֥וֹר כֹּל֙

"the firstborn of all"

Here and throughout this chapter, the implication is that firstborn refers specifically to firstborn males. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the firstborn males of]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:16 (#7)
content:
לָקַ֥חְתִּי אֹתָ֖⁠ם לִֽ⁠י

"I have taken them for me"

By taken them for me, God means he has selected them to serve him at the tent of meeting. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I have selected them to serve me at the tent of meeting]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:17 (#1)
content:
בָּ⁠אָדָ֖ם וּ⁠בַ⁠בְּהֵמָ֑ה

"among the man and among the animal"

Here, man and animal represent people and animals in general, not specific people or animals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [among the men and among the animals]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 8:17 (#2)
content:
בָּ⁠אָדָ֖ם

"among the man"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [among the human]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 8:17 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠י֗וֹם הַכֹּתִ֤⁠י

"On the day of my striking down"

The expression On the day of is a common expression of his culture to mean “at the time when.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [At the time when I struck down]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 8:17 (#4)
content:
הַכֹּתִ֤⁠י

"my striking down"

By my striking down, God means when he killed all the firstborn sons of the Egyptians. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to Numbers. Alternate translation: [my slaying]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:18 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶקַּח֙ אֶת־הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֔ם

"And I took the Levites"

By I have taken the Levites, God means he selected and set apart the Levites for special service to him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And I have selected the Levites to serve me at the tent of meeting]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:19 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶתְּנָ֨⁠ה אֶת־הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֜ם נְתֻנִ֣ים

"And I gave the Levites {as} given ones"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the Levites were actually given ones who were presented as gifts to Aaron and his sons. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I appointed the Levites as appointed ones]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:19 (#2)
content:
וָ⁠אֶתְּנָ֨⁠ה אֶת־הַ⁠לְוִיִּ֜ם נְתֻנִ֣ים

"And I gave the Levites {as} given ones"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And I gave the Levites]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 8:19 (#3)
content:
לַ⁠עֲבֹ֞ד אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֤ת

"to serve the service of"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [to serve]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 8:19 (#4)
content:
אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֤ת בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙

"the service of the sons of Israel"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a service that is done for the sons of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the service they do for the sake of the sons of Israel]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 8:19 (#5)
content:
אֶת־עֲבֹדַ֤ת בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙

"the service of the sons of Israel"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the sake of serving the sons of Israel]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 8:19 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠כַפֵּ֖ר עַל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"and to make atonement for the sons of Israel"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of atonement, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to redeem the sons of Israel]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 8:19 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֨א יִהְיֶ֜ה & נֶ֔גֶף

"And a plague will not be"

The word translated as And here indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [As a result, a plague will not be]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 8:19 (#8)
content:
נֶ֔גֶף

"a plague"

The term plague refers to any kind of severe disaster or terrible trouble. If your readers would not be familiar with what a plague is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [a disaster] or [terrible trouble]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 8:20 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֨עַשׂ מֹשֶׁ֧ה וְ⁠אַהֲרֹ֛ן וְ⁠כָל־עֲדַ֥ת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לַ⁠לְוִיִּ֑ם כְּ֠⁠כֹל אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֨ה יְהוָ֤ה אֶת־מֹשֶׁה֙ לַ⁠לְוִיִּ֔ם כֵּן־עָשׂ֥וּ לָ⁠הֶ֖ם בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"And Moses, and Aaron and all the congregation of the sons of Israel, did to the Levites according to all that Yahweh had commanded Moses for the Levites; thus the sons of Israel did to them"

It might seem that the expression thus the sons of Israel did to them contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And Moses, and Aaron and all the congregation of the sons of Israel, did to the Levites exactly according to all that Yahweh had commanded Moses for the Levites]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 8:20 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־עֲדַ֥ת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל

"and all the congregation of the sons of Israel"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a congregation that is made up of the sons of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 8:9. Alternate translation: [the congregation that consists of all the sons of Israel]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 8:21 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֨נֶף אַהֲרֹ֥ן אֹתָ֛⁠ם תְּנוּפָ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"and Aaron raised them {as} a raised offering to the face of Yahweh"

See how you translated the similar phrase in 8:11.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:21 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יְכַפֵּ֧ר עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם אַהֲרֹ֖ן

"and Aaron made atonement for them"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of atonement, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And Aaron offered sacrifices to redeem the Levites and restore them to Yahweh]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 8:22 (#1)
content:
בָּ֣אוּ & לַ⁠עֲבֹ֤ד

"went to serve"

The phrase went to serve is a common expression of his culture to mean “were capable of serving” or “began their service.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 8:15. Alternate translation: [were capable of serving]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 8:22 (#2)
content:
לַ⁠עֲבֹ֤ד אֶת־עֲבֹֽדָתָ⁠ם֙

"to serve their service"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [to serve]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 8:22 (#3)
content:
אֶת־עֲבֹֽדָתָ⁠ם֙

"their service"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as they must serve]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 8:22 (#4)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י אַהֲרֹ֖ן וְ⁠לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י בָנָ֑י⁠ו

"to the face of Aaron and to the face of his sons"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Aaron and his sons. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. See how you translated these words in 8:13. Alternate translation: [before Aaron and before his sons]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 8:22 (#5)
content:
עָשׂ֥וּ

"they did"

The pronoun they refers to the Levites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 8:24 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠צְבֹ֣א צָבָ֔א

"to fight in the army"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of serving in the tabernacle as if it were fighting in the army. This metaphor implies dedication and discipline in service. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 4:23. Alternate translation: [to be part of the group of workers]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:24 (#2)
content:
זֹ֖את אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַ⁠לְוִיִּ֑ם

"This {is} what {is} for the Levites"

Yahweh is using This is what is for the Levites as a common expression of his culture to mean “Here is what the Levites should do.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Here is what the Levites should do]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 8:24 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠בֶּן֩ חָמֵ֨שׁ וְ⁠עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ וָ⁠מַ֔עְלָ⁠ה יָבוֹא֙

"From a son of 25 years and upward he shall come"

Yahweh is not referring to a specific Levite. He means Levites who meet this requirement in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [From sons of 25 years and upward they shall come]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 8:24 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠בֶּן֩ חָמֵ֨שׁ וְ⁠עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ וָ⁠מַ֔עְלָ⁠ה יָבוֹא֙

"From a son of 25 years and upward he shall come"

The phrase from a son of 25 years is a common expression of this culture that means “from age 25” or “starting at 25 years old.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 1:3. Alternate translation: [Those who are 25 years old or older shall come] or [Those aged 25 and above shall come]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 8:24 (#5)
content:
יָבוֹא֙ לִ⁠צְבֹ֣א

"he shall come to fight"

Yahweh is using come to fight as a common expression of this culture to mean “begin doing military service.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 4:23. Alternate translation: [he can fight]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 8:24 (#6)
content:
לִ⁠צְבֹ֣א צָבָ֔א

"to fight in the army"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb (fight) and its object (army) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [to be in the army]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 8:24 (#7)
content:
בַּ⁠עֲבֹדַ֖ת אֹ֥הֶל

"in the service of the tent of"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to serve at]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 8:25 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠צְּבָ֣א הָ⁠עֲבֹדָ֑ה

"from the army of the service"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of the group of workers as if it were an army. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar figure of speech in 8:24. Alternate translation: [from being part of the group of workers for]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:25 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מִ⁠בֶּן֙ חֲמִשִּׁ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה יָשׁ֖וּב מִ⁠צְּבָ֣א הָ⁠עֲבֹדָ֑ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א יַעֲבֹ֖ד עֽוֹד

"And from a son of 50 years he shall return from the army of the service, and he shall not serve more"

Yahweh is not referring to a specific Levite. He means Levites who meet this qualification in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. See how you chose to translate 8:24. Alternate translation: [And from sons of 50 years old they shall return from the army of service, and they shall not serve more]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 8:25 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠מִ⁠בֶּן֙ חֲמִשִּׁ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה יָשׁ֖וּב

"And from a son of 50 years he shall return"

The phrase a son of 50 years is a common expression of this culture that means that a person has the characteristic of being at least 50 years old. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Those who are 50 years old or older shall return] or [Those aged 50 and above shall return]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 8:25 (#4)
content:
יָשׁ֖וּב מִ⁠צְּבָ֣א

"he shall return from the army of"

Yahweh is using he shall return from the army as a common expression of this culture to mean “he cannot be in the army.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the opposite figure of speech in 8:24. Alternate translation: [he cannot be in the army]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 8:25 (#5)
content:
מִ⁠צְּבָ֣א הָ⁠עֲבֹדָ֑ה

"from the army of the service"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the army that serves]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 8:26 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שֵׁרֵ֨ת אֶת־אֶחָ֜י⁠ו בְּ⁠אֹ֤הֶל מוֹעֵד֙ לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֣ר מִשְׁמֶ֔רֶת וַ⁠עֲבֹדָ֖ה לֹ֣א יַעֲבֹ֑ד

"And he shall minister to his brothers in the tent of meeting to keep keeping, but he shall not serve service"

Yahweh is not referring to one specific Levite. He means Levites over 50 years old in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. See how you chose to translate 8:24–25. Alternate translation: [And they shall minister to their brothers in the tent of meeting to keep keeping, but they shall not serve service]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 8:26 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠שֵׁרֵ֨ת אֶת־אֶחָ֜י⁠ו

"And he shall minister to his brothers"

Here, Yahweh is using the term brothers to describe fellow members of the tribe of Levi. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the other Levites]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 8:26 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֣ר מִשְׁמֶ֔רֶת וַ⁠עֲבֹדָ֖ה לֹ֣א יַעֲבֹ֑ד

"to keep keeping, but he shall not serve service"

By keep keeping and serve service, Yahweh means to guard the holy things and do the physical work associated with moving them. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [to guard the holy things, but he shall not do the physical labor required to move them]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:26 (#4)
content:
לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֣ר מִשְׁמֶ֔רֶת וַ⁠עֲבֹדָ֖ה לֹ֣א יַעֲבֹ֑ד

"to keep keeping, but he shall not serve service"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [to keep, but he shall not serve]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 8:26 (#5)
content:
יַעֲבֹ֑ד

"service"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in any way that the Levites serve]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 8:26 (#6)
content:
כָּ֛כָה תַּעֲשֶׂ֥ה לַ⁠לְוִיִּ֖ם בְּ⁠מִשְׁמְרֹתָֽ⁠ם

"Thus you shall do for the Levites in their keepings"

By their keepings, Yahweh means the duties and responsibilities that God has assigned to the Levites. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [That is what you must command the Levites concerning their keepings]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 8:26 (#7)
content:
בְּ⁠מִשְׁמְרֹתָֽ⁠ם

"in their keepings"

The implication is that the Levites had specific duties guarding the sanctuary and assisting with its maintenance. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [in their guard duties]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers - Chapter 9 Introduction
content:
Numbers 9 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter briefly narrates how the Israelites celebrated the Passover for the first time since they left Egypt, and it also gives instructions for a celebration of the Passover in the second month for those who were unable to celebrate it in the first month. Then, the author describes how a cloud visually represented Yahweh’s commands to the Israelites concerning when to travel and where to camp.

  1. Israel celebrates the Passover, and Yahweh provides for those unable to celebrate at the appointed time (1–14)
  2. Yahweh uses the cloud over the tabernacle to show Israel when to camp and when to travel (15–23)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Passover

The Passover was a festival that celebrated how God delivered the Israelites from Egypt. You can read more about the Passover in Exodus 12. This chapter records the first celebration of this festival after God delivered the Israelites from Egypt. The festival was celebrated on the fourteenth day of the first month, and it included a special meal at which the Israelites ate unleavened bread and a special lamb. In this chapter, Yahweh allows any Israelites who were unable to celebrate on that day (because of impurity or travel) to celebrate on a backup day, which was the fourteenth day of the second month. This festival was a very important one, so Yahweh indicates that anyone who chooses not to celebrate it must be expelled from the community.

Being “cut off” from the people

The punishment for failing to celebrate the Passover (except for impurity or travel) was being “cut off” from the rest of the Israelites. Scholars are unsure exactly what penalty this phrase implies. It could refer to death by execution. It could refer to punishment from Yahweh in a way of his choice. It could refer to expulsion from the Israelite community. The UST and notes follow this last option. If possible, use a word or phrase that could be understood in several of these ways. If you must specify, it is recommended that you follow the UST and notes.

The cloud

This chapter refers to “the cloud” that was over the sacred tent during the Israelites’ travels in the wilderness. This cloud appeared when the Israelites left Egypt (see Exodus 13:21–22). There it is described as a pillar that is a cloud during the day and fire at night. Here, the cloud also looks like fire at night. In this chapter, the cloud visually shows Yahweh’s commands for when and where the Israelites should travel. Be sure that it is clear to your readers that Yahweh controls the cloud.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Order of events

As with Numbers 7, this chapter occurs before the events in Numbers 1–6. In fact, 9:15 refers to the same day as 7:1 does. Within this chapter, the exact timing of the events in 9:1–4 is uncertain, since the author only mentions the month (although these must have happened before the fourteenth day, when Passover was celebrated). The events in 9:5–14 took place on the fourteenth day of the first month. Then, the event in 9:15 took place on the first day of the first month. So, these events are not in sequential order. Consider how to make this clear to your readers. See the notes on 9:15 for translation options.

Present tense for repeated past actions

In 9:15–23, the author uses the present tense to refer to repeated actions in the past. He means that the events he describes with the present tense happened many times. Consider what tense or form to use to make that clear. The UST uses the English form “would” to refer to these repeated past events.

Personification of the cloud

The author speaks of the cloud as if it were a person who could “dwell” and “prolong” in certain places. He uses this figure of speech to describe how the cloud moved and to imply that Yahweh controlled the cloud. If you would not speak of a cloud as if it were a person, you could use words that you would normally use to describe clouds moving, or you could indicate that Yahweh controlled the cloud.

title: Numbers 9:1 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֣ר יְהוָ֣ה אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֣ה בְ⁠מִדְבַּר־סִ֠ינַי בַּ⁠שָּׁנָ֨ה הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֜ית לְ⁠צֵאתָ֨⁠ם מֵ⁠אֶ֧רֶץ מִצְרַ֛יִם בַּ⁠חֹ֥דֶשׁ הָ⁠רִאשׁ֖וֹן

"And Yahweh spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the second year of their going out from the land of Egypt, in the first month"

The events in this chapter occurred during the same month as the events in Numbers 7. See the note on 7:1. That means that these events occurred before the events in Numbers 1–6, which took place during the second month. You could include a footnote to make the timing of this chapter clear to your readers.

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 9:1 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠שָּׁנָ֨ה הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֜ית & בַּ⁠חֹ֥דֶשׁ הָ⁠רִאשׁ֖וֹן

"in the second year of & in the first month"

If your language would not represent numbers in forms such as in the second year and in the first month, you could represent these numbers in forms that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year two … in month one]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 9:1 (#3)
content:
בַּ⁠חֹ֥דֶשׁ הָ⁠רִאשׁ֖וֹן

"in the first month"

The first month of the Hebrew calendar includes parts of March and April on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

See: Hebrew Months

title: Numbers 9:1 (#4)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"saying"

Here, the word saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 9:2 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יַעֲשׂ֧וּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל

"And the sons of Israel shall do"

Here the word And introduces additional instructions that Yahweh is giving to the Israelites. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Also, the sons of Israel shall do]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 9:3 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠אַרְבָּעָ֣ה עָשָֽׂר־י֠וֹם

"On day 14"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as day 14, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [On the fourteenth day]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 9:3 (#2)
content:
בֵּ֧ין הָֽ⁠עֲרְבַּ֛יִם

"between the evenings"

Yahweh is using between the evenings as a common expression of this culture to mean “when evening begins.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when evening begins]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:3 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠כָל־חֻקֹּתָ֥י⁠ו וּ⁠כְ⁠כָל־מִשְׁפָּטָ֖י⁠ו

"According to all its statutes and according to all its ordinances"

These two phrases according to all its statutes and according to all its ordinances mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [According to all its statutes] or [According to all its ordinances]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 9:4 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֥ר מֹשֶׁ֛ה אֶל־בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לַ⁠עֲשֹׂ֥ת הַ⁠פָּֽסַח

"And Moses spoke to the sons of Israel to do the Passover"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [And Moses said to the sons of Israel, “Do the Passover”]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Numbers 9:5 (#1)
content:
בָּ⁠רִאשׁ֡וֹן בְּ⁠אַרְבָּעָה֩ עָשָׂ֨ר י֥וֹם לַ⁠חֹ֛דֶשׁ

"in the first, on day 14 of the month"

The first month of the Hebrew calendar includes March and April on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar. See how you referred to this month in 9:1.

See: Hebrew Months

title: Numbers 9:5 (#2)
content:
בָּ⁠רִאשׁ֡וֹן

"in the first"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. Here in the first refers to the first month, as in verse 1. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [in the first month]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 9:5 (#3)
content:
בָּ⁠רִאשׁ֡וֹן

"in the first"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as in the first, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [on one]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 9:5 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠אַרְבָּעָה֩ עָשָׂ֨ר י֥וֹם

"on day 14"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as day 14, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. See how you referred to this day in 9:3. Alternate translation: [on the fourteenth day]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 9:5 (#5)
content:
בֵּ֥ין הָ⁠עַרְבַּ֖יִם

"between the evenings"

See how you translated this phrase in 9:3. Alternate translation: [when evening began]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:6 (#1)
content:
אֲנָשִׁ֗ים & אָדָ֔ם

"men & a man"

Here the masculine terms men and a man have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [people … human]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 9:6 (#2)
content:
טְמֵאִים֙ לְ⁠נֶ֣פֶשׁ אָדָ֔ם

"unclean to a person of a man"

The author is using unclean to a person of a man as a common expression of this culture to mean “unclean because of contact with a dead person’s body.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [unclean because of coming into contact with a corpse]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:6 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא־יָכְל֥וּ

"and they were not able"

The word translated as and indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and since they were unclean, they were not able]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 9:6 (#4)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י מֹשֶׁ֛ה וְ⁠לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י אַהֲרֹ֖ן

"to the face of Moses and to the face of Aaron"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Moses and Aaron. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Moses and before Aaron]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 9:6 (#5)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠ה֑וּא

"on that day"

The author assumes that readers will know that day refers to the fourteenth day of the first month when the Passover was to be celebrated. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on the day when the Passover would be celebrated]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:7 (#1)
content:
הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֤ים & אָדָ֑ם

"men & a man"

Here the masculine terms men and man have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [people … a human]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 9:7 (#2)
content:
אֵלָ֔י⁠ו

"to him"

The pronoun him refers to Moses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to Moses]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 9:7 (#3)
content:
טְמֵאִ֖ים לְ⁠נֶ֣פֶשׁ אָדָ֑ם

"unclean to a person of a man"

See how you translated this phrase in 9:6. Alternate translation: [unclean because of coming into contact with a corpse]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:7 (#4)
content:
לָ֣⁠מָּה נִגָּרַ֗ע לְ⁠בִלְתִּ֨י הַקְרִ֜ב אֶת־קָרְבַּ֤ן יְהוָה֙ בְּ⁠מֹ֣עֲד֔⁠וֹ בְּ⁠ת֖וֹךְ בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"Why are we taken away not to present the offering of Yahweh in its appointed time in the midst of the sons of Israel"

The men are using the question form to express their strong desire to participate in the Passover celebration. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Yet, we still want to be able to present the offering of Yahweh in its appointed time in the midst of the sons of Israel.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 9:7 (#5)
content:
נִגָּרַ֗ע לְ⁠בִלְתִּ֨י הַקְרִ֜ב

"are we taken away not to present"

The men are using the phrase are we taken away not to present as a common expression of their culture to mean “are we prevented from presenting” or “are we forbidden to present.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are we prevented from presenting]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:7 (#6)
content:
נִגָּרַ֗ע

"are we taken away"

The expression are we taken away is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [does our uncleanness take us away]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 9:7 (#7)
content:
הַקְרִ֜ב אֶת־קָרְבַּ֤ן

"to present the offering of"

The phrase present the offering is a construction in which a verb (present) and its object (offering) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [to give the offering]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 9:7 (#8)
content:
אֶת־קָרְבַּ֤ן יְהוָה֙

"the offering of Yahweh"

The people are using the possessive form to describe an offering that is for Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the offering for Yahweh]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 9:7 (#9)
content:
אֶת־קָרְבַּ֤ן

"the offering of"

The people assume that Moses will know that the offering refers to the lamb that was killed and eaten during the Passover celebration. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the Passover lamb offering]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:8 (#1)
content:
עִמְד֣וּ

"Stand"

By Stand, Moses means to wait where they were while he went to ask Yahweh about their situation. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Stand here as you wait]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:8 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אֶשְׁמְעָ֔ה מַה־יְצַוֶּ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה לָ⁠כֶֽם

"and I shall hear what Yahweh commands for you"

By I shall hear what Yahweh commands, Moses means he will go to the sacred tent to receive instructions from Yahweh and then report back to tell them. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I shall go to the sacred tent, find out what Yahweh commands for you, and tell you]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:10 (#1)
content:
דַּבֵּ֛ר אֶל־בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר אִ֣ישׁ אִ֣ישׁ כִּי־יִהְיֶֽה־טָמֵ֣א ׀ לָ⁠נֶ֡פֶשׁ אוֹ֩ בְ⁠דֶ֨רֶךְ רְחֹקָ֜הׄ לָ⁠כֶ֗ם א֚וֹ לְ⁠דֹרֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"Speak to the sons of Israel, saying, ‘A man, a man, when he is unclean to a person or is on a distant way, for you or for your generations"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Speak to the sons of Israel. Say to them that a man, a man, when he is unclean to a person or is on a distant way, for them or for their generations]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 9:10 (#2)
content:
אִ֣ישׁ אִ֣ישׁ כִּי־יִהְיֶֽה־טָמֵ֣א & וְ⁠עָ֥שָׂה

"A man, a man, when he is unclean & then he will do"

Here the masculine terms a man, a man and he have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Since the verses that follow use plural forms, you could also use plural forms here. Alternate translation: [A person, a person, when he or she is unclean … then he or she shall do]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 9:10 (#3)
content:
אִ֣ישׁ אִ֣ישׁ

"A man, a man"

In Hebrew, the repetition of A man, a man creates emphasis. If your language has different ways to show emphasis, you could use one of those instead. See how you translated this phrase in 5:12. Alternate translation: [Any man]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 9:10 (#4)
content:
טָמֵ֣א ׀ לָ⁠נֶ֡פֶשׁ

"unclean to a person"

See how you translated the similar phrase in 9:6. Alternate translation: [unclean because of coming into contact with a corpse]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:10 (#5)
content:
בְ⁠דֶ֨רֶךְ רְחֹקָ֜הׄ

"is on a distant way"

The phrase on a distant way was a common expression meaning “on a long journey” or “traveling far away.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on a journey far away]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:10 (#6)
content:
לָ⁠כֶ֗ם א֚וֹ לְ⁠דֹרֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"for you or for your generations"

By for you or for your generations, Yahweh means that these instructions apply both to the people who were alive at that time and to all their descendants who would live later. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [which applies to you and to your generations]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:10 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠עָ֥שָׂה

"then he will do"

Yahweh is using a future statement to give an instruction or command. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words then he will do using a command or instruction form. Alternate translation: [then he may do]

See: Statements — Other Uses

title: Numbers 9:11 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠חֹ֨דֶשׁ הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֜י בְּ⁠אַרְבָּעָ֨ה עָשָׂ֥ר י֛וֹם

"In the second month on day 14"

The second month of the Hebrew calendar includes April and May on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

See: Hebrew Months

title: Numbers 9:11 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠חֹ֨דֶשׁ הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֜י

"In the second month"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as In the second month, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [On month two]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 9:11 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠אַרְבָּעָ֨ה עָשָׂ֥ר י֛וֹם

"on day 14"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as on day 14, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [on the fourteenth day]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 9:11 (#4)
content:
בֵּ֥ין הָ⁠עַרְבַּ֖יִם

"between the evenings"

See how you translated this phrase in 9:3. Alternate translation: [when evening began]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:11 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠מְרֹרִ֖ים

"and bitter herbs"

These bitter herbs are a kind of vegetable or plant that has a strong and sour taste. If your readers would not be familiar with what bitter herbs are, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and small plants that taste bitter]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 9:11 (#6)
content:
יֹאכְלֻֽ⁠הוּ

"they shall eat it"

The pronoun it refers to the Passover lamb. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [they shall eat the Passover lamb]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 9:12 (#1)
content:
מִמֶּ֨⁠נּוּ֙ & ב֑⁠וֹ & יַעֲשׂ֥וּ אֹתֽ⁠וֹ

"from it & in it & they shall do it"

The pronoun it in the phrases from it and in it refers to the Passover lamb. The pronoun it in the phrase they shall do it refers to the Passover celebration. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from the Passover lamb … in the Passover lamb … they shall do the Passover]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 9:12 (#2)
content:
לֹֽא־יַשְׁאִ֤ירוּ מִמֶּ֨⁠נּוּ֙ עַד־בֹּ֔קֶר

"They shall not leave from it until morning"

Yahweh is using a figure of speech here that emphasizes a positive meaning by using a negative word, not, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. It is clear in Exodus 12:10 that they must eat all the food or burn any leftovers. Alternate translation: [They shall eat it all or burn any leftovers before morning]

See: Litotes

title: Numbers 9:13 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נִכְרְתָ֛ה הַ⁠נֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַ⁠הִ֖וא מֵֽ⁠עַמֶּ֑י⁠הָ

"then that person shall be cut off from his people"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of separating a person from his community as if that person were cut off from his people like a branch being cut from a tree. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [then that person shall be expelled from his people]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 9:13 (#2)
content:
חֶטְא֥⁠וֹ יִשָּׂ֖א הָ⁠אִ֥ישׁ הַ⁠הֽוּא

"That man shall lift up his sin"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of sin as if it were a burden that a person could lift up or carry. This speaks of experiencing the consequences of sin. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [That man shall bear his sin] or [That man will be punished for his sin]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 9:13 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠אִישׁ֩ אֲשֶׁר־ה֨וּא טָה֜וֹר וּ⁠בְ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ לֹא־הָיָ֗ה וְ⁠חָדַל֙ לַ⁠עֲשׂ֣וֹת הַ⁠פֶּ֔סַח וְ⁠נִכְרְתָ֛ה הַ⁠נֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַ⁠הִ֖וא מֵֽ⁠עַמֶּ֑י⁠הָ כִּ֣י ׀ קָרְבַּ֣ן יְהוָ֗ה לֹ֤א הִקְרִיב֙ בְּ⁠מֹ֣עֲד֔⁠וֹ חֶטְא֥⁠וֹ יִשָּׂ֖א הָ⁠אִ֥ישׁ הַ⁠הֽוּא

"And the man who is clean and is not on a way and ceases to do the Passover, then that person shall be cut off from his people, for he did not present the offering of Yahweh in its appointed time. That man shall lift up his sin"

Here the masculine terms man, he, and his have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [And the person who is clean and is not on a way and ceases to do the Passover, then that person shall be cut off from his or her people, for he or she did not present the offering of Yahweh in its appointed time. That person shall lift up his or her sin]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 9:13 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ לֹא־הָיָ֗ה

"and is not on a way"

Yahweh is using is not on a way as a common expression of this culture to mean “is not traveling” or “is not on a journey.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 9:10. Alternate translation: [is not on a journey]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:13 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠נִכְרְתָ֛ה הַ⁠נֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַ⁠הִ֖וא מֵֽ⁠עַמֶּ֑י⁠הָ

"then that person shall be cut off from his people"

The expression shall be cut off from his people is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the rest of the Israelites. Alternate translation: [then the rest of the Israelites must cut off that person from among them]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 9:13 (#6)
content:
קָרְבַּ֣ן & לֹ֤א הִקְרִיב֙

"he did not present the offering of"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb (present) and its object (offering) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [he did not give the offering]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 9:13 (#7)
content:
קָרְבַּ֣ן יְהוָ֗ה

"the offering of Yahweh"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe an offering that is for Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 9:7. Alternate translation: [the offering for Yahweh]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 9:13 (#8)
content:
קָרְבַּ֣ן

"the offering of"

Yahweh assumes that readers will know that the offering refers to the Passover lamb that the Israelites were commanded to sacrifice. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated this word in 9:7. Alternate translation: [the Passover lamb offering]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:14 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כִֽי־יָג֨וּר אִתְּ⁠כֶ֜ם גֵּ֗ר & לָ⁠כֶ֔ם

"And if a sojourner sojourns with you & for you"

If you decided in 9:10 to translate these verses in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [And if a sojourner sojourns with them … for them]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 9:14 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠חֻקַּ֥ת הַ⁠פֶּ֛סַח וּ⁠כְ⁠מִשְׁפָּט֖⁠וֹ

"according to the statute of the Passover and according to its ordinance"

These two phrases according to the statute of the Passover and according to its ordinance mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [according to the statute of the Passover] or [according to the ordinance of the Passover]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 9:14 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠חֻקַּ֥ת הַ⁠פֶּ֛סַח וּ⁠כְ⁠מִשְׁפָּט֖⁠וֹ & חֻקָּ֤ה אַחַת֙

"according to the statute of the Passover and according to its ordinance & One statute"

Here, statute and ordinance represent laws about the Passover in general, not one specific law. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [according to the statutes of the Passover and according to its ordinances … The same statutes]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 9:14 (#4)
content:
כֵּ֣ן יַעֲשֶׂ֑ה

"so he shall do"

The implication is that foreigners must follow all the Passover regulations, but if they do, they can celebrate the Passover. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he may do the Passover in that way]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:14 (#5)
content:
כֵּ֣ן יַעֲשֶׂ֑ה

"so he shall do"

Here the masculine term he has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [so he or she shall do]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 9:14 (#6)
content:
לָ⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֖ר וּ⁠לְ⁠אֶזְרַ֥ח הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"for you and for the sojourner and for the native of the land"

The implication is that you includes both the sojourner and the native of the land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for you, both for the sojourner and for the native of the land]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:14 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֖ר וּ⁠לְ⁠אֶזְרַ֥ח הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"and for the sojourner and for the native of the land"

Here, sojourner and native represent sojourners and natives in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and for the sojourners and for the natives of]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 9:14 (#8)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠אֶזְרַ֥ח הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"and for the native of the land"

Yahweh is using the native of the land as a common expression of this culture to mean “people who were born as Israelites.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and for people who were born as Israelites]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:15 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠יוֹם֙ הָקִ֣ים אֶת־הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּ֔ן

"And on the day of the raising up of the Dwelling"

This day is the day that Exodus 40:17 refers to, which is the first day of the first month of the second year. So, this event occurred before the Passover described in the first half of this chapter, which took place on the fourteenth day of the first month. If it is helpful in your language, you might want to make it clear that the account that starts in this verse happened before the Passover in 9:1–14. Alternate translation: [Now previously, on the day of the raising up of the Dwelling]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 9:15 (#2)
content:
הֶֽ⁠עָנָן֙

"the cloud"

The author assumes that readers will know that the cloud is the same cloud that led the Israelites when they left Egypt as described in Exodus 13:21–22. You could say this explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the same cloud that went before them when they left Egypt]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:15 (#3)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּ֔ן לְ⁠אֹ֖הֶל הָ⁠עֵדֻ֑ת

"the Dwelling of the Tent of the Testimony"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a Dwelling that was inside the Tent of the Testimony. The Dwelling was the inner part of the sacred tent, and the Tent of the Testimony was the outer part that enclosed it. See Exodus 26:1–13 for details, and see how you translated the similar words in 3:25. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the Dwelling that was inside the Tent of the Testimony]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 9:15 (#4)
content:
יִהְיֶ֧ה עַֽל־הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּ֛ן כְּ⁠מַרְאֵה־אֵ֖שׁ

"it is upon the Dwelling like the appearance of fire"

The point of this comparison is that just as fire is bright and visible at night, so was the appearance over the Dwelling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [it is bright upon the Dwelling, like the appearance of fire]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 9:15 (#5)
content:
יִהְיֶ֧ה

"it is"

Here and in 9:16–23, the author uses the present tense to describe things that happened regularly and repeatedly in the past. See the chapter introduction for more information. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a tense that can refer to regular or repeated actions. Alternate translation: [it was]

See: Irregular Use of Tenses

title: Numbers 9:16 (#1)
content:
כֵּ֚ן יִהְיֶ֣ה תָמִ֔יד

"So it is continually"

The implication is that this situation with the cloud covering the tent in the daytime and appearing as fire at night continued throughout the entire time that the Israelites traveled in the wilderness. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [So it is continually while the Israelites traveled through the wilderness]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:16 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מַרְאֵה־אֵ֖שׁ לָֽיְלָה

"and the appearance of fire {is} at night"

By the appearance of fire is at night, the author means that the cloud that covered the sacred tent appeared like fire during the night. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the fuller expression of this idea in 9:15. Alternate translation: [and the cloud appeared like fire at night]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 9:17 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠פִ֞י הֵעָלֹ֤ת הֶֽ⁠עָנָן֙

"And to the mouth of the cloud being taken up"

The author is using to the mouth of the cloud as a common expression of his culture to mean “when” or “at the time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And at any time the cloud could be taken up]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 9:17 (#2)
content:
הֵעָלֹ֤ת הֶֽ⁠עָנָן֙

"of the cloud being taken up"

The expression being taken up is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [Yahweh taking up the cloud]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 9:17 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בִ⁠מְק֗וֹם אֲשֶׁ֤ר יִשְׁכָּן־שָׁם֙ הֶֽ⁠עָנָ֔ן

"And in a place where the cloud dwells there"

It might seem that the expression where the cloud dwells there contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And in any place where the cloud dwells]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 9:17 (#4)
content:
יִשְׁכָּן & הֶֽ⁠עָנָ֔ן

"the cloud dwells"

title: Numbers - Chapter 10 Introduction
content:
Numbers 10 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter provides the commands Yahweh gave to Moses about silver trumpets to be used for signaling the people. It also describes the order in which the Israelites set out, Moses’ request to Hobab, and the blessings Moses spoke when the sacred chest was picked up at the beginning of each day and set down at the end of each day.

  1. Yahweh commands Moses to make silver trumpets and explains their uses (1–10)
  2. Israel leaves Sinai and travels in the assigned order (11–28)
  3. Moses asks Hobab to accompany Israel and help guide the people (29–32)
  4. The ark goes ahead of Israel, and Moses calls on Yahweh when it sets out and rests (33–36)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Trumpets

The trumpets mentioned in this chapter are metal instruments that make a loud sound when people blow into them. This chapter refers to “blowing” the trumpets as well as “blowing an alarm.” These are two different ways of making sounds with the trumpets. It is not clear exactly what sound the “alarm” was. Some scholars think that the sound was very loud. Others think the sound was repeated. Use a general expression in your language, but be sure to distinguish “blowing” and “blowing an alarm.”

Israel sets out

In 10:11–28, the author describes the order in which the Israelite tribes set out from their camp at Sinai. While the author is explicitly describing the first time they left, he implies that this is also how they normally traveled. The four camps that Yahweh outlined in Numbers 2 set out in the same order in this chapter: east, south, west, north. It is also important to note that the Levites set out in two different groups: first the Gershonites and Merarites, who carried the pieces of the sacred tent, and later the Kohathites, who carried the things that belonged inside the sacred tent.

“According to their armies”

As in Numbers 2, the phrase “according to their armies” indicates that each tribe and camp was organized and arranged into military units or divisions. The people in each military unit would camp together, and their names were listed together when the census was recorded. The UST expresses this idea with the phrase “by their army divisions.”

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Order of events

The events in this chapter occur after the events in Numbers 1–9. The events in Numbers 7–9 happened first, followed by the events in Numbers 1–6. Then, the events in this chapter happened. This chapter repeatedly refers to the same event: the Israelites setting out from Mount Sinai. The author mentions this event directly in 10:12–13, 10:28, and 10:33. Be sure that your readers know that these verses all refer to the same event.

Repetition

The list in 10:14–27 includes many repeated structures. Each of the camps, made up of three tribes, is described with almost the same words, except for the names. After you have translated 10:14–16, use the same forms for the following sections. Remember to pay attention to differences in names and details, as illustrated in the ULT and by the notes.

Names from earlier in Numbers

In this chapter, the author includes the name of each tribe’s leader and the name of each leader’s father. These names already appeared in Numbers 1 in identical form. Be sure that you translate them in exactly the same way in this chapter.

Moses’ father-in-law

In 10:29, the author refers to Hobab and Reuel, identifying one of them as Moses’ father-in-law, but it is not clear which one. In Judges 4:11, Hobab is called Moses’ father-in-law. However, in Exodus 2:18, Reuel is named as the father of Moses’ (future) wife. Finally, elsewhere in Exodus (for example, see Exodus 3:1 and 4:18), Jethro is the name of Moses’ father-in-law. In this time period, people often had multiple names. Also, some scholars think that the word for “father-in-law” can refer to any male relative by marriage. So, it may be that Hobab is Moses’ brother-in-law and that Reuel was also named Jethro and was Moses’ father-in-law. It may be that Hobab was also named Jethro and was Moses’ father-in-law and that Reuel was Hobab’s father and Moses’ wife’s grandfather. It may be that one man had all three names (Hobab, Reuel, and Jethro) and had a father whose name was also Reuel. Here, the Hebrew most naturally identifies Hobab as Moses’ father-in-law, and the UST follows that interpretation. Consider how translations that your readers might be familiar with treat this verse.

By Make for you, Yahweh means that Moses should have someone make the trumpets for him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Let two trumpets of silver be made for you. Let them be made of]

title: Numbers 10:6 (#8)
content:
תְּרוּעָ֥ה יִתְקְע֖וּ לְ⁠מַסְעֵי⁠הֶֽם

"They shall blow an alarm for their setting out"

The implication is that the same trumpet signal used for the eastern and southern camps was also to be used when the western and northern camps set out. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They shall blow alarms for the setting out of each other camp in the same way]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:7 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠הַקְהִ֖יל אֶת־הַ⁠קָּהָ֑ל

"And when assembling the assembly"

This is poetic language where the verb “assemble” and its object “assembly” come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And when assembling the people]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 10:7 (#2)
content:
תִּתְקְע֖וּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א תָרִֽיעוּ

"you shall blow but you shall not blow an alarm"

The word you is plural here because God is speaking to all the Israelites along with Moses. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 10:7 (#3)
content:
תִּתְקְע֖וּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א תָרִֽיעוּ

"you shall blow but you shall not blow an alarm"

The implication is that it is the priests who blow the trumpets, as stated explicitly in 10:8. You could make this explicit by saying who does the blowing. See how you translated “you shall blow” in 10:5. Alternate translation: [you shall have the priests blow but you shall not have them blow]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:7 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א תָרִֽיעוּ

"but you shall not blow an alarm"

See how you translated alarm in 10:5.

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 10:8 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בְנֵ֤י אַהֲרֹן֙

"And the sons of Aaron"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the priests were actually sons of Aaron. This refers to the descendants of Aaron who served as priests. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the men descended from Aaron]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 10:8 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָי֥וּ

"and they shall be"

The pronoun they refers to the trumpets. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the trumpets shall be]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 10:8 (#3)
content:
לָ⁠כֶ֛ם & לְ⁠דֹרֹתֵי⁠כֶֽם

"for you & for your generations"

The word you is plural here because it refers to the Israelites. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 10:8 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠חֻקַּ֥ת עוֹלָ֖ם

"for a statute of eternity"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a statute that applies for eternity. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for a statute that applies for eternity]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 10:8 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠חֻקַּ֥ת עוֹלָ֖ם

"for a statute of eternity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of eternity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for an eternal statute]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 10:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כִֽי־תָבֹ֨אוּ

"And when you go"

The word you here and in the rest of this verse is plural because Yahweh is addressing all the Israelites along with Moses. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 10:9 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠צַּר֙ הַ⁠צֹּרֵ֣ר אֶתְ⁠כֶ֔ם

"the opponent who opposes you"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [those who oppose you]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 10:9 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠הֲרֵעֹתֶ֖ם

"then you shall blow an alarm"

See how you translated this phrase in 10:5.

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 10:9 (#4)
content:
וֲ⁠נִזְכַּרְתֶּ֗ם לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠נוֹשַׁעְתֶּ֖ם

"and you shall be remembered to the face of Yahweh your God, and you shall be saved"

The expressions shall be remembered and shall be saved are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the actions, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh your God shall remember you, and he shall save you]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 10:9 (#5)
content:
וֲ⁠נִזְכַּרְתֶּ֗ם

"and you shall be remembered"

The word translated as and indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and in response you shall be remembered]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 10:9 (#6)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"to the face of Yahweh your God"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh your God]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 10:9 (#7)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"to the face of Yahweh your God"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh your God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [to my face, who am Yahweh your God]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 10:10 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠רָאשֵׁ֣י חָדְשֵׁי⁠כֶם֒

"and at the heads of your months"

Here, heads of your months refers to the beginning of each month as if each month were a person or animal and its first day were its head. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and during the festivals at the beginning of each month]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 10:10 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠י֨וֹם שִׂמְחַתְ⁠כֶ֥ם וּֽ⁠בְ⁠מוֹעֲדֵי⁠כֶם֮ וּ⁠בְ⁠רָאשֵׁ֣י חָדְשֵׁי⁠כֶם֒ וּ⁠תְקַעְתֶּ֣ם בַּ⁠חֲצֹֽצְרֹ֗ת עַ֚ל עֹלֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠עַ֖ל זִבְחֵ֣י שַׁלְמֵי⁠כֶ֑ם וְ⁠הָי֨וּ לָ⁠כֶ֤ם לְ⁠זִכָּרוֹן֙ לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶ֔ם אֲנִ֖י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵי⁠כֶֽם

"And on the day of your joy and at your appointed times and at the heads of your months, then you shall blow the trumpets upon your burnt offerings and upon the sacrifices of your peace offerings, and they will be for you for a memorial to the face of your God. I {am} Yahweh your God"

The word you is plural here and in the rest of the verse because Yahweh is addressing all the Israelites along with Moses. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 10:10 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠י֨וֹם שִׂמְחַתְ⁠כֶ֥ם וּֽ⁠בְ⁠מוֹעֲדֵי⁠כֶם֮ וּ⁠בְ⁠רָאשֵׁ֣י חָדְשֵׁי⁠כֶם֒

"And on the day of your joy and at your appointed times and at the heads of your months"

Here, the word and in the phrase and at your appointed times could mean that: (1) your appointed times and the heads of your months are examples of the day of your. Alternate translation: [And on the day of your joy, that is, at your appointed times and at the heads of your months]; or (2) your appointed times and the heads of your months are in addition to the day of your joy. Alternate translation: [And on the day of your joy and also at your appointed times and at the heads of your months]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 10:10 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠י֨וֹם שִׂמְחַתְ⁠כֶ֥ם

"And on the day of your joy"

Here, day represents a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And at the time of your joy]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 10:10 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠י֨וֹם שִׂמְחַתְ⁠כֶ֥ם

"And on the day of your joy"
