If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of joy, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And on the day when you are joyful]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 10:10 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠י֨וֹם

"And on the day"

Yahweh is not referring to a specific day. He means days in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And on the days]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 10:10 (#7)
content:
וּֽ⁠בְ⁠מוֹעֲדֵי⁠כֶם֮

"and at your appointed times"

By appointed times, Yahweh means the special festivals that God commanded the Israelites to celebrate each year. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at your yearly festivals]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:10 (#8)
content:
וּ⁠תְקַעְתֶּ֣ם

"then you shall blow"

The implication is that the priests, not the general population, were to blow the trumpets. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [then you shall have the priests blow]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:10 (#9)
content:
עַ֚ל עֹלֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠עַ֖ל זִבְחֵ֣י שַׁלְמֵי⁠כֶ֑ם

"upon your burnt offerings and upon the sacrifices of your peace offerings"

Yahweh is using upon your burnt offerings and upon the sacrifices of your peace offerings as a common expression of this culture to mean “when you offer your burnt offerings and when you offer the sacrifices of your peace offerings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when you offer your burnt offerings and when you offer the sacrifices of your peace offerings]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 10:10 (#10)
content:
וְ⁠עַ֖ל זִבְחֵ֣י שַׁלְמֵי⁠כֶ֑ם

"and upon the sacrifices of your peace offerings"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe sacrifices that are part of peace offerings. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and upon the animal sacrifices that are part of your peace offerings]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 10:10 (#11)
content:
וְ⁠הָי֨וּ לָ⁠כֶ֤ם לְ⁠זִכָּרוֹן֙

"and they will be for you for a memorial"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of memorial, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they will cause you to be remembered]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 10:10 (#12)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"to the face of your God"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before your God]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 10:10 (#13)
content:
אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"of your God"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as your God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, your God]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 10:11 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְהִ֞י

"And it happened"

The phrase And it happened introduces a new event in the story. This is a common way in biblical Hebrew to signal the beginning of a new section. If your language has a natural way to mark the start of a new event, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [Then] or [After this]

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 10:11 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠שָּׁנָ֧ה הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֛ית בַּ⁠חֹ֥דֶשׁ הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֖י בְּ⁠עֶשְׂרִ֣ים בַּ⁠חֹ֑דֶשׁ

"in the second year, in the second month, on 20 in the month"

This event took place after the events narrated in Numbers 1–6, which took place after the events in Numbers 7–9. If it is helpful in your language, you might want to make it clear that the account that starts in this verse happened after the events in chapters 1–6. Alternate translation: [after the census, in the second year, in the second month, on 20 in the month]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 10:11 (#3)
content:
בַּ⁠שָּׁנָ֧ה הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֛ית בַּ⁠חֹ֥דֶשׁ הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֖י

"in the second year, in the second month"

If your language would not represent numbers in forms such as in the second year and in the second month, you could represent these numbers in forms that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year two, in month two]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 10:11 (#4)
content:
בַּ⁠שָּׁנָ֧ה הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֛ית

"in the second year"

The implication is that this was two years after the Israelites had left Egypt. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the second year after the Israelites left Egypt]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:11 (#5)
content:
בַּ⁠חֹ֥דֶשׁ הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֖י

"in the second month"

The second month of the Hebrew calendar includes April and May on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

See: Hebrew Months

title: Numbers 10:11 (#6)
content:
בְּ⁠עֶשְׂרִ֣ים

"on 20"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [on day 20]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 10:11 (#7)
content:
בְּ⁠עֶשְׂרִ֣ים

"on 20"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as on 20, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [on the twentieth]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 10:11 (#8)
content:
נַעֲלָה֙ הֶֽ⁠עָנָ֔ן

"the cloud was taken up"

The expression was taken up is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh took the cloud up]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 10:11 (#9)
content:
מִשְׁכַּ֥ן הָ⁠עֵדֻֽת

"the Dwelling of the Testimony"

The implication is that the tent housed the stone tablets on which Yahweh had written the Ten Commandments, which were called “the Testimony.” The ark containing these tablets was kept in the Most Holy Place in this tent. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated this phrase in 1:50. Alternate translation: [the tent holding the ark containing the Ten Commandments]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:12 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠מַסְעֵי⁠הֶ֖ם

"according to their departures"

Here, the word departures could refer to: (1) the way each group of three tribes left its campsite. This is probably what the word means in 10:28. Alternate translation: [according to their order of departure]; or (2) multiple times in a row when the Israelites left their campsite. This is what the word means in 33:1–2. Alternate translation: [with many campsites] or [on their many journeys]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:12 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠מַסְעֵי⁠הֶ֖ם

"according to their departures"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of departures, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to how they departed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 10:12 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁכֹּ֥ן הֶ⁠עָנָ֖ן

"and the cloud dwelled"

The author is speaking of the cloud as if it were a living thing that could dwell in a place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 9:17. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh had the cloud stop and stay]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 10:12 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠מִדְבַּ֥ר פָּארָֽן

"in the wilderness of Paran"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a wilderness that is near Paran. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in the wilderness that was near Paran]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 10:13 (#1)
content:
בָּ⁠רִאשֹׁנָ֑ה

"in the first"

The phrase in the first is a common expression of this culture to mean “for the first time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the first time]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 10:13 (#2)
content:
בָּ⁠רִאשֹׁנָ֑ה

"in the first"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as in the first, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [for time one]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 10:13 (#3)
content:
עַל־פִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה בְּ⁠יַד־מֹשֶֽׁה

"upon the mouth of Yahweh in the hand of Moses"

See how you translated this phrase in 9:23. Alternate translation: [as Yahweh commanded them under the control of Moses]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 10:14 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסַּ֞ע דֶּ֣גֶל מַחֲנֵ֧ה בְנֵֽי־יְהוּדָ֛ה

"And the banner of the camp of the sons of Judah set out"

The author is speaking of the banner as if it were a living thing that could set out on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And those who camped at the banner of the camp of the sons of Judah set out]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 10:14 (#2)
content:
דֶּ֣גֶל

"the banner of"

A banner is a kind of flag that represents a group of people. If your readers would not be familiar with what a banner is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. See how you translated banner in 1:52. Alternate translation: [the flag of]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 10:14 (#3)
content:
מַחֲנֵ֧ה בְנֵֽי־יְהוּדָ֛ה

"the camp of the sons of Judah"

The implication is that this group, who followed the tribal flag of Judah, included the troops not only from Judah but also from the tribes of Issachar and Zebulun, as shown in 10:15–16. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the camp of the sons of Judah, which included the sons of Issachar and Zebulun,]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:14 (#4)
content:
בָּ⁠רִאשֹׁנָ֖ה

"in the first"

The author is using in the first as a common expression of his culture to mean “as the first to leave” or “in the first position.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as the first to leave]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 10:14 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֑⁠ם

"according to their armies"

Here and throughout the chapter, the phrase according to their armies implies that the tribes were organized like armies, with leaders and orderly groups. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [according to their military divisions]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:14 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠עַל־צְבָא֔⁠וֹ

"and over his army"

The pronoun his refers to Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and over Judah’s army]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 10:14 (#7)
content:
נַחְשׁ֖וֹן בֶּן־עַמִּינָדָֽב

"was} Nahshon, the son of Amminadab"

For these and the other names in the list in 10:14–27, translate them as you did in chapter 1. See the chapter introduction for more information.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 10:17 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הוּרַ֖ד הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּ֑ן

"And the Dwelling was taken down"

The expression was taken down is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Gershonites and the Merarites. Alternate translation: [And the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari took down the Dwelling]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 10:17 (#2)
content:
גֵרְשׁוֹן֙ & מְרָרִ֔י

"of Gershon & of Merari"

See how you translated these men’s names in Numbers 3:17.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 10:17 (#3)
content:
נֹשְׂאֵ֖י הַ⁠מִּשְׁכָּֽן

"the ones carrying the Dwelling"

The implication is that these men were assigned this task as their specific responsibility. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [whose job it was to carry the Dwelling]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:18 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נָסַ֗ע דֶּ֛גֶל מַחֲנֵ֥ה רְאוּבֵ֖ן

"And the banner of the camp of Reuben set out"

The author is speaking of the banner as if it were a living thing that could move forward. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar clause in 10:14. Alternate translation: [And those who camped at the banner of the camp of Reuben set out]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 10:18 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נָסַ֗ע דֶּ֛גֶל מַחֲנֵ֥ה רְאוּבֵ֖ן

"And the banner of the camp of Reuben set out"

See how you translated banner in 10:14.

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 10:18 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠עַל־צְבָא֔⁠וֹ

"and over his army"

The pronoun his refers to Reuben. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. See how you translated the similar phrase in 10:14. Alternate translation: [and over Reuben’s camp]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 10:18 (#4)
content:
מַחֲנֵ֥ה רְאוּבֵ֖ן

"the camp of Reuben"

The implication is that the camp of Reuben included the tribes of Simeon and Gad, who followed Reuben’s leadership and camped near his tribal flag. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the camp of Reuben, which included the sons of Simeon and Gad]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:21 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠קְּהָתִ֔ים

"the Kohathites"

This refers to the descendants of Kohath. See how you translated this in Numbers 3:27.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 10:21 (#2)
content:
נֹשְׂאֵ֖י הַ⁠מִּקְדָּ֑שׁ

"the ones carrying the holy place"

The implication is that this group of people had the special duty of carrying the holy place. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar phrase in 10:17. Alternate translation: [whose job it was to carry the holy place]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:21 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠מִּקְדָּ֑שׁ

"the holy place"

Here, the holy place represents the sacred objects that were inside the holy place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. See how you translated the similar phrase in 4:15. Alternate translation: [the things that belong in the holy place]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 10:21 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הֵקִ֥ימוּ

"and they raised up"

The pronoun they refers to the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari who were mentioned in 2:17. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari raised up]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 10:21 (#5)
content:
עַד־בֹּאָֽ⁠ם

"until their coming"

The author is using until their coming as a common expression of his culture to mean “before they arrived.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before they came]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 10:22 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נָסַ֗ע דֶּ֛גֶל מַחֲנֵ֥ה בְנֵֽי־אֶפְרַ֖יִם לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠עַל־צְבָא֔⁠וֹ אֱלִישָׁמָ֖ע בֶּן־עַמִּיהֽוּד

"And the banner of the camp of the sons of Ephraim set out according to their armies: and over his army {was} Elishama, the son of Ammihud"

This verse is identical in structure with 10:19 except that this verse includes the sons of in front of Ephraim. Translate this verse as you translated 10:19, changing only the names as well as the sons of, if necessary. The tribes associated with this camp were Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin.

title: Numbers 10:25 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נָסַ֗ע דֶּ֚גֶל מַחֲנֵ֣ה בְנֵי־דָ֔ן מְאַסֵּ֥ף לְ⁠כָל־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֹ֖ת לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠עַל־צְבָא֔⁠וֹ אֲחִיעֶ֖זֶר בֶּן־עַמִּישַׁדָּֽי

"And the banner of the camp of the sons of Dan, the one gathering for all the camps, set out according to their armies: and over his army was Ahiezer, the son of Ammishaddai"

This verse is identical in structure with 10:14 except that it uses the phrase the one gathering for all the camps instead of in the first. For the phrase the one gathering for all the camps, see the note below. Except for that, translate this verse as you translated 10:14. The tribes associated with this camp were Dan, Asher, and Naphtali.

title: Numbers 10:25 (#2)
content:
מְאַסֵּ֥ף לְ⁠כָל־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֹ֖ת

"the one gathering for all the camps"

The author is using the one gathering for all the camps as a common expression of this culture to mean “the rearguard” or “the one walking at the rear of the group.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one walking at the rear of the group]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 10:28 (#1)
content:
אֵ֛לֶּה מַסְעֵ֥י בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל

"These were the departures of the sons of Israel"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of departures, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [This was how the sons of Israel departed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 10:28 (#2)
content:
אֵ֛לֶּה מַסְעֵ֥י בְנֵֽי

"These were the departures of the sons"

Here, the word departures could refer to: (1) the way each group of three tribes left its campsite. This is probably what the word means in 10:12. Alternate translation: [This was the order of departure of]; or (2) multiple times in a row when the Israelites left their campsite. This is what the word means in 33:1–2. Alternate translation: [These were the many journeys of]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:28 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסָּֽעוּ

"And they set out"

The author assumes that readers will know that he is summarizing what has already been said about how the Israelites arranged themselves for travel. This statement in verse 28 follows the detailed description of the marching order that began in 10:12. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [That is how they set out]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:29 (#1)
content:
נֹסְעִ֣ים ׀ אֲנַ֗חְנוּ & אִתָּ֨⁠נוּ֙ וְ⁠הֵטַ֣בְנוּ

"We are setting out & with us, and we will do good"

Here and in 10:31–32, when Moses says we and us, he is including himself and the Israelites but not Hobab, to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of those words if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 10:29 (#2)
content:
לְ֠⁠חֹבָב בֶּן־רְעוּאֵ֣ל הַ⁠מִּדְיָנִי֮ חֹתֵ֣ן מֹשֶׁה֒

"to Hobab, the son of Reuel, the Midianite, the father-in-law of Moses"

It is not totally clear which of these men was Moses’ father-in-law. See the chapter introduction for more information. Moses’ father-in-law could be: (1) Hobab. Alternate translation: [to the father-in-law of Moses, Hobab the son of Reuel the Midianite]; or (2) Reuel. Alternate translation: [to Hobab, the son of the father-in-law of Moses, Reuel the Midianite]

See: Kinship

title: Numbers 10:29 (#3)
content:
לְ֠⁠חֹבָב בֶּן־רְעוּאֵ֣ל הַ⁠מִּדְיָנִי֮

"to Hobab, the son of Reuel, the Midianite"

The phrase the Midianite could go with: (1) Hobab. Alternate translation: [to Hobab the Midianite, the son of Reuel]; or (2) Reuel. Alternate translation: [to Hobab, the son of Reuel the Midianite]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:29 (#4)
content:
לְ֠⁠חֹבָב בֶּן־רְעוּאֵ֣ל

"to Hobab, the son of Reuel"

The words Hobab and Reuel are the names of men.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 10:29 (#5)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה אֹת֖⁠וֹ אֶתֵּ֣ן לָ⁠כֶ֑ם

"that Yahweh said, ‘I shall give it to you"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that Yahweh said that he would give to us]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 10:29 (#6)
content:
לְכָ֤⁠ה אִתָּ֨⁠נוּ֙ וְ⁠הֵטַ֣בְנוּ לָ֔⁠ךְ כִּֽי־יְהוָ֥ה דִּבֶּר־ט֖וֹב עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"Go with us, and we will do good to you. For Yahweh has spoken good upon Israel"

The word translated as For indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has spoken good upon Israel. So, go with us, and we will do good to you]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 10:29 (#7)
content:
לְכָ֤⁠ה אִתָּ֨⁠נוּ֙

"Go with us"

In a context such as this, your language might say “Come” instead of Go. Alternate translation: [Come with us]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 10:29 (#8)
content:
דִּבֶּר־ט֖וֹב עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"has spoken good upon Israel"

Moses is using has spoken good upon Israel as a common expression of his culture to mean “has promised to do good things for Israel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has said that good things will happen to Israel]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 10:29 (#9)
content:
עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"upon Israel"

Moses is speaking of himself and his fellow Israelites in the third person as Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this form in the first person. Alternate translation: [upon us Israelites]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 10:30 (#1)
content:
לֹ֣א אֵלֵ֑ךְ כִּ֧י אִם־אֶל־אַרְצִ֛⁠י וְ⁠אֶל־מוֹלַדְתִּ֖⁠י אֵלֵֽךְ

"I will not go, except I will go to my land and to my relatives"

If it would appear in your language that Hobab was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [I will not go with you. Rather, I will go to my land and to my relatives.]

See: Connect — Exception Clauses

title: Numbers 10:30 (#2)
content:
אֶל־אַרְצִ֛⁠י וְ⁠אֶל־מוֹלַדְתִּ֖⁠י

"to my land and to my relatives"

The phrase land and relatives expresses a single idea. The word relatives tells more about land. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [to my land where my relatives are]

See: Hendiadys

title: Numbers 10:31 (#1)
content:
אֹתָ֑⁠נוּ & חֲנֹתֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ & לָּ֖⁠נוּ

"us & our camping & for us"

Here and in 10:32, the words us and our include Moses and the Israelites but not Hobab, to whom Moses is speaking, so use the exclusive form of these words if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [myself and all the Israelites … our camping … for myself and all the Israelites]

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 10:31 (#2)
content:
כִּ֣י ׀ עַל־כֵּ֣ן יָדַ֗עְתָּ

"For upon this, you know"

Moses is using For upon this as a common expression of his culture to mean “Here is why I ask.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Here is why I ask: you know]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 10:31 (#3)
content:
חֲנֹתֵ֨⁠נוּ֙

"our camping"

Here, camping represents places of encampment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [where we can camp]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 10:31 (#4)
content:
לָּ֖⁠נוּ לְ⁠עֵינָֽיִם

"for us for eyes"

Moses is using the expression for us for eyes as a common expression of his culture to mean “a guide for us.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a guide for us]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 10:32 (#1)
content:
תֵלֵ֣ךְ עִמָּ֑⁠נוּ וְ⁠הָיָ֣ה

"when you go with us, then it will happen that"

Moses is describing a possible condition in which it will happen that that good that Yahweh shall do good with us will take place only if you go with us occurs first. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [if you go with us, then it will happen]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 10:32 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֣ה ׀ הַ⁠טּ֣וֹב הַ⁠ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר יֵיטִ֧יב יְהוָ֛ה עִמָּ֖⁠נוּ וְ⁠הֵטַ֥בְנוּ לָֽ⁠ךְ

"then it will happen that that good that Yahweh shall do good with us, also we shall do good to you"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about that good that Yahweh shall do good with us with the information about we shall do good to you. Alternate translation: [that we shall do the same good to you that Yahweh shall do with us]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 10:32 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הֵטַ֥בְנוּ לָֽ⁠ךְ

"also we shall do good to you"

The author does not explicitly indicate whether Hobab went with the Israelites. The narrative may imply that he did. However, because the author does not include Hobab’s response, it is recommended that you do not make his response explicit in your translation.

See: When to Keep Information Implicit

title: Numbers 10:33 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסְעוּ֙ מֵ⁠הַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה דֶּ֖רֶךְ שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת יָמִ֑ים

"And they set out from the mountain of Yahweh a way of three days"

The term appointed is a formal way of saying “arranged for” or “selected for.” If it would be clearer in your language, you could express this idea in a less formal way, such as “he chose” or “he picked.” Alternate translation: [And when they set out from the mountain of Yahweh, they traveled a way of three days]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:33 (#2)
content:
מֵ⁠הַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה

"from the mountain of Yahweh"

The implication is that Mount Sinai was the mountain where Yahweh had revealed himself to the Israelites and given them his law. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from Sinai, the mountain of Yahweh]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:33 (#3)
content:
מֵ⁠הַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה

"from the mountain of Yahweh"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a mountain that is characterized by being the place where Yahweh had revealed himself to Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the mountain where Yahweh had spoken to them]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 10:33 (#4)
content:
דֶּ֖רֶךְ שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת יָמִ֑ים & דֶּ֚רֶךְ שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת יָמִ֔ים

"a way of three days & a way of three days"

The phrase a way of three days was a common expression of his culture to mean “a three-day journey” or “a distance that would take three days to travel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and walked for three days … for those three days]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 10:33 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠אֲר֨וֹן בְּרִית־יְהוָ֜ה נֹסֵ֣עַ

"and the box of the covenant of Yahweh was setting out"

The author is speaking of the box of the covenant of Yahweh as if it were a living thing that could travel on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the men who carried the box of the covenant of Yahweh were setting out]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 10:33 (#6)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵי⁠הֶ֗ם

"to their face"

Here, to their face represents being in front of the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [ahead of them]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 10:33 (#7)
content:
מְנוּחָֽה

"rest"

Here, rest represents a place to camp. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a place to rest]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 10:34 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠עֲנַ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֖ם יוֹמָ֑ם בְּ⁠נָסְעָ֖⁠ם מִן־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶֽה

"and the cloud of Yahweh {was} over them by day when they set out from the camp"

By the cloud of Yahweh was over them, the author means this happened regularly whenever they traveled. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the cloud of Yahweh would be over them by day each time they set out from the camp]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:34 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠עֲנַ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה

"and the cloud of Yahweh"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a cloud that was controlled by Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the cloud that Yahweh controlled]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 10:35 (#1)
content:
קוּמָ֣⁠ה

"Rise up"

Here, Moses is speaking of the command Rise up as if Yahweh were a person who could physically stand up and begin to act. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Begin to act]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 10:35 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠נְסֹ֥עַ הָ⁠אָרֹ֖ן

"when the box set out"

The author is speaking of the box as if it were a living thing that could set out. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when the people who carried the box set out]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 10:35 (#3)
content:
קוּמָ֣⁠ה

"Rise up"

The word translated as Rise up is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [I ask you to rise up]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

title: Numbers 10:35 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יָפֻ֨צוּ֙ אֹֽיְבֶ֔י⁠ךָ וְ⁠יָנֻ֥סוּ מְשַׂנְאֶ֖י⁠ךָ

"and your enemies will scatter, and the ones hating you will flee"

The phrases your enemies will scatter and the ones hating you will flee are results that will follow when Moses says “Rise up, Yahweh.” If it would be clearer in your language, you could use words that show that these are results that will happen when Yahweh acts. Alternate translation: [and in response your enemies will scatter, and in response the ones having you will flee]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 10:35 (#5)
content:
מִ⁠פָּנֶֽי⁠ךָ

"from your face"

Here, from your face represents being in the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before you]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 10:36 (#1)
content:
שׁוּבָ֣⁠ה

"Return"

Here, Moses is speaking as if Yahweh were actually going to Return to a physical location with Israel. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Be with us]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 10:36 (#2)
content:
אַלְפֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"the thousands of Israel"

Here, Moses is speaking as if the tribes of Israel were thousands of military divisions. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the military divisions of]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 10:36 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠נֻחֹ֖⁠ה

"And when it rested"

The author is speaking of the box as if it were a living thing that could rest. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And when the men carrying it rested]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 10:36 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠נֻחֹ֖⁠ה

"And when it rested"

The implication is that it refers to the sacred chest or ark of the covenant that was mentioned in 10:35. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And when it stopped and stayed in one place]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:36 (#5)
content:
יֹאמַ֑ר

"he says"

The author is using the present tense in says to refer to a repeated past action. If it would not be natural to do that in your language, you could use the past tense in your translation. Alternate translation: [he would say]

See: Irregular Use of Tenses

title: Numbers 10:36 (#6)
content:
שׁוּבָ֣⁠ה יְהוָ֔ה רִֽבְב֖וֹת אַלְפֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"Return, Yahweh, the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel"

This clause could mean that: (1) Moses is asking Yahweh to Return to the Israelites after arising (10:35). Alternate translation: [Return, Yahweh, to the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel]; or (2) Moses is describing Yahweh as the leader of the Israelites. Alternate translation: [Return, Yahweh who is over the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 10:36 (#7)
content:
שׁוּבָ֣⁠ה

"Return"

The word translated as Return is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [I ask you to return]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

title: Numbers 10:36 (#8)
content:
רִֽבְב֖וֹת אַלְפֵ֥י

"the ten thousands of the thousands of"

The expression ten thousands stands approximately for a very large number. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [the enormous number of]

See: Numbers

title: Numbers - Chapter 11 Introduction
content:
Numbers 11 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the Israelites complain about the manna that Yahweh provided for them and ask for meat instead. Yahweh gives them meat but also punishes them. Yahweh also appoints 70 men to help Moses lead the Israelites.

  1. The people complain, and Yahweh sends fire against the camp (1–3)
  2. The people complain about food, and Moses asks Yahweh for help (4–15)
  3. Yahweh promises helpers for Moses and meat for the people (16–23)
  4. Yahweh gives his Spirit to 70 leaders to help Moses (24–30)
  5. Yahweh sends quail and punishes the people (31–35)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The manna

In this chapter, the Israelites complain about the food that Yahweh provided for them, which was called “manna.” See Exodus 16 for more information about how God provided the manna for them. Here, the Israelites want meat instead of manna. God provides them with meat, but he also punishes them for failing to be content with the manna. The author also briefly describes the manner. It is shaped like small seeds, and it has the consistency or color of gum resin.

The Spirit

In 11:17, 25–26, and 29, the “Spirit” is mentioned. Scholars debate whether the word refers to God’s own Spirit, which he gave to Moses, or whether it refers to Moses’ spirit, which Yahweh had enabled in a special way. Either way, it is clear that Yahweh enabled Moses to lead the Israelites, and now Yahweh also enables the 70 men to lead the Israelites too. It is recommended that you follow the UST and indicate that the Spirit is God’s Spirit. However, also consider how translations that your readers might be familiar with treat the word “Spirit” here.

Prophesying

In this chapter, Yahweh sends his Spirit on 70 leaders. When they receive the Spirit, they “prophesy.” The author does not indicate exactly what they said or did. In some cases, “prophesying” means not being in control of one’s body and saying strange things. In other cases, “prophesying” means speaking words from God. In this context, it is likely that the leaders “prophesied” by speaking words from God, but they may also have acted strangely as they did so.

The quails

In this chapter, Yahweh sends birds called “quails” to the Israelites. These birds are good to eat. They are brown and have a wingspan of around 32–35 centimeters. They migrate in large numbers through the Sinai area twice a year.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

“People” as singular and plural

The singular word “people” occurs frequently in this chapter. Sometimes, plural words refer to “people” (for example, see 11:8), and sometimes singular words refer to “people” (for example, see 11:10). This happens because the word “people” is singular in form but refers to many persons. The ULT preserves the singular and plural alternation, and the UST models how to express the ideas in plural form. Consider how you would naturally refer to a group of people in your language.

Quotes in quotes

There are several times in this chapter where there are quotes inside quotes. In fact, 11:18 includes a quote inside a quote inside a quote. Consider how your language indicates that a quote contains a quote. The UST models how to express the idea with only one level of quotations.

Metaphors with the Spirit

In this chapter, Yahweh and the author speak as if the Spirit were an object that could be taken from one person, given to another person, and “rest” on top of them. This metaphor portrays how Yahweh shared the Spirit that he gave to Moses with the 70 leaders, who now also received the Spirit from Yahweh. Yahweh and the author do not mean that Moses had less of the Spirit now. Rather, they mean that the Spirit now enables the 70 leaders to lead the Israelites along with Moses. See the notes for translation options.

title: Numbers 11:1 (#1)
content:
הָ⁠עָם֙ כְּ⁠מִתְאֹ֣נְנִ֔ים רַ֖ע בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"the people {were} like those complaining of evil in the ears of Yahweh"

The point of this comparison is that just as those complaining speaks of people who make complaints, so the Israelites were actually doing this in the ears of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the people complained of evil in the ears of Yahweh]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 11:1 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠מִתְאֹ֣נְנִ֔ים רַ֖ע בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"like those complaining of evil in the ears of Yahweh"

Here, the word evil could go with: (1) complaining as its object. Alternate translation: [like those complaining about evil in the ears of Yahweh]; or (2) in the ears of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [like those complaining, and it was evil in the ears of Yahweh]; or (3) complaining as a descriptor. Alternate translation: [like those complaining bitterly in the ears of Yahweh]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 11:1 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠מִתְאֹ֣נְנִ֔ים רַ֖ע

"like those complaining of evil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of evil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like those complaining that things were evil]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 11:1 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֤ע יְהוָה֙ וַ⁠יִּ֣חַר אַפּ֔⁠וֹ

"in the ears of Yahweh, and Yahweh heard, and his nose burned"

It might seem that the expression in the ears of Yahweh contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [while Yahweh heard, and his nose burned]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 11:1 (#5)
content:
בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"in the ears of Yahweh"

The phrase in the ears of Yahweh means in Yahweh’s hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while Yahweh could hear]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 11:1 (#6)
content:
וַ⁠יִּ֣חַר אַפּ֔⁠וֹ

"and his nose burned"

The phrase his nose burned is a common expression of this culture that means that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his anger burned] or [and he was enraged]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:1 (#7)
content:
וַ⁠תִּבְעַר־בָּ⁠ם֙ אֵ֣שׁ יְהוָ֔ה וַ⁠תֹּ֖אכַל בִּ⁠קְצֵ֥ה הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶֽה

"and the fire of Yahweh burned among them, and it ate at the end of the camp"

Here, the author could be implying that: (1) the fire burned the edges of the camp but did not kill anyone. Alternate translation: [and the fire of Yahweh burned among then, and it ate tents and belongings at the edges of the camp]; or (2) the fire burned in the camp near its edges and did kill some people. Alternate translation: [and the fire of Yahweh burned among them, and it ate some people at the edges of the camp]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:1 (#8)
content:
וַ⁠תִּבְעַר & אֵ֣שׁ יְהוָ֔ה

"and the fire of Yahweh burned"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a fire that was sent by Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the fire that Yahweh sent]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 11:1 (#9)
content:
וַ⁠תֹּ֖אכַל

"and it ate"

The author is speaking of fire as if it were a living thing that could eat or devour things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it ravaged]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 11:2 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תִּשְׁקַ֖ע הָ⁠אֵֽשׁ

"and the fire sank"

The expression the fire sank is a common expression of this culture to mean “the fire went out” or “the fire died down.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the fire went out] or [and the fire died down]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:3 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקְרָ֛א שֵֽׁם־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠ה֖וּא תַּבְעֵרָ֑ה כִּֽי־בָעֲרָ֥ה בָ֖⁠ם אֵ֥שׁ יְהוָֽה

"and he called the name of that place Taberah, for the fire of Yahweh burned among them"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and because the fire of Yahweh burned among them, he called the name of that place Taberah]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 11:3 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקְרָ֛א

"and he called"

The pronoun he could refer: (1) generically to anyone who used this name. Alternate translation: [and people called]; or (2) to Moses. Alternate translation: [and Moses called]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 11:3 (#3)
content:
תַּבְעֵרָ֑ה

"Taberah"

The word Taberah is the name of a place. This name sounds like the Hebrew word for “burning.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain this in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [the place of burning]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 11:3 (#4)
content:
כִּֽי & אֵ֥שׁ יְהוָֽה

"for the fire of Yahweh"

See how you translated this phrase in 11:1. Alternate translation: [for the fire that Yahweh sent]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 11:4 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠קִרְבּ֔⁠וֹ

"in its midst"

Here, the author is speaking as if the non-Israelite people were actually in the midst of all the Israelites. He means that the non-Israelites were living among the Israelites. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among the people]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:4 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָֽ⁠אסַפְסֻף֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּ⁠קִרְבּ֔⁠וֹ

"And the rabble that {was} in its midst"

The implication is that there were some people among the Israelites who were not Israelites themselves and who were causing trouble by encouraging the Israelites to complain. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And some non-Israelite troublemakers that were]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:4 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠קִרְבּ֔⁠וֹ

"in its midst"

The pronoun its refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the midst of the people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 11:4 (#4)
content:
הִתְאַוּ֖וּ תַּאֲוָ֑ה

"desired a desire"

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [had a strong desire]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 11:4 (#5)
content:
תַּאֲוָ֑ה

"a desire"

By a desire, the author means a desire to eat meat. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a desire to eat meat]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:4 (#6)
content:
תַּאֲוָ֑ה

"a desire"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of desire, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what they desired]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 11:4 (#7)
content:
וַ⁠יָּשֻׁ֣בוּ וַ⁠יִּבְכּ֗וּ

"and & returned, and they wept"

The author is using returned, and they wept as a common expression of his culture to mean “they wept again.” The text in 11:1–2 implies that they had already wept once. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [wept again]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:4 (#8)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ

"And they said"

The pronoun they refers to the Israelites who were complaining. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites said]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 11:4 (#9)
content:
מִ֥י יַאֲכִלֵ֖⁠נוּ בָּשָֽׂר

"Who will feed us flesh"

The Israelites are using the question form to express their strong desire for meat. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [If only someone would feed us flesh!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 11:5 (#1)
content:
זָכַ֨רְנוּ֙ אֶת־הַ⁠דָּגָ֔ה אֲשֶׁר־נֹאכַ֥ל

"We remember the fish that we ate"

By we, the Israelites mean to include both themselves and their listeners, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 11:5 (#2)
content:
אֵ֣ת הַ⁠קִּשֻּׁאִ֗ים וְ⁠אֵת֙ הָֽ⁠אֲבַטִּחִ֔ים וְ⁠אֶת־הֶ⁠חָצִ֥יר וְ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠בְּצָלִ֖ים וְ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠שּׁוּמִֽים

"the cucumbers, and the watermelons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic"

The cucumbers and watermelons are kinds of gourds, and leeks, onions, and garlic are kinds of vegetables used for seasoning. If your readers would not be familiar with what these foods are, you could use more general terms or explain them in a footnote. Alternate translation: [the fruits with rinds, and the savory vegetables]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 11:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עַתָּ֛ה נַפְשֵׁ֥⁠נוּ יְבֵשָׁ֖ה

"And now our life {is} dry"

Here the Israelites speak as if their lives were dry. They could mean that: (1) they have lost their strength because they do not have enough to eat. Alternate translation: [And now we have lost our strength]; or (2) they have lost their appetite for food because they do not like eating only manna. Alternate translation: [And now we have lost our appetite]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:6 (#2)
content:
נַפְשֵׁ֥⁠נוּ יְבֵשָׁ֖ה

"our life {is} dry"

In this verse, the word life is singular in form, but it refers to all the lives of the Israelites as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “life.” Alternate translation: [our lives are dry]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 11:6 (#3)
content:
נַפְשֵׁ֥⁠נוּ & עֵינֵֽי⁠נוּ

"our life & in} our eyes"

By our, the Israelites mean to include both themselves and their listeners, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 11:6 (#4)
content:
אֵ֣ין כֹּ֑ל בִּלְתִּ֖י אֶל־הַ⁠מָּ֥ן עֵינֵֽי⁠נוּ

"there is not anything except for the manna {in} our eyes"

If it would appear in your language that the Israelites were making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [the only thing in our eyes is the manna]

See: Connect — Exception Clauses

title: Numbers 11:6 (#5)
content:
אֵ֣ין כֹּ֑ל

"there is not anything"

The implication is that the people meant there was nothing worth eating except manna. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [there is not any food]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:6 (#6)
content:
עֵינֵֽי⁠נוּ

"in} our eyes"

The people are using the common expression of their culture in our eyes to mean “that we can see” or “that is available to us.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that we can observe]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:7 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠מָּ֕ן

"And the manna"

Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. The phrase And the manna introduces an explanation of the manna, how it appeared, and what the people did with it in 11:7–9. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [Now about this manna:]

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 11:7 (#2)
content:
כִּ⁠זְרַע־גַּ֖ד ה֑וּא

"it {was} like the seed of coriander"

The point of this comparison is that just as the seed of coriander is small and round, so is the manna. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [it was small and round like the seed of coriander]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 11:7 (#3)
content:
כִּ⁠זְרַע־גַּ֖ד

"like the seed of coriander"

The author is using the possessive form to describe seed that is from the coriander plant. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [coriander seeds]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 11:7 (#4)
content:
כִּ⁠זְרַע־גַּ֖ד

"like the seed of coriander"

The plant named coriander produces leaves that people use for seasoning and call “cilantro.” It also produces small, round seeds that are 3–5 millimeters in diameter. If your readers would not be familiar with what coriander is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the small, round seed of a plant called coriander]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 11:7 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠עֵינ֖⁠וֹ כְּ⁠עֵ֥ין הַ⁠בְּדֹֽלַח

"and its eye {was} like the eye of bdellium"

The point of this comparison is that just as bdellium is yellowish-brown in color, so is the eye (the appearance) of the manna. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and it was yellowish-brown, like bdellium]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 11:7 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠עֵינ֖⁠וֹ כְּ⁠עֵ֥ין הַ⁠בְּדֹֽלַח

"and its eye {was} like the eye of bdellium"

Here, eye represents appearance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and its appearance was like the appearance of bdellium]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 11:7 (#7)
content:
הַ⁠בְּדֹֽלַח

"bdellium"

A bdellium is a kind of gum resin that comes from certain trees. If your readers would not be familiar with what bdellium is, you could use the name of a similar resin that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a gum resin called bdellium]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 11:8 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לָֽקְט֜וּ וְ⁠טָחֲנ֣וּ בָ⁠רֵחַ֗יִם א֤וֹ דָכוּ֙ בַּ⁠מְּדֹכָ֔ה וּ⁠בִשְּׁלוּ֙ בַּ⁠פָּר֔וּר

"and they gathered, and they ground in the mill or crushed in the mortar, and they boiled in the pot"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they gathered the manna, and they ground it in the mill or crushed it in the mortar, and they boiled it in the pot]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 11:8 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠טָחֲנ֣וּ בָ⁠רֵחַ֗יִם א֤וֹ דָכוּ֙ בַּ⁠מְּדֹכָ֔ה

"and they ground in the mill or crushed in the mortar"

A mill is a kind of stone tool used for grinding grain. A mortar is a stone bowl in which people would crush grain. If your readers would not be familiar with what a mill or a mortar is, you could use more general terms or explain them in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and they ground with stones that they used for grinding grain or crushed in bowls with special stones]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 11:8 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠טָחֲנ֣וּ בָ⁠רֵחַ֗יִם א֤וֹ דָכוּ֙ בַּ⁠מְּדֹכָ֔ה

"and they ground in the mill or crushed in the mortar"

Here, mill and mortar represent grinding tools in general, not specific grinding tools. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they ground in mills or crushed in mortars]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 11:8 (#4)
content:
עֻג֑וֹת

"cakes"

Here, cakes are a kind of bread baked in a flat, round shape. If your readers would not be familiar with what cakes are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [flat, round loaves]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 11:8 (#5)
content:
הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶן

"the oil"

The author is not referring to a specific oil. He means oil in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [oil]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 11:8–9 (#1)
content:
שָׁטוּ֩ הָ⁠עָ֨ם וְ⁠לָֽקְט֜וּ וְ⁠טָחֲנ֣וּ בָ⁠רֵחַ֗יִם א֤וֹ דָכוּ֙ בַּ⁠מְּדֹכָ֔ה וּ⁠בִשְּׁלוּ֙ בַּ⁠פָּר֔וּר וְ⁠עָשׂ֥וּ אֹת֖⁠וֹ עֻג֑וֹת וְ⁠הָיָ֣ה טַעְמ֔⁠וֹ כְּ⁠טַ֖עַם לְשַׁ֥ד הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶן׃ וּ⁠בְ⁠רֶ֧דֶת הַ⁠טַּ֛ל עַל־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֖ה לָ֑יְלָה יֵרֵ֥ד הַ⁠מָּ֖ן עָלָֽי⁠ו

"The people went about, and they gathered, and they ground in the mill or crushed in the mortar, and they boiled in the pot, and they made it cakes, and its taste was like the taste of the freshness of the oil. And when the dew came down on the camp at night, the manna came down upon it"

If it is more natural in your language to indicate how the manna appeared before indicating what the people did with it, you could move the information from verse 9 before the information in verse 8. You would then present the combined verses as 11:8–9. See the UST for an example.

See: Verse Bridges

title: Numbers 11:9 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠רֶ֧דֶת הַ⁠טַּ֛ל עַל־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֖ה

"And when the dew came down on the camp"

The author is using came down as a common expression of his culture to mean “settled” or “formed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And when the dew condensed in the camp]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:9 (#2)
content:
יֵרֵ֥ד הַ⁠מָּ֖ן עָלָֽי⁠ו

"the manna came down upon it"

The implication is that when the dew came down at night, the manna appeared along with it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the manna was there along with it]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:10 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֨ע מֹשֶׁ֜ה

"And Moses heard"

The previous verses include background information about the manna. Here, the author returns to the main storyline. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a form that makes this explicit. Alternate translation: [Now when the people said those things, Moses heard]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 11:10 (#2)
content:
אִ֖ישׁ לְ⁠פֶ֣תַח אָהֳל֑⁠וֹ

"a man to the opening of his tent"

The author is not referring to a specific man. He means all the men in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [each of the men at the openings of their tents]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 11:10 (#3)
content:
אִ֖ישׁ לְ⁠פֶ֣תַח אָהֳל֑⁠וֹ

"a man to the opening of his tent"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a person at the opening of his or her tent]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 11:10 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יִּֽחַר־אַ֤ף יְהוָה֙ מְאֹ֔ד

"and the nose of Yahweh burned exceedingly"

The phrase the nose of Yahweh burned is a common expression of this culture that means that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh’s anger greatly burned] or [and Yahweh was very enraged]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:10 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠עֵינֵ֥י מֹשֶׁ֖ה

"and in the eyes of Moses"

The phrase in the eyes of is a common expression of this culture that means “in the judgment of” or “in the opinion of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in the judgment of Moses]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:10 (#6)
content:
רָֽע

"it was} evil"

Here, the author could mean that Moses considers evil: (1) what the people did. Alternate translation: [what the people did was evil]; or (2) that the people made Yahweh angry. Alternate translation: [it was evil that the people made Yahweh angry]; or (3) that Yahweh was angry. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s anger was evil]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:11 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠שׂ֗וּם אֶת־מַשָּׂ֛א כָּל־הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה עָלָֽ⁠י

"to put the burden of all this people on me"

Here, Moses is speaking of his responsibility to care for the Israelites as if it were a heavy burden that he had to carry. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to make me work very hard to care for all this people]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:11 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֨אמֶר מֹשֶׁ֜ה

"And Moses said"

The implication is that Moses went to the tent of meeting to speak with Yahweh. This is shown clearly when it says “And Moses went out” in 11:24. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Moses went to the tent of meeting and said]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:11 (#3)
content:
לָ⁠מָ֤ה הֲרֵעֹ֨תָ֙ לְ⁠עַבְדֶּ֔⁠ךָ וְ⁠לָ֛⁠מָּה לֹא־מָצָ֥תִי חֵ֖ן בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֑י⁠ךָ לָ⁠שׂ֗וּם אֶת־מַשָּׂ֛א כָּל־הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה עָלָֽ⁠י

"Why do you do evil to your servant? And why have I not found favor in your eyes, to put the burden of all this people on me"

Moses is using the question form to express strong negative emotions and to complain about his situation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [You are doing evil to your servant. I clearly have not found favor in your eyes, since you have put the burden of all this people on me.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 11:11 (#4)
content:
הֲרֵעֹ֨תָ֙ לְ⁠עַבְדֶּ֔⁠ךָ

"do you do evil to your servant"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of evil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [do you harm your servant]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 11:11 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠עַבְדֶּ֔⁠ךָ

"to your servant"

Moses is speaking of himself in the third person as your servant to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to me, who serves you]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 11:11 (#6)
content:
לֹא־מָצָ֥תִי חֵ֖ן בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"have I not found favor in your eyes"

Moses is using the common expression of his culture found favor in your eyes to mean “gained your approval” or “pleased you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do you not approve of me] or [do you not show me favor]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:11 (#7)
content:
לֹא־מָצָ֥תִי חֵ֖ן בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"have I not found favor in your eyes"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of favor, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [am I not favored in your eyes]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 11:12 (#1)
content:
הֶ⁠אָנֹכִ֣י הָרִ֗יתִי אֵ֚ת כָּל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אִם־אָנֹכִ֖י יְלִדְתִּ֑י⁠הוּ

"Did I, I conceive all this people? Or did I, I bear him"

Here, Moses is speaking as if he were actually a mother who had conceived and given birth to all the Israelites. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Am I like a mother who conceived all these people? Am I like the mother that bore them]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:12 (#2)
content:
שָׂאֵ֣⁠הוּ בְ⁠חֵיקֶ֗⁠ךָ & לַ⁠אֲבֹתָֽי⁠ו

"Carry him in your bosom & to his fathers"

Here, Moses is speaking as if the Israelites were actually a child whom he had to carry in his bosom and nurse. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take care of them as if you were carrying them in your bosom … to their fathers]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:12 (#3)
content:
הֶ⁠אָנֹכִ֣י הָרִ֗יתִי אֵ֚ת כָּל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אִם־אָנֹכִ֖י יְלִדְתִּ֑י⁠הוּ כִּֽי־תֹאמַ֨ר אֵלַ֜⁠י שָׂאֵ֣⁠הוּ בְ⁠חֵיקֶ֗⁠ךָ כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִשָּׂ֤א הָ⁠אֹמֵן֙ אֶת־הַ⁠יֹּנֵ֔ק עַ֚ל הָֽ⁠אֲדָמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִשְׁבַּ֖עְתָּ לַ⁠אֲבֹתָֽי⁠ו

"Did I, I conceive all this people? Or did I, I bear him, that you say to me, ‘Carry him in your bosom just as the one nursing carries the one sucking,’ over the ground that you swore to his fathers"

Moses is using the question form for emphasis and to express his frustration at being expected to care for the Israelites like a mother. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [I, I did not conceive all this people. I, I did not bear him, that you say to me, ‘Carry him in your bosom just as the one nursing carries the one sucking,’ upon the ground that you swore to his fathers.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 11:12 (#4)
content:
הֶ⁠אָנֹכִ֣י הָרִ֗יתִי & אָנֹכִ֖י יְלִדְתִּ֑י⁠הוּ

"Did I, I conceive & did I, I bear him"

Moses is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verbs translated as I conceive and I bear already include this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is definitely not he who did those things. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [Was it I who conceived … was it I who bore him]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 11:12 (#5)
content:
שָׂאֵ֣⁠הוּ בְ⁠חֵיקֶ֗⁠ךָ כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִשָּׂ֤א הָ⁠אֹמֵן֙ אֶת־הַ⁠יֹּנֵ֔ק עַ֚ל הָֽ⁠אֲדָמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִשְׁבַּ֖עְתָּ לַ⁠אֲבֹתָֽי⁠ו

"Carry him in your bosom just as the one nursing carries the one sucking,’ over the ground that you swore to his fathers"

Here, the quotation could end after: (1) the word sucking. Moses speaks the rest of the sentence to Yahweh. See the ULT. (2) the word father. This implies either that Moses swore the promise or that Yahweh is speaking about himself in the second person. Alternate translation: [‘Carry him in your bosom just as the one nursing carries the one sucking upon the ground that you swore to his fathers?’]

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 11:12 (#6)
content:
כִּֽי־תֹאמַ֨ר אֵלַ֜⁠י שָׂאֵ֣⁠הוּ בְ⁠חֵיקֶ֗⁠ךָ כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִשָּׂ֤א הָ⁠אֹמֵן֙ אֶת־הַ⁠יֹּנֵ֔ק עַ֚ל הָֽ⁠אֲדָמָ֔ה

"that you say to me, ‘Carry him in your bosom just as the one nursing carries the one sucking,’ over the ground"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that you tell me to carry him in my bosom just as the one nursing carries the one sucking, upon the ground]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 11:12 (#7)
content:
כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִשָּׂ֤א הָ⁠אֹמֵן֙ אֶת־הַ⁠יֹּנֵ֔ק

"just as the one nursing carries the one sucking"

The point of this comparison is that just as the one nursing carries the one sucking is gentle and caring, so Moses should care for the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [with the tenderness of a nurse carrying the one sucking]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 11:12 (#8)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִשְׁבַּ֖עְתָּ לַ⁠אֲבֹתָֽי⁠ו

"that you swore to his fathers"

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply the words “to give to” from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [that you swore to give to his fathers]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 11:12 (#9)
content:
לַ⁠אֲבֹתָֽי⁠ו

"to his fathers"

Moses is using the term fathers to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to his predecessors]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:12 (#10)
content:
עַ֚ל הָֽ⁠אֲדָמָ֔ה

"over the ground"

Moses is using over the ground as a common expression of his culture to mean “to the land.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the place]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:13 (#1)
content:
מֵ⁠אַ֤יִן לִ⁠י֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר לָ⁠תֵ֖ת לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה כִּֽי־יִבְכּ֤וּ עָלַ⁠י֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר תְּנָ⁠ה־לָּ֥⁠נוּ בָשָׂ֖ר וְ⁠נֹאכֵֽלָה

"From where {is} flesh for me to give to all this people? For they weep upon me, saying, ‘Give to us flesh and let us eat"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [These people weep upon me, saying, ‘Give to us flesh and let us eat.’ But from where is meat for me to give to all this people?]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 11:13 (#2)
content:
מֵ⁠אַ֤יִן לִ⁠י֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר לָ⁠תֵ֖ת לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה

"From where {is} flesh for me to give to all this people"

Moses is using the question form to emphasize that it would be impossible for him to get enough meat to feed all the Israelite people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no place for me to acquire meat to give to all this people.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 11:13 (#3)
content:
עָלַ⁠י֙

"upon me"

The phrase upon me is a common expression of this culture that means “near me” or “to me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [near me] or [to me]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:13 (#4)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר תְּנָ⁠ה־לָּ֥⁠נוּ בָשָׂ֖ר וְ⁠נֹאכֵֽלָה

"saying, ‘Give to us flesh and let us eat"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [demanding that I give them flesh so that they can eat it]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 11:13 (#5)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר

"saying"

Here, the word saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 11:14 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠שֵׂ֖את אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה

"to carry all this people"

Here, Moses is speaking of the responsibility to lead and care for the Israelites as if it were a heavy object that he had to carry. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to care for all this people]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:14 (#2)
content:
כָבֵ֖ד מִמֶּֽ⁠נִּי

"it is} heavy from me"

Here, Moses is speaking of taking care of the Israelites as if it were a heavy burden that he must carry. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it is too hard for me to do]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:14 (#3)
content:
לֹֽא־אוּכַ֤ל אָנֹכִי֙ לְ⁠בַדִּ֔⁠י לָ⁠שֵׂ֖את אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה כִּ֥י כָבֵ֖ד מִמֶּֽ⁠נִּי

"I, I am not able by myself to carry all this people, for {it is} heavy from me"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since heavy from me gives the reason for the result that I myself am not able by myself to carry all this people describes. Alternate translation: [Carrying all this people by myself is heavy from me. So, I, I am not able to do it]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 11:14 (#4)
content:
לֹֽא־אוּכַ֤ל אָנֹכִי֙

"I, I am not able"

Moses is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I am … able already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is definitely not able to do this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [I am certainly not able]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 11:14 (#5)
content:
כָבֵ֖ד

"it is} heavy"

Here, the word heavy could describe: (1) carrying the people. Alternate translation: [this burden is heavy]; or (2) the people. Alternate translation: [they are heavy]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 11:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אַל־אֶרְאֶ֖ה בְּ⁠רָעָתִֽ⁠י

"and let me not look on my evil"

Here, Moses is speaking of his suffering as if it were his own evil that he needed to look at. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I do not want to experience my evil]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אִם־כָּ֣כָה ׀ אַתְּ־עֹ֣שֶׂה לִּ֗⁠י הָרְגֵ֤⁠נִי נָא֙ הָרֹ֔ג אִם־מָצָ֥אתִי חֵ֖ן בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"And if you are doing thus to me, killing, please kill me, if I have found favor in your eyes"

Moses is describing a possible condition in which God will kill him only if two conditions are both true: God is going to continue treating him in this way, and Moses has found favor in God’s eyes. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Suppose that you are doing thus to me, and suppose that I have found favor in your eyes. In that case, killing, please kill me]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 11:15 (#3)
content:
הָרְגֵ֤⁠נִי נָא֙ הָרֹ֔ג

"killing, please kill me"

Moses is repeating forms of the verb kill in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [please kill me immediately]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 11:15 (#4)
content:
אִם־מָצָ֥אתִי חֵ֖ן בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"if I have found favor in your eyes"

Moses is using the common expression of his culture found favor in your eyes to mean “you approve of me” or “you show me favor.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the negative form of this clause in 11:11. Alternate translation: [if you approve of me] or [if you show me favor]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:15 (#5)
content:
אִם־מָצָ֥אתִי חֵ֖ן בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"if I have found favor in your eyes"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of favor, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the negative form of this clause in 11:11. Alternate translation: [if I am favored in your eyes]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 11:15 (#6)
content:
בְּ⁠רָעָתִֽ⁠י

"on my evil"

Moses is using the possessive form to describe evil that is happening to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the evil that is happening to me]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 11:15 (#7)
content:
בְּ⁠רָעָתִֽ⁠י

"on my evil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of evil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the evil things that are happening to me]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 11:16 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שֹׁטְרָ֑י⁠ו

"and its officers"

A officer is a kind of leader with authority over others. If your readers would not be familiar with what an officer is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and ones with authority over it]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 11:16 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לָקַחְתָּ֤ אֹתָ⁠ם֙

"and you shall take them"

In a context such as this, your language might say bring instead of “take.” Alternate translation: [and you shall bring them]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 11:17 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יָרַדְתִּ֗י

"And I will come down"

Here, God is speaking of his coming to Moses as if he would physically come down from heaven to earth. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will meet you]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:17 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אָצַלְתִּ֗י מִן־הָ⁠ר֛וּחַ אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָלֶ֖י⁠ךָ וְ⁠שַׂמְתִּ֣י עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֑ם

"and I will take away from the Spirit that {is} on you, and I will put on them"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of the Spirit that empowered Moses as if it were a physical substance that could be taken away from one person and put on others. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will share with them some of the authority and power that I gave you through my Spirit]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:17 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠נָשְׂא֤וּ אִתְּ⁠ךָ֙ בְּ⁠מַשָּׂ֣א הָ⁠עָ֔ם וְ⁠לֹא־תִשָּׂ֥א אַתָּ֖ה לְ⁠בַדֶּֽ⁠ךָ

"and they will carry the burden of the people with you, and you, you will not carry by yourself"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of taking care of the people as if it were a heavy burden to carry. The image emphasizes how difficult and wearisome this responsibility is. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar metaphor in 11:11. Alternate translation: [and they will work hard to care for the people with you, and you, you will not have to care for them by yourself]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:17 (#4)
content:
מִן־הָ⁠ר֛וּחַ

"from the Spirit"
