On this issue, see the chapter introduction for more information. Here, the word Spirit could refer to: (1) God’s Spirit. Alternate translation: [from my Spirit]; or (2) Moses’ own spirit that Yahweh has specially equipped. Alternate translation: [from the spirit]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:17 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠שַׂמְתִּ֣י עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֑ם

"and I will put on them"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will put some of that Spirit on them]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 11:17 (#6)
content:
בְּ⁠מַשָּׂ֣א הָ⁠עָ֔ם

"the burden of the people"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the burden that is made up of the people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the burden that the people create]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 11:17 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא־תִשָּׂ֥א אַתָּ֖ה

"and you, you will not carry"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun you separately, even though the verb translated as you will … carry already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Moses will definitely not need to do this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [and you will no longer carry]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 11:18 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֶל־הָ⁠עָ֨ם תֹּאמַ֜ר הִתְקַדְּשׁ֣וּ לְ⁠מָחָר֮ וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּ֣ם בָּשָׂר֒ כִּ֡י בְּכִיתֶם֩ בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֨י יְהוָ֜ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר מִ֤י יַאֲכִלֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר כִּי־ט֥וֹב לָ֖⁠נוּ בְּ⁠מִצְרָ֑יִם וְ⁠נָתַ֨ן יְהוָ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֛ם בָּשָׂ֖ר וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּֽם

"And to the people you shall say, ‘Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat flesh. For you wept in the ears of Yahweh, saying, “Who will feed us flesh? For {it was} good for us in Egypt.” And Yahweh shall give to you flesh, and you shall eat"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And you shall say to the people that they must consecrate themselves for tomorrow, and they shall eat flesh, for they wept in my ears, asking who would feed them flesh and declaring that it was good for them in Egypt. Say to them that I shall give to them flesh, and they shall eat.]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 11:18 (#2)
content:
הִתְקַדְּשׁ֣וּ לְ⁠מָחָר֮ וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּ֣ם בָּשָׂר֒ כִּ֡י בְּכִיתֶם֩ בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֨י יְהוָ֜ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר מִ֤י יַאֲכִלֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר כִּי־ט֥וֹב לָ֖⁠נוּ בְּ⁠מִצְרָ֑יִם וְ⁠נָתַ֨ן יְהוָ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֛ם בָּשָׂ֖ר וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּֽם

"Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat flesh. For you wept in the ears of Yahweh, saying, “Who will feed us flesh? For {it was} good for us in Egypt.” And Yahweh shall give to you flesh, and you shall eat"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about you shall eat flesh with the information about Yahweh shall give to you flesh, since these are related events that are separated by the reason For you wept in the ears of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and Yahweh shall give to you flesh, and you shall eat it. For you wept in the ears of Yahweh, saying, “Who will feed us flesh? For it was good for us in Egypt.”]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 11:18 (#3)
content:
הִתְקַדְּשׁ֣וּ לְ⁠מָחָר֮ וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּ֣ם בָּשָׂר֒ כִּ֡י בְּכִיתֶם֩ בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֨י יְהוָ֜ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר מִ֤י יַאֲכִלֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר כִּי־ט֥וֹב לָ֖⁠נוּ בְּ⁠מִצְרָ֑יִם

"Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat flesh. For you wept in the ears of Yahweh, saying, “Who will feed us flesh? For {it was} good for us in Egypt"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since For you wept in the ears of Yahweh gives the reason for the result that consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat flesh describes. Alternate translation: [You wept in the ears of Yahweh, saying, “Who will feed us flesh? For it was good for us in Egypt.” So, consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat flesh.]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 11:18 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠אָזְנֵ֨י יְהוָ֜ה

"in the ears of Yahweh"

Here, in the ears of represents that Yahweh heard what the people said. See how you translated this phrase in 11:1. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [while Yahweh could hear]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 11:18 (#5)
content:
מִ֤י יַאֲכִלֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר

"Who will feed us flesh"

The Israelites are using the question form to express their strong desire for meat to eat. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [If only someone would feed us flesh!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 11:18 (#6)
content:
כִּי־ט֥וֹב

"For {it was} good"

The word translated as For indicates that what follows is the reason why they asked the question. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [We ask that because it used to be]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 11:18 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠נָתַ֨ן יְהוָ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֛ם בָּשָׂ֖ר וַ⁠אֲכַלְתֶּֽם

"And Yahweh shall give to you flesh, and you shall eat"

It might seem that the expression Yahweh shall give to you flesh, and you shall eat contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language since Yahweh has already said that they will eat flesh. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh shall give to you flesh]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 11:19 (#1)
content:
לֹ֣א י֥וֹם אֶחָ֛ד תֹּאכְל֖וּ⁠ן וְ⁠לֹ֣א יוֹמָ֑יִם וְ⁠לֹ֣א ׀ חֲמִשָּׁ֣ה יָמִ֗ים וְ⁠לֹא֙ עֲשָׂרָ֣ה יָמִ֔ים וְ⁠לֹ֖א עֶשְׂרִ֥ים יֽוֹם

"You shall eat not one day and not two days and not five days and not ten days and not 20 days"

If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Say to them that they shall eat not one day and not two days and not five days and not ten days and not 20 days]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 11:19 (#2)
content:
לֹ֣א י֥וֹם אֶחָ֛ד תֹּאכְל֖וּ⁠ן וְ⁠לֹ֣א יוֹמָ֑יִם וְ⁠לֹ֣א ׀ חֲמִשָּׁ֣ה יָמִ֗ים וְ⁠לֹא֙ עֲשָׂרָ֣ה יָמִ֔ים וְ⁠לֹ֖א עֶשְׂרִ֥ים יֽוֹם

"You shall eat not one day and not two days and not five days and not ten days and not 20 days"

The implication is that Yahweh will give them meat for a much longer time than any of these shorter periods. Yahweh lists increasingly longer periods of time to emphasize that Yahweh will give them more meat than they expect. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You shall eat not just for one day or two days or five days or ten days or 20 days]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:19 (#3)
content:
תֹּאכְל֖וּ⁠ן

"You shall eat"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [You shall eat flesh]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 11:20 (#1)
content:
עַ֤ד אֲשֶׁר־יֵצֵא֙ מֵֽ⁠אַפְּ⁠כֶ֔ם

"until when it goes out from your nose"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the meat were actually going out from your nose. This means that they will become very sick of the meat. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until when you are too full] or [until when you gag on it]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:20 (#2)
content:
עַ֣ד ׀ חֹ֣דֶשׁ יָמִ֗ים עַ֤ד אֲשֶׁר־יֵצֵא֙ מֵֽ⁠אַפְּ⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠הָיָ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֖ם לְ⁠זָרָ֑א יַ֗עַן כִּֽי־מְאַסְתֶּ֤ם אֶת־יְהוָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּ⁠קִרְבְּ⁠כֶ֔ם וַ⁠תִּבְכּ֤וּ לְ⁠פָנָי⁠ו֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר לָ֥⁠מָּה זֶּ֖ה יָצָ֥אנוּ מִ⁠מִּצְרָֽיִם

"until a month of days, until when it goes out from your nose. And it shall be for nausea for you because you rejected Yahweh who is in your midst, and you wept to his face, saying, “Why {is} this: we went out from Egypt"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [until a month of days, until when it goes out from their nose. Say to them that it shall be for nausea for them because they rejected me who is in their midst, and they wept to my face, asking why they went out from Egypt.]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 11:20 (#3)
content:
עַ֣ד ׀ חֹ֣דֶשׁ יָמִ֗ים

"until a month of days"

The implication is that they would eat meat for 30 days. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [but for a month of days] or [but for 30 days]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:20 (#4)
content:
חֹ֣דֶשׁ יָמִ֗ים

"a month of days"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a month that is made up of all its days. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the days in a month]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 11:20 (#5)
content:
מֵֽ⁠אַפְּ⁠כֶ֔ם

"from your nose"

Yahweh is not referring to a specific nose. He means their noses in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from your noses]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 11:20 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֖ם לְ⁠זָרָ֑א

"And it shall be for nausea for you"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of nausea, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And it shall make you nauseous]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 11:20 (#7)
content:
לְ⁠פָנָי⁠ו֙

"to his face"

Here, to his face represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before him]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 11:20 (#8)
content:
לָ֥⁠מָּה זֶּ֖ה יָצָ֥אנוּ מִ⁠מִּצְרָֽיִם

"Why {is} this: we went out from Egypt"

The people are using the question form to complain about leaving Egypt and to express their regret that they left. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We should never have gone out from Egypt!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 11:20 (#9)
content:
לָ֥⁠מָּה זֶּ֖ה יָצָ֥אנוּ

"Why {is} this: we went out"

It might seem that the word this contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [Why did we go out]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 11:20 (#10)
content:
יָצָ֥אנוּ

"we went out"

In a context such as this, your language might say “came” instead of went. Alternate translation: [we came out]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 11:21 (#1)
content:
שֵׁשׁ־מֵא֥וֹת אֶ֨לֶף֙ רַגְלִ֔י

"are} 600,000 on foot"

The implication is that this number represents only the adult men who could walk, since the census in Numbers 1 only counted adult men. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [are 600,000 men on foot, plus the women and children]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:21 (#2)
content:
שֵׁשׁ־מֵא֥וֹת אֶ֨לֶף֙

"are} 600,000"

The number 600,000 is a round number, since 1:46 indicates that there were 603,550 men. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [six hundred thousand]

See: Numbers

title: Numbers 11:21 (#3)
content:
רַגְלִ֔י

"on foot"

The phrase on foot is a common expression of this culture that means “who walk.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who walk]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:21 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אַתָּ֣ה אָמַ֗רְתָּ בָּשָׂר֙ אֶתֵּ֣ן לָ⁠הֶ֔ם וְ⁠אָכְל֖וּ חֹ֥דֶשׁ יָמִֽים

"but you, you said, ‘I shall give flesh to them, and they shall eat a month of days"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [but you, you said that you shall give flesh to them, and they shall eat a month of days]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 11:21 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אַתָּ֣ה אָמַ֗רְתָּ

"but you, you said"

Moses is stating the pronoun you separately, even though the verb translated as you said already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh was the one who said this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [but you definitely said]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 11:21 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠אָכְל֖וּ

"and they shall eat"

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they shall eat flesh]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 11:21 (#7)
content:
חֹ֥דֶשׁ יָמִֽים

"a month of days"

Moses is using the possessive form to describe a month that is made up of all its days. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 11:20. Alternate translation: [all the days in a month]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 11:22 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠צֹ֧אן וּ⁠בָקָ֛ר יִשָּׁחֵ֥ט לָ⁠הֶ֖ם וּ⁠מָצָ֣א לָ⁠הֶ֑ם אִ֣ם אֶֽת־כָּל־דְּגֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּ֛ם יֵאָסֵ֥ף לָ⁠הֶ֖ם וּ⁠מָצָ֥א לָ⁠הֶֽם

"Shall flock and cattle be slaughtered for them, and it shall find for them? Or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered for them, and it shall find for them"

These two phrases Shall flock and cattle be slaughtered for them, and it shall find for them and shall all the fish of the sea be gathered for them, and it shall find for them mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Shall flock and cattle be slaughtered for them or all the fish of the sea be gathered for them, and it shall find for them?]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 11:22 (#2)
content:
הֲ⁠צֹ֧אן וּ⁠בָקָ֛ר יִשָּׁחֵ֥ט לָ⁠הֶ֖ם וּ⁠מָצָ֣א לָ⁠הֶ֑ם אִ֣ם אֶֽת־כָּל־דְּגֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּ֛ם יֵאָסֵ֥ף לָ⁠הֶ֖ם וּ⁠מָצָ֥א לָ⁠הֶֽם

"Shall flock and cattle be slaughtered for them, and it shall find for them? Or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered for them, and it shall find for them"

Moses is using the question form for emphasis to point out the impossibility of what God had promised to do. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [Were flock and cattle to be slaughtered for them, it would not find for them. Or were all the fish of the sea to be gathered for them, it would not find for them.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 11:22 (#3)
content:
הֲ⁠צֹ֧אן וּ⁠בָקָ֛ר יִשָּׁחֵ֥ט & אֶֽת־כָּל־דְּגֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּ֛ם יֵאָסֵ֥ף

"Shall flock and cattle be slaughtered & shall all the fish of the sea be gathered"

The expressions be slaughtered and be gathered are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Shall someone slaughter flock and cattle … shall someone gather all the fish of the sea]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 11:22 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠מָצָ֣א לָ⁠הֶ֑ם & וּ⁠מָצָ֥א לָ⁠הֶֽם

"and it shall find for them & and it shall find for them"

The phrase it shall find for them is a common expression of this culture that means “it will be enough for them” or “it will satisfy them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it satisfy them … and it satisfy them]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:23 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠יַ֥ד יְהוָ֖ה תִּקְצָ֑ר

"Is the hand of Yahweh short"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if he had a hand that could be too short to reach what he wanted. He means that his power is not limited. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Is the power of Yahweh limited?]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:23 (#2)
content:
הֲ⁠יַ֥ד יְהוָ֖ה תִּקְצָ֑ר

"Is the hand of Yahweh short"

Yahweh is using the question form Is the hand of Yahweh short? to strongly emphasize that he is fully able to do what he has promised. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The hand of Yahweh is not short!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 11:23 (#3)
content:
הֲ⁠יַ֥ד יְהוָ֖ה

"Is the hand of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [my hand]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 11:23 (#4)
content:
עַתָּ֥ה תִרְאֶ֛ה הֲ⁠יִקְרְ⁠ךָ֥ דְבָרִ֖⁠י

"Now you will see whether my word will happen to you"

The word you is singular here because Yahweh is speaking directly to Moses. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [Now Moses, you will see whether my word will happen to you or not]

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 11:23 (#5)
content:
עַתָּ֥ה תִרְאֶ֛ה

"Now you will see"

Here, see represents experiencing or knowing something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Now you will experience]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 11:23 (#6)
content:
דְבָרִ֖⁠י

"my word"

Here, word represents what Yahweh said he would do. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what I said]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 11:24 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּצֵ֣א מֹשֶׁ֗ה

"And Moses went out"

The implication is that Moses went out of the tent of meeting where he had been speaking with Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Moses went out of the tent of meeting]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:24 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּצֵ֣א מֹשֶׁ֗ה

"And Moses went out"

In a context such as this, your language might say “came” instead of went. Alternate translation: [And Moses came out]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 11:24 (#3)
content:
אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"the words of Yahweh"

Here, words of Yahweh represents what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh had spoken]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 11:25 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּ֨רֶד יְהוָ֥ה

"And Yahweh came down"

Here the author is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who could move up and down in space. This was a common way of describing God appearing to humans to interact with them. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 11:17. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh met them]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:25 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֗אצֶל מִן־הָ⁠ר֨וּחַ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָלָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יִּתֵּ֕ן עַל־שִׁבְעִ֥ים אִ֖ישׁ

"and he took away from the Spirit that {was} on him, and he gave on 70 men"

Here, the author is speaking as if the Spirit that empowered Moses were a physical substance that could be removed from one person and distributed to others. This represents God sharing his power and authority. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar construction in 11:17. Alternate translation: [and he shared some of the authority and power that he gave Moses through his Spirit with 70 men]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:25 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠נ֤וֹחַ עֲלֵי⁠הֶם֙ הָ⁠ר֔וּחַ

"as the Spirit rested on them"

Here, the author is speaking of the Spirit as if it were a physical being that could rest on people. This represents God giving these men authority and power to serve as leaders. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as they received the authority and power through God’s Spirit]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:25 (#4)
content:
בֶּ⁠עָנָן֮

"in the cloud"

The implication is that this was the same cloud that represented Yahweh’s presence, which descended on and remained above the sacred tent as described in 9:15–23. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the cloud that was over the Dwelling]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:25 (#5)
content:
מִן־הָ⁠ר֨וּחַ֙ & הָ⁠ר֔וּחַ

"from the Spirit & the Spirit"

On this issue, see the chapter introduction for more information, and see how you referred to Spirit in 11:17. Here, the word Spirit could refer to: (1) God’s Spirit. Alternate translation: [from God’s Spirit … God’s Spirit]; or (2) Moses’ own spirit that Yahweh has specially equipped. Alternate translation: [from the spirit … the spirit]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:25 (#6)
content:
וַ⁠יִּתֵּ֕ן עַל־שִׁבְעִ֥ים אִ֖ישׁ

"and he gave on 70 men"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. See how you translated the similar clause in 11:17. Alternate translation: [and he gave some of that Spirit on 70 men]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 11:25 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א יָסָֽפוּ

"and they did not add"

The phrase they did not add is a common expression of this culture that means “they did not do it again” or “it happened only that one time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but they did so only that time]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:26 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשָּׁאֲר֣וּ שְׁנֵֽי־אֲנָשִׁ֣ים

"And two of the men were left"

The expression were left is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And two of the men remained]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 11:26 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠אֶחָ֣ד

"the one"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as the one, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [the first]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 11:26 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֨י

"the second"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as the second, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [the other] or [number two]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 11:26 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠תָּ֧נַח עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֣ם הָ⁠ר֗וּחַ וְ⁠הֵ֨מָּה֙ בַּ⁠כְּתֻבִ֔ים וְ⁠לֹ֥א יָצְא֖וּ הָ⁠אֹ֑הֱלָ⁠ה וַ⁠יִּֽתְנַבְּא֖וּ בַּֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶֽה

"And the Spirit rested on them, and they {were} among the written ones, but they did not go out to the tent; and they prophesied in the camp"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about they were among the written ones with the information about they did not go out to the tent before stating that the Spirit rested on them, and they prophesied in the camp. Alternate translation: [And they were among the written ones, but they did not go out to the tent. And the spirit rested on them, and they prophesied in the camp]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 11:26 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠תָּ֧נַח עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֣ם הָ⁠ר֗וּחַ

"And the Spirit rested on them"

See how you translated the similar phrase in 11:26.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:26 (#6)
content:
בַּ⁠כְּתֻבִ֔ים

"among the written ones"

The implication is that these men were among those who had been selected and registered as leaders. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [among those whose names were written down as chosen leaders]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:26 (#7)
content:
בַּ⁠כְּתֻבִ֔ים

"among the written ones"

The expression among the written ones is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Moses. Alternate translation: [among the ones whose names Moses had written down]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 11:26 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א יָצְא֖וּ

"but they did not go out"

Here, the author speaks of going to the sacred tent as “going out.” However, the sacred tent was in the center of the campsite. If a speaker of your language would not use the phrase go out for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but they did not approach]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 11:27 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠נַּ֔עַר

"the young man"

The author is not referring to a young man who has already been mentioned in the story. He means an unidentified young man. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a certain young man]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 11:27 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּאמַ֑ר

"and he said"

The term and he said introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 11:28 (#1)
content:
נ֗וּן

"Nun"

The word Nun is the name of a man.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 11:28 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠בְּחֻרָ֖י⁠ו

"from his youth"

Here, the phrase the ULT translates as from his youth could mean: (1) that Joshua had been ministering to Moses since Joshua was young. Alternate translation: [since he was young]; or (2) that Joshua was one of Moses’ “chosen,” or best, men. Alternate translation: [as one of his chosen men]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:28 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּאמַ֑ר

"and said"

The terms answered and said introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent both of these terms explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 11:28 (#4)
content:
אֲדֹנִ֥⁠י מֹשֶׁ֖ה

"My lord Moses"

Joshua is referring to Moses by a respectful title. Use a comparable title or expression for addressing someone respectfully in your language. Alternate translation: [My master Moses] or [Moses my leader]

See: Politeness

title: Numbers 11:29 (#1)
content:
הַֽ⁠מְקַנֵּ֥א אַתָּ֖ה לִ֑⁠י

"Are} you being jealous for me"

Moses is using the question form to rebuke Joshua’s concern. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not be jealous for me!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 11:29 (#2)
content:
הַֽ⁠מְקַנֵּ֥א אַתָּ֖ה לִ֑⁠י

"Are} you being jealous for me"

By Are you being jealous for me, Moses means “Are you trying to protect my authority as leader?” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Are you trying to protect my leadership]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:29 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠מִ֨י יִתֵּ֜ן כָּל־עַ֤ם יְהוָה֙ נְבִיאִ֔ים כִּי־יִתֵּ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־רוּח֖⁠וֹ עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם

"And who will give all the people of Yahweh {as} prophets, that Yahweh will give his Spirit on them"

Moses is using the question form to express his wish or desire that all of Yahweh’s people would be prophets. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [If only all the people of Yahweh would be prophets, that Yahweh would give his Spirit on them!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 11:29 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠מִ֨י יִתֵּ֜ן כָּל־עַ֤ם יְהוָה֙ נְבִיאִ֔ים כִּי־יִתֵּ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־רוּח֖⁠וֹ עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם

"And who will give all the people of Yahweh {as} prophets, that Yahweh will give his Spirit on them"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Yahweh giving his Spirit before the information about the people becoming prophets, since in the context, Yahweh gives his Spirit before people prophesy. Alternate translation: [And when will Yahweh give his Spirit on all the people of Yahweh, and who will give them as prophets]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 11:29 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠מִ֨י יִתֵּ֜ן כָּל־עַ֤ם יְהוָה֙ נְבִיאִ֔ים

"And who will give all the people of Yahweh {as} prophets"

Moses is using the phrase who will give as a common expression of his culture to mean “who will make” or “who will cause.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And who will make all the people of Yahweh prophets]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:29 (#6)
content:
כִּי־יִתֵּ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־רוּח֖⁠וֹ עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם

"that Yahweh will give his Spirit on them"

See how you translated the similar words in 11:25.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:29 (#7)
content:
כִּי

"that"

Here the word that introduces a second wish. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [and that]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 11:30 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּאָסֵ֥ף מֹשֶׁ֖ה אֶל־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֑ה ה֖וּא וְ⁠זִקְנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"And Moses was gathered to the camp, he and the elders of Israel"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about he and the elders of Israel with the information about Moses at the beginning of the sentence. Alternate translation: [And Moses and the elders of Israel were gathered to the camp]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 11:30 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּאָסֵ֥ף מֹשֶׁ֖ה

"And Moses was gathered"

The expression was gathered is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And Moses returned]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 11:31 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠ר֜וּחַ נָסַ֣ע ׀ מֵ⁠אֵ֣ת יְהוָ֗ה

"And a wind set out from with Yahweh"

Here, the author is speaking as if the wind were actually a person that Yahweh sent on a mission. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh sent a wind]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 11:31 (#2)
content:
שַׂלְוִים֮

"quails"

A quail is a kind of small, plump game bird. If your readers would not be familiar with what a quail is, you could use the name of a similar bird that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [small, plump game birds]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 11:31 (#3)
content:
מִן־הַ⁠יָּם֒

"from the sea"

The author assumes that readers will know that the sea refers to the Gulf of Aqaba, on the eastern side of the Sinai region. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from the nearby gulf]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:31 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יִּטֹּ֨שׁ עַל־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֜ה

"and it left upon the camp"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and it left the quails upon the camp]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 11:31 (#5)
content:
כְּ⁠דֶ֧רֶךְ י֣וֹם כֹּ֗ה וּ⁠כְ⁠דֶ֤רֶךְ יוֹם֙ כֹּ֔ה סְבִיב֖וֹת הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֑ה

"as a way of a day this way and as a way of a day that way around the camp"

The phrase as a way of a day this way and as a way of a day that way was a common expression of this culture that means “about a day’s journey in each direction.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and about a day’s journey in each direction from the camp]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:31 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠כְ⁠אַמָּתַ֖יִם עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"and about two cubits on the face of the land"

Here, the author could be indicating that: (1) the quails lay in piles on the ground, and the piles were about two cubits high. Alternate translation: [and in piles about two cubits high on the face of]; or (2) the quails were flying about two cubits above the ground. Alternate translation: [and flying about cubits above the face of]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:31 (#7)
content:
וּ⁠כְ⁠אַמָּתַ֖יִם

"and about two cubits"

The term two cubits refers to a unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or 18 inches. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this distance in modern measurements, either in the text or a footnote. Alternate translation: [and about three feet]

See: Biblical Distance

title: Numbers 11:31 (#8)
content:
עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"on the face of the land"

Here, face of the land represents the surface of the ground. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [on top of the land]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 11:32 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֣קָם הָ⁠עָ֡ם

"And the people rose"

The author is using rose as a common expression of his culture to mean “got up and started working.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the people worked]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:32 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠כֹ֣ל ׀ י֣וֹם הַֽ⁠מָּחֳרָ֗ת

"and all the day of the next day"

It might seem that the expression the day of contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and all the next day]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 11:32 (#3)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠שְּׂלָ֔ו

"the quail"

In this verse, the word quail is singular in form, but it refers to all the birds as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “quail.” Alternate translation: [the quail birds]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 11:32 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠מַּמְעִ֕יט אָסַ֖ף עֲשָׂרָ֣ה חֳמָרִ֑ים

"The one making little gathered ten homers"

The implication is that even the person who gathered the least amount still gathered a very large quantity of quail. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Even the one making little gathered very much: ten homers]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:32 (#5)
content:
הַ⁠מַּמְעִ֕יט

"The one making little"

The phrase making little is a common expression of this culture that means “doing the least work” or “gathering the least amount.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one who did the least work]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:32 (#6)
content:
עֲשָׂרָ֣ה חֳמָרִ֑ים

"ten homers"

The term homer was equivalent to 220 liters or about 6.5 bushels. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this in terms of modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote.

See: Biblical Volume

title: Numbers 11:32 (#7)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁטְח֤וּ לָ⁠הֶם֙ שָׁט֔וֹחַ סְבִיב֖וֹת הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶֽה

"And spreading, they spread for them around the camp"

The author does not state why the people spread the quails around the camp. Some scholars think that they did this so that the meat from the quails would dry out and last longer. However, it is not certain that this is why they spread them out. So it is recommended that you do not explain in your translation why they spread out the quails. You could include possible interpretations in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

See: When to Keep Information Implicit

title: Numbers 11:32 (#8)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁטְח֤וּ & שָׁט֔וֹחַ

"And spreading, they spread"

The author is repeating forms of the verb spread in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And they spread widely]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 11:32 (#9)
content:
לָ⁠הֶם֙

"for them"

The pronoun them refers to the Israelites who gathered the quails. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for themselves]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 11:33 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠בָּשָׂ֗ר עוֹדֶ֨⁠נּוּ֙ בֵּ֣ין שִׁנֵּי⁠הֶ֔ם טֶ֖רֶם יִכָּרֵ֑ת

"The flesh {was} still between their teeth, before it was cut off"

The expression The flesh was still between their teeth, before it was cut off was a common expression of this culture that means “before they had even chewed and swallowed the meat.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They were about to bite off some of the flesh and chew it]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:33 (#2)
content:
טֶ֖רֶם יִכָּרֵ֑ת

"before it was cut off"

The expression was cut off is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. Alternate translation: [before they cut it off]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 11:33 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אַ֤ף יְהוָה֙ חָרָ֣ה בָ⁠עָ֔ם

"and the nose of Yahweh burned against the people"

The phrase the nose of Yahweh burned is a common expression of this culture that means that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh’s anger burned against the people] or [and Yahweh was enraged with the people]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 11:33 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֤ךְ יְהוָה֙ בָּ⁠עָ֔ם מַכָּ֖ה רַבָּ֥ה מְאֹֽד

"and Yahweh struck the people an exceedingly great striking"

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh struck the people very hard]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 11:33 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֤ךְ יְהוָה֙ בָּ⁠עָ֔ם מַכָּ֖ה רַבָּ֥ה מְאֹֽד

"and Yahweh struck the people an exceedingly great striking"

The implication is that Yahweh caused a large number of people to die, possibly through a disease or plague. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to Numbers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh caused many of the people to die] or [and Yahweh sent a terrible plague among the people]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 11:34 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקְרָ֛א אֶת־שֵֽׁם־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠ה֖וּא קִבְר֣וֹת הַֽתַּאֲוָ֑ה כִּי־שָׁם֙ קָֽבְר֔וּ אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֖ם הַ⁠מִּתְאַוִּֽים

"and he called the name of that place Kibroth Hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had desired"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and because there they buried the people who had desired, he called the name of that place Kibroth Hattaavah]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 11:34 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקְרָ֛א

"and he called"

See how you translated the similar form in 11:3. Here, the pronoun he could refer: (1) generically to anyone who used this name. Alternate translation: [and people called]; or (2) to Moses. Alternate translation: [and Moses called]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 11:34 (#3)
content:
קִבְר֣וֹת הַֽתַּאֲוָ֑ה

"Kibroth Hattaavah"

This name Kibroth Hattaavah sounds like the Hebrew words for “graves of desire.” This place got this name because the Israelites buried there the people who had strongly desired meat. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain this in the text of your translation or in a footnote.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 11:35 (#1)
content:
חֲצֵר֑וֹת

"to} Hazeroth"

The word Hazeroth is the name of a place in the desert. Alternate translation: [the place called Hazeroth]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 11:35 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּהְי֖וּ בַּ⁠חֲצֵרֽוֹת

"And they were in Hazeroth"

The implication is that the Israelites stayed in Hazeroth, and this is where the events in chapter 12 took place. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And they camped in Hazeroth]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers - Chapter 12 Introduction
content:
Numbers 12 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses and claim authority like his authority. God punishes Miriam, but then he restores her when Moses intercedes for her.

  1. Miriam and Aaron question Moses’ authority (1–3)
  2. Yahweh explains Moses’ special role as his servant (4–9)
  3. Miriam receives a skin disease and stays outside the camp for seven days (10–16)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Miriam and Aaron

Miriam was Moses’ older sister. Aaron was Moses’ older brother, although Aaron was younger than Miriam. In this story, they claim to have the authority to speak for God as Moses did. However, by the end of the chapter, God has shown that Moses is the one who has this authority.

Moses’ wife

This chapter refers to a wife of Moses who was a Cushite, which means that she was from the area that is now southern Egypt and northern Sudan. In Exodus 2:21, Moses marries a woman named Zipporah, but it is clear in the context that she is a Midianite (see Exodus 2:16). It is possible that Zipporah could be identified both as a Cushite and as a Midianite. It is more likely that Moses married a second woman, who was a Cushite. However, since the text does not directly identify this woman, it is recommended that you refer to her as generally as 12:1 does.

Skin disease

God punishes Miriam by making her suffer a skin disease. This specific skin disease disfigures her skin and makes it white. It is not certain exactly what skin disease it is. It is recommended that you use a general term for a skin disease.

title: Numbers 12:1 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תְּדַבֵּ֨ר מִרְיָ֤ם וְ⁠אַהֲרֹן֙ בְּ⁠מֹשֶׁ֔ה עַל־אֹד֛וֹת הָ⁠אִשָּׁ֥ה הַ⁠כֻּשִׁ֖ית אֲשֶׁ֣ר לָקָ֑ח כִּֽי־אִשָּׁ֥ה כֻשִׁ֖ית לָקָֽח

"And Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses on account of the woman, the Cushitess, that he took. For he took a woman, a Cushitess"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Now Moses had taken a woman, a Cushitess. And Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses on account of this woman, this Cushitess]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 12:1 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠אִשָּׁ֥ה הַ⁠כֻּשִׁ֖ית

"the woman, the Cushitess"

Some scholars argue that this woman was Zipporah, whom Moses married in Exodus 2:21. Other scholars argue that this is another woman to whom Moses was also married. It is recommended that you do not identify this woman beyond identifying her as a Cushitess.

See: When to Keep Information Implicit

title: Numbers 12:1 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠כֻּשִׁ֖ית & כֻשִׁ֖ית

"the Cushitess & a Cushitess"

Here, the word Cushitess refers to a woman from the area south of Egypt, sometimes known as Nubia. This is modern day southern Egypt and northern Sudan. Alternate translation: [the one from Cush … one from Cush]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 12:2 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠רַ֤ק אַךְ־בְּ⁠מֹשֶׁה֙ דִּבֶּ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה הֲ⁠לֹ֖א גַּם־בָּ֣⁠נוּ דִבֵּ֑ר

"Did Yahweh really only speak in Moses? Did he not speak also in us"

Aaron and Miriam are using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [Yahweh did not only speak in Moses. He also spoke in us!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 12:2 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠מֹשֶׁה֙ & בָּ֣⁠נוּ

"in Moses & in us"

The phrases in Moses and in us are common expressions of this culture that mean “by means of Moses” and “by means of us.” If these phrases do not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by means of Moses … by means of us]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 12:2 (#3)
content:
בָּ֣⁠נוּ

"in us"

By in us, Miriam and Aaron mean themselves but not Moses to whom they are referring, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 12:3 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠אִ֥ישׁ מֹשֶׁ֖ה ענו מְאֹ֑ד מִ⁠כֹּל֙ הָֽ⁠אָדָ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֖ר עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אֲדָמָֽה

"And the man Moses {was} very meek, more than the man who {was} upon the face of the ground"

Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. The ULT indicates this with parentheses. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [Now it is important to know that the man Moses was very meek, more than the man who was upon the face of the ground]

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 12:3 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠אִ֥ישׁ

"And the man"

The author is not referring to a specific man. The author means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any human]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 12:3 (#3)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֖ר עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אֲדָמָֽה

"who {was} upon the face of the ground"

The author is using upon the face of the ground as a common expression of his culture to mean “in the world” or “on the earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who was alive] or [who was in the world]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 12:3 (#4)
content:
פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אֲדָמָֽה

"the face of the ground"

Here, the face of the ground represents the surface of the ground. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the surface of the land] or [the land]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 12:4 (#1)
content:
צְא֥וּ & וַ⁠יֵּצְא֖וּ שְׁלָשְׁתָּֽ⁠ם

"Go out & And the three of them went out"

In a context such as this, your language might say “approach” instead of go. The tent was in the middle of the camp, not outside it. See how you translated the similar expression in 11:26. Alternate translation: [Approach … And the three of them approached]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 12:4 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּצְא֖וּ שְׁלָשְׁתָּֽ⁠ם

"And the three of them went out"

By the three of them went out, the author means they went out to the tent of meeting. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the three of them went out to the tent of meeting]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 12:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּ֤רֶד יְהוָה֙

"And Yahweh came down"

Here, the author is speaking as if Yahweh had actually moved physically downward. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 11:25. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh met them]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 12:5 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠עַמּ֣וּד עָנָ֔ן

"in a pillar of cloud"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a cloud that is in the shape of a pillar. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in a cloud in the shape of a pillar]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 12:5 (#3)
content:
וַֽ⁠יַּעֲמֹ֖ד

"and it stood"

The author is speaking of the cloud column as if it were a living thing that could stand. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh had it stay]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 12:5 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּצְא֖וּ שְׁנֵי⁠הֶֽם

"and the two of them went out"

In a context such as this, your language might say “approached” instead of went out. The tent was in the middle of the camp, not outside it. See how you translated the similar expression in 12:4. Alternate translation: [and the two of them approached]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 12:6 (#1)
content:
דְבָרָ֑⁠י

"my words"

Here, words represents what God will say by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what I am about to say]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 12:6 (#2)
content:
אִם־יִֽהְיֶה֙ נְבִ֣יאֲ⁠כֶ֔ם יְהוָ֗ה בַּ⁠מַּרְאָה֙ אֵלָ֣י⁠ו אֶתְוַדָּ֔ע

"If there is a prophet of yours of Yahweh, in the vision I will make myself known to him"

Yahweh is describing a possible condition in which he will make himself known in a vision only if there is a prophet of Yahweh. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Suppose that there is a prophet of yours of Yahweh. In that case, in the vision I will make myself known to him]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 12:6 (#3)
content:
נְבִ֣יאֲ⁠כֶ֔ם יְהוָ֗ה

"a prophet of yours of Yahweh"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a prophet who belongs to and speaks for Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a prophet among you through whom I speak]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 12:6 (#4)
content:
יְהוָ֗ה

"of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [of mine]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 12:6 (#5)
content:
בַּ⁠מַּרְאָה֙ אֵלָ֣י⁠ו אֶתְוַדָּ֔ע בַּ⁠חֲל֖וֹם אֲדַבֶּר־בּֽ⁠וֹ

"in the vision I will make myself known to him. In the dream I will speak with him"

These two phrases in the vision I will make myself known to him and In the dream I will speak with him mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [in the vision or the dream I will reveal myself to him]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 12:6 (#6)
content:
בַּ⁠מַּרְאָה֙ & בַּ⁠חֲל֖וֹם

"in the vision & In the dream"

Here, vision and dream represent supernatural revelations in general, not specific visions or dreams. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in a vision … In a dream]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 12:6 (#7)
content:
אֵלָ֣י⁠ו & בּֽ⁠וֹ

"to him & with him"

Here the masculine terms to him and with him have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [to that person … with that person]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 12:7 (#1)
content:
לֹא־כֵ֖ן עַבְדִּ֣⁠י מֹשֶׁ֑ה

"Not so my servant Moses"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Not so do I make myself known to my servant Moses]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 12:7 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠כָל־בֵּיתִ֖⁠י נֶאֱמָ֥ן הֽוּא

"in all my house, he, he is faithful"

Here, the phrase he himself is faithful could indicate that: (1) Moses faithfully does what God requires. Alternate translation: [in all my house he, he acts faithfully]; or (2) Moses is entrusted with the house. Alternate translation: [with all my house he, he is entrusted]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 12:7 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠כָל־בֵּיתִ֖⁠י

"in all my house"

God is using the term house to mean all the people who serve and worship him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among all my people]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 12:7 (#4)
content:
נֶאֱמָ֥ן הֽוּא

"he, he is faithful"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun he separately, even though the verb translated as he is faithful already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Moses is very faithful. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [he certainly is faithful]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 12:8 (#1)
content:
פֶּ֣ה אֶל־פֶּ֞ה

"Mouth to mouth"

Yahweh is using mouth to mouth as a common expression of his culture to mean “face to face” or “directly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Face to face] or [Directly]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 12:8 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מַרְאֶה֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א בְ⁠חִידֹ֔ת

"and appearance and not in riddles"

By appearance and not in riddles, Yahweh means that he spoke to Moses plainly and directly rather than in ways that were difficult to understand. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and clearly instead of in complicated ways]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 12:8 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠תְמֻנַ֥ת יְהוָ֖ה

"and & the form of Yahweh"

By the form of Yahweh, Yahweh means the visible way in which he reveals himself. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the visible way in which Yahweh reveals himself]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 12:8 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠תְמֻנַ֥ת יְהוָ֖ה

"and & the form of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [my form]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 12:8 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠מַדּ֨וּעַ֙ לֹ֣א יְרֵאתֶ֔ם לְ⁠דַבֵּ֖ר בְּ⁠עַבְדִּ֥⁠י בְ⁠מֹשֶֽׁה

"And why do you not fear to speak against my servant, against Moses"

God is using the question form to rebuke Aaron and Miriam. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [So you should fear to speak against my servant, against Moses.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 12:8 (#6)
content:
בְּ⁠עַבְדִּ֥⁠י בְ⁠מֹשֶֽׁה

"against my servant, against Moses"

It might seem that the expression against my servant, against Moses contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [against my servant Moses]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 12:9 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּֽחַר אַ֧ף יְהוָ֛ה בָּ֖⁠ם

"And the nose of Yahweh burned against them"

The phrase the nose of Yahweh burned is a common expression of this culture that means that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh’s anger burned against them] or [and Yahweh was enraged with them]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 12:9 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּלַֽךְ

"and he went"

The implication is that Yahweh left the sacred tent where he had been speaking with Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and he left the sacred tent]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 12:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֶ⁠עָנָ֗ן סָ֚ר

"and the cloud turned aside"

The author is speaking of the cloud as if it were a living thing that could move away on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh had the cloud depart]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 12:10 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֥ה & וְ⁠הִנֵּ֥ה

"And behold & and behold"

The author is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And look … and look]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 12:10 (#3)
content:
כַּ⁠שָּׁ֑לֶג

"like the snow"

The point of this comparison is that just as snow is white, so was her skin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [white like snow] or [white like wool]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 12:10 (#4)
content:
כַּ⁠שָּׁ֑לֶג

"like the snow"

The author is not referring to a specific snow. He means snow in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like snow]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 12:10 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֥ה מְצֹרָֽעַת

"and behold, she was with a skin disease"

It might seem that the expression she was with a skin disease contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, since the author stated it earlier in the verse. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and he saw what had happened]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 12:11 (#1)
content:
אַל & תָשֵׁ֤ת עָלֵ֨י⁠נוּ֙ חַטָּ֔את

"do not put upon us sin"

Here, Aaron is speaking as if sin were actually something that could be put upon a person. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not make us suffer the punishment for the sin]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 12:11 (#2)
content:
בִּ֣י אֲדֹנִ֔⁠י & נָ֨א

"Please, my lord, please"

Aaron uses two words that mean please to indicate his own low status and the urgency of his request. Use a comparable title or expression for addressing someone respectfully in your language. Alternate translation: [I beg you, my lord,]

See: Politeness

title: Numbers 12:11 (#3)
content:
אֲדֹנִ֔⁠י

"my lord"

Aaron is referring to Moses by the respectful title my lord. Use a comparable title or expression for addressing someone respectfully in your language. See how you translated the similar phrase in 11:28. Alternate translation: [my master] or [my leader]

See: Politeness

title: Numbers 12:11 (#4)
content:
עָלֵ֨י⁠נוּ֙ & נוֹאַ֖לְנוּ & חָטָֽאנוּ

"upon us & we did foolishly & we sinned"

By us, Aaron means himself and Miriam but not Moses to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 12:11 (#5)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֥ר נוֹאַ֖לְנוּ וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר חָטָֽאנוּ

"which we did foolishly and which we sinned"

The expression which we did foolishly and which we sinned expresses a single idea. The word foolishly tells more about sinned. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [which we foolishly sinned] or [which we did so foolishly]

See: Hendiadys

title: Numbers 12:12 (#1)
content:
אַל־נָ֥א תְהִ֖י כַּ⁠מֵּ֑ת אֲשֶׁ֤ר בְּ⁠צֵאת⁠וֹ֙ מֵ⁠רֶ֣חֶם אִמּ֔⁠וֹ וַ⁠יֵּאָכֵ֖ל חֲצִ֥י בְשָׂרֽ⁠וֹ

"May she not be like the one having died, who, when he comes out from the womb of his mother, then half of his flesh was eaten"

The point of this comparison is that just as one having died has decaying flesh, so Miriam has decaying flesh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [May her skin not be like the skin of the one having died, who, when he comes out from the womb of his mother, then half of his flesh was eaten]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 12:12 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠צֵאת⁠וֹ֙ מֵ⁠רֶ֣חֶם אִמּ֔⁠וֹ

"when he comes out from the womb of his mother"

The author is using when he comes out from the womb of his mother as a common expression of his culture to mean “when he is born.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he is born]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 12:12 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּאָכֵ֖ל חֲצִ֥י בְשָׂרֽ⁠וֹ

"then half of his flesh was eaten"

The expression was eaten is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [then half of his flesh has wasted away] or [then half of his flesh has rotted]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 12:13 (#1)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר

"saying"

Here, the word saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 12:13 (#2)
content:
אֵ֕ל נָ֛א & נָ֖א

"God, please, please"

Here Moses repeats the word please to show that he is speaking humbly and pleading urgently with God. To show humility and urgency in your language, you may need to use different words or expressions rather than repeating “please.” See how you translated the similar repetition in 12:11. Alternate translation: [God, I respectfully and urgently ask you,]

See: Politeness

title: Numbers 12:14 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אָבִ֨י⁠הָ֙ יָרֹ֤ק יָרַק֙ בְּ⁠פָנֶ֔י⁠הָ הֲ⁠לֹ֥א תִכָּלֵ֖ם שִׁבְעַ֣ת יָמִ֑ים

"And her father, spitting, spit in her face, would she not be humiliated seven days"

The author is using the question form to emphasize that being spit in the face by her father would certainly humiliate her for seven days. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And her father, spitting, spit in her face, she would be humiliated seven days.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 12:14 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אָבִ֨י⁠הָ֙ יָרֹ֤ק יָרַק֙ בְּ⁠פָנֶ֔י⁠הָ הֲ⁠לֹ֥א תִכָּלֵ֖ם שִׁבְעַ֣ת יָמִ֑ים

"And her father, spitting, spit in her face, would she not be humiliated seven days"

The author says And her father, spitting, spit in her face, would she not be humiliated seven days to introduce an imaginary situation to help explain how long Miriam should be isolated outside the camp. Use a natural method in your language for introducing an imaginary situation. Alternate translation: [Imagine that her father, spitting, spit in her face. In that case, would she not be humiliated seven days]

See: Hypothetical Situations

title: Numbers 12:14 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אָבִ֨י⁠הָ֙ יָרֹ֤ק יָרַק֙ בְּ⁠פָנֶ֔י⁠הָ

"And her father, spitting, spit in her face"

Spitting in her face was a symbolic action by which her father showed that she was disgraced and unclean. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And her father humiliated her by spitting in her face]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Numbers 12:14 (#4)
content:
יָרֹ֤ק יָרַק֙

"spitting, spit"

The author is repeating forms of the verb spit in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [spit directly]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 12:14 (#5)
content:
הֲ⁠לֹ֥א תִכָּלֵ֖ם

"would she not be humiliated"

The expression would she not be humiliated is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [would that not cause humiliation for her]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 12:14 (#6)
content:
תִּסָּגֵ֞ר

"She shall be shut up"

The expression she shall be shut up is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. Alternate translation: [You Israelites must shut her up]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 12:14 (#7)
content:
תִּסָּגֵ֞ר

"She shall be shut up"

The implication is that she must be excluded from the camp, not that she must be locked up. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [She shall be banished]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 12:14 (#8)
content:
מִ⁠ח֣וּץ לַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֔ה

"from outside to the camp"

The phrase from outside to the camp is a common expression of this culture to mean “in the area outside the camp.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the area outside the camp]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 12:14 (#9)
content:
תֵּאָסֵֽף

"she shall be gathered"

The expression she shall be gathered is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. See how you translated the similar construction in 11:30. Alternate translation: [And she shall return]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 12:15 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תִּסָּגֵ֥ר מִרְיָ֛ם

"And Miriam was shut up"

The expression was shut up is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. See how you translated the similar clause in 12:14. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites shut up Miriam]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 12:15 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠תִּסָּגֵ֥ר מִרְיָ֛ם

"And Miriam was shut up"

The implication is that Miriam was shut up outside the camp, not that she was locked up. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar clause in 12:14. Alternate translation: [And Miriam was banished]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 12:15 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠ח֥וּץ לַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֖ה

"from outside to the camp"

The phrase from outside to the camp is a common expression of this culture that means “in the area away from the camp.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 12:14. Alternate translation: [in the area outside the camp]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 12:15 (#4)
content:
עַד־הֵאָסֵ֖ף מִרְיָֽם

"until Miriam was gathered"

The expression was gathered is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. See how you translated the similar clause in 12:14. Alternate translation: [until Miriam returned]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 12:16 (#1)
content:
מֵ⁠חֲצֵר֑וֹת

"from Hazeroth"

The word Hazeroth is the name of a place in the desert. See how you translated this name in 11:35.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 12:16 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠מִדְבַּ֥ר פָּארָֽן

"in the wilderness of Paran"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a wilderness that is characterized by being near Paran. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 10:12. Alternate translation: [in the wilderness that was near Paran]

See: Possession

title: Numbers - Chapter 13 Introduction
content:
Numbers 13 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh has Moses send 12 leaders to explore the land of Canaan. They explore it from south to north and then return to the Israelites. They report that the land is good, but most of them discourage the Israelites from going there because the inhabitants are big and strong.

  1. Yahweh commands Moses to send leaders to explore the land of Canaan, and Moses gives them instructions (1–20)
  2. The leaders explore Canaan and gather fruit (21–25)
  3. The leaders report what they have seen, and Caleb urges Israel to take the land (26–33)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Exploring Canaan

In this chapter, Moses sends 12 leaders to explore the land of Canaan. Moses asks them to find out how the area is laid out, how fertile it is, what its people are like, and what their defenses are like. Moses asks for this information because it will help him plan how to take over the area.

Areas within Canaan

Moses tells the leaders to go from the Negeb in the south to the hill country, which is the central area to the north of the Negeb. When the leaders travel, they go from the wilderness of Zin in the southern part of the region to Lebo Hamath in the northern part of the region. The author also mentions Hebron, which is in the southern part of the hill country, and Wadi Eshcol, whose location is unknown. The mentioned locations indicate that the leaders did explore the entire land of Canaan, from south to north and then back south.

The Anak and the Nephils

In this chapter, the author mentions that there are “sons of the Anak” living at Hebron. These “Anakites” were tall and powerful men. The author mentions three names: Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai. These could be names of three tribes or, more likely, three men. At the end of the chapter, the Israelite leaders mention “Nephils,” and the author notes that the sons of Anak are a type of Nephil. The Nephils are also mentioned in Genesis 6:4, where they are described as mighty men. Scholars do not agree on exactly what the Nephils and the Anakites were. It is clear that they were tall and powerful people.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Order of events

There are two places in this chapter where events are not narrated in sequence. First, 13:3 states that Moses sent the leaders to Canaan. Then, after a list of these leaders, 13:17 again states that Moses sent the leaders, followed by the instructions that Moses gave to them. This second statement about Moses sending them resumes the main storyline after the list. Consider how you would resume the main storyline in your language. Second, 13:21 provides a summary statement that indicates that the leaders explored the entire region of Canaan. Then, 13:22 begins a more detailed narrative of how they explored the region, which ends in 13:26. Consider how you might express a summary statement followed by a more detailed explanation.

“Go up”

Multiple times in this chapter, the author or characters use the word “up” with verbs of movement, such as “go” or “come.” This language often includes elevation in its descriptions of movement. For example, going from the Negeb to the hill country is going “up” because elevation is gained during the travel. For some languages, “up” would give the wrong meaning or is not necessary.

Indirect questions

In 13:18–20, Moses uses indirect questions to tell the leaders what he wants to know about Canaan. These questions begin with “what” or “whether.” The ULT and UST both use indirect questions here. However, you could use direct questions if it would be helpful in your language. Here is the ULT but with the indirect questions expressed as direct questions:

[18] And you shall see the land. What {is} it? And the people dwelling upon it, {is} it strong or weak? {Is} it few or many? [19] And what {is} the land in which it is dwelling? {Is} it good or evil? And what {are} the cities in which it is dwelling? Is it in camps or in fortresses? [20] And what {is} the land? {Is} it fat or lean? Are there trees in it or not? And you shall strengthen yourselves, and you shall take from the fruit of the land.

title: Numbers 13:1 (#1)
content:
לֵּ⁠אמֹֽר

"saying"

Here, the word saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 13:2 (#1)
content:
שְׁלַח־לְ⁠ךָ֣ & תִּשְׁלָ֔חוּ

"Send for you & you shall send"

The first instance of you (in Send for you) is singular and refers only to Moses. The second instance of you (in you shall send) is plural and refers to Moses and the Israelites. Use the appropriate singular or plural form of “you” in your language if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 13:2 (#2)
content:
אֲנִ֥י נֹתֵ֖ן

"I am giving"

Yahweh is using the present tense am giving to describe something that is going to happen in the future in order to show that the event will happen soon. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the future tense. Alternate translation: [I am about to give]

See: Irregular Use of Tenses

title: Numbers 13:2 (#3)
content:
אִ֣ישׁ אֶחָד֩ אִ֨ישׁ אֶחָ֜ד לְ⁠מַטֵּ֤ה אֲבֹתָי⁠ו֙

"One man, one man to the tribe of his fathers"

The phrase one man, one man to the tribe of is a common expression of this culture that means “one man for each tribe.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [One man for each tribe of]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 13:2 (#4)
content:
אֲבֹתָי⁠ו֙

"his fathers"

God is using the term fathers to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his ancestors]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 13:2 (#5)
content:
בָ⁠הֶֽם

"among them"

The pronoun them refers to the people in the man’s tribe. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [among the people of his tribe]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 13:3 (#1)
content:
רָאשֵׁ֥י בְנֵֽי

"heads of the sons"

Here, heads represents leaders. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar metaphor in 10:4. Alternate translation: [chiefs of]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 13:3 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠מִּדְבַּ֥ר פָּארָ֖ן

"from the wilderness of Paran"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a wilderness that is near Paran.
