If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 10:12. Alternate translation: [from the wilderness that was near Paran]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 13:3 (#3)
content:
עַל־פִּ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"upon the mouth of Yahweh"

Here, upon the mouth of Yahweh represents what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 9:23. Alternate translation: [according to what Yahweh commanded him]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 13:4 (#1)
content:
רְאוּבֵ֔ן שַׁמּ֖וּעַ בֶּן־זַכּֽוּר

"of Reuben, Shammua, the son of Zaccur"

Here and in 13:5–16, all the names are names of tribes or men.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 13:8 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠מַטֵּ֥ה אֶפְרָ֖יִם

"for the tribe of Ephraim"

The author assumes that readers will know that Ephraim was the son of Joseph, just as Manasseh was (see 13:11). You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for the tribe of Joseph, for the tribe of Ephraim]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:11 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠מַטֵּ֥ה יוֹסֵ֖ף לְ⁠מַטֵּ֣ה מְנַשֶּׁ֑ה

"for the tribe of Joseph, for the tribe of Manasseh"

The implication is that Manasseh was a subdivision of the larger tribe of Joseph. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for the tribe of Manasseh, which is part of the tribe of Joseph]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:16 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקְרָ֥א מֹשֶׁ֛ה

"and Moses called"

The author does not state directly when Moses did this. It could be: (1) at some earlier time. In this case, the author includes this information here to explain the name “Hoshea” in the list. Alternate translation: [and previously Moses had called]; or (2) at this time, when he sent the leaders to explore Canaan. Alternate translation: [and at that time Moses called]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:16 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠הוֹשֵׁ֥עַ בִּן־נ֖וּן יְהוֹשֻֽׁעַ

"Hoshea, the son of Nun, Joshua"

The name Hoshea means “he saved.” The name Joshua means “Yahweh saved.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could give the meaning of these names in your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Hoshea (which means “he saved”), the son of Nun, Joshua (which means “Yahweh saved”)]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 13:17 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֤ח אֹתָ⁠ם֙ מֹשֶׁ֔ה לָ⁠ת֖וּר אֶת־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּנָ֑עַן וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר

"And Moses sent them to explore the land of Canaan, and he said"

The author is describing one event, Moses sent them to explore the land of Canaan, after already having described it in 13:3. If it would be helpful in your language, you may wish to relate these events in a different way to avoid repetition. Alternate translation: [And at the time when Moses sent them to explore the land of Canaan, he said]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 13:17 (#2)
content:
עֲל֥וּ & וַ⁠עֲלִיתֶ֖ם

"Go up & and you shall go up"

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, Moses is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [Go on … and you shall go to]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 13:17 (#3)
content:
זֶה֙

"this"

The pronoun this refers to the way ahead of them through the Negeb. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [by the way in front of you] or [this way]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 13:18 (#1)
content:
מַה־הִ֑וא

"what it {is"

The implication is that Moses is asking about the land in general: its quality, characteristics, and suitability for settlement. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [what kind of place it is]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:18 (#2)
content:
הֶ⁠חָזָ֥ק הוּא֙ הֲ⁠רָפֶ֔ה הַ⁠מְעַ֥ט ה֖וּא אִם־רָֽב

"whether it {is} strong or weak, whether it {is} few or many"

The pronoun it refers to the group of people living in the land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [whether those people are strong or weak, whether those people are few or many]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 13:19 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠בְּ⁠מַֽחֲנִ֖ים

"whether in camps"

Here, Moses is speaking of unprotected settlements where people live as if they were camps, which were temporary settlements made of tents. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whether in unfortified towns]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 13:19 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מָ֣ה הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ

"and what {is} the land"

By what is the land, Moses means what the land looks like and how people live in it. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and what are the features of the land]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:19 (#3)
content:
הוּא֙ יֹשֵׁ֣ב & הוּא֙ יוֹשֵׁ֣ב

"it is dwelling & it is dwelling"

The pronoun it refers to the people group who are living in the land that Moses told the men to explore. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [those people are dwelling … those people are dwelling]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 13:19 (#4)
content:
הֲ⁠טוֹבָ֥ה הִ֖וא אִם־רָעָ֑ה

"whether it {is} good or evil"

The implication is that the land could be good or bad for the people to live in. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [whether it is good to live in or bad to live in]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:20 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מָ֣ה הָ֠⁠אָרֶץ

"and what {is} the land"

The implication is that Moses wanted the spies to observe the quality of the soil itself. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and what kind of ground it is]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:20 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠שְּׁמֵנָ֨ה הִ֜וא אִם־רָזָ֗ה

"whether it {is} fat or lean"

The author is speaking of the land as if it were a living thing that could be fat or lean. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whether it can produce many crops or few crops]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 13:20 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִ֨תְחַזַּקְתֶּ֔ם וּ⁠לְקַחְתֶּ֖ם

"and you shall strengthen yourselves, and you shall take"

Here, the phrase strengthen yourselves could mean that: (1) the leaders should work hard to do something. Alternate translation: [and you shall try hard to take]; or (2) the leaders should be courageous. Alternate translation: [and you shall be courageous, and you shall take]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 13:20 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠פְּרִ֣י הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ

"from the fruit of the land"

In this verse, the word fruit is singular in form, but it refers to all the produce of the land as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “fruit.” Alternate translation: [from the fruits of the land]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 13:20 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הַ֨⁠יָּמִ֔ים יְמֵ֖י בִּכּוּרֵ֥י עֲנָבִֽים

"And the days {were} the days of the firstfruits of the grapes"

Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [Now it is important to know that the days were the days of the firstfruits of the grapes]

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 13:20 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠הַ֨⁠יָּמִ֔ים יְמֵ֖י

"And the days {were} the days of"

The author is using the term days to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it was the time of year for]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 13:21 (#1)
content:
וַֽ⁠יַּעֲל֖וּ

"And they went up"

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. See how you expressed this idea in 13:17. Alternate translation: [And they went]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 13:21 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠מִּדְבַּר־צִ֥ן עַד־רְחֹ֖ב

"from the wilderness of Zin up to Rehob"

The words Zin and Rehob are the names of places. Zin refers to a wilderness area in the southern part of the land, and Rehob refers to a city in the northern part of the land.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 13:21 (#3)
content:
עַד־רְחֹ֖ב לְבֹ֥א חֲמָֽת

"up to Rehob, Lebo Hamath"

Here, the phrase Lebo Hamath could be: (1) the name of a city which is near Rehob. Alternate translation: [up to Rehob, near the city of Lebo Hamath]; or (2) a phrase that refers to the entrance or way to a place called Hamath. Alternate translation: [up to Rehob, at the entrance to Hamath]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:22 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּעֲל֣וּ בַ⁠נֶּגֶב֮

"And they went up in the Negeb"

Here and in the following verses, the author provides the details of the travel that was summarized in 13:21. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate explicitly that the events in this and the following verses happened during the time described in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [Specifically, they went up in the Negeb] or [Here is how they did that. They went up in the Negeb]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 13:22 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יַּעֲל֣וּ

"And they went up"

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. See how you expressed this idea in 13:17. Alternate translation: [And they went]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 13:22 (#3)
content:
אֲחִימַן֙ שֵׁשַׁ֣י וְ⁠תַלְמַ֔י

"were} Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai"

Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai could be the names of: (1) individual men. Alternate translation: [the men named Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai]; or (2) clans. Alternate translation: [the clans of Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 13:22 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠חֶבְר֗וֹן שֶׁ֤בַע שָׁנִים֙ נִבְנְתָ֔ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י צֹ֥עַן מִצְרָֽיִם

"And Hebron was built seven years to the face of Zoan, Egypt"

Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand what is happening in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [It is important to know that Hebron was built seven years to the face of Zoan, Egypt]

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 13:22 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠חֶבְר֗וֹן & נִבְנְתָ֔ה

"And Hebron was built"

The expression was built is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And its founders built Hebron]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 13:22 (#6)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י

"to the face of"

The author is using the expression to the face of to mean “before” or “previous to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [prior to]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 13:22 (#7)
content:
צֹ֥עַן מִצְרָֽיִם

"Zoan, Egypt"

The words Zoan and Egypt are the names of a city and a country.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 13:23 (#1)
content:
נַ֣חַל אֶשְׁכֹּ֗ל

"Wadi Eshcol"

The word Wadi Eshcol is the name of a place. Here “Wadi” means a valley or streambed.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 13:23 (#2)
content:
זְמוֹרָה֙ וְ⁠אֶשְׁכּ֤וֹל עֲנָבִים֙ אֶחָ֔ד

"a branch and one cluster of grapes"

The phrase branch and one cluster of grapes expresses a single idea. The word branch tells more about the cluster of grapes. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [a branch with one cluster of grapes]

See: Hendiadys

title: Numbers 13:23 (#3)
content:
בַ⁠מּ֖וֹט

"on the carrying pole"

The author is not referring to a specific carrying pole that the reader knows about. He means any carrying pole. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [on a carrying pole]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 13:23 (#4)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנָ֑יִם

"with two"

The implication is that there were two men who carried the cluster of grapes. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with two men carrying it at a time]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:23 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠מִן־הָ⁠רִמֹּנִ֖ים וּ⁠מִן־הַ⁠תְּאֵנִֽים

"and from the pomegranates and from the figs"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they also took from the pomegranates and from the figs]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 13:23 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠מִן־הָ⁠רִמֹּנִ֖ים וּ⁠מִן־הַ⁠תְּאֵנִֽים

"and from the pomegranates and from the figs"

Here, pomegranates and figs represent these fruits in general, not specific ones. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and some pomegranates and some figs]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 13:24 (#1)
content:
קָרָ֖א

"He called"

See how you translated the similar form in 11:3. Here, the pronoun He could refer: (1) generically to anyone who used this name. Alternate translation: [People called]; or (2) to Moses. Alternate translation: [Moses called]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 13:24 (#2)
content:
נַ֣חַל אֶשְׁכּ֑וֹל עַ֚ל אֹד֣וֹת הָֽ⁠אֶשְׁכּ֔וֹל

"Wadi Eshcol on account of the cluster"

The name Eshcol sounds like the Hebrew word for cluster. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could make that explicit in your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Wadi Eshcol (which means “Cluster Wadi”) on account of the cluster]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 13:25 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּשֻׁ֖בוּ

"And they returned"

The pronoun they refers to the 12 men who explored Canaan. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the 12 leaders returned]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 13:26 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּלְכ֡וּ וַ⁠יָּבֹאוּ֩

"and they went and they came"

It might seem that the expression and they went and they came contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and they went] or [and they came]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 13:26 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אֶל־כָּל־עֲדַ֧ת בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל

"and to all the congregation of the sons of Israel"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a congregation that is made up of the sons of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 8:9. Alternate translation: [and to the congregation that consists of all the sons of Israel]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 13:26 (#3)
content:
אֶל־מִדְבַּ֥ר פָּארָ֖ן קָדֵ֑שָׁ⁠ה

"to the wilderness of Paran at Kadesh"

The implication is that the people of Israel were located in both the wilderness of Paran and specifically at the city of Kadesh when the scouts returned. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who were in the wilderness of Paran at Kadesh]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:26 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יָּשִׁ֨יבוּ אוֹתָ֤⁠ם דָּבָר֙ וְ⁠אֶת־כָּל־הָ֣⁠עֵדָ֔ה

"And they returned them and all the congregation a word"

The phrase returned them and all the congregation a word is a common expression of this culture that means “gave them all a report” or “told them what they learned.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they told what they had learned to them and all the congregation]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 13:26 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠יָּשִׁ֨יבוּ אוֹתָ֤⁠ם & וַ⁠יַּרְא֖וּ⁠ם

"And they returned them & and they showed them"

The pronoun they refers to the 12 men who scouted out Canaan, the first pronoun them refers to Moses and Aaron, and the second pronoun them refers to Moses, Aaron, and the congregation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the 12 leaders returned Moses and Aaron … and the 12 leaders showed Moses, Aaron, and the congregation]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 13:26 (#6)
content:
אֶת־פְּרִ֥י הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"the fruit of the land"

In this verse, the word fruit is singular in form, but it refers to all the produce as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “fruit.” See how you translated this phrase in 13:20. Alternate translation: [the fruits of]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 13:27 (#1)
content:
זָבַ֨ת חָלָ֥ב וּ⁠דְבַ֛שׁ הִ֖וא

"it is flowing {with} milk and honey"

Here, the author is speaking as if the land were actually flowing with milk and honey. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it is rich and fertile] or [it is very productive]

See: Metaphor

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 13:27 (#2)
content:
ל⁠וֹ֙

"to him"

The pronoun him refers to Moses. The men who explored Canaan spoke this report to Moses, but everyone else who was present also heard it. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to Moses publicly]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 13:27 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ

"and they said"

The term and they said introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 13:27 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֣ר שְׁלַחְתָּ֑⁠נוּ

"where you sent us"

The phrase where you sent us shows that “us” refers to the 12 men who explored Canaan, but not to Moses, whom they are addressing, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 13:27 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠זֶה־פִּרְיָֽ⁠הּ

"and this {is} its fruit"

In this verse, the word fruit is singular in form, but it refers to all the fruit (grapes, pomegranates, and figs) as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “fruit.” See how you translated this phrase in 13:20. Alternate translation: [and these are its fruits]

See: Collective Nouns

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 13:28 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֶֽ⁠עָרִ֗ים בְּצֻר֤וֹת גְּדֹלֹת֙ מְאֹ֔ד

"and the cities are fortified very great"

The expression are fortified is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they have fortified their cities very greatly]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 13:28 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠גַם & רָאִ֥ינוּ

"and also we saw"

By we saw, the spies mean themselves but not Moses to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 13:29 (#1)
content:
עֲמָלֵ֥ק יוֹשֵׁ֖ב

"Amalek is dwelling"

Here, Amalek represents the Amalekite people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The Amalekites are dwelling]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 13:29 (#2)
content:
וְ֠⁠הַֽ⁠חִתִּי וְ⁠הַ⁠יְבוּסִ֤י וְ⁠הָֽ⁠אֱמֹרִי֙ יוֹשֵׁ֣ב & וְ⁠הַֽ⁠כְּנַעֲנִי֙ יֹשֵׁ֣ב

"and the Hittite and the Jebusite and the Amorite is dwelling & and the Canaanite is dwelling"

The men are not referring to specific Hittite, Jebusite, Amorite, and Canaanite people. They mean Hittites, Jebusites, Amorites, and Canaanites in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the Hittites and the Jebusites and the Amorites are dwelling … and the Canaanites are dwelling]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 13:29 (#3)
content:
עַל־הַ⁠יָּ֔ם

"upon the sea"

The author is using upon the sea as a common expression of his culture to mean “next to the sea” or “along the coast.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [next to the sea]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 13:29 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠עַ֖ל יַ֥ד הַ⁠יַּרְדֵּֽן

"and upon the hand of the Jordan"

The author is using upon the hand of the Jordan as a common expression of his culture to mean “along the Jordan River.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and along the Jordan]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 13:30 (#1)
content:
אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֑ה

"to Moses"

Here, the phrase to Moses could mean that Caleb hushed: (1) all the people who were assembled with Moses. Alternate translation: [who were assembled before Moses]; or (2) the people who were near Moses. Alternate translation: [near Moses]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:30 (#2)
content:
עָלֹ֤ה נַעֲלֶה֙ וְ⁠יָרַ֣שְׁנוּ אֹתָ֔⁠הּ כִּֽי־יָכ֥וֹל נוּכַ֖ל לָֽ⁠הּ

"Going up, we will go up, and we will possess it, for being able, we are able against it"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since being able, we are able against it gives the reason for the result that going up, we will go up, and we will possess it describes. Alternate translation: [Being able, we are able against it. So, going up, we will go up, and we will possess it]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 13:30 (#3)
content:
עָלֹ֤ה נַעֲלֶה֙ & יָכ֥וֹל נוּכַ֖ל

"Going up, we will go up & being able, we are able"

The author is repeating forms of the verbs go up and able in order to intensify his expression of the ideas that they convey. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [We will certainly go up … for we are certainly able]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 13:30 (#4)
content:
עָלֹ֤ה נַעֲלֶה֙

"Going up, we will go up"

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. See how you expressed the idea in 13:17. Alternate translation: [Going, we will go]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 13:30 (#5)
content:
נַעֲלֶה֙ וְ⁠יָרַ֣שְׁנוּ אֹתָ֔⁠הּ & נוּכַ֖ל

"we will go up, and we will possess it & we are able"

By we will go up … and we will possess it … we are able, Caleb means to include both himself and his listeners, so use the inclusive form of those words if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 13:30 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠יָרַ֣שְׁנוּ אֹתָ֔⁠הּ & לָֽ⁠הּ

"and we will possess it & against it"

The pronoun it refers to the land that the Israelites will possess and go up against. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and we will possess the land … against the land]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 13:30 (#7)
content:
נוּכַ֖ל לָֽ⁠הּ

"we are able against it"

Caleb is using we are able against it as a common expression of his culture to mean “we are able to conquer it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are able to conquer it]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 13:31 (#1)
content:
עָל֤וּ

"went up"

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. See how you expressed the idea in 13:17. Alternate translation: [went]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 13:31 (#2)
content:
לֹ֥א נוּכַ֖ל לַ⁠עֲל֣וֹת אֶל־הָ⁠עָ֑ם כִּֽי־חָזָ֥ק ה֖וּא מִמֶּֽ⁠נּוּ

"We are not able to go up against the people, for it {is} stronger than us"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since it is stronger than us gives the reason for the result that we are not able to go up against the people describes. Alternate translation: [The people is stronger than us, so we are not able to go up against it]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 13:31 (#3)
content:
לֹ֥א נוּכַ֖ל & מִמֶּֽ⁠נּוּ

"We are not able & than us"

By us, the men who went up with Caleb mean themselves and the rest of the Israelites, so use the inclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 13:31 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠עֲל֣וֹת אֶל־הָ⁠עָ֑ם

"to go up against the people"

The spies are using to go up against the people as a common expression of their culture to mean “to fight against” or “to defeat.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to fight against the people] or [to defeat the people]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 13:31 (#5)
content:
חָזָ֥ק ה֖וּא

"it {is} stronger"

The pronoun it refers to the people of Canaan. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [those people are stronger]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 13:32 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יּוֹצִ֜יאוּ דִּבַּ֤ת הָ⁠אָ֨רֶץ֙

"And they brought out a bad report of the land"

Here, the scouts are speaking as if a report were an object that could be brought out. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they gave a bad report]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 13:32 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠אָ֡רֶץ אֲשֶׁר֩ עָבַ֨רְנוּ בָ֜⁠הּ לָ⁠ת֣וּר אֹתָ֗⁠הּ אֶ֣רֶץ אֹכֶ֤לֶת יוֹשְׁבֶ֨י⁠הָ֙ הִ֔וא

"The land through which we passed to explore it, it {is} a land eating the ones dwelling in it"

It might seem that the expression it is a land contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [The land through which we passed to explore it eats the ones dwelling in it]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 13:32 (#3)
content:
עָבַ֨רְנוּ

"we passed"

By we passed, the spies mean themselves but not Moses and the other Israelites to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 13:32 (#4)
content:
אֶ֣רֶץ אֹכֶ֤לֶת יוֹשְׁבֶ֨י⁠הָ֙

"a land eating the ones dwelling in it"

Here, the spies speak as if the land were a person that could eat the people who live there. Some scholars think this refers to a specific danger, like famine or war. However, it is recommended that you refer generally to dangers that people would experience living in the land. Alternate translation: [a land that is as dangerous as if it ate the ones dwelling in it] or [a land that is dangerous for the ones dwelling in it]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 13:32 (#5)
content:
אַנְשֵׁ֥י מִדּֽוֹת

"were} men of size"

The author is using the possessive form to describe men that are characterized by size. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [sizable men] or [large men]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 13:32 (#6)
content:
אַנְשֵׁ֥י מִדּֽוֹת

"were} men of size"

Here the masculine term men of has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [humans of]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 13:33 (#1)
content:
בְּנֵ֥י עֲנָ֖ק

"the sons of Anak"

Here, the author is speaking as if the people of the tribes descended from Anak were actually his sons. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those descended from Anak]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 13:33 (#2)
content:
רָאִ֗ינוּ & וַ⁠נְּהִ֤י & הָיִ֖ינוּ

"we saw & and we were & we were"

By we, the spies mean to include themselves but not Moses and the other Israelites to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your language if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 13:33 (#3)
content:
בְּנֵ֥י עֲנָ֖ק מִן־הַ⁠נְּפִלִ֑ים

"the sons of Anak {are} from the Nephils"

Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand the identity of the sons of Anak. He interrupts the quote to do so. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [it is important to know that the sons of Anak are from the Nephils]

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 13:33 (#4)
content:
מִן־הַ⁠נְּפִלִ֑ים

"are} from the Nephils"

Here, the phrase from the Nephils could mean: (1) that the sons of Anak are Nephils. Alternate translation: [are a type of Nephil]; or (2) that the sons of Anak are descended from Nephils. Alternate translation: [are descended from the Nephils]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 13:33 (#5)
content:
בְ⁠עֵינֵ֨י⁠נוּ֙ & בְּ⁠עֵינֵי⁠הֶֽם

"in our eyes & in their eyes"

Here, eyes represents what people thought or perceived about themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in our sight … in their sight] or [in our perception … in their perception]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 13:33 (#6)
content:
כַּֽ⁠חֲגָבִ֔ים

"like the grasshoppers"

The point of this comparison is that just as grasshoppers are small and insignificant compared to humans, so the Israelite spies felt small and insignificant compared to the people of Canaan. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as small and insignificant as grasshoppers]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 13:33 (#7)
content:
כַּֽ⁠חֲגָבִ֔ים

"like the grasshoppers"

A grasshopper is a kind of jumping insect. If your readers would not be familiar with what a grasshopper is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like the small jumping insects]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 13:33 (#8)
content:
כַּֽ⁠חֲגָבִ֔ים

"like the grasshoppers"

The men are not referring to specific grasshoppers. They mean grasshoppers in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like grasshoppers]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers - Chapter 14 Introduction
content:
Numbers 14 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the Israelites refuse to enter Canaan. Yahweh then declares how he will punish them. When the Israelites hear this, they decide to go to Canaan after all. However, Yahweh does not help them, and they are defeated.

  1. Israel refuses to enter Canaan despite Joshua and Caleb’s appeal (1–12)
  2. Moses asks Yahweh to forgive the people (13–19)
  3. Yahweh declares that the rebellious generation will not enter the land (20–38)
  4. Israel tries to enter the land without Yahweh’s help and is defeated (39–45)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Murmuring

In this chapter, “murmuring” refers to speaking against someone else. In this context, it means that people say that their leader is doing a bad job leading them. Consider how you would express this idea in your language.

Forgiveness and punishment

In this chapter, Moses quotes what Yahweh had previously said about himself: he both forgives and punishes. In response to Moses asking Yahweh to forgive the Israelites, that is exactly what Yahweh does. He forgives them, but he also punishes them for their disobedience. More specifically, all the people who refused to go to Canaan will die in the wilderness, but their children will enter and live in Canaan.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

“Go up”

Multiple times in this chapter, the author or characters use the word “up” or “down” with verbs of movement, such as “go” or “come.” This language often includes elevation in its descriptions of movement. For example, going from the Israelite camp to the hill country is going “up” because elevation is gained during the travel. For some languages, “up” or “down” would give the wrong meaning or is not necessary.

Oath formulas

Yahweh uses several different oath formulas in this chapter. One formula includes something that the oath-taker swears by. Yahweh swears by his own life and by the fact that his glory fills the earth. This formula indicates that what Yahweh swears is as certain as his glory and as his life. A second formula uses a conditional form but does not include what will happen if the condition is met. In these cases, the oath formula implies that something terrible will happen to the oath-taker if the condition is met. See the notes for specific cases and translation options.

Rhetorical Questions

Several times in this chapter, characters ask rhetorical questions. The characters are using the question form to express strong emotions. They do not actually want answers. See the notes for translation options.

title: Numbers 14:1 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תִּשָּׂא֙ כָּל־הָ֣⁠עֵדָ֔ה וַֽ⁠יִּתְּנ֖וּ אֶת־קוֹלָ֑⁠ם

"And all the congregation lifted up, and they gave their voice"

Here, the author is speaking as if the voices of the people were objects that they could lift up and give. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all the congregation made loud noises] or [And all the congregation cried out]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:1 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠תִּשָּׂא֙ כָּל־הָ֣⁠עֵדָ֔ה וַֽ⁠יִּתְּנ֖וּ אֶת־קוֹלָ֑⁠ם וַ⁠יִּבְכּ֥וּ הָ⁠עָ֖ם בַּ⁠לַּ֥יְלָה הַ⁠הֽוּא

"And all the congregation lifted up, and they gave their voice, and the people wept in that night"

The clauses And all the congregation lifted up, and they gave their voice and and the people wept mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [And all the congregation wept very loudly in that night]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 14:1 (#3)
content:
אֶת־קוֹלָ֑⁠ם

"their voice"

In this verse, the word voice is singular in form, but it refers to all the Israelites as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “voice.” Alternate translation: [their voices]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 14:2 (#1)
content:
לוּ־מַ֨תְנוּ֙ בְּ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֔יִם א֛וֹ בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֥ר הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לוּ־מָֽתְנוּ

"If only we died in the land of Egypt, or if only we died in this wilderness"

The Israelites are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, hopelessness and despair. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what the Israelites were feeling, or you could say what made them sad. Alternate translation: [It would have been better for us to die in the land of Egypt! It would be better for us to die in this wilderness!]

See: Exclamations

title: Numbers 14:2 (#2)
content:
לוּ־מַ֨תְנוּ֙ בְּ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֔יִם א֛וֹ בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֥ר הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לוּ־מָֽתְנוּ

"If only we died in the land of Egypt, or if only we died in this wilderness"

It might seem that the expression if only we died contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [If only we died in the land of Egypt or in this wilderness!]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:2 (#3)
content:
מַ֨תְנוּ֙ & מָֽתְנוּ

"we died & we died"

By we, the Israelites mean to include themselves but not Moses and Aaron to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 14:3 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לָ⁠מָ֣ה יְ֠הוָה מֵבִ֨יא אֹתָ֜⁠נוּ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֤רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּאת֙ לִ⁠נְפֹּ֣ל בַּ⁠חֶ֔רֶב

"And why is Yahweh bringing us to this land to fall by the sword"

The Israelites are using the question form to express their complaint against Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We do not like how Yahweh has brought us to this land, since we will fall by the sword.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 14:3 (#2)
content:
אֹתָ֜⁠נוּ & נָשֵׁ֥י⁠נוּ וְ⁠טַפֵּ֖⁠נוּ & לָ֖⁠נוּ

"us & Our wives and our children & for us"

By us … Our wives and our children … for us, the Israelites mean themselves, their families, and others in the congregation, but excluding Moses and Aaron to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of those words if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 14:3 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠נְפֹּ֣ל בַּ⁠חֶ֔רֶב

"to fall by the sword"

The phrase to fall by the sword is a common expression of this culture that means “to die in battle.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to die in battle]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:3 (#4)
content:
לָ⁠בַ֑ז

"for plunder"

By for plunder, the Israelites mean that their families would be taken away as slaves. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [slaves]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:3 (#5)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֧וֹא ט֦וֹב לָ֖⁠נוּ שׁ֥וּב מִצְרָֽיְמָ⁠ה

"Is it not good for us to return to Egypt"

The Israelites are using the question form to make a strong statement that they believe returning to Egypt would be good for them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is good for us to return to Egypt.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 14:4 (#1)
content:
נִתְּנָ֥ה רֹ֖אשׁ

"We shall give a head"

Here, the Israelites are speaking of appointing a leader as if they would give a head. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We shall appoint a chief]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:4 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּאמְר֖וּ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־אָחִ֑י⁠ו

"And they said, a man to his brother"

The phrase a man to his brother is a common expression of this culture that means “to one another.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they said to one another]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:4 (#3)
content:
נִתְּנָ֥ה & וְ⁠נָשׁ֥וּבָה

"We shall give & and we shall return"

By We, the Israelites mean to include themselves and also the other Israelites to whom they are speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word in your language if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 14:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּפֹּ֥ל מֹשֶׁ֛ה וְ⁠אַהֲרֹ֖ן עַל־פְּנֵי⁠הֶ֑ם

"And Moses fell and Aaron on their faces"

Falling on their faces was a symbolic action by which Moses and Aaron showed their dismay and grief at the Israelites’ rebellion. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And Moses lay and Aaron with their faces on the ground to show their grief] or [And Moses bowed and Aaron with their faces to the ground in sorrow]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Numbers 14:5 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּפֹּ֥ל מֹשֶׁ֛ה וְ⁠אַהֲרֹ֖ן

"And Moses fell and Aaron"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Aaron with the information about Moses. Alternate translation: [And Moses and Aaron fell]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 14:5 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֕י

"to the face of"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of the Israelite assembly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:5 (#4)
content:
כָּל־קְהַ֥ל עֲדַ֖ת בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"all the assembly of the congregation of the sons of Israel"

The author is using the possessive form to describe an assembly that is made up of the congregation that is the sons of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the congregation that consists of all the sons of Israel assembled together]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 14:5 (#5)
content:
קְהַ֥ל עֲדַ֖ת

"the assembly of the congregation of"

The terms assembly and congregation mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the congregation]

See: Doublet

title: Numbers 14:6 (#1)
content:
נ֗וּן & יְפֻנֶּ֔ה

"Nun & Jephunneh"

The words Nun and Jephunneh are the names of men.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 14:6 (#2)
content:
מִן־הַ⁠תָּרִ֖ים אֶת־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ

"from the ones exploring the land"

The phrase from the ones exploring the land is a common expression of this culture that means “who were among those who explored the land.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who were among those who explored the land]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:6 (#3)
content:
קָרְע֖וּ בִּגְדֵי⁠הֶֽם

"tore their clothes"

The act of tearing their clothes was a symbolic action by which Joshua and Caleb showed their extreme distress and grief over the people’s unbelief. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [tore their clothes in sorrow] or [were so distressed that they ripped their clothes]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Numbers 14:7 (#1)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר

"saying"

Here, the word saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 14:7 (#2)
content:
עָבַ֤רְנוּ

"we passed"

By we, Joshua and Caleb mean themselves but not the other Israelites to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 14:7 (#3)
content:
טוֹבָ֥ה הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ מְאֹ֥ד מְאֹֽד

"is} a very, very good land"

The author is repeating forms of the word very in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [an incredibly good land]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 14:8 (#1)
content:
הִ֛וא זָבַ֥ת חָלָ֖ב וּ⁠דְבָֽשׁ

"is flowing {with} milk and honey"

Here, Joshua and Caleb are speaking of Canaan as if it were a land that had streams of milk and honey flowing through it. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this clause in 13:27. Alternate translation: [is rich and fertile] or [is very productive]

See: Metaphor

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 14:8 (#2)
content:
אִם־חָפֵ֥ץ בָּ֨⁠נוּ֙ יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠הֵבִ֤יא אֹתָ֨⁠נוּ֙ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֔את

"If Yahweh delights in us, then he will bring us to this land"

The author is describing a possible condition in which he will bring us to this land will take place only if Yahweh delights in us occurs first. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Suppose that Yahweh delights in us. In that case, he will bring us to this land]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 14:8 (#3)
content:
בָּ֨⁠נוּ֙ & אֹתָ֨⁠נוּ֙ & לָ֑⁠נוּ

"in us & us & to us"

By us, Joshua and Caleb mean to include both themselves and their Israelite listeners, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 14:9 (#1)
content:
לַחְמֵ֖⁠נוּ הֵ֑ם

"they {are} our bread"

Here, Joshua and Caleb are speaking as if the Canaanites were actually bread. They mean that the Israelites will defeat them as easily as they eat food. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are like our bread] or [we will conquer them as easily as eating bread]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:9 (#2)
content:
סָ֣ר צִלָּ֧⁠ם מֵ⁠עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם

"Their shadow turned aside from upon them"

Here, Joshua and Caleb are speaking as if the protection the Canaanites had were actually a shadow that had departed from them. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Any protection they had is gone]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:9 (#3)
content:
אַ֣ךְ

"Only"

Here the word Only introduces something that is very important because of the previous statement. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [So it is important that]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 14:9 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אַתֶּ֗ם אַל־תִּֽירְאוּ֙ אֶת־עַ֣ם הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ כִּ֥י לַחְמֵ֖⁠נוּ הֵ֑ם

"and you, you shall not fear the people of the land, for they {are} our bread"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that you shall not fear the people of the land describes. Alternate translation: [and because the people of the land are our bread, you, you shall not fear them]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 14:9 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אַתֶּ֗ם אַל־תִּֽירְאוּ֙

"and you, you shall not fear"

Here the author is repeating the pronoun you along with the verb translated as shall not fear, which already includes its meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that the Israelites should trust God rather than be afraid. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [and you shall not fear]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 14:10 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ כָּל־הָ֣⁠עֵדָ֔ה לִ⁠רְגּ֥וֹם אֹתָ֖⁠ם בָּ⁠אֲבָנִ֑ים

"And all the congregation said to stone them with stones"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [And all the congregation said, “Stone them with stones!”]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Numbers 14:10 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠רְגּ֥וֹם אֹתָ֖⁠ם בָּ⁠אֲבָנִ֑ים

"to stone them with stones"

It might seem that the expression to stone them with stones contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [to stone them]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:10 (#3)
content:
אֹתָ֖⁠ם

"them"

Here, the pronoun them could refer to: (1) Caleb and Joshua. Alternate translation: [them, that is, Caleb and Joshua,]; or (2) Moses and Aaron. Alternate translation: [Moses and Aaron]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 14:10 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠כְב֣וֹד יְהוָ֗ה נִרְאָה֙

"But the glory of Yahweh appeared"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of glory, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh showed himself gloriously]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:10 (#5)
content:
בְּ⁠אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֔ד

"in the tent of meeting"

Here, the author could mean that Yahweh’s glory appeared: (1) at or near the tent of meeting. Alternate translation: [near the tent of meeting]; or (2) inside the tent of meeting. Alternate translation: [inside the tent of meeting]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:11 (#1)
content:
עַד־אָ֥נָה יְנַאֲצֻ֖⁠נִי הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה וְ⁠עַד־אָ֨נָה֙ לֹא־יַאֲמִ֣ינוּ בִ֔⁠י בְּ⁠כֹל֙ הָֽ⁠אֹת֔וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשִׂ֖יתִי בְּ⁠קִרְבּֽ⁠וֹ

"Until when will this people spurn me? And until when will it not believe in me, in all the signs that I have done in its midst"

Yahweh is using the question form to express his anger and frustration that the people keep rejecting him and not believing in him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [This people needs to stop spurning me! And they need to stop not believing in me, in all the signs that I have done in its midst!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 14:11 (#2)
content:
לֹא־יַאֲמִ֣ינוּ & בְּ⁠קִרְבּֽ⁠וֹ

"will it not believe & in its midst"

The pronoun it refers to the people of Israel, and the pronoun its refers to the same group. In Hebrew, these pronouns are singular, even though they refer to a group of people. If it would be more natural in your language, you could use plural pronouns as in the alternate translation. Alternate translation: [will this people not believe … in their midst]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 14:12 (#1)
content:
אַכֶּ֥⁠נּוּ & וְ⁠אוֹרִשֶׁ֑⁠נּוּ & מִמֶּֽ⁠נּוּ

"I will strike it & and I will dispossess it & than it"

The pronoun it refers to the Israelite people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I will strike this people … and I will dispossess them … than they]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 14:12 (#2)
content:
אַכֶּ֥⁠נּוּ

"I will strike it"

The implication is that Yahweh will kill the people with a plague. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to Numbers. Alternate translation: [I will make it die]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:12 (#3)
content:
בַ⁠דֶּ֖בֶר

"with the plague"

Yahweh is not referring to a specific plague. He means an unspecified plague. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with a plague]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 14:12 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אֶֽעֱשֶׂה֙ אֹֽתְ⁠ךָ֔ לְ⁠גוֹי

"and I will make you into a nation"

By I will make you into a nation, Yahweh means he will make Moses’ descendants into a nation. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will make your offspring into a nation]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:13 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁמְע֣וּ מִצְרַ֔יִם

"And Egypt shall hear"

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [But Egypt shall hear] or [Then Egypt shall hear]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 14:13 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁמְע֣וּ מִצְרַ֔יִם

"And Egypt shall hear"

By Egypt shall hear, Moses means that the Egyptians will hear about what Yahweh has done to the Israelites. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Egypt shall hear if you do those things]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:13 (#3)
content:
מִצְרַ֔יִם

"Egypt"

Here, Egypt represents the people of Egypt. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Egypt]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:13 (#4)
content:
כִּֽי־הֶעֱלִ֧יתָ & אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה

"for you brought this people up"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. In this case, the Egyptians will hear because they are the ones from whom God rescued the Israelites. Alternate translation: [for they are paying attention because you brought this people up]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 14:13 (#5)
content:
הֶעֱלִ֧יתָ & אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה

"you brought this people up"

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, Moses is marking travel for change in elevation. If the expression you brought this people up contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [you brought this people]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:13 (#6)
content:
בְ⁠כֹחֲ⁠ךָ֛

"with your power"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of power, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in a powerful way]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:14 (#1)
content:
אַתָּ֨ה הֹלֵ֤ךְ לִ⁠פְנֵי⁠הֶם֙

"you are going before to their face"

Here, Moses is speaking of Yahweh as if he were going before the people to show them the way. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are guiding]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:14 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אָמְר֗וּ

"and they shall say"

The implication is that they will tell others about what Yahweh had done to Israel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they shall tell what you did]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:14 (#3)
content:
אֶל־יוֹשֵׁב֮

"to the one dwelling in"

In this verse, the word one dwelling is singular in form, but it refers to all inhabitants of Canaan as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “one dwelling.” Alternate translation: [to the ones dwelling]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 14:14 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־עַ֨יִן בְּ⁠עַ֜יִן נִרְאָ֣ה ׀ אַתָּ֣ה יְהוָ֗ה

"who appears eye in eye, you, Yahweh"

Moses is using the expression eye in eye as a common expression of his culture to mean “face to face” or “directly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who appears face to face, you, Yahweh] or [who appears so that they can see you plainly, Yahweh]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:14 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠עֲנָֽנְ⁠ךָ֙ עֹמֵ֣ד עֲלֵ⁠הֶ֔ם

"and your cloud is standing over them"

Here Moses is speaking of the cloud as if it were a living thing that could stand over people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar figures of speech in Numbers 9:17–19. Alternate translation: [and you have your cloud hover over them]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 14:14 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠עַמֻּ֣ד עָנָ֗ן & וּ⁠בְ⁠עַמּ֥וּד אֵ֖שׁ

"and in a pillar of cloud & and in a pillar of fire"

Moses is using the possessive form to describe a cloud that looks like a pillar and fire that looks like a pillar. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and in a cloud in the shape of a pillar … and in fire in the shape of a pillar]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 14:14 (#7)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵי⁠הֶם֙

"before to their face"

Here, to their face represents being in front of the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before them]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֵמַתָּ֛ה

"And you kill"

The word And introduces the “if” portion of a hypothetical statement. Moses is describing a possible condition in which the nations saying certain things will take place only if Yahweh kills all the Israelites. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [If you kill]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 14:15 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠אִ֣ישׁ אֶחָ֑ד

"as one man"

The point of this comparison is that just as killing one man is quick and complete, so would be killing all the Israelites at once. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [at one time] or [as quickly as killing one man]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 14:15 (#3)
content:
שָׁמְע֥וּ אֶֽת־שִׁמְעֲ⁠ךָ֖

"heard your hearing"

Moses is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [heard about you]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 14:15 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אָֽמְרוּ֙ הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֔ם אֲשֶׁר־שָׁמְע֥וּ אֶֽת־שִׁמְעֲ⁠ךָ֖ לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"then the nations who heard your hearing will say, saying"

The term saying introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent the term explicitly. Alternate translation: [then the nations who heard your hearing will say]

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 14:16 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠בִּלְתִּ֞י יְכֹ֣לֶת יְהוָ֗ה לְ⁠הָבִיא֙ אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ אֲשֶׁר־נִשְׁבַּ֣ע לָ⁠הֶ֑ם וַ⁠יִּשְׁחָטֵ֖⁠ם בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּֽר

"From Yahweh not being able to bring this people to the land that he swore to them, so he slaughtered them in the wilderness"

The word translated as From indicates that what follows is a reason for what comes after. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what comes after. Alternate translation: [‘Because Yahweh was not able to bring this people to the land that he swore to them, he slaughtered them in the wilderness’]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 14:16 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־נִשְׁבַּ֣ע לָ⁠הֶ֑ם

"that he swore to them"

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [that he swore to hand over to them]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 14:17 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עַתָּ֕ה

"And now"

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Therefore]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 14:17 (#2)
content:
יִגְדַּל & כֹּ֣חַ אֲדֹנָ֑⁠י

"may the power of my Lord be great"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of power, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [may my Lord act very powerfully]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:17 (#3)
content:
אֲדֹנָ֑⁠י

"of my Lord"

Even though Moses is addressing Yahweh directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as my Lord to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [of you, my Lord,]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 14:17–18 (#1)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹֽר & אֶ֤רֶךְ אַפַּ֨יִם֙ וְ⁠רַב־חֶ֔סֶד נֹשֵׂ֥א עָוֺ֖ן וָ⁠פָ֑שַׁע וְ⁠נַקֵּה֙ לֹ֣א יְנַקֶּ֔ה פֹּקֵ֞ד עֲוֺ֤ן אָבוֹת֙ עַל־בָּנִ֔ים עַל־שִׁלֵּשִׁ֖ים וְ⁠עַל־רִבֵּעִֽים

"saying & long of nostrils and great of covenant faithfulness, lifting up iniquity and transgression. But leaving unpunished, he will not leave unpunished, visiting iniquity of fathers upon sons, upon thirds, and upon fourths"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [saying that Yahweh is long of nostrils and great of covenant faithfulness, lifting up iniquity and transgression, and that leaving unpunished, he will not leave unpunished, counting iniquity of fathers upon sons, upon thirds, and upon fourths.]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 14:18 (#1)
content:
נֹשֵׂ֥א עָוֺ֖ן וָ⁠פָ֑שַׁע

"lifting up iniquity and transgression"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of forgiving sins as if a person were lifting up a heavy object and taking it away. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [granting forgiveness for]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:18 (#2)
content:
פֹּקֵ֞ד עֲוֺ֤ן אָבוֹת֙ עַל־בָּנִ֔ים עַל־שִׁלֵּשִׁ֖ים וְ⁠עַל־רִבֵּעִֽים

"visiting iniquity of fathers upon sons, upon thirds, and upon fourths"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of passing down the consequences of sin as if it were visiting iniquity upon later generations. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [making iniquity of fathers apply to sons, to thirds, and to fourths]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:18 (#3)
content:
יְהוָ֗ה אֶ֤רֶךְ & לֹ֣א יְנַקֶּ֔ה

"Yahweh {is} long of & he will not leave unpunished"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, am … I will not leave unpunished]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 14:18 (#4)
content:
אֶ֤רֶךְ אַפַּ֨יִם֙

"long of nostrils"

The phrase long of nostrils is a common expression of this culture that means “slow to anger” or “patient.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [slow to anger] or [patient]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:18 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠רַב־חֶ֔סֶד

"and great of covenant faithfulness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of covenant faithfulness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and completely faithful to his promises]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:18 (#6)
content:
עָוֺ֖ן וָ⁠פָ֑שַׁע

"iniquity and transgression"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of iniquity and transgression, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what people do that is evil and that breaks my laws]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:18 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠נַקֵּה֙ לֹ֣א יְנַקֶּ֔ה

"But leaving unpunished, he will not leave unpunished"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb leave unpunished in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [But he will definitely not leave unpunished]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 14:18 (#8)
content:
לֹ֣א יְנַקֶּ֔ה

"he will not leave unpunished"

Here, Yahweh could be implying that he will not leave unpunished: (1) a different group of people than the ones he forgives. Alternate translation: [he will not leave other people unpunished]; or (2) the same group of people he forgives, who will receive some punishment despite being forgiven. Alternate translation: [he will not leave them completely unpunished]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:18 (#9)
content:
עֲוֺ֤ן אָבוֹת֙

"iniquity of fathers"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of iniquity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what fathers did that was evil]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:18 (#10)
content:
עָוֺ֖ן

"iniquity"

Here, iniquity represents the punishment for wrongdoing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the punishment for iniquity]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:18 (#11)
content:
עַל־שִׁלֵּשִׁ֖ים וְ⁠עַל־רִבֵּעִֽים

"upon thirds, and upon fourths"

Yahweh assumes that readers will know that thirds and fourths refer to the third and fourth generations of descendants. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [upon the people of the third generation, and upon the people of the fourth generation]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:19 (#1)
content:
לַ⁠עֲוֺ֛ן

"for the iniquity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of iniquity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for what they did that was evil]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:19 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠גֹ֣דֶל חַסְדֶּ֑⁠ךָ

"according to the greatness of your covenant faithfulness"

If your language does not use an abstract nouns for the ideas of greatness and covenant faithfulness, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [according to how much you are completely faithful to your promises]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:19 (#3)
content:
נָשָׂ֨אתָה֙

"you lifted up"

Here, Moses is speaking of forgiveness as if it were “lifting up.” You may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 14:18. Alternate translation: [you granted forgiveness]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:19 (#4)
content:
לָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֖יִם וְ⁠עַד־הֵֽנָּה

"for this people from Egypt and as far as here"

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [for this people as they came from Egypt to this place]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 14:20 (#1)
content:
סָלַ֖חְתִּי

"I have forgiven"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I have forgiven their iniquity]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 14:20 (#2)
content:
כִּ⁠דְבָרֶֽ⁠ךָ

"according to your word"

Yahweh is using the term word to represent what Moses said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to your request]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:21 (#1)
content:
חַי־אָ֑נִי וְ⁠יִמָּלֵ֥א כְבוֹד־יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"as} I live and {as} all the land is filled with the glory of Yahweh"

Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by his own life and by how all the land is filled with the glory of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [I swear by my life and by how all the land is filled with the glory of Yahweh]

See: Oath Formulas

title: Numbers 14:21 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יִמָּלֵ֥א & אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"and {as} all the land is filled"

The expression is filled is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [as I fill all the land]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 14:21 (#3)
content:
כְבוֹד־יְהוָ֖ה

"with the glory of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [with my glory]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 14:21 (#4)
content:
כְבוֹד־יְהוָ֖ה

"with the glory of Yahweh"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of glory, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with my glorious presence]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:21–22 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אוּלָ֖ם חַי־אָ֑נִי וְ⁠יִמָּלֵ֥א כְבוֹד־יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ׃ כִּ֣י כָל־הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֗ים הָ⁠רֹאִ֤ים אֶת־כְּבֹדִ⁠י֙

"However, {as} I live and {as} all the land is filled with the glory of Yahweh, that all the men seeing my glory"

Here, the phrase all the land is filled with the glory of Yahweh could be: (1) a second thing that Yahweh swears by. In this case, the phrase that all the men introduces what Yahweh swears. Alternate translation: [However, just as I live and just as all the land is filled with the glory of Yahweh, so all the men seeing my glory]; or (2) what Yahweh swears. In this case, the phrase that all the men introduces the reason for what Yahweh says in 14:23. Alternate translation: [However, as I live, so all the land shall be filled with the glory of Yahweh. Because all the men saw my glory]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 14:22 (#1)
content:
הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֗ים

"the men"

Here the masculine term men has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [the men and women]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 14:22 (#2)
content:
אֶת־כְּבֹדִ⁠י֙

"my glory"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of glory, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how glorious I am]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:22 (#3)
content:
זֶ֚ה עֶ֣שֶׂר פְּעָמִ֔ים

"this ten times"

Here, the phrase ten times could refer to: (1) many times, with ten standing for a significant number of times. Alternate translation: [these many times]; or (2) ten specific times. Alternate translation: [these ten individual times]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:22 (#4)
content:
זֶ֚ה

"this"

The pronoun this refers to the ten times when the Israelites tested God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 14:22 (#5)
content:
בְּ⁠קוֹלִֽ⁠י

"my voice"

Here, my voice represents what Yahweh told them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [what I told them]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:23 (#1)
content:
לֹ֥א יִרְאֽוּ⁠הָ

"will not see it"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of seeing the land to mean entering and experiencing it personally. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will not enter it] or [will not live in it]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:23 (#2)
content:
אִם־יִרְאוּ֙ אֶת־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִשְׁבַּ֖עְתִּי לַ⁠אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם

"if they see the land that I swore to their fathers"

Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (if they see the land that I swore to their fathers) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [if they see the land that I swore to their fathers, may I strike myself dead]

See: Oath Formulas

title: Numbers 14:23 (#3)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִשְׁבַּ֖עְתִּי לַ⁠אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם

"that I swore to their fathers"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. See how you translated the similar clause in verse 16. Alternate translation: [that I swore to hand over to their fathers]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 14:23 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠אֲבֹתָ֑⁠ם

"to their fathers"

Yahweh is using the term fathers to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to their predecessors]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:23 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠כָל

"And all"

Here the word And introduces a restatement that affirms the oath. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [In the end, all]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 14:24 (#1)
content:
עֵ֣קֶב הָֽיְתָ֞ה ר֤וּחַ אַחֶ֨רֶת֙ עִמּ֔⁠וֹ

"because another spirit was with him"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of Caleb’s attitude and character as if it were a spirit that was with him. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because he had a different attitude]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:24 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יְמַלֵּ֖א אַחֲרָ֑⁠י

"and he filled after me"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of Caleb’s faithfulness as if it were physically filling up the space behind Yahweh. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he was fully obedient to me] or [he was completely loyal to me]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:24 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠זַרְע֖⁠וֹ

"and his seed"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of Caleb’s descendants as if they were actually his seed. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his offspring]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:24 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠הֲבִֽיאֹתִ֗י⁠ו

"so I will bring him"

In a context such as this, your language might say “take” instead of bring. Alternate translation: [so I will take him]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 14:25 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָֽ⁠עֲמָלֵקִ֥י וְ⁠הַֽ⁠כְּנַעֲנִ֖י יוֹשֵׁ֣ב בָּ⁠עֵ֑מֶק

"And the Amalekite and the Canaanite are dwelling in the valley"

The sentence And the Amalekite and the Canaanite are dwelling in the valley could be: (1) a reason why the Israelites must go back to the wilderness. Alternate translation: [Now here is why you travel as I command: the Amalekite and the Canaanite are dwelling in the valley.]; or (2) a description of the area that Caleb’s offspring will inherit.
