Alternate translation: [His seed will possess a valley where the Amalekite and the Canaanite are dwelling]; or (3) an explanation that the author has included inside the quote. Alternate translation: [(It is important to know that the Amalekite and the Canaanite are dwelling in the valley.)]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:25 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָֽ⁠עֲמָלֵקִ֥י וְ⁠הַֽ⁠כְּנַעֲנִ֖י

"And the Amalekite and the Canaanite"

Here, the Amalekite and the Canaanite represent Amalekites and Canaanites in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Amalekites and the Canaanites]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 14:25 (#3)
content:
בָּ⁠עֵ֑מֶק

"in the valley"

Here, the phrase the valley could refer to: (1) a specific, nearby valley. Alternate translation: [in the valley near here]; or (2) many valleys in the region. Alternate translation: [in the valleys]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:25 (#4)
content:
פְּנ֨וּ וּ⁠סְע֥וּ לָ⁠כֶ֛ם

"turn and set out for you"

The word you is plural here because Yahweh is addressing the Israelites, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 14:25 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠סְע֥וּ לָ⁠כֶ֛ם

"and set out for you"

It might seem that the expression for you contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and set out]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:25 (#6)
content:
דֶּ֥רֶךְ יַם־סֽוּף

"the way of the Sea of Reeds"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a way that leads to the Sea of Reeds. This may refer to a well-known road. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way that leads to the Sea of Reeds]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 14:27 (#1)
content:
עַד־מָתַ֗י לָ⁠עֵדָ֤ה הָֽ⁠רָעָה֙ הַ⁠זֹּ֔את אֲשֶׁ֛ר הֵ֥מָּה מַלִּינִ֖ים עָלָ֑⁠י אֶת־תְּלֻנּ֞וֹת בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵ֧מָּה מַלִּינִ֛ים עָלַ֖⁠י שָׁמָֽעְתִּי

"Until when to this evil congregation, that they are murmuring against me? I have heard the murmurings of the sons of Israel, which they are murmuring against me"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Yahweh hearing the complaints of the Israelites before his question about how long he must endure this evil congregation, that they are murmuring against me. Alternate translation: [I have heard the murmurings of the sons of Israel, which they are murmuring against me. Until when to this evil congregation, that they are murmuring against me?]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 14:27 (#2)
content:
עַד־מָתַ֗י לָ⁠עֵדָ֤ה הָֽ⁠רָעָה֙ הַ⁠זֹּ֔את אֲשֶׁ֛ר הֵ֥מָּה מַלִּינִ֖ים עָלָ֑⁠י

"Until when to this evil congregation, that they are murmuring against me"

Yahweh is using the question form to express his frustration with the Israelites’ constant complaining. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This evil congregation needs to stop murmuring against me!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 14:27 (#3)
content:
עַד־מָתַ֗י לָ⁠עֵדָ֤ה הָֽ⁠רָעָה֙ הַ⁠זֹּ֔את אֲשֶׁ֛ר הֵ֥מָּה מַלִּינִ֖ים

"Until when to this evil congregation, that they are murmuring"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Until when will this evil congregation escape punishment, for they are murmuring]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 14:27 (#4)
content:
אֶת־תְּלֻנּ֞וֹת בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵ֧מָּה מַלִּינִ֛ים עָלַ֖⁠י

"the murmurings of the sons of Israel, which they are murmuring against me"

The term murmurings and the phrase they are murmuring come from the same root word. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [what the sons of Israel are murmuring against me]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 14:28 (#1)
content:
אֱמֹ֣ר אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֗ם חַי־אָ֨נִי֙ נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה אִם־לֹ֕א כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּרְתֶּ֖ם בְּ⁠אָזְנָ֑⁠י כֵּ֖ן אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֥ה לָ⁠כֶֽם

"Say to them, ‘{As} I live—the declaration of Yahweh—if not just as you spoke in my ears, thus I will do to you"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Say to them that as I live—the declaration of Yahweh—if not just as they spoke in my ears, thus I will do to them]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 14:28 (#2)
content:
אֱמֹ֣ר

"Say"

The word Say is singular here because Yahweh is speaking only to Moses. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 14:28 (#3)
content:
חַי־אָ֨נִי֙

"As} I live"

Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred: his life. For another example of this kind of oath, see verse 21. Alternate translation: [I swear by my life]

See: Oath Formulas

title: Numbers 14:28 (#4)
content:
חַי־אָ֨נִי֙ נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה אִם־לֹ֕א

"As} I live—the declaration of Yahweh—if not"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the declaration of Yahweh before the oath rather than interrupting the oath. Alternate translation: [This is the declaration of Yahweh: As I live, if not]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 14:28 (#5)
content:
אִם־לֹ֕א כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּרְתֶּ֖ם בְּ⁠אָזְנָ֑⁠י כֵּ֖ן אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֥ה לָ⁠כֶֽם

"if not just as you spoke in my ears, thus I will do to you"

Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (if not just as you spoke in my ears, thus I will do to you) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [if I do not do to you exactly what you spoke in my ears, may I strike myself dead]

See: Oath Formulas

title: Numbers 14:28 (#6)
content:
בְּ⁠אָזְנָ֑⁠י

"in my ears"

Yahweh is using the term in my ears to mean hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 11:1. Alternate translation: [while I could hear]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:29 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֣ר הַ֠⁠זֶּה יִפְּל֨וּ פִגְרֵי⁠כֶ֜ם וְ⁠כָל־פְּקֻדֵי⁠כֶם֙ לְ⁠כָל־מִסְפַּרְ⁠כֶ֔ם מִ⁠בֶּ֛ן עֶשְׂרִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וָ⁠מָ֑עְלָ⁠ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֲלִֽינֹתֶ֖ם עָלָֽ⁠י

"In this wilderness your corpses will fall and all your counted ones according to all your number, from a son of 20 years and upward, who murmured against me"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [In this wilderness their corpses will fall and all their counted ones according to all their number, from a son of 20 years and upward, who murmured against me]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 14:29 (#2)
content:
יִפְּל֨וּ פִגְרֵי⁠כֶ֜ם

"your corpses will fall"

Yahweh is using your corpses will fall as a common expression of this culture to mean “you will die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will experience death]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:29 (#3)
content:
יִפְּל֨וּ & וְ⁠כָל

"will fall and all"

Here the word and introduces an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [will fall, that is, all]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 14:29 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־פְּקֻדֵי⁠כֶם֙

"and all your counted ones"

The expression counted ones is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelite leaders. See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4. Alternate translation: [and all of you whom your leaders counted]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 14:29 (#5)
content:
מִ⁠בֶּ֛ן עֶשְׂרִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וָ⁠מָ֑עְלָ⁠ה

"from a son of 20 years and upward"

The phrase from a son of 20 years and upward is a common expression of this culture that means “those who were 20 years old or older.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 1:3. Alternate translation: [those who were 20 years old or older]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:30 (#1)
content:
אִם־אַתֶּם֙ תָּבֹ֣אוּ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָשָׂ֨אתִי֙ אֶת־יָדִ֔⁠י לְ⁠שַׁכֵּ֥ן אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם בָּ֑⁠הּ כִּ֚י אִם־כָּלֵ֣ב בֶּן־יְפֻנֶּ֔ה וִ⁠יהוֹשֻׁ֖עַ בִּן־נֽוּן

"if you go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make you dwell in it, except Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, the son of Nun"

If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [if they go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make them dwell in it, except Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, the son of Nun]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 14:30 (#2)
content:
אִם־אַתֶּם֙ תָּבֹ֣אוּ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָשָׂ֨אתִי֙ אֶת־יָדִ֔⁠י לְ⁠שַׁכֵּ֥ן אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם בָּ֑⁠הּ

"if you go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make you dwell in it"

Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (if you go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make you dwell in it) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [may I strike myself dead if you go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make you dwell in it]

See: Oath Formulas

title: Numbers 14:30 (#3)
content:
נָשָׂ֨אתִי֙ אֶת־יָדִ֔⁠י

"I have lifted up my hand"

The expression lifted up my hand was a symbolic action by which Yahweh showed that he was making a solemn oath or promise. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I have sworn by lifting up my hand]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Numbers 14:30–31 (#1)
content:
אִם־אַתֶּם֙ תָּבֹ֣אוּ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָשָׂ֨אתִי֙ אֶת־יָדִ֔⁠י לְ⁠שַׁכֵּ֥ן אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם בָּ֑⁠הּ כִּ֚י אִם־כָּלֵ֣ב בֶּן־יְפֻנֶּ֔ה וִ⁠יהוֹשֻׁ֖עַ בִּן־נֽוּן׃ וְ⁠טַ֨פְּ⁠כֶ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲמַרְתֶּ֖ם לָ⁠בַ֣ז יִהְיֶ֑ה

"if you go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make you dwell in it, except Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, the son of Nun, and your children whom you said will be for plunder"

If, in your language, it would appear that Yahweh was making a statement here and then contradicting it, you could reverse the order of the clauses so that the exception is stated first and then the larger group is named second. If you do, you may need to combine 14:30 and 14:31. Alternate translation: [except for Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, the son of Nun, and your children whom you said will be for plunder, if you go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make you dwell in it]

See: Connect — Exception Clauses

title: Numbers 14:31 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠טַ֨פְּ⁠כֶ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲמַרְתֶּ֖ם לָ⁠בַ֣ז יִהְיֶ֑ה וְ⁠הֵבֵיאתִ֣י אֹתָ֔⁠ם וְ⁠יָֽדְעוּ֙ אֶת־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר מְאַסְתֶּ֖ם בָּֽ⁠הּ

"and your children whom you said will be for plunder. And I will bring them, and they will know the land that you rejected"

If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [and their children whom they said will be for plunder. And I will bring those children, and they will know the land that their parents rejected]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 14:31 (#2)
content:
לָ⁠בַ֣ז

"for plunder"

The implication is that some people had said the Israelite children would be taken as plunder or slaves by the Canaanites. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 3. Alternate translation: [slaves]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:31 (#3)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲמַרְתֶּ֖ם לָ⁠בַ֣ז יִהְיֶ֑ה

"whom you said will be for plunder"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [about whom you said, “They will be for plunder.”]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Numbers 14:31 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הֵבֵיאתִ֣י אֹתָ֔⁠ם

"And I will bring them"

By I will bring them, Yahweh means he will bring them to the land of Canaan. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And I will bring them to Canaan]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:31 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הֵבֵיאתִ֣י אֹתָ֔⁠ם

"And I will bring them"

In a context such as this, your language might say “take” instead of bring. Alternate translation: [And I will take them]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 14:31 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠יָֽדְעוּ֙

"and they will know"

Here, know represents experiencing and being familiar with the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and they will live in] or [and they will enjoy]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:32 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠פִגְרֵי⁠כֶ֖ם אַתֶּ֑ם יִפְּל֖וּ בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֥ר הַ⁠זֶּֽה

"And you, your corpses will fall in this wilderness"

If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [And they, their corpses will fall in this wilderness]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 14:32 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠פִגְרֵי⁠כֶ֖ם אַתֶּ֑ם

"And you, your corpses"

Yahweh is stating the pronoun you separately, even though the phrase translated as your corpses already includes this meaning. He is doing that to transition clearly from speaking about the children of the Israelites to the Israelites themselves. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But concerning you, your corpses]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 14:32 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠פִגְרֵי⁠כֶ֖ם אַתֶּ֑ם יִפְּל֖וּ

"And you, your corpses will fall"

Yahweh is using your corpses will fall as a common expression of this culture to mean “you will die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in verse 29. Alternate translation: [And you, you will experience death]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:33 (#1)
content:
אֶת־זְנוּתֵי⁠כֶ֑ם

"your fornications"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of the Israelites’ unfaithfulness to him as if it were sexual unfaithfulness (fornications). If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your faithlessness]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:33 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נָשְׂא֖וּ אֶת־זְנוּתֵי⁠כֶ֑ם

"and they will lift up your fornications"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of the Israelites’ fornications as if they were a burden that their children would carry. This refers to the consequences of their unfaithfulness to Yahweh that their children would experience. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will be punished for your fornications] or [they will bear the penalty of your fornications]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:33 (#3)
content:
וּ֠⁠בְנֵי⁠כֶם יִהְי֨וּ רֹעִ֤ים בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּר֙ אַרְבָּעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה וְ⁠נָשְׂא֖וּ אֶת־זְנוּתֵי⁠כֶ֑ם עַד־תֹּ֥ם פִּגְרֵי⁠כֶ֖ם בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּֽר

"and your sons will be shepherds in the wilderness 40 years, and they will lift up your fornications until the finishing of your corpses in the wilderness"

If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [and their sons will be shepherds in the wilderness 40 years, and their sons will lift up their fornications until the finishing of their corpses in the wilderness]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 14:33 (#4)
content:
וּ֠⁠בְנֵי⁠כֶם

"and your sons"

Here the masculine term sons has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and your sons and daughters]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 14:33 (#5)
content:
יִהְי֨וּ רֹעִ֤ים

"will be shepherds"

The implication is that the sons will wander from place to place in the wilderness as they care for their flocks. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will be shepherds who roam]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:33 (#6)
content:
עַד־תֹּ֥ם פִּגְרֵי⁠כֶ֖ם

"until the finishing of your corpses"

The phrase until the finishing of your corpses is a common expression of this culture that means “until the last one of you has died.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until the last one of you experiences death]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:34 (#1)
content:
תִּשְׂאוּ֙ אֶת־עֲוֺנֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"you will lift up your iniquities"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if iniquities were a physical burden that the Israelites could lift up. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar clause in verse 33. Alternate translation: [you will be punished for your iniquities] or [you will bear the penalty of your iniquities]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:34 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠מִסְפַּ֨ר הַ⁠יָּמִ֜ים אֲשֶׁר־תַּרְתֶּ֣ם אֶת־הָ⁠אָרֶץ֮ אַרְבָּעִ֣ים יוֹם֒ י֣וֹם לַ⁠שָּׁנָ֞ה י֣וֹם לַ⁠שָּׁנָ֗ה תִּשְׂאוּ֙ אֶת־עֲוֺנֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם אַרְבָּעִ֖ים שָׁנָ֑ה וִֽ⁠ידַעְתֶּ֖ם אֶת־תְּנוּאָתִֽ⁠י

"By the number of the days that you explored the land, 40 days, a day for the year, a day for the year, you will lift up your iniquities 40 years. And you will know my opposition"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [By the number of the days that they explored the land, 40 days, a day for the year, a day for the year, they will lift up their iniquities 40 years. And they will know my opposition.]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 14:34 (#3)
content:
י֣וֹם לַ⁠שָּׁנָ֞ה י֣וֹם לַ⁠שָּׁנָ֗ה

"a day for the year, a day for the year"

Yahweh is using the common expression of this culture a day for the year, a day for the year to mean “one year for each day.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [one day to one year] or [one year for each day]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:34 (#4)
content:
אֶת־עֲוֺנֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"your iniquities"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the idea of iniquities, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what you did that was evil]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:34 (#5)
content:
אֶת־תְּנוּאָתִֽ⁠י

"my opposition"

Here, the word translated opposition could refer to: (1) enmity. Alternate translation: [my enmity]; or (2) displeasure. Alternate translation: [my displeasure]; or (3) absence. Alternate translation: [my absence]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:34 (#6)
content:
אֶת־תְּנוּאָתִֽ⁠י

"my opposition"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of opposition, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what it is like for me to oppose you]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 14:35 (#1)
content:
אֲנִ֣י יְהוָה֮ דִּבַּרְתִּי֒

"I, Yahweh, have spoken"

The implication is that when Yahweh speaks something, it will certainly happen. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, have spoken, so it will happen]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:35 (#2)
content:
אִם־לֹ֣א ׀ זֹ֣את אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֗ה לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עֵדָ֤ה הָֽ⁠רָעָה֙ הַ⁠זֹּ֔את הַ⁠נּוֹעָדִ֖ים עָלָ֑⁠י

"If I do not do this to all this evil congregation, the ones congregating against me"

Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (if I do not do this to all this evil congregation, the ones congregating against me) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [If I do not do this to all this evil congregation, the ones congregating against me, may I strike myself dead]

See: Oath Formulas

title: Numbers 14:35 (#3)
content:
זֹ֣את

"this"

Here, the pronoun this could refer to: (1) what Yahweh has declared in the previous verses. Alternate translation: [those things]; or (2) what he says at the end of this verse. Alternate translation: [what I am about to say]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 14:35 (#4)
content:
בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֥ר הַ⁠זֶּ֛ה יִתַּ֖מּוּ וְ⁠שָׁ֥ם יָמֻֽתוּ

"In this wilderness they will finish, and there they will die"

These two phrases In this wilderness they will finish and there they will die mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [In this wilderness they will end their lives and die]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 14:35 (#5)
content:
יִתַּ֖מּוּ

"they will finish"

Yahweh is using they will finish as a common expression of his culture to mean “they will die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will end their lives] or [they will experience death]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:36 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠הוֹצִ֥יא דִבָּ֖ה

"by bringing out a bad report"

Here, the author is speaking as if words were actually something that could be brought out, like items that can be carried. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar clause in chapter 13:32. Alternate translation: [by giving a bad report]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:36 (#2)
content:
עָלָי⁠ו֙

"against him"

Here, the pronoun him could refer to: (1) Moses. Alternate translation: [against Moses]; or (2) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [against Yahweh]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 14:37 (#1)
content:
מוֹצִאֵ֥י דִבַּת־הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ רָעָ֑ה

"bringing out an evil bad report of the land"

Here, the author is speaking as if words were actually something that could be brought out, like items that can be carried. See how you translated the similar clause in verse 36. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [giving an evil bad report of]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:37 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יָּמֻ֨תוּ֙ הָֽ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֔ים מוֹצִאֵ֥י דִבַּת־הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ רָעָ֑ה

"and they died, the men bringing out an evil bad report of the land"

It might seem that the expression the men bringing out an evil bad report of the land contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and those men died]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:37 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יָּמֻ֨תוּ֙

"and they died"

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [also they died] or [they died]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 14:37 (#4)
content:
בַּ⁠מַּגֵּפָ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"in the plague to the face of Yahweh"

The implication is that Yahweh sent the plague to punish these men. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to the face of Yahweh in the plague that he sent]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:37 (#5)
content:
בַּ⁠מַּגֵּפָ֖ה

"in the plague"

The author is not referring to a specific plague. He means an unspecified plague. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in a plague]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 14:37 (#6)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:38 (#1)
content:
חָיוּ֙ מִן־הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֣ים הָ⁠הֵ֔ם הַֽ⁠הֹלְכִ֖ים לָ⁠ת֥וּר אֶת־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"lived from those men, the ones having gone to explore the land"

The author is using from those men as a common expression of his culture to mean “among those men” or “out of those men.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [lived. They were the only ones who lived among those men, the ones having gone to explore the land]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:39 (#1)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֣ים הָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה

"these words"

Moses is using the term these words to represent what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh had declared]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:40 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּֽעֲל֥וּ

"and went up"

The implication is that the Israelites are preparing to leave. In verse 44, the text shows that they actually started marching up to fight. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and prepared to go up] or [and got ready to go up]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:40 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יַּֽעֲל֥וּ

"and went up"

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and went]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:40 (#3)
content:
אֶל־רֹאשׁ־הָ⁠הָ֖ר

"to the head of the hill country"

Here, the author is speaking as if a hill were a person with a head. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the heights of the hill country] or [to the top of the hill country]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 14:40 (#4)
content:
הִנֶּ֗⁠נּוּ וְ⁠עָלִ֛ינוּ & חָטָֽאנוּ

"Behold us! And we will go up & we sinned"

By us, the people mean to include themselves but not Moses to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 14:40 (#5)
content:
הִנֶּ֗⁠נּוּ

"Behold us"

The Israelites are using the term Behold us to focus their listeners’ attention on what they are about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen to us]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:40 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠עָלִ֛ינוּ אֶל־הַ⁠מָּק֛וֹם אֲשֶׁר־אָמַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה כִּ֥י חָטָֽאנוּ

"And we will go up to the place that Yahweh said, for we sinned"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [We sinned. So, now we will go up to the place that Yahweh said]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 14:40 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠עָלִ֛ינוּ

"And we will go up"

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And we will go]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:41 (#1)
content:
אַתֶּ֥ם עֹבְרִ֖ים

"are you passing over"

Here, Moses is speaking of disobedience as if it were physically passing over God’s command. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are you transgressing]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:41 (#2)
content:
לָ֥⁠מָּה זֶּ֛ה אַתֶּ֥ם עֹבְרִ֖ים אֶת־פִּ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"Why {is} this—are you passing over the mouth of Yahweh"

Moses is using the question form to rebuke the Israelites. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not pass over the mouth of Yahweh!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 14:41 (#3)
content:
לָ֥⁠מָּה זֶּ֛ה אַתֶּ֥ם עֹבְרִ֖ים

"Why {is} this—are you passing over"

It might seem that the expression is this contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [Why are you passing over]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:41 (#4)
content:
אֶת־פִּ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"the mouth of Yahweh"

Here, the mouth of Yahweh represents what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s command]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:41 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הִ֖וא

"And it will"

The pronoun it refers to their plan to go up to the high hill country. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And your plan]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 14:42 (#1)
content:
אֵ֥ין יְהוָ֖ה בְּ⁠קִרְבְּ⁠כֶ֑ם

"Yahweh is not in your midst"

Here, Moses is speaking of Yahweh as if he were physically present among the Israelites. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is not with you] or [Yahweh will not help you]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:42 (#2)
content:
אַֽל־תַּעֲל֔וּ כִּ֛י אֵ֥ין יְהוָ֖ה בְּ⁠קִרְבְּ⁠כֶ֑ם

"You shall not go up, for Yahweh is not in your midst"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is not in your midst, so you shall not go up]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 14:42 (#3)
content:
אַֽל־תַּעֲל֔וּ

"You shall not go up"

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, Moses is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression go up contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [You shall not go]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:42 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא֙ תִּנָּ֣גְפ֔וּ לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י אֹיְבֵי⁠כֶֽם

"and you shall not be struck to the face of your enemies"

The expression shall not be struck is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and your enemies shall not strike you to their face]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 14:42 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא֙ תִּנָּ֣גְפ֔וּ

"and you shall not be struck"

The words translated as and introduce what will happen if they do not go up. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and that way you shall not be struck]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 14:42 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא֙ תִּנָּ֣גְפ֔וּ

"and you shall not be struck"

The implication is that the Israelites will be defeated in battle by their enemies. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to Numbers. Alternate translation: [and you shall not be defeated]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:42 (#7)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י אֹיְבֵי⁠כֶֽם

"to the face of your enemies"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of your enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before your enemies]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:43 (#1)
content:
כִּי֩

"For"

Here the word For introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [More specifically,]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 14:43 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠עֲמָלֵקִ֨י וְ⁠הַ⁠כְּנַעֲנִ֥י

"the Amalekite and the Canaanite"

Here, the Amalekite and the Canaanite represent Amalekites and Canaanites in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. See how you translated the similar forms in verse 25. Alternate translation: [the Amalekites and the Canaanites]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 14:43 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"to your face"

Here, to your face represents being in front of you. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of you]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 14:43 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠נְפַלְתֶּ֖ם בֶּ⁠חָ֑רֶב

"and you will fall by the sword"

Moses is using fall by the sword as a common expression of his culture to mean “die in battle.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar words in verse 3. Alternate translation: [and you will die in battle]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 14:43 (#5)
content:
כִּֽי־עַל־כֵּ֤ן שַׁבְתֶּם֙ מֵ⁠אַחֲרֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠לֹא־יִהְיֶ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה עִמָּ⁠כֶֽם

"for upon this, you returned from after Yahweh, and Yahweh will not be with you"

Here, the phrase for upon this introduces a reason, which is you returned from after Yahweh. This clause could be the reason: (1) why the Israelites will fall by the sword. Alternate translation: [since you returned from after Yahweh. And Yahweh will not be with you]; or (2) why Yahweh will not be with them. Alternate translation: [and because you returned from after Yahweh, Yahweh will not be with you]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 14:43 (#6)
content:
שַׁבְתֶּם֙ מֵ⁠אַחֲרֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה

"you returned from after Yahweh"

Here, Moses is speaking as if the Israelites had literally been walking behind Yahweh but then returned from after him. He means that they stopped living in the manner in which Yahweh wants people to live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you stopped following Yahweh] or [you did not do what Yahweh said]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:44 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּעְפִּ֕לוּ לַ⁠עֲל֖וֹת

"And they presumed to go up"

The implication is that the Israelites were deliberately disobeying Moses and Yahweh by going up to the hill country. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And they disobeyed Moses and went up]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:44 (#2)
content:
לַ⁠עֲל֖וֹת

"to go up"

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation in to go up. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [to go]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:44 (#3)
content:
אֶל־רֹ֣אשׁ הָ⁠הָ֑ר

"to the head of the hill country"

Here, the author is speaking of the hill country as if it had a head, meaning its highest point or peak. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in verse 40. Alternate translation: [to the heights of the hill country] or [to the top of the hill country]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 14:44 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠אֲר֤וֹן בְּרִית־יְהוָה֙ וּ⁠מֹשֶׁ֔ה לֹא־מָ֖שׁוּ מִ⁠קֶּ֥רֶב הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶֽה

"but the box of the covenant of Yahweh and Moses did not depart from the midst of the camp"

The author is speaking of the box of the covenant of Yahweh as if it were a living thing that could depart or stay. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but no one carried the box of the covenant of Yahweh from the midst of the camp, and Moses also did not depart from the midst of the camp] or [but the box of the covenant of Yahweh and Moses stayed in the midst of the camp]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 14:45 (#1)
content:
וַֽ⁠יַּכְּת֖וּ⁠ם

"and beat them to pieces"

Here, the author is speaking of defeating the Israelites as if they were objects that they could beat … to pieces. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and pursued the scattered Israelite soldiers]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 14:45 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּ֤רֶד הָ⁠עֲמָלֵקִי֙ וְ⁠הַֽ⁠כְּנַעֲנִ֔י הַ⁠יֹּשֵׁ֖ב

"And the Amalekite and the Canaanite, the one dwelling & came down"

Here, the Amalekite and the Canaanite represent Amalekites and Canaanites in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. See how you translated the similar forms in verse 25. Alternate translation: [And the Amalekites and the Canaanites, the ones dwelling]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 14:45 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּ֤רֶד

"And & came down"

The expression came down marks a change in elevation that was usual for the author to express in his language and culture. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [came] or [arrived]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 14:45 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יַּכּ֥וּ⁠ם

"And they struck them"

The implication is that the Amalekites and Canaanites defeated the Israelites in battle and killed many of them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to Numbers. Alternate translation: [And they overpowered them] or [And they won the battle with them]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 14:45 (#5)
content:
הַֽ⁠חָרְמָֽה

"the Hormah"

The word Hormah is the name of a city. It was located south of Beersheba.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 14:45 (#6)
content:
הַֽ⁠חָרְמָֽה

"the Hormah"

It is very unusual for a name to have the word the with it in this language. The use of the here may imply that the author intended his readers to think about the meaning of the name Hormah, which comes from a word that means “to devote to destruction.” You could consider including this information in a footnote if it would be helpful to your readers.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers - Chapter 15 Introduction
content:
Numbers 15 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh gives instructions for grain and drink offerings, contributions from first batches of bread, atonement for unintentional sins, punishment for intentional sins, and tassels on clothing. The author also narrates a story about a man who gathered wood on the Sabbath.

  1. Yahweh gives instructions for offerings in the land of Canaan (1–21)
  2. Yahweh explains how to make offerings for sins committed by mistake (22–29)
  3. Yahweh warns against deliberate disobedience (30–31)
  4. A man is put to death for breaking the Sabbath law (32–36)
  5. Yahweh commands Israel to wear tassels as reminders of his commands (37–41)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Grain and drink offerings

This chapter includes instructions for what the Israelites were supposed to offer along with animal sacrifices. For each male lamb, ram, and bull that they offered, they needed to offer also a specific portion of grain and wine. The portion size was different for each animal. When the Israelites included the grain and drink offerings with each animal, Yahweh was pleased.

Contributions from first dough

This chapter includes instructions on contributions from the dough that the Israelites made from the first grain that they harvested each year. They were to make one loaf from this dough to give to Yahweh. This contribution would be similar to the contribution that farmers made from the first grain that they harvested. Some scholars think that the contribution of a loaf was specifically intended for Israelites who were not farmers and who did not have grain from a harvest to contribute.

Deliberate and unintentional sins

This chapter includes information on deliberate and unintentional sins. Deliberate sins are when people know that they are disobeying God and continue to do so anyway. They do not feel any regret or guilt for what they have done. Those people cannot atone for their sins but instead are punished. Unintentional sins are when people disobey God without realizing that they are disobeying. Those people can atone for their sins, and God gives instructions on what sacrifices to offer. Unintentional sins can be committed by many people together or by one person, and the sacrifices are different in these two cases.

The Sabbath

On the Sabbath, which was the seventh day of the week, the Israelites were not allowed to do any work. See Exodus 20:10 for the basic command. In this chapter, a man does work on the Sabbath (gathering firewood), and the Israelite leaders know that he did something wrong. However, they wait to hear from Yahweh how the man should be punished. Yahweh declares that the Israelites must kill him by throwing stones at him, so that is what they do. This story emphasizes how important keeping the Sabbath is to Yahweh.

Tassels

This chapter includes instructions on “tassels” that the Israelites were supposed to attach to their clothing. Tassels are groups of threads connected together that hang down from whatever they are attached to. In this case, the Israelites were supposed to attach the tassels to the corners of their garments. The outer garments that the Israelites wore were usually in the shape of a rectangle, so there would be four tassels, one at each corner. Each tassel needed to have one cord or thread of blue in it. These tassels functioned as visual reminders that the Israelites were supposed to think about and obey God’s commands.

Sojourners

The instructions in this chapter on grain and drink offerings and on atonement for unintentional sins apply to “sojourners” as well as to native Israelites. Sojourners were non-Israelites who lived among the Israelites. They were considered sojourners as long as they lived among the Israelites. The laws that include sojourners indicate that these foreigners could participate in worshiping and honoring Yahweh.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Order of events

This chapter includes both instructions that Yahweh gives Moses and a story about a man working on the Sabbath. The author does not clarify in what order these events happened or whether they happened before or after the events narrated in the previous chapter. It is recommended that you avoid using time words to connect these instructions and stories.

“a scent of pleasing”

Multiple times in this chapter, Yahweh describes a sacrifice as “a scent of pleasing” to or for him. This phrase refers to burning the sacrifice in a way that causes smoke to go up, picturing the sacrifice as being converted to pleasant-smelling smoke by the fire and arising to Yahweh in heaven, where he would smell the smoke and be pleased. That the sacrifice was accompanied by the gift of the pleasant-smelling smoke of the sacrifice was apparently crucial to the acceptance of the offering as an appropriate sacrifice on a person’s behalf.

Being “cut off” from the people

The punishment for deliberate sins was being “cut off” from the rest of the Israelites. Scholars are unsure exactly what penalty this phrase implies. It could refer to death by execution. It could refer to punishment from Yahweh in a way of his choice. It could refer to expulsion from the Israelite community. The UST and notes follow this last option. If possible, use a word or phrase that could be understood in several of these ways. If you must specify, it is recommended that you follow the UST and notes.

title: Numbers 15:2 (#4)

content:
וְ⁠עָשָׂ֛ה & יַעֲשֶֽׂה

"and he makes & he shall do"

Here the masculine terms he makes and he shall do have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and he or she makes … he or she shall do]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 15:14 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠יהוָ֑ה

"for Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [for me]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:15 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠קָּהָ֕ל חֻקָּ֥ה אַחַ֛ת לָ⁠כֶ֖ם וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֣ר הַ⁠גָּ֑ר חֻקַּ֤ת עוֹלָם֙ לְ⁠דֹרֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם כָּ⁠כֶ֛ם כַּ⁠גֵּ֥ר יִהְיֶ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"For} the assembly, a statute {is} one for you and for the sojourner, the one sojourning, a statute of eternity for your generations. As you, so the sojourner shall be to the face of Yahweh"

Here, the word statute could be referring to: (1) the specific instructions that Yahweh just told Moses concerning grain and drink offerings with animal sacrifices. Alternate translation: [For the assembly, this statute is the same for you and for the sojourner, the one sojourning, a statute of eternity for your generations. As you, so the sojourner shall be to the face of Yahweh in this case]; or (2) the instructions that Yahweh gave to Moses more generally. Alternate translation: [For the assembly, each statute is the same for you and for the sojourner, the one sojourning, statutes of eternity for your generations. As you, so the sojourner shall be to the face of Yahweh]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֣ר הַ⁠גָּ֑ר

"and for the sojourner, the one sojourning"

It might seem that the expression the sojourner, the one sojourning contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and for the one sojourning]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 15:15 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֣ר הַ⁠גָּ֑ר & כַּ⁠גֵּ֥ר

"and for the sojourner, the one sojourning & so the sojourner"

The author is not referring to a specific sojourner. He means foreigners in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and for the sojourners, the ones sojourning … so the sojourners]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 15:15 (#4)
content:
חֻקַּ֤ת עוֹלָם֙

"a statute of eternity"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a statute that is characterized by eternity. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 10:8. Alternate translation: [a statute that applies for eternity]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 15:15 (#5)
content:
חֻקַּ֤ת עוֹלָם֙

"a statute of eternity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of eternity, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 10:8. Alternate translation: [an eternal statute]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 15:15 (#6)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh] or [in Yahweh’s consideration]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 15:15 (#7)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [to my face]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:16 (#1)
content:
תּוֹרָ֥ה אַחַ֛ת וּ⁠מִשְׁפָּ֥ט אֶחָ֖ד יִהְיֶ֣ה לָ⁠כֶ֑ם וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֖ר הַ⁠גָּ֥ר אִתְּ⁠כֶֽם

"One law and one ordinance shall be for you and for the sojourner, the one sojourning with you"

Here, just as in 15:15, the words law and ordinance could be referring to: (1) the specific instructions that Yahweh just told Moses concerning grain and drink offerings with animal sacrifices. Alternate translation: [Concerning those instructions, the same law and the same ordinance shall be for you and for the sojourner, the one sojourning with you]; or (2) the instructions that Yahweh gave to Moses more generally. Alternate translation: [The same laws and the same ordinances shall be for you and for the sojourner, the one sojourning with you]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:16 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֖ר הַ⁠גָּ֥ר אִתְּ⁠כֶֽם

"and for the sojourner, the one sojourning with you"

It might seem that the expression the sojourner, the one sojourning with you contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and for the one sojourning with you]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 15:16 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֖ר הַ⁠גָּ֥ר

"and for the sojourner, the one sojourning"

The author is not referring to a specific sojourner. He means foreigners in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and for the sojourners, the ones sojourning]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 15:18 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֖ אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֑ם בְּ⁠בֹֽאֲ⁠כֶם֙ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲנִ֛י מֵבִ֥יא אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם שָֽׁמָּ⁠ה

"and say to them, ‘When you go to the land where I am bringing you"

In 15:18–31, Yahweh tells Moses to speak for him to the Israelites. To do so, he uses a quote inside another quote. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. See the book introduction for more information, and see the UST for an example.

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 15:18 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֖ אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֑ם

"and say to them"

The term and say to them introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 15:18 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠בֹֽאֲ⁠כֶם֙

"When you go"

In a context such as this, your language might say “come” instead of go. Alternate translation: [When you come]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 15:18 (#4)
content:
אֲנִ֛י מֵבִ֥יא אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם שָֽׁמָּ⁠ה

"I am bringing you"

In a context such as this, your language might say “taking” instead of bringing. Alternate translation: [I am taking you]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 15:19 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠לֶּ֣חֶם הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ

"from the bread of the land"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a bread that is made from what is produced by the land. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the bread that is made from what the land produces]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 15:19 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠לֶּ֣חֶם

"from the bread of"

The author is using one kind of food, bread, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the food]

See: Synecdoche

title: Numbers 15:19 (#3)
content:
תָּרִ֥ימוּ

"you shall raise"

Here, Moses is speaking of dedicating food to God as if a person could raise it up to him. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you shall set apart]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 15:19 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠יהוָֽה

"to Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [to me, Yahweh]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:20 (#1)
content:
רֵאשִׁית֙ עֲרִסֹ֣תֵ⁠כֶ֔ם חַלָּ֖ה תָּרִ֣ימוּ

"The first of your dough, a loaf, you shall raise"

By the first of your dough, the author means the first dough made from a new harvest of grain. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you first make dough from a new harvest of grain, you must make a loaf that you shall raise]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:20 (#2)
content:
רֵאשִׁית֙ עֲרִסֹ֣תֵ⁠כֶ֔ם

"The first of your dough"

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as first, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [Some of the initial batch of]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 15:20 (#3)
content:
תָּרִ֣ימוּ & תָּרִ֥ימוּ אֹתָֽ⁠הּ

"you shall raise & you shall raise it"

Here, Moses is speaking of setting grain aside as if it were actually raising it up to God. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 19. Alternate translation: [you shall set apart … you shall set it apart]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 15:20 (#4)
content:
כִּ⁠תְרוּמַ֣ת גֹּ֔רֶן כֵּ֖ן תָּרִ֥ימוּ אֹתָֽ⁠הּ

"As a contribution of the threshing floor, so you shall raise it"

The implication is that the contribution from the first dough should be treated the same way as contributions from grain harvested at the threshing floor. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When you raise it, it counts as a contribution of the threshing floor] or [You shall raise it in the same way that you raise a contribution of the threshing floor]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:20 (#5)
content:
כִּ⁠תְרוּמַ֣ת גֹּ֔רֶן

"As a contribution of the threshing floor"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a contribution that is characterized by coming from the threshing floor. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a contribution that comes from the threshing floor]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 15:21 (#1)
content:
מֵ⁠רֵאשִׁית֙ עֲרִסֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם תִּתְּנ֥וּ

"From the first of your dough you shall give"

The implication is that they will be making dough from newly harvested grain. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar words in verse 20. Alternate translation: [When you first make dough from a new harvest of grain, you shall give]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:21 (#2)
content:
מֵ⁠רֵאשִׁית֙ עֲרִסֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"From the first of your dough"

The word first refers to the beginning portion or initial batch of the dough. If your language would not represent this idea with an ordinal number, you could represent it in a form that your language would use. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 20. Alternate translation: [From the initial batch of]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Numbers 15:21 (#3)
content:
לַ⁠יהוָ֖ה

"to Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [to me, Yahweh,]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:22 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כִ֣י תִשְׁגּ֔וּ וְ⁠לֹ֣א תַעֲשׂ֔וּ

"And when you err and do not do"

The phrase err and do not do expresses a single idea. The phrase do not do tells more about err. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [And when you err by not doing]

See: Hendiadys

title: Numbers 15:22 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠כִ֣י תִשְׁגּ֔וּ

"And when you err"

To err is to make a mistake or do something wrong. If your readers would not be familiar with what erring is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And when you do something wrong by accident]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 15:22 (#3)
content:
דִּבֶּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה

"Yahweh has spoken"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I have spoken]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:23 (#1)
content:
צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה & צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה

"Yahweh has commanded & Yahweh commanded"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I have commanded … I commanded]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:23 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠יַד־מֹשֶׁ֑ה

"in the hand of Moses"

The author is using in the hand of Moses as a common expression of this culture to mean “under Moses’ authority” or “through Moses.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 4:37. Alternate translation: [under the supervision of Moses]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 15:23 (#3)
content:
מִן־הַ⁠יּ֞וֹם

"from the day"

The author is using the term day to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the moment]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 15:23 (#4)
content:
וָ⁠הָ֖לְאָה

"and beyond"

The author is using and beyond as a common expression of this culture to mean “and ever since and into the future.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and onward] or [and ever since and into the future]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 15:24 (#1)
content:
מֵ⁠עֵינֵ֣י הָ⁠עֵדָה֮

"from the eyes of the congregation"

Here, from the eyes of represents the knowledge or awareness of the congregation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [without the knowledge of the congregation]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 15:24 (#2)
content:
נֶעֶשְׂתָ֣ה

"it was done"

The expression it was done is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. Alternate translation: [you did it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 15:24 (#3)
content:
בֶּן־בָּקָר֩ אֶחָ֨ד

"one son of cattle"

Here, the author is speaking of a young bull as if it were actually a son of cattle. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 8. Alternate translation: [one that is young]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 15:24 (#4)
content:
כַּ⁠מִּשְׁפָּ֑ט

"according to the ordinance"

The implication is that these offerings must be made according to the instructions that Yahweh had already given about grain and drink offerings. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [according to the ordinance about grain and drink offerings I just gave you]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:24 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠שְׂעִיר־עִזִּ֥ים אֶחָ֖ד

"and one buck of the goats"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a buck that is characterized by being one of the goats. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in chapter 7:16. Alternate translation: [and a goat that is a buck] or [and an adult male goat]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 15:25 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כִפֶּ֣ר הַ⁠כֹּהֵ֗ן עַֽל־כָּל־עֲדַ֛ת בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל

"And the priest shall make atonement for all the congregation of the sons of Israel"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of atonement, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And the priest shall offer the sacrifices to restore all the congregation of the sons of Israel to Yahweh]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 15:25 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נִסְלַ֣ח לָ⁠הֶ֑ם כִּֽי־שְׁגָגָ֣ה הִ֔וא וְ⁠הֵם֩ הֵבִ֨יאוּ אֶת־קָרְבָּנָ֜⁠ם אִשֶּׁ֣ה לַֽ⁠יהוָ֗ה וְ⁠חַטָּאתָ֛⁠ם לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה עַל־שִׁגְגָתָֽ⁠ם

"and it shall be forgiven for them, for it {was} a mistake, and they, they brought their offering, a gift, to Yahweh, and their sin offering to the face of Yahweh according to their mistake"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase it shall be forgiven for them describes. Alternate translation: [and because it was a mistake, and they, they brought their offering, a gift, to Yahweh, and their sin offering to the face of Yahweh according to their mistake, it shall be forgiven for them]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 15:25 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠נִסְלַ֣ח לָ⁠הֶ֑ם

"and it shall be forgiven for them"

The expression it shall be forgiven for them is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh shall forgive them]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 15:25 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הֵם֩ הֵבִ֨יאוּ

"and they, they brought"

The author is stating the pronoun they separately, even though the verb translated as brought already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that the Israelites themselves were the ones who brought the offering. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and as for them, they brought] or [and they brought]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 15:25 (#5)
content:
אֶת־קָרְבָּנָ֜⁠ם אִשֶּׁ֣ה לַֽ⁠יהוָ֗ה וְ⁠חַטָּאתָ֛⁠ם

"their offering, a gift, to Yahweh, and their sin offering"

By their offering, a gift, the author means the bull mentioned in verse 24, and by their sin offering, he means the male goat also mentioned in verse 24. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [their offering, a gift of the bull, and their sin offering, the male goat,]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:25 (#6)
content:
לַֽ⁠יהוָ֗ה & לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה

"to Yahweh & to the face of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [to me … to my face]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:25 (#7)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 15:26 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נִסְלַ֗ח לְ⁠כָל־עֲדַת֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֖ר הַ⁠גָּ֣ר בְּ⁠תוֹכָ֑⁠ם כִּ֥י לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֖ם בִּ⁠שְׁגָגָֽה

"And it shall be forgiven for all the congregation of the sons of Israel and for the sojourner, the one sojourning in their midst, for {it was} to all the people by mistake"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [It was to all the people by mistake. So, it shall be forgiven for all the congregation of the sons of Israel and for the sojourner, the one sojourning in their midst]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 15:26 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נִסְלַ֗ח לְ⁠כָל־עֲדַת֙

"And it shall be forgiven for all the congregation of"

The expression it shall be forgiven is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh shall forgive all the congregation]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 15:26 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֖ר הַ⁠גָּ֣ר בְּ⁠תוֹכָ֑⁠ם

"and for the sojourner, the one sojourning in their midst"

It might seem that the expression the sojourner, the one sojourning in their midst contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and for the one sojourning in their midst]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 15:26 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֖ר הַ⁠גָּ֣ר

"and for the sojourner, the one sojourning"

Here, sojourner and the one sojourning represent foreigners in general, not specific foreigners. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and for the sojourners, the ones sojourning]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 15:26 (#5)
content:
כִּ֥י לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֖ם בִּ⁠שְׁגָגָֽה

"for {it was} to all the people by mistake"

By it was to all the people by mistake, the author means that all the people had disobeyed unintentionally. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for all the people disobeyed by mistake]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:27 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִקְרִ֛יבָה

"then he shall present"

Here the masculine term he has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [then he or she shall present]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 15:27 (#2)
content:
בַּת־שְׁנָתָ֖⁠הּ

"a daughter of her year"

The author is using a daughter of her year as a common expression of this culture to mean “one year old.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase “a son of his year” in Numbers 6:12. Alternate translation: [a year old]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 15:28 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כִפֶּ֣ר הַ⁠כֹּהֵ֗ן עַל־הַ⁠נֶּ֧פֶשׁ הַ⁠שֹּׁגֶ֛גֶת בְּ⁠חֶטְאָ֥ה בִ⁠שְׁגָגָ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה לְ⁠כַפֵּ֥ר עָלָ֖י⁠ו

"And the priest shall make atonement for the person, the one erring in a sin by mistake to the face of Yahweh, to make atonement for him"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the idea of atonement, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And the priest shall offer the sacrifice to restore the person, the one erring in a sin by mistake to the face of Yahweh, to restore him]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 15:28 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 15:28 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [to my face]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:28 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠כַפֵּ֥ר עָלָ֖י⁠ו

"to make atonement for him"

It might seem that the expression to make atonement for him contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language since this has already been stated. If so, you could omit these words.

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 15:28 (#5)
content:
עָלָ֖י⁠ו & לֽ⁠וֹ

"for him & for him"

Here the masculine term him has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [for him or her … for him or her]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 15:28 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠נִסְלַ֥ח לֽ⁠וֹ

"and it shall be forgiven for him"

The expression it shall be forgiven for him is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh shall forgive him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 15:29 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֖ר הַ⁠גָּ֣ר בְּ⁠תוֹכָ֑⁠ם

"and for the sojourner, the one sojourning in their midst"

It might seem that the expression the sojourner, the one sojourning in their midst contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. See how you translated these phrases in verse 26. Alternate translation: [and for the one sojourning in their midst]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 15:29 (#2)
content:
הָֽ⁠אֶזְרָח֙ בִּ⁠בְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֖ר הַ⁠גָּ֣ר

"The native among the sons of Israel and for the sojourner, the one sojourning"

Here, native and sojourner, the one sojourning represent Israelites and foreigners in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The natives among the sons of Israel and for the sojourners, the ones sojourning]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 15:29 (#3)
content:
תּוֹרָ֤ה אַחַת֙ יִהְיֶ֣ה לָ⁠כֶ֔ם

"one law shall be for you"

The implication is that both native Israelites and sojourners must follow the same law when dealing with unintentional sins. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the same law shall apply for any of you]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:29 (#4)
content:
לָ⁠כֶ֔ם

"for you"

The word you is plural here because Yahweh is addressing all the Israelites and foreigners who live among them, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 15:30 (#1)
content:
אֲשֶֽׁר־תַּעֲשֶׂ֣ה ׀ בְּ⁠יָ֣ד רָמָ֗ה

"who does with a hand being high"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of doing something deliberately and defiantly as if it were done with a hand being high. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who sins boldly and deliberately] or [who transgresses on purpose]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 15:30 (#2)
content:
מִן־הָֽ⁠אֶזְרָח֙ וּ⁠מִן־הַ⁠גֵּ֔ר

"from the native and from the sojourner"

Here, native and sojourner represent Israelites and foreigners in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from natives and from sojourners]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 15:30 (#3)
content:
ה֣וּא מְגַדֵּ֑ף & עַמָּֽ⁠הּ

"he is blaspheming & his people"

Here the masculine terms he and his have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [he or she is blaspheming … his or her people]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 15:30 (#4)
content:
אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה

"Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, Yahweh]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:30 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠נִכְרְתָ֛ה הַ⁠נֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַ⁠הִ֖וא מִ⁠קֶּ֥רֶב עַמָּֽ⁠הּ

"and that person shall be cut off from the midst of his people"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of separating someone from the community as if that person were actually being cut off from the group. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [and that person shall be expelled from the midst of his people]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 15:30 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠נִכְרְתָ֛ה הַ⁠נֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַ⁠הִ֖וא מִ⁠קֶּ֥רֶב עַמָּֽ⁠הּ

"and that person shall be cut off from the midst of his people"

The expression shall be cut off is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. Alternate translation: [and the rest of the Israelites must cut off that person from their midst]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 15:31 (#1)
content:
כִּ֤י דְבַר־יְהוָה֙ בָּזָ֔ה וְ⁠אֶת־מִצְוָת֖⁠וֹ הֵפַ֑ר הִכָּרֵ֧ת

"for he despised the word of Yahweh and broke his commandment. Being cut off"

Here, the clause for he despised the word of Yahweh and broke his commandment could give a reason for: (1) the person being “cut off” in 15:30. Alternate translation: [which must happen because he despised the word of Yahweh and broke his commandment. Being cut off]; or (2) the person being “cut off” in this verse. Alternate translation: [Because he despised the word of Yahweh and broke his commandment, being cut off]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 15:31 (#2)
content:
דְבַר־יְהוָה֙ & מִצְוָת֖⁠וֹ

"the word of Yahweh & his commandment"
