Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [my word … my commandment]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:31 (#3)
content:
דְבַר־יְהוָה֙

"the word of Yahweh"

The author is using the term word of Yahweh to represent what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh spoke]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 15:31 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אֶת & הֵפַ֑ר

"and broke"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of his commandment as if it were an object that they broke when they disobeyed. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and failed to obey]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 15:31 (#5)
content:
הִכָּרֵ֧ת ׀ תִּכָּרֵ֛ת הַ⁠נֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַ⁠הִ֖וא

"Being cut off, that person shall be cut off"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb cut off in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [That person must certainly be cut off]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 15:31 (#6)
content:
הִכָּרֵ֧ת ׀ תִּכָּרֵ֛ת הַ⁠נֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַ⁠הִ֖וא

"Being cut off, that person shall be cut off"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of separating someone from the community as if that person were actually being cut off from the group. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [Being expelled, that person shall be expelled]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 15:31 (#7)
content:
הִכָּרֵ֧ת ׀ תִּכָּרֵ֛ת הַ⁠נֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַ⁠הִ֖וא

"Being cut off, that person shall be cut off"

The expressions Being cut off and shall be cut off are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the actions, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. Alternate translation: [Cutting off, the rest of the Israelites must cut off that person]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 15:31 (#8)
content:
עֲוֺנָ֥⁠ה בָֽ⁠הּ

"His iniquity {is} on him"

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if iniquity were a physical burden that a person could carry. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will be punished for his iniquity] or [He will bear the penalty of his iniquity]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 15:31 (#9)
content:
עֲוֺנָ֥⁠ה בָֽ⁠הּ

"His iniquity {is} on him"

Here the masculine terms him and his have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [His or her iniquity is on him or her]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 15:32 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּהְי֥וּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֑ר וַֽ⁠יִּמְצְא֗וּ

"And the sons of Israel were in the wilderness, and they found"

The story that this clause introduces probably did not happen immediately after the commands that Yahweh gave to Moses in the previous verses. It may have happened some time before or some time after the events in the previous verses. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use a word or phrase that introduces an event that may not be in sequence. Alternate translation: [Once, when the sons of Israel were in the wilderness, they found]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 15:32 (#2)
content:
וַֽ⁠יִּמְצְא֗וּ

"and they found"

The implication is that the Israelites were not looking for this man, but they happened to notice him gathering wood. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they saw]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:32 (#3)
content:
מְקֹשֵׁ֥שׁ עֵצִ֖ים

"gathering wood"

By gathering wood, the author means the man was gathering pieces of wood to use as fuel for a fire. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [gathering pieces of wood for a fire]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:33 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּקְרִ֣יבוּ & הַ⁠מֹּצְאִ֥ים אֹת֖⁠וֹ

"and the ones finding him & presented"

The implication is that the Israelites were not looking for this man, but they happened to notice him gathering wood. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 32. Alternate translation: [and the ones seeing him]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:33 (#2)
content:
מְקֹשֵׁ֣שׁ עֵצִ֑ים

"gathering wood"

By gathering wood, the author means that the man was gathering pieces of wood to use as fuel for a fire. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated this phrase in verse 32. Alternate translation: [gathering pieces of wood for a fire]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:34 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּנִּ֥יחוּ אֹת֖⁠וֹ בַּ⁠מִּשְׁמָ֑ר כִּ֚י לֹ֣א פֹרַ֔שׁ מַה־יֵּעָשֶׂ֖ה לֽ⁠וֹ

"And they made him rest in custody, for it had not been declared what should be done to him"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because it had not been declared what should be done to him, they made him rest in custody]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 15:34 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יַּנִּ֥יחוּ אֹת֖⁠וֹ בַּ⁠מִּשְׁמָ֑ר

"And they made him rest in custody"

The author is using made him rest in custody as a common expression of his culture to mean “put him under guard” or “kept him confined.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they put him under guard] or [And they kept him in a place for retraining people]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 15:34 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יַּנִּ֥יחוּ אֹת֖⁠וֹ

"And they made him rest"

The pronoun they refers to the leaders of the congregation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And those in charge made him rest]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 15:34 (#4)
content:
לֹ֣א פֹרַ֔שׁ

"it had not been declared"

The expression it had not been declared is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [there was no declaration about] or [Yahweh had not declared]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 15:34 (#5)
content:
מַה־יֵּעָשֶׂ֖ה לֽ⁠וֹ

"what should be done to him"

The expression what should be done to him is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. Alternate translation: [what they should do to him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 15:35 (#1)
content:
מ֥וֹת יוּמַ֖ת הָ⁠אִ֑ישׁ

"Dying, the man shall be put to death"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb dying in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [The man shall surely be put to death]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 15:35 (#2)
content:
מ֥וֹת יוּמַ֖ת הָ⁠אִ֑ישׁ

"Dying, the man shall be put to death"

The expression shall be put to death is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. Alternate translation: [The Israelites shall put the man, dying, to death]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 15:35 (#3)
content:
יוּמַ֖ת הָ⁠אִ֑ישׁ

"the man shall be put to death"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of death, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the man shall be killed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 15:35 (#4)
content:
רָג֨וֹם אֹת֤⁠וֹ בָֽ⁠אֲבָנִים֙

"stoning him with the stones"

It might seem that the expression stoning him with the stones contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [stoning him]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 15:35 (#5)
content:
בָֽ⁠אֲבָנִים֙

"with the stones"

Here, stones means stones in general, not specific stones. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with stones]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 15:35 (#6)
content:
מִ⁠ח֖וּץ לַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶֽה

"from outside to the camp"

Yahweh is using from outside to the camp as a common expression of this culture to mean “in the area outside the camp.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 12:14. Alternate translation: [in the area outside the camp]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 15:36 (#1)
content:
אֶל־מִ⁠חוּץ֙ לַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֔ה

"to from outside to the camp"

The expression to from outside to the camp is a common expression of this culture that means “to the area outside the camp.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 35. Alternate translation: [to the area outside the camp]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 15:36 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּרְגְּמ֥וּ אֹת֛⁠וֹ בָּ⁠אֲבָנִ֖ים

"and they stoned him with the stones"

It might seem that the expression stoned him with the stones contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. See how you translated the similar words in verse 35. Alternate translation: [and they stoned him]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 15:36 (#3)
content:
בָּ⁠אֲבָנִ֖ים

"with the stones"

The author is not referring to specific stones. He means stones in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with stones]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 15:37 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוָ֖ה

"And Yahweh spoke"

The author does not indicate exactly when Yahweh spoke the following words. It may have been before or after the events narrated in the previous verses. Avoid implying a time relationship with the previous section. Alternate translation: [One day, Yahweh spoke]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 15:38 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֔ם וְ⁠עָשׂ֨וּ לָ⁠הֶ֥ם

"and say to them, ‘And they shall make for themselves"

In 15:38–41, Yahweh tells Moses to speak for him to the Israelites. To do so, he uses a quote inside another quote. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. See the book introduction for more information, and see the UST for an example.

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 15:38 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֔ם

"and say to them"

The term and say to them introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 15:38 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠עָשׂ֨וּ לָ⁠הֶ֥ם צִיצִ֛ת עַל־כַּנְפֵ֥י בִגְדֵי⁠הֶ֖ם לְ⁠דֹרֹתָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠נָֽתְנ֛וּ

"And they shall make for themselves a tassel on the hems of their clothes for their generations, and they shall put"

Yahweh switches from the third person (they) to second person (“you”) in verse 39. This shows that Moses was supposed to tell the Israelites what they should do, and then tell them directly what the purpose was. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate all of these statements in the second person. Alternate translation: [And you shall make for yourselves a tassel on the hems of your clothes for your generations, and you shall put]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:38 (#4)
content:
צִיצִ֛ת & עַל־צִיצִ֥ת

"a tassel & on the tassel of"

A tassel is a kind of decorative tuft of threads or cords that hangs down. If your readers would not be familiar with what a tassel is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a tuft of threads … on the tuft of threads]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 15:38 (#5)
content:
עַל־כַּנְפֵ֥י בִגְדֵי⁠הֶ֖ם

"on the hems of their clothes"

The author assumes that readers will know that a typical garment in ancient Israel was a rectangular cloth with four corners at the hems or edges. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at each of the four places where the edges of your clothes meet]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:38 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠נָֽתְנ֛וּ עַל־צִיצִ֥ת הַ⁠כָּנָ֖ף פְּתִ֥יל תְּכֵֽלֶת

"and they shall put on the tassel of the hem a cord of blue"

The implication is that the blue cord needs to be attached to the tassel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they shall add to each tassel of the hem a cord of blue]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:38 (#7)
content:
עַל־צִיצִ֥ת הַ⁠כָּנָ֖ף

"on the tassel of the hem"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a tassel that is attached to the hem. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the tassel at each of the hems]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 15:39 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֣ה לָ⁠כֶם֮ לְ⁠צִיצִת֒ וּ⁠רְאִיתֶ֣ם אֹת֗⁠וֹ וּ⁠זְכַרְתֶּם֙ אֶת־כָּל־מִצְוֺ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה

"and it shall be for you for a tassel, and you shall see it, and you shall remember all the commandments of Yahweh"

The implication is that the Israelites will remember the commandments when they see the tassels. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and it shall be for you for a tassel, and when you see it, you shall remember all the commandments of Yahweh]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 15:39 (#2)
content:
אֶת־כָּל־מִצְוֺ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה

"all the commandments of Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [all my commandments]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:39 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־תָתֻ֜רוּ אַחֲרֵ֤י לְבַבְ⁠כֶם֙ וְ⁠אַחֲרֵ֣י עֵֽינֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"and you shall not explore after your heart and after your eyes"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of following sinful desires as if a person were exploring a path, going after their heart and eyes. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you shall not follow your heart and your eyes] or [And you shall not do whatever your heart and your eyes want]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 15:39 (#4)
content:
אַחֲרֵ֤י לְבַבְ⁠כֶם֙ וְ⁠אַחֲרֵ֣י עֵֽינֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"after your heart and after your eyes"

Here, heart represents thoughts or desires, and eyes represents what a person sees and desires. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [after your what you think and after what you see] or [after your thoughts and after your desires]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 15:39 (#5)
content:
אֲשֶׁר & אַחֲרֵי⁠הֶֽם

"after which"

Yahweh is using after which as a common expression of this culture to mean “because of which” or “at whose prompting.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at whose prompting] or [because of which]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 15:39 (#6)
content:
אַתֶּ֥ם זֹנִ֖ים

"you are committing fornication"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of the people’s disobedience as if it were committing fornication. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are being faithless]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 15:40 (#1)
content:
לְמַ֣עַן תִּזְכְּר֔וּ

"so that you shall remember"

Here, so that marks you shall remember as the goal or purpose of having tassels with blue cords. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [and so you shall remember] or [and the tassels will help you remember]

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Numbers 15:40 (#2)
content:
וִ⁠הְיִיתֶ֥ם קְדֹשִׁ֖ים

"and you shall be holy"

The word translated as and indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and that way you shall be holy]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 15:40 (#3)
content:
לֵֽ⁠אלֹהֵי⁠כֶֽם

"for your God"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as your God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [for me, your God]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 15:41 (#1)
content:
הוֹצֵ֤אתִי אֶתְ⁠כֶם֙

"brought you out"

In a context such as this, your language might say “took” instead of brought. Alternate translation: [took you out]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers - Chapter 16 Introduction
content:
Numbers 16 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, three men (Korah, Dathan, and Abiram) lead others in rebelling against Moses and Aaron. They want to be the leaders of the Israelites. However, Yahweh kills them and the people who agreed with them. After that, all the Israelites grumble against Moses and Aaron, and Yahweh begins to kill them too. However, Aaron offers incense for them, and Yahweh spares everyone who is still alive.

  1. Korah and other leaders challenge Moses and Aaron (1–19)
  2. Yahweh punishes the rebels with the opening of the ground and with fire (20–35)
  3. The rebels’ incense burners become a covering for the altar and a warning to Israel (36–40)
  4. The people complain, and Aaron makes atonement to stop a plague (41–50)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Korah, Dathan, and Abiram rebel

Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, along with many men who agreed with them, rebelled against Moses and Aaron. They argued that all the Israelites were holy, and that Aaron was improperly preventing them from approaching Yahweh. They argued that Moses was a bad leader who had not brought them to a fertile land as he had promised. They think that they should be leaders and priests instead of Moses and Aaron. Moses responds by telling them that they are not really rebelling against Moses and Aaron but against Yahweh, who appointed them. Yahweh then punishes Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and the people who agreed with them.

The Israelites rebel

After Yahweh punished Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and the people who agreed with them, the rest of the Israelites blame Moses and Aaron for killing them. Yahweh is angry and begins to kill them. Again, when the Israelites rebel against Moses and Aaron, they are rebelling against Yahweh, who appointed them.

Offering incense

In this chapter, people offer incense in several situations. To offer incense, they put hot coals or embers in a special pan and sprinkled incense on top of them. The incense would burn, creating a smoke that had a pungent smell. Moses had the 250 leaders who agreed with Korah, as well as Korah and Aaron, offer incense in Yahweh’s presence as a test. The person whom Yahweh chose would be the one he wanted to be priest. Later in the chapter, Aaron fulfilled the function of priest by burning incense among the people to make atonement for their sin of speaking against Moses and Aaron. Both times that people burn incense, it proves that Aaron is the real priest.

The plague

When Yahweh punishes the Israelites for rebelling against Moses and Aaron, he sends a “plague.” The word can refer to many different kinds of disasters. Some translations suggest that the “plague” is a kind of disease. The UST illustrates that option. Other translations use a more general word or phrase that refers to any kind of disaster that kills people.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Did Korah and Dathan and Abiram rebel in the same way?

Korah is a Levite, while Dathan and Abiram are Reubenites. When Moses responds to Korah, he speaks about Levites and priests, and the test for him and the people who agree with him includes offering incense to Yahweh. On the other hand, Dathan and Abiram critique Moses for how he has led them out of Egypt and into the wilderness. Therefore, it is likely that Korah wanted to remove Aaron from being priest, and Dathan and Abiram wanted to remove Moses from being leader. However, these three men and the people who agreed with them did work together. So, this is one rebellion that targets both Moses and Aaron.

When is each group of people punished?

Dathan, Abiram, and their families are punished when the ground opens and swallows them up. Some of the people who agreed with Korah are also punished at this time. While this chapter does not directly state when Korah himself was punished, 26:10–11 indicates that Korah too was swallowed up when the ground opened, although his sons did not die at this time. The 250 leaders of Israel were punished when they offered incense, and fire burned them up.

title: Numbers 16:1 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקַּ֣ח קֹ֔רַח בֶּן־יִצְהָ֥ר בֶּן־קְהָ֖ת בֶּן־לֵוִ֑י וְ⁠דָתָ֨ן וַ⁠אֲבִירָ֜ם בְּנֵ֧י אֱלִיאָ֛ב וְ⁠א֥וֹן בֶּן־פֶּ֖לֶת בְּנֵ֥י רְאוּבֵֽן

"And Korah, the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, took, and Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, and On, the son of Peleth, the sons of Reuben"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put all the names of the people who took before indicating that they took. Alternate translation: [And Korah, the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, and On, the son of Peleth, the sons of Reuben, took]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 16:1 (#2)
content:
יִצְהָ֥ר & קְהָ֖ת & וְ⁠דָתָ֨ן וַ⁠אֲבִירָ֜ם & אֱלִיאָ֛ב וְ⁠א֥וֹן & פֶּ֖לֶת

"Izhar & Kohath & and Dathan and Abiram & Eliab, and On & Peleth"

The words Izhar, Kohath, Dathan, Abiram, Eliab, On, and Peleth are the names of men.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 16:1 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקַּ֣ח

"And & took"

Here, the word took could imply that they: (1) took action, or decided to do something. Alternate translation: [took action]; or (2) took men with them. Alternate translation: [took men]; or (3) took confidence or boldness that they should not have had. Alternate translation: [became bold] or [rebelled]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:2 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּקֻ֨מוּ֙

"and they rose"

Here, the author is speaking of opposition as if it were physically rising against Moses. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they opposed]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:2 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י מֹשֶׁ֔ה

"to the face of Moses"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Moses. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in Moses’ presence]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 16:2 (#3)
content:
חֲמִשִּׁ֣ים וּ⁠מָאתָ֑יִם

"250"

Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [two hundred and fifty]

See: Numbers

title: Numbers 16:2 (#4)
content:
קְרִאֵ֥י מוֹעֵ֖ד

"called ones of meeting"

The expression called ones is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, it could be: (1) the other Israelites, who called them to participate in important meetings. Alternate translation: [whom the Israelites called to be at important meetings]; or (2) people at the meeting, who selected these men to be leaders. Alternate translation: [whom the people at a meeting had called]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 16:2 (#5)
content:
קְרִאֵ֥י מוֹעֵ֖ד

"called ones of meeting"

By called ones of, the author means they were selected or chosen for a specific purpose. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [chosen ones of]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:2 (#6)
content:
אַנְשֵׁי־שֵֽׁם

"men of name"

The author is using men of name as a common expression of his culture to mean “respected men” or “men of importance.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [respected men] or [well-known men]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:3 (#1)
content:
תִּֽתְנַשְּׂא֖וּ עַל־קְהַ֥ל יְהוָֽה

"do you lift yourselves up above the assembly of Yahweh"

Here, the protesters are speaking as if Moses and Aaron could physically lift themselves up above the rest of the people. They mean that Moses and Aaron had claimed authority over the assembly. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do you take authority for yourselves over the assembly of Yahweh] or [do you claim to be more important than the rest of the assembly of Yahweh]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:3 (#2)
content:
רַב־לָ⁠כֶם֒

"Great to you"

The Israelites are using Great to you as a common expression of their culture to mean “You take too much authority for yourself.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You make much of yourselves] or [You take too much authority]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:3 (#3)
content:
כִּ֤י

"For"

The word translated as For indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [We say that because]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 16:3 (#4)
content:
כָל־הָֽ⁠עֵדָה֙ כֻּלָּ֣⁠ם

"all of the congregation, all of them"

These two phrases all of the congregation and all of them mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [every single one of the congregation]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 16:3 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠מַדּ֥וּעַ תִּֽתְנַשְּׂא֖וּ עַל־קְהַ֥ל יְהוָֽה

"And why do you lift yourselves up above the assembly of Yahweh"

Korah and his followers are using the question form to express their disapproval and criticism of Moses and Aaron. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is wrong for you to lift yourselves up above the assembly of Yahweh!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 16:3 (#6)
content:
קְהַ֥ל יְהוָֽה

"the assembly of Yahweh"

The author is using the possessive form to describe an assembly that serves or worships Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the assembly that worships Yahweh]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 16:4 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּפֹּ֖ל עַל־פָּנָֽי⁠ו

"and fell on his face"

Fell on his face was a symbolic action by which Moses showed his grief and humility before Yahweh at the rebellion of Korah and his followers. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. See how you translated the similar words in 14:5. Alternate translation: [lay with his face on the ground to show his grief] or [and bowed with his face to the ground in sorrow]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Numbers 16:5 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֶֽל־כָּל־עֲדָת⁠וֹ֮

"and to all his congregation"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a congregation that is characterized by following Korah. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and to all the people who had joined him]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 16:5 (#2)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹר֒

"saying"

Here, the word saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 16:5 (#3)
content:
בֹּ֠קֶר

"Morning"

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Wait for the morning] or [Morning will come]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 16:5 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יֹדַ֨ע יְהוָ֧ה אֶת־אֲשֶׁר־ל֛⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠קָּד֖וֹשׁ וְ⁠הִקְרִ֣יב אֵלָ֑י⁠ו וְ⁠אֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִבְחַר־בּ֖⁠וֹ יַקְרִ֥יב אֵלָֽי⁠ו

"and Yahweh will make known who {is} to him and the holy one, and he will present to him, and whom he chooses he will present to him"

These two phrases Yahweh will make known who is to him and the holy one, and he will present to him and whom he chooses he will present to him mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will make known who is to him and the holy one, and he will present to him. Indeed, whom he chooses he will present to him]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 16:5 (#5)
content:
אֶת־אֲשֶׁר־ל֛⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠קָּד֖וֹשׁ

"who {is} to him and the holy one"

The phrase to him and the holy one expresses a single idea. The word holy one tells more about who belongs to him. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [who is the holy one who is to him]

See: Hendiadys

title: Numbers 16:5 (#6)
content:
אֶת־אֲשֶׁר־ל֛⁠וֹ

"who {is} to him"

The implication is that Yahweh will show who truly belongs to him and has his approval. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who is his] or [whom he has chosen]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:5 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠הִקְרִ֣יב אֵלָ֑י⁠ו וְ⁠אֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִבְחַר־בּ֖⁠וֹ יַקְרִ֥יב אֵלָֽי⁠ו

"and he will present to him, and whom he chooses he will present to him"

The implication is that Yahweh will enable certain people to come into his presence and serve him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and he will enable to come near to himself, and whom he chooses he will enable to come near to himself]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:5 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠הִקְרִ֣יב אֵלָ֑י⁠ו

"and he will present to him"

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will present that person to him]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 16:6 (#1)
content:
מַחְתּ֔וֹת

"censers"

A censer is a kind of container used for burning incense. If your readers would not be familiar with what a censer is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [containers for incense]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 16:6 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־עֲדָתֽ⁠וֹ

"and all his congregation"

Here Moses is using the possessive form to describe a congregation that is characterized by following Korah. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated the similar form in verse 5. Alternate translation: [and all the people who have joined him]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 16:7 (#1)
content:
אֵ֡שׁ

"fire"

Here, fire represents burning coals. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [embers]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 16:7 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֤י יְהוָה֙

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 16:7 (#3)
content:
הָ⁠אִ֛ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִבְחַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה ה֣וּא הַ⁠קָּד֑וֹשׁ

"the man whom Yahweh chooses, he {is} the holy one"

It might seem that the expression the man whom Yahweh chooses, he is the holy one contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [the man whom Yahweh chooses is the holy one]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 16:7 (#4)
content:
רַב־לָ⁠כֶ֖ם

"Great to you"

Moses is using the phrase Great to you as a common expression of his culture to mean “You take too much authority” or “You make too much of yourselves.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 3. Alternate translation: [You make much of yourselves] or [You take too much authority]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:7 (#5)
content:
בְּנֵ֥י לֵוִֽי

"sons of Levi"

Here, Moses is speaking as if all the people who were descended from Levi were actually sons of Levi. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [men descended from Levi]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:8 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֥אמֶר מֹשֶׁ֖ה אֶל־קֹ֑רַח

"And Moses said to Korah"

Here, Moses continues speaking with Korah. The author states that Moses addressed Korah specifically, but Moses also addresses all the Levites who are with Korah. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate more explicitly that Moses continues to speak, addressing himself directly to Korah but including other Levites as well. Alternate translation: [And Moses continued to speak with Korah as well as the Levites who were with him. He said]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:8 (#2)
content:
בְּנֵ֥י לֵוִֽי

"sons of Levi"

Moses is speaking of the tribe of Levi as if they were literally the sons of Levi. They were actually his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in verse 7. Alternate translation: [men descended from Levi]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠עֲמֹ֛ד לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הָ⁠עֵדָ֖ה

"and to stand to the face of the congregation"

Here, Moses is speaking of the Levites serving in front of the congregation as if they were standing to the face of the congregation. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to be ready to serve the congregation]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:9 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠מְעַ֣ט מִ⁠כֶּ֗ם כִּֽי־הִבְדִּיל֩ אֱלֹהֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל אֶתְ⁠כֶם֙ מֵ⁠עֲדַ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לְ⁠הַקְרִ֥יב אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם אֵלָ֑י⁠ו לַ⁠עֲבֹ֗ד אֶת־עֲבֹדַת֙ מִשְׁכַּ֣ן יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠לַ⁠עֲמֹ֛ד לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הָ⁠עֵדָ֖ה לְ⁠שָׁרְתָֽ⁠ם

"Is it} small from you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel to present you to him to serve the service of the Dwelling of Yahweh and to stand to the face of the congregation to minister to them"

Moses is using the question form to rebuke Korah for not being content with his role. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not consider it small from you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel to present you to him to serve the service of the Dwelling of Yahweh and to stand to the face of the congregation to minister to them!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 16:9 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠מְעַ֣ט מִ⁠כֶּ֗ם כִּֽי

"Is it} small from you that"

Moses is using Is it small from you as a common expression of his culture to mean “Do you consider it insignificant?” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do you consider it insignificant]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:9 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠עֲבֹ֗ד אֶת־עֲבֹדַת֙ מִשְׁכַּ֣ן

"to serve the service of the Dwelling of"

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [to serve]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 16:9 (#5)
content:
אֶת־עֲבֹדַת֙ מִשְׁכַּ֣ן יְהוָ֔ה

"the service of the Dwelling of Yahweh"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of service, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as the Dwelling of Yahweh needs to be served]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 16:9 (#6)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הָ⁠עֵדָ֖ה

"to the face of the congregation"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of the congregation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before the congregation]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 16:9–10 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠מְעַ֣ט מִ⁠כֶּ֗ם כִּֽי־הִבְדִּיל֩ אֱלֹהֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל אֶתְ⁠כֶם֙ מֵ⁠עֲדַ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לְ⁠הַקְרִ֥יב אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם אֵלָ֑י⁠ו לַ⁠עֲבֹ֗ד אֶת־עֲבֹדַת֙ מִשְׁכַּ֣ן יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠לַ⁠עֲמֹ֛ד לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הָ⁠עֵדָ֖ה לְ⁠שָׁרְתָֽ⁠ם׃ וַ⁠יַּקְרֵב֙ אֹֽתְ⁠ךָ֔ וְ⁠אֶת־כָּל־אַחֶ֥י⁠ךָ בְנֵי־לֵוִ֖י אִתָּ֑⁠ךְ וּ⁠בִקַּשְׁתֶּ֖ם גַּם־כְּהֻנָּֽה

"Is it} small from you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel to present you to him to serve the service of the Dwelling of Yahweh and to stand to the face of the congregation to minister to them? And he has presented you and all your brothers, the sons of Levi, with you, but do you seek the priesthood also"

The question that begins in 16:9 could end at: (1) the end of verse 9. In this case, verse 10 is its own question. See the ULT. (2) the words the sons of Levi, with you in verse 10. Alternate translation: [Is it small from you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel to present you to him to serve the service of the Dwelling of Yahweh and to stand to the face of the congregation to minister to them and has presented you and all your brothers, the sons of Levi, with you? But do you seek the priesthood also?]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 16:10 (#1)
content:
בְנֵי־לֵוִ֖י

"the sons of Levi"

Here, Moses is speaking as if the people of the tribe of Levi were literally the sons of Levi. They were actually his descendants. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in verse 7. Alternate translation: [the men descended from Levi]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:10 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יַּקְרֵב֙ אֹֽתְ⁠ךָ֔

"And he has presented you"

The implication is that God enabled the Levites to serve at his sanctuary. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar phrases in verse 5. Alternate translation: [And he has enabled you and all your brothers, the sons of Levi, with you to come near to himself]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:10 (#3)
content:
אֹֽתְ⁠ךָ֔ וְ⁠אֶת־כָּל־אַחֶ֥י⁠ךָ & אִתָּ֑⁠ךְ וּ⁠בִקַּשְׁתֶּ֖ם

"you and all your brothers & with you, but do you seek"

The word you is singular in most of this verse because Moses is speaking to Korah, but in you seek it is plural because Moses is speaking about Korah and his fellow Levites. Use the correct singular and plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 16:10 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אֶת־כָּל־אַחֶ֥י⁠ךָ

"and all your brothers"

Here, Moses is using the term brothers to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and all your relatives]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:10 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠בִקַּשְׁתֶּ֖ם גַּם־כְּהֻנָּֽה

"but do you seek the priesthood also"

Moses is using the question form to express disapproval of Korah’s desire for the priesthood. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [but you are seeking the priesthood also!] or [and despite that you are seeking the priesthood also.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 16:10 (#6)
content:
כְּהֻנָּֽה

"the priesthood"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of priesthood, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to serve as priests]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 16:11 (#1)
content:
אַתָּה֙ וְ⁠כָל־עֲדָ֣תְ⁠ךָ֔ & תלונו

"you and all your congregation & you murmur"

In this verse, forms of you are singular except for the word you in you murmur, which is plural because it refers to both Korah and his followers. So use the plural form in that place in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 16:11 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־עֲדָ֣תְ⁠ךָ֔

"and all your congregation"

Moses is using the possessive form to describe a congregation that is characterized by following Korah. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated the similar words in verse 5. Alternate translation: [and all the people who have joined you]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 16:11 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אַהֲרֹ֣ן מַה־ה֔וּא כִּ֥י תלונו עָלָֽי⁠ו

"and Aaron, what is he that you murmur against him"

Moses is using the question form to emphasize that Aaron is not really the one they are rebelling against. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [and Aaron is not actually the one whom you are murmuring against] or [and since Yahweh appointed Aaron, Aaron is not the one whom you are actually murmuring against]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 16:11 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אַהֲרֹ֣ן מַה־ה֔וּא כִּ֥י

"and Aaron, what is he that"

It might seem that the expression and Aaron, what is he contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and what is Aaron that]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 16:12 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֣ח מֹשֶׁ֔ה לִ⁠קְרֹ֛א

"And Moses sent to call"

The implication is that Moses sent someone to call Dathan and Abiram. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Moses sent someone to call]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:12 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠דָתָ֥ן וְ⁠לַ⁠אֲבִירָ֖ם בְּנֵ֣י אֱלִיאָ֑ב

"for Dathan and for Abiram, the sons of Eliab"

The words Dathan and Abiram are the names of men, and Eliab is also the name of a man. See how you translated these names in verse 1.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 16:12 (#3)
content:
לֹ֥א נַעֲלֶֽה

"We will not go up"

Dathan and Abiram are using go up as a common expression of their culture to mean “present ourselves to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We will not present ourselves to you]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:13 (#1)
content:
מֵ⁠אֶ֨רֶץ זָבַ֤ת חָלָב֙ וּ⁠דְבַ֔שׁ

"up from a land flowing {with} milk and honey"

Here, Dathan and Abiram are speaking of Egypt as if it were a land actually flowing with milk and honey. This was a way of saying that it was a very fertile and productive place. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 13:27. Alternate translation: [from a land that is rich and fertile] or [from a land that is very productive]

See: Metaphor

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 16:13 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠מְעַ֗ט כִּ֤י הֶֽעֱלִיתָ֨⁠נוּ֙ מֵ⁠אֶ֨רֶץ זָבַ֤ת חָלָב֙ וּ⁠דְבַ֔שׁ לַ⁠הֲמִיתֵ֖⁠נוּ בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֑ר כִּֽי־תִשְׂתָּרֵ֥ר עָלֵ֖י⁠נוּ גַּם־הִשְׂתָּרֵֽר

"Is it} small that you have brought us up from a land flowing {with} milk and honey to kill us in the wilderness that you make yourself rule over us, also making yourself rule"

Dathan and Abiram are using the question form to express indignation at Moses’ leadership. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not consider it so small that you have brought us up from a land flowing with milk and honey to kill us in the wilderness that you make yourself rule over us, also making yourself rule!]

See: Rhetorical Question

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 16:13 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠מְעַ֗ט כִּ֤י

"Is it} small that"

The phrase Is it small that is a common expression of this culture that means “Do you consider it insignificant that” or “Is it not enough that.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 9. Alternate translation: [Do you consider it so insignificant that]

See: Idiom

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 16:13 (#4)
content:
תִשְׂתָּרֵ֥ר עָלֵ֖י⁠נוּ גַּם־הִשְׂתָּרֵֽר

"you make yourself rule over us, also making yourself rule"

Dathan and Abiram are repeating forms of the verb rule in order to intensify their expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you make yourself rule over us completely]

See: Reduplication

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 16:14 (#1)
content:
אֶל־אֶרֶץ֩ זָבַ֨ת חָלָ֤ב וּ⁠דְבַשׁ֙

"to a land flowing {with} milk and honey"

Here, Dathan and Abiram are speaking as if the land were actually flowing with milk and honey. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 13. Alternate translation: [to a land that is rich and fertile] or [to a land that is very productive]

See: Metaphor

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 16:14 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠עֵינֵ֞י הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֥ים הָ⁠הֵ֛ם תְּנַקֵּ֖ר

"Will you gouge out the eyes of these men"

Here, Dathan and Abiram are speaking of deceiving people as if it were gouging out their eyes. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Will you mislead these men] or [Will you trick these men]

See: Metaphor

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 16:14 (#3)
content:
נַחֲלַ֖ת שָׂדֶ֣ה

"an inheritance of field"

Dathan and Abiram are using the term inheritance by association to mean a lasting possession that would be passed down to future generations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a lasting possession of]

See: Metonymy

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 16:14 (#4)
content:
שָׂדֶ֣ה וָ⁠כָ֑רֶם

"field and vineyard"

Here, field and vineyard represent agricultural land in general, not specific fields and vineyards. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [of fields and vineyards]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 16:14 (#5)
content:
הַ⁠עֵינֵ֞י הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֥ים הָ⁠הֵ֛ם תְּנַקֵּ֖ר

"Will you gouge out the eyes of these men"

Dathan and Abiram are using the question form to make a strong negative statement. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You cannot gouge out the eyes of these men!]

See: Rhetorical Question

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 16:14 (#6)
content:
לֹ֥א נַעֲלֶֽה

"We will not go up"

See how you translated this clause in 16:12. Alternate translation: [We will not present ourselves to you]

See: Idiom

acai.preferred_label: Land Flowing of Milk and Honey

title: Numbers 16:15 (#1)
content:
אַל־תֵּ֖פֶן אֶל

"Do not turn to"

Here, Moses is speaking of accepting an offering as if Yahweh would turn to look at it. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not receive]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:15 (#2)
content:
לֹ֠א חֲמ֨וֹר אֶחָ֤ד מֵ⁠הֶם֙ נָשָׂ֔אתִי

"I have not lifted up one donkey from them"

Here, Moses is speaking of stealing as if it were lifting something up. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have not stolen one donkey from them]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:15 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּ֤חַר לְ⁠מֹשֶׁה֙ מְאֹ֔ד

"And it burned exceedingly for Moses"

The author is using it burned exceedingly as a common expression of this culture to mean “he became very angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Moses’ anger burned greatly] or [and Moses was enraged]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:15 (#4)
content:
מִנְחָתָ֑⁠ם

"their grain offering"

By grain offering, Moses means any offering from them at all. He is using a grain offering as an example because it was a small offering. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [any offering from them, even a grain offering]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:15 (#5)
content:
חֲמ֨וֹר אֶחָ֤ד

"one donkey"

By one donkey, Moses means he has not taken anything from the Israelites, not even something as insignificant as a donkey. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [something as insignificant as one donkey]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:16 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־עֲדָ֣תְ⁠ךָ֔

"and all your congregation"

Moses is using the possessive form to describe a congregation that is characterized by following Korah. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in verse 11. Alternate translation: [all the people who have joined you]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 16:16 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 16:17 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠קְח֣וּ ׀ אִ֣ישׁ מַחְתָּת֗⁠וֹ וּ⁠נְתַתֶּ֤ם עֲלֵי⁠הֶם֙ קְטֹ֔רֶת וְ⁠הִקְרַבְתֶּ֞ם לִ⁠פְנֵ֤י יְהוָה֙ אִ֣ישׁ מַחְתָּת֔⁠וֹ חֲמִשִּׁ֥ים וּ⁠מָאתַ֖יִם מַחְתֹּ֑ת

"And take a man his censer, and put incense on them, and present to the face of Yahweh, a man his censer, 250 censers"

It might seem that the second occurrence of the expression a man his censer contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And take a man his censer, and put incense on them, and present to the face of Yahweh, 250 censers]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Numbers 16:17 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠קְח֣וּ ׀ אִ֣ישׁ מַחְתָּת֗⁠וֹ

"And take a man his censer"

Moses is using take a man his censer as a common expression of his culture to mean “each man must take his censer.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all the men must take their censers]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:17 (#3)
content:
מַחְתָּת֗⁠וֹ & מַחְתָּת֔⁠וֹ & מַחְתֹּ֑ת & מַחְתָּתֽ⁠וֹ

"his censer & his censer & censers & his censer"

A censer is a kind of metal container used for burning incense. If your readers would not be familiar with what a censer is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. See how you translated censer in verse 6. Alternate translation: [his container for incense … his container for incense … containers for incense … his container for incense]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 16:17 (#4)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֤י יְהוָה֙

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 16:17 (#5)
content:
חֲמִשִּׁ֥ים וּ⁠מָאתַ֖יִם

"250"

Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [two hundred and fifty]

See: Numbers

title: Numbers 16:17 (#6)
content:
אִ֣ישׁ מַחְתָּת֗⁠וֹ & אִ֣ישׁ מַחְתָּת֔⁠וֹ

"a man his censer & a man his censer"

Moses is using a man his censer as a common expression of his culture to mean “each person with his own censer.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all the men with their censers … each with your own censer]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:18 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקְח֞וּ אִ֣ישׁ מַחְתָּת֗⁠וֹ

"And they took a man his censer"

Moses is using a man his censer as a common expression of his culture to mean “each man took his own censer.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar words in verse 17. Alternate translation: [And all the men took their censers]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:18 (#2)
content:
וַֽ⁠יַּעַמְד֗וּ פֶּ֛תַח אֹ֥הֶל מוֹעֵ֖ד וּ⁠מֹשֶׁ֥ה וְ⁠אַהֲרֹֽן

"and they stood {at} the opening of the tent of meeting, and Moses and Aaron"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Moses and Aaron with the information about the others who stood at the entrance. Alternate translation: [and they and Moses and Aaron stood at the opening of the tent of meeting]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 16:19 (#1)
content:
אֶת־כָּל־הָ֣⁠עֵדָ֔ה

"all the congregation"

Here, the congregation could be: (1) the Israelite community. Alternate translation: [all the Israelite congregation]; or (2) just the men with Korah, referred to as “his congregation” in 16:5. Alternate translation: [all his congregation] or [all his followers]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:19 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּרָ֥א כְבוֹד־יְהוָ֖ה

"and the glory of Yahweh appeared"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of glory, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the similar clause in 14:10. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh showed himself gloriously]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 16:21 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אַכַלֶּ֥ה אֹתָ֖⁠ם

"and I shall finish them"

Yahweh is using I shall finish them as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will make them die” or “I will cause them to cease to exist.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I shall end their lives] or [and I will make them experience death]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:21 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠רָֽגַע

"according to a moment"

Yahweh is using according to a moment as a common expression of the culture to mean “instantly” or “immediately.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [instantly]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:22 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּפְּל֤וּ עַל־פְּנֵי⁠הֶם֙

"And they fell on their faces"

Falling on their faces was a symbolic action by which Moses and Aaron showed their grief and submission to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. See how you translated the similar words in chapter 14:5. Alternate translation: [And they lay with their faces on the ground to show their grief] or [And they bowed with their faces to the ground in sorrow]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Numbers 16:22 (#2)
content:
אֱלֹהֵ֥י הָ⁠רוּחֹ֖ת לְ⁠כָל־בָּשָׂ֑ר

"the God of the spirits of all flesh"

The author is using the possessive form to describe God who gives or rules the spirits that belong to or are in all flesh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who rules the spirits in all flesh] or [the God who gave the spirits to all flesh]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 16:22 (#3)
content:
הָ⁠רוּחֹ֖ת לְ⁠כָל־בָּשָׂ֑ר

"the spirits of all flesh"

Moses and Aaron are using the spirits of all flesh as a common expression of their culture to mean “the life that is in all living things.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the life that is in all living things] or [everything that lives]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:22 (#4)
content:
הָ⁠אִ֤ישׁ אֶחָד֙ יֶחֱטָ֔א וְ⁠עַ֥ל כָּל־הָ⁠עֵדָ֖ה תִּקְצֹֽף

"will one man sin and you be angry against all the congregation"

Moses and Aaron are using the question form to protest the unfairness of punishing everyone for one person’s sin. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [when one man sins, surely you will not be angry against all the congregation.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 16:24 (#1)
content:
הֵֽעָלוּ֙

"Be taken up"

Here, Yahweh is speaking of moving away from Korah’s dwelling as if people could be taken up from that place. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Move away]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:24 (#2)
content:
דַּבֵּ֥ר אֶל־הָ⁠עֵדָ֖ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר הֵֽעָלוּ֙ מִ⁠סָּבִ֔יב לְ⁠מִשְׁכַּן־קֹ֖רַח דָּתָ֥ן וַ⁠אֲבִירָֽם

"Speak to the congregation, saying, ‘Be taken up from around to the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Tell the congregation that they must be taken up from around to the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 16:24 (#3)
content:
הֵֽעָלוּ֙

"Be taken up"

The expression Be taken up is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. Alternate translation: [Take yourselves up]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 16:24 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠סָּבִ֔יב לְ⁠מִשְׁכַּן־קֹ֖רַח דָּתָ֥ן וַ⁠אֲבִירָֽם

"from around to the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram"

By from around to the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, Yahweh means that the people should move away from all sides of where these men were living. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram on every side]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:25 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֣קָם מֹשֶׁ֔ה

"And Moses rose"

The author is using rose as a common expression of the culture to mean “began to do something.” He is not saying that Moses got up from a seated position. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Moses got ready]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:25 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּ֖לֶךְ

"and went"

In a context such as this, your language might say “came” instead of went. Alternate translation: [and came]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 16:26 (#1)
content:
תִּסָּפ֖וּ בְּ⁠כָל־חַטֹּאתָֽ⁠ם

"you be swept away in all their sins"

Here, Moses is speaking as if the punishment of others’ sins were a flood that could sweep away those who are nearby. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you be included when God punishes them for their sins] or [you too experience the punishment for their sins]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:26 (#2)
content:
מֵ⁠עַל֩ אָהֳלֵ֨י הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֤ים

"from upon the tents of & men"

Moses is using from upon the tents of as a common expression of his culture to mean “from near the tents of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from near the tents of]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:26 (#3)
content:
פֶּן־תִּסָּפ֖וּ

"lest you be swept away"

Moses is using the word translated as lest to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives the people an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [or else you will be swept away]

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Numbers 16:27 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּעָל֗וּ

"And they were taken up"

Here, the author is speaking of moving physically away from a place as if the people were being taken up. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar form in verse 24. Alternate translation: [And they moved away]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:27 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּעָל֗וּ

"And they were taken up"

The expression were taken up is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. See how you translated the similar form in verse 24. Alternate translation: [And they took themselves up]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 16:27 (#3)
content:
מֵ⁠עַ֧ל מִשְׁכַּן־קֹ֛רֶח

"from upon the dwelling of Korah"

The expression from upon the dwelling of is a common expression of the culture that means “from the area around” or “from near.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar form in verse 26. Alternate translation: [from near the dwelling of]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:27 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠סָּבִ֑יב

"from around"

The implication is that the people moved away from all sides of where the men were living. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. (See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 24.) Alternate translation: [on every side]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:27 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠דָתָ֨ן וַ⁠אֲבִירָ֜ם יָצְא֣וּ נִצָּבִ֗ים פֶּ֚תַח אָֽהֳלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם וּ⁠נְשֵׁי⁠הֶ֥ם וּ⁠בְנֵי⁠הֶ֖ם וְ⁠טַפָּֽ⁠ם

"and Dathan and Abiram went out, standing {at} the opening of their tents, and their wives and their sons and their children"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the wives, sons, and children with the information about Dathan and Abiram before saying that they were standing at the opening of their tents. Alternate translation: [and Dathan and Abiram and their wives and their sons and their children went out, standing at the opening of their tents]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 16:27 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠דָתָ֨ן וַ⁠אֲבִירָ֜ם יָצְא֣וּ

"and Dathan and Abiram went out"

Here, the author implies that Dathan, Abiram, and their families went out of their tents before the Israelites moved away from them. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could make the sequence of events more explicit. Alternate translation: [and meanwhile, Dathan and Abiram had gone out]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 16:27 (#7)
content:
יָצְא֣וּ

"went out"

The implication is that Dathan and Abiram went out of their tents. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [went out of their tents]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:27 (#8)
content:
יָצְא֣וּ

"went out"

In a context such as this, your language might say “came” instead of went out. Alternate translation: [came out]

See: Go and Come

title: Numbers 16:27 (#9)
content:
וּ⁠בְנֵי⁠הֶ֖ם וְ⁠טַפָּֽ⁠ם

"and their sons and their children"

The implication is that their sons and their children refer to the same group, with the second phrase being more general. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and their sons and the rest of their children]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:28 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠זֹאת֙

"By this"

The phrase By this refers to what Moses is about to say in verses 29–30. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [By what I am about to say]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 16:28 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠לִּבִּֽ⁠י

"they are & from my heart"

Here, heart represents Moses’ own thoughts, desires, or will. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from my own prompting] or [from my own choice]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 16:29 (#1)
content:
כְּ⁠מ֤וֹת כָּל־הָֽ⁠אָדָם֙ יְמֻת֣וּ⁠ן אֵ֔לֶּה וּ⁠פְקֻדַּת֙ כָּל־הָ֣⁠אָדָ֔ם יִפָּקֵ֖ד עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֑ם

"as the death of every man these die, and the oversight of every man is counted upon them"

These two phrases as the death of every man these die and the oversight of every man is counted upon them mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [as the death of every man these die in an ordinary way]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 16:29 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠מ֤וֹת כָּל־הָֽ⁠אָדָם֙

"as the death of every man"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of death, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as every man dies]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 16:29 (#3)
content:
כָּל־הָֽ⁠אָדָם֙ & כָּל־הָ֣⁠אָדָ֔ם

"every man & every man"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [every human … every human]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 16:29 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠פְקֻדַּת֙ כָּל־הָ֣⁠אָדָ֔ם יִפָּקֵ֖ד עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֑ם

"and the oversight of every man is counted upon them"

Moses is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase the oversight of every man is counted upon them. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and the fate of every man happens to them] or [and they experience death like everyone else does]

See: Euphemism

title: Numbers 16:29 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠פְקֻדַּת֙ כָּל־הָ֣⁠אָדָ֔ם

"and the oversight of every man"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of oversight, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and how every man is overseen]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 16:29 (#6)
content:
לֹ֥א יְהוָ֖ה שְׁלָחָֽ⁠נִי

"Yahweh did not send me"

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [then you will know that Yahweh did not send me]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 16:30 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יָרְד֥וּ חַיִּ֖ים שְׁאֹ֑לָ⁠ה

"and they go down living to Sheol"

Here, Moses is speaking of death as if it were going to a place called Sheol that these people would enter while still alive. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it is as if they arrive at the place of the dead while they are still alive] or [and they die after they are buried instead of before]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:30 (#2)
content:
בְּרִיאָ֞ה יִבְרָ֣א

"creates a creation"

Moses is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [creates something] or [makes a creation]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 16:30 (#3)
content:
בְּרִיאָ֞ה

"a creation"

By a creation, Moses means something that has never happened before. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a new thing]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:30 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠פָצְתָ֨ה הָ⁠אֲדָמָ֤ה אֶת־פִּ֨י⁠הָ֙ וּ⁠בָלְעָ֤ה אֹתָ⁠ם֙

"and the ground opens its mouth and swallows them"

Moses is speaking of the ground as if it were a living thing that could open its mouth and swallow. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a hole forms in the ground and engulfs them]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 16:31 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תִּבָּקַ֥ע

"that & was split open"

The expression was split open is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the ground. Alternate translation: [split open] or [broke apart]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 16:31 (#2)
content:
תַּחְתֵּי⁠הֶֽם

"was} under them"

The pronoun them refers to Dathan, Abiram, and their families. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [under Dathan, Abiram, and their families]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 16:32 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֶת־בָּתֵּי⁠הֶ֑ם

"and their houses"

Here, the author is speaking of the people and animals and objects that belonged to these men as if they were houses in which they lived. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their households]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 16:32 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠תִּפְתַּ֤ח הָ⁠אָ֨רֶץ֙ אֶת־פִּ֔י⁠הָ וַ⁠תִּבְלַ֥ע אֹתָ֖⁠ם

"and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them"

The author is speaking of the earth as if it were a living thing that could open its mouth and swallow people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar clause in verse 30. Alternate translation: [and a hole formed in the earth and engulfed them]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 16:32 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אֶת־בָּתֵּי⁠הֶ֑ם וְ⁠אֵ֤ת כָּל־הָ⁠אָדָם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְ⁠קֹ֔רַח וְ⁠אֵ֖ת כָּל־הָ⁠רֲכֽוּשׁ

"and their houses and every man who {was} to Korah and all the property"

Here, every man and all the property could refer to: (1) people and their property in addition to Dathan, Abiram, and their families. These people agreed with Korah, but they were not among the 250 men who offered incense at the sacred tent. Alternate translation: [and their houses, and in addition every man who was to Korah besides the 250 men and all their property]; or (2) Dathan, Abiram, and their families. The author is simply giving more information about them. Alternate translation: [and their houses, that is, every man who was to Korah and all their property]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 16:32 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֤ת כָּל־הָ⁠אָדָם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְ⁠קֹ֔רַח

"and every man who {was} to Korah"

The author is using who was to Korah as a common expression of the culture to mean “who had followed Korah” or “who had supported Korah.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and every man who had followed Korah]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 16:32 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֤ת כָּל־הָ⁠אָדָם֙

"and every man"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and every person]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 16:33 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּ֨רְד֜וּ הֵ֣ם וְ⁠כָל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר לָ⁠הֶ֛ם חַיִּ֖ים שְׁאֹ֑לָ⁠ה

"and they went down, they and all that {was} to them, living to Sheol"

Here, the author is speaking of death as if it were going to a place called Sheol that these people would enter while still alive. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar clause in verse 30. Alternate translation: [and it as if they arrived, they and all that was to them, at the place of the dead while they were still alive] or [and they died, they and all that was to them, after they were buried instead of before]
