"And the sons of Israel, all the congregation, came to the wilderness of Zin in the first month"

The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 20:1 (#2)
content:
בְנֵֽי־יִ֠שְׂרָאֵל

"the sons of Israel"

See how you translated these same phrases in Numbers 1:2. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 20:1 (#3)
content:
בַּ⁠חֹ֣דֶשׁ הָֽ⁠רִאשׁ֔וֹן

"in the first month"

This is the first month of the Hebrew calendar. It marks when God rescued the Israelites from the Egyptians. The first month is during the last part of March and the first part of April on the Western calendar.

See: Hebrew Months

title: Numbers 20:1 (#4)
content:
בַּ⁠חֹ֣דֶשׁ הָֽ⁠רִאשׁ֔וֹן

"in the first month"

Here the author implies that this is the first month of the fortieth year since the Israelites left the land of Egypt. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [in the first month of the year that was forty years after they left Egypt]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 20:1 (#5)
content:
מִדְבַּר־צִן֙

"the wilderness of Zin"

The word “Zin” here is the Hebrew name of the wilderness.

See: Copy or Borrow Words

title: Numbers 20:1 (#6)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּ֥שֶׁב הָ⁠עָ֖ם

"and the people dwelt"

The phrase the people refers to the sons of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the Israelites dwelt]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:1 (#7)
content:
וַ⁠תִּקָּבֵ֖ר שָֽׁם

"and she was buried there"

The expression she was buried is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they buried her there]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 20:2 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא־הָ֥יָה מַ֖יִם לָ⁠עֵדָ֑ה

"And there was no water for the congregation"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 20:2 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא־הָ֥יָה מַ֖יִם

"And there was no water"

Here, the author implies that there was no water in or near the city of Kadesh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could make that explicit. Alternate translation: [And there was no water in Kadesh]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 20:2 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקָּ֣הֲל֔וּ

"and they assembled"

The pronoun they refers to the congregation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the congregation assembled]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:2 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקָּ֣הֲל֔וּ

"and they assembled"

Alternate translation: [came as a mob]

title: Numbers 20:3 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּאמְר֣וּ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר

"and they said, saying"

Here and throughout the chapter, the term saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 20:3 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠ל֥וּ גָוַ֛עְנוּ

"If only we had expired"

The people are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, a desperate wish that they had already died. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [We would rather have died]

See: Exclamations

title: Numbers 20:3 (#3)
content:
גָוַ֛עְנוּ

"we had expired"

By we, the people mean themselves and their fellow Israelites but not those to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 20:3 (#4)
content:
גָוַ֛עְנוּ בִּ⁠גְוַ֥ע אַחֵ֖י⁠נוּ

"we had expired when our brothers expired"

The people are referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase we had expired when our brothers expired. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [we had died when our brothers died]

See: Euphemism

title: Numbers 20:3 (#5)
content:
אַחֵ֖י⁠נוּ

"our brothers"

Here the people are speaking as if their fellow Israelites were their brothers. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our kinsmen]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 20:3 (#6)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"to the face of Yahweh"

Here, to the face of Yahweh represents being in Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:4 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לָ⁠מָ֤ה הֲבֵאתֶם֙ אֶת־קְהַ֣ל יְהוָ֔ה אֶל־הַ⁠מִּדְבָּ֖ר הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה לָ⁠מ֣וּת שָׁ֔ם אֲנַ֖חְנוּ וּ⁠בְעִירֵֽ⁠נוּ

"And why have you brought the assembly of Yahweh to this wilderness to die there, we and our livestock"

Here, the word to marks die there as the purpose of have you brought the assembly of Yahweh to this wilderness. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Numbers 20:4 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לָ⁠מָ֤ה הֲבֵאתֶם֙ אֶת־קְהַ֣ל יְהוָ֔ה אֶל־הַ⁠מִּדְבָּ֖ר הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה לָ⁠מ֣וּת שָׁ֔ם

"And why have you brought the assembly of Yahweh to this wilderness to die there"

The people are using the question form to rebuke Moses and Aaron for bringing them into the wilderness to die. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have brought the assembly of Yahweh to this wilderness to die there!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 20:4 (#3)
content:
הֲבֵאתֶם֙

"have you brought"

The pronoun you refers to Moses and Aaron. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [have Moses and Aaron brought]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:4 (#4)
content:
אֶת־קְהַ֣ל יְהוָ֔ה

"the assembly of Yahweh"

The people are using the possessive form to describe an assembly that is characterized by belonging to Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the assembly that worships Yahweh]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 20:4 (#5)
content:
אֲנַ֖חְנוּ וּ⁠בְעִירֵֽ⁠נוּ

"we and our livestock"

By we, the people mean themselves and their fellow Israelites but not those to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 20:5 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לָ⁠מָ֤ה הֶֽעֱלִיתֻ֨⁠נוּ֙ מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֔יִם לְ⁠הָבִ֣יא אֹתָ֔⁠נוּ אֶל־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הָ⁠רָ֖ע הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה לֹ֣א ׀ מְק֣וֹם זֶ֗רַע וּ⁠תְאֵנָ֤ה וְ⁠גֶ֨פֶן֙ וְ⁠רִמּ֔וֹן וּ⁠מַ֥יִם אַ֖יִן לִ⁠שְׁתּֽוֹת

"And why did you bring us up from Egypt to bring us to this evil place? {It is} not a place of seed and fig and vine and pomegranate, and there is no water to drink"

Here, the word to marks bring us to this evil place as the purpose of did you bring us up from Egypt. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Numbers 20:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לָ⁠מָ֤ה הֶֽעֱלִיתֻ֨⁠נוּ֙ מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֔יִם לְ⁠הָבִ֣יא אֹתָ֔⁠נוּ אֶל־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הָ⁠רָ֖ע הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה

"And why did you bring us up from Egypt to bring us to this evil place"

The people are using the question form to rebuke Moses and Aaron for bringing them up out of Egypt to this evil place. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not have brought us up from Egypt to bring us to this evil place!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 20:6 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠פְּנֵ֣י הַ⁠קָּהָ֗ל

"from the face of the assembly"

Here, from the face of the assembly represents being in front of the assembly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [away from the assembly]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:6 (#2)
content:
וַֽ⁠יִּפְּל֖וּ עַל־פְּנֵי⁠הֶ֑ם

"and they fell on their faces"

The pronouns they and their refer to Moses and Aaron. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Moses and Aaron fell on their faces]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:6 (#3)
content:
כְבוֹד־יְהוָ֖ה

"the glory of Yahweh"

Moses is using the possessive form to describe the glory that is characterized by belonging to Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the divine glory]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 20:6 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּרָ֥א כְבוֹד־יְהוָ֖ה

"And the glory of Yahweh appeared"

Here, the glory of Yahweh represents a visible display of Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh himself appeared]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:6 (#5)
content:
כְבוֹד־יְהוָ֖ה

"the glory of Yahweh"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of glory, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the glorious Yahweh]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 20:8 (#1)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠מַּטֶּ֗ה

"the staff"

Here, the staff could be: (1) the staff with Aaron’s name on it from Numbers 17. That was the staff that budded and produced almonds, which proved that Aaron was the priest that Yahweh had chosen. Alternate translation: [Aaron’s staff that budded]; or (2) the staff that Moses used when he performed miracles in Egypt. Alternate translation: [your staff] or [the staff that you used in Egypt]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 20:8 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠דִבַּרְתֶּ֧ם אֶל־הַ⁠סֶּ֛לַע לְ⁠עֵינֵי⁠הֶ֖ם

"and you shall speak to the rock to their eyes"

The pronoun their refers to the congregation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and you shall speak to the rock while the congregation watches]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:8 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠עֵינֵי⁠הֶ֖ם

"to their eyes"

Yahweh is using to their eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean “in their sight.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their sight]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 20:8 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠נָתַ֣ן מֵימָ֑י⁠ו

"and it will give its water"

Yahweh is speaking of the rock as if it were a living thing that could give its water. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and water will flow from it]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 20:8 (#5)
content:
מֵימָ֑י⁠ו

"its water"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the water that is characterized by coming from the rock. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the water it holds]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 20:9 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה

"from before the face of Yahweh"

Here, from before the face of Yahweh represents being in Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from Yahweh’s presence]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:9 (#2)
content:
כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֖ר צִוָּֽ⁠הוּ

"just as he commanded him"

The pronoun he refers to Yahweh, and the pronoun him refers to Moses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [just as Yahweh commanded him]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:10 (#1)
content:
אֶל־פְּנֵ֣י הַ⁠סָּ֑לַע

"to the face of the rock"

The author is using to the face of the rock as a common expression of the culture to mean “in front of the rock.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before the rock]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 20:10 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר לָ⁠הֶ֗ם

"and he said to them"

The pronoun he refers to Moses, and the pronoun them refers to the assembly. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Moses said to the assembly]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:10 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠מֹּרִ֔ים

"the rebellious ones"

Moses is using the adjective rebellious as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [you rebellious people]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Numbers 20:10 (#4)
content:
הֲ⁠מִן־הַ⁠סֶּ֣לַע הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה נוֹצִ֥יא לָ⁠כֶ֖ם מָֽיִם

"From this rock shall we bring out water for you"

Moses is using the question form to express his frustration and doubt about bringing water out of the rock for the people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [From this rock we can actually bring out water for you!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 20:10 (#5)
content:
נוֹצִ֥יא

"we bring out"

By we, Moses means himself and Aaron but not the people to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 20:11 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תֵּ֥שְׁתְּ הָ⁠עֵדָ֖ה וּ⁠בְעִירָֽ⁠ם

"and the congregation drank and their livestock"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the congregation drank, and their livestock drank too]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 20:12 (#1)
content:
לֹא־הֶאֱמַנְתֶּ֣ם

"you did not believe"

The pronoun you refers to Moses and Aaron. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the two of you did not believe]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:12 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠עֵינֵ֖י בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"to the eyes of the sons of Israel"

Yahweh is using to the eyes of the sons of Israel as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the sight of the sons of Israel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before the sons of Israel]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 20:12 (#3)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־נָתַ֥תִּי לָ⁠הֶֽם

"that I have given to them"

The pronoun them refers to the sons of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that I have given to the sons of Israel]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:13 (#1)
content:
הֵ֚מָּה מֵ֣י מְרִיבָ֔ה

"They {are} the waters of Meribah"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 20:13 (#2)
content:
בָּֽ⁠ם

"in them"

Here, the pronoun them could refer to: (1) the Israelites. In this case, Yahweh showed that he is holy to the Israelites. Alternate translation: [among the Israelites]; or (2) the waters. In this case, Yahweh used the waters to show that he is holy. Alternate translation: [through the waters]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:14 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֨ח מֹשֶׁ֧ה מַלְאָכִ֛ים מִ⁠קָּדֵ֖שׁ

"And Moses sent messengers from Kadesh"

The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 20:14 (#2)
content:
כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ אָחִ֣י⁠ךָ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"Thus says your brother Israel"

The phrase Thus says your brother Israel introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 20:14 (#3)
content:
כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ אָחִ֣י⁠ךָ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אַתָּ֣ה יָדַ֔עְתָּ אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַ⁠תְּלָאָ֖ה

"Thus says your brother Israel: ‘You, you know all of the hardship"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Your brother Israel says that you know all of the hardship]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 20:14 (#4)
content:
אָחִ֣י⁠ךָ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"your brother Israel"

Here the people of Israel are speaking as if their nation were the brother of the king of Edom, because the two nations descended from the brothers Jacob and Esau. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the nation descended from your brother Jacob]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 20:14 (#5)
content:
אָחִ֣י⁠ךָ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"your brother Israel"

The pronoun your refers to the king of Edom. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Edom’s brother Israel]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:14 (#6)
content:
הַ⁠תְּלָאָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר מְצָאָֽתְ⁠נוּ

"the hardship that has found us"

The people of Israel are speaking of the hardship as if it were a living thing that could find them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the hardship we have experienced]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 20:14 (#7)
content:
הַ⁠תְּלָאָ֖ה

"the hardship"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of hardship, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the trouble]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 20:15 (#1)
content:
אֲבֹתֵ֨י⁠נוּ֙

"our fathers"

Here the people of Israel are speaking as if their ancestors were their literal fathers. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our forefathers]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 20:15 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠נֵּ֥שֶׁב בְּ⁠מִצְרַ֖יִם

"and we dwelled in Egypt"

By we, the people of Israel mean themselves and their ancestors but not the king of Edom to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 20:16 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠נִּצְעַ֤ק & וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֣ע קֹלֵ֔⁠נוּ & וַ⁠יֹּצִאֵ֖⁠נוּ

"And we cried out & and he heard our voice & and he brought us out"

By we, our, and us, the people of Israel mean themselves and their ancestors but not the king of Edom to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of those words in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 20:16 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֣ע קֹלֵ֔⁠נוּ וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֣ח מַלְאָ֔ךְ וַ⁠יֹּצִאֵ֖⁠נוּ

"and he heard our voice, and he sent a messenger, and he brought us out"

The pronoun he, used three times here, refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh heard our voice, and Yahweh sent a messenger, and Yahweh brought us out]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:16 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֣ע קֹלֵ֔⁠נוּ

"and he heard our voice"

Here, our voice represents the cry for help that the people of Israel called out. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he heard our plea]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:16 (#4)
content:
מַלְאָ֔ךְ

"a messenger"

Here, the messenger could be: (1) an angel that Yahweh sent to help the Israelites. Alternate translation: [an angel]; or (2) a human representative, probably Moses. Alternate translation: [a representative]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 20:16 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּה֙

"And behold"

Here the people of Israel are speaking as if there were something for the king of Edom to look at, using the word behold to focus his attention on what they say next. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And so now]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 20:17 (#1)
content:
לֹ֤א נַעֲבֹר֙ בְּ⁠שָׂדֶ֣ה וּ⁠בְ⁠כֶ֔רֶם

"We will not pass over in a field or in a vineyard"

By We, the people of Israel mean themselves but not the king of Edom to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Numbers 20:17 (#2)
content:
מֵ֣י בְאֵ֑ר

"water of a well"

The people of Israel are using the possessive form to describe water that is characterized by coming from a well. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [water from a well]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 20:17 (#3)
content:
דֶּ֧רֶךְ הַ⁠מֶּ֣לֶךְ

"on the way of the king"

The people of Israel are using the possessive form to describe a way that is characterized by belonging to the king. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the royal road]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 20:17 (#4)
content:
לֹ֤א נִטֶּה֙ יָמִ֣ין וּ⁠שְׂמֹ֔אול

"We will not turn aside right or left"

The people of Israel are referring to all possible directions by naming two major components, the right and the left. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [We will not turn aside in any direction]

See: Merism

title: Numbers 20:18 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָי⁠ו֙ אֱד֔וֹם לֹ֥א תַעֲבֹ֖ר בִּ֑⁠י פֶּן־בַּ⁠חֶ֖רֶב אֵצֵ֥א לִ⁠קְרָאתֶֽ⁠ךָ

"And Edom said to him, “You shall not pass over in me, lest with the sword I come out to meet you"

Here, the word lest marks with the sword I come out to meet you as the outcome that the king of Edom warns will happen if the Israelites try to pass through. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of his warning.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Numbers 20:18 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָי⁠ו֙ אֱד֔וֹם

"And Edom said to him"

Here, Edom represents the king of Edom, its ruler, who is speaking on the nation’s behalf. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the king of Edom said to him]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:18 (#3)
content:
לֹ֥א תַעֲבֹ֖ר בִּ֑⁠י

"You shall not pass over in me"

The pronoun me refers to Edom and its land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You shall not pass over my land]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:18 (#4)
content:
בַּ⁠חֶ֖רֶב

"with the sword"

Here, the sword represents military force or armed attack. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with my armed forces]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:19 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אִם־מֵימֶ֤י⁠ךָ נִשְׁתֶּה֙ אֲנִ֣י וּ⁠מִקְנַ֔⁠י וְ⁠נָתַתִּ֖י מִכְרָ֑⁠ם

"And if we drink your water, I and my livestock, then I will give its price"

The people of Israel are presenting a possible condition, that they will pay for any water that they or their livestock drink. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [And if we or our livestock drink your water, then we will pay for it]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 20:19 (#2)
content:
אֲנִ֣י וּ⁠מִקְנַ֔⁠י

"I and my livestock"

The pronoun I refers to the people of Israel, speaking as a single group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I, all Israel, and my livestock]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:19 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠נָתַתִּ֖י מִכְרָ֑⁠ם

"then I will give its price"

The pronoun its refers to the water. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [then I will give the price of the water I drank]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:19 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠רַגְלַ֥⁠י

"on my feet"

The people of Israel are using on my feet as a common expression of the culture to mean “on foot” or “by walking.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [walking]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 20:20 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֖אמֶר

"And he said"

The pronoun he refers to the king of Edom. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The king of Edom said]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:20 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּצֵ֤א אֱדוֹם֙ לִ⁠קְרָאת֔⁠וֹ

"And Edom came out to meet him"

Here, Edom represents the people of Edom. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the Edomites came out to meet him]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:20 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠יָ֥ד חֲזָקָֽה

"and with a strong hand"

Here, a strong hand represents great military power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and with a powerful army]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:21 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְמָאֵ֣ן ׀ אֱד֗וֹם נְתֹן֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל עֲבֹ֖ר בִּ⁠גְבֻל֑⁠וֹ וַ⁠יֵּ֥ט יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל מֵ⁠עָלָֽי⁠ו

"And Edom refused to give Israel to pass over in his border. And Israel turned aside from upon him"

Here, Edom represents the Edomite king and his people, and Israel represents the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The Edomite king and his people refused to give the Israelites to pass over in their border. And the Israelites turned aside from upon them.]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:21 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠גְבֻל֑⁠וֹ & מֵ⁠עָלָֽי⁠ו

"in his border & from upon him"

The pronouns his and him refer to Edom. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in Edom’s territory … away from Edom]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:21 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּ֥ט יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל מֵ⁠עָלָֽי⁠ו

"And Israel turned aside from upon him"

The author is using turned aside from upon him as a common expression of the culture to mean that Israel went away from Edom. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Israel went away from him]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 20:22 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסְע֖וּ מִ⁠קָּדֵ֑שׁ

"And they set out from Kadesh"

The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 20:22 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסְע֖וּ

"And they set out"

The pronoun they refers to the sons of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites set out]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:23 (#1)
content:
גְּב֥וּל אֶֽרֶץ־אֱד֖וֹם

"the border of the land of Edom"

Moses is using the possessive form to describe a border that is characterized by being part of the land of Edom. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the border next to Edom]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 20:24 (#1)
content:
יֵאָסֵ֤ף אַהֲרֹן֙ אֶל־עַמָּ֔י⁠ו כִּ֣י לֹ֤א יָבֹא֙ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָתַ֖תִּי לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל עַ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־מְרִיתֶ֥ם אֶת־פִּ֖⁠י לְ⁠מֵ֥י מְרִיבָֽה

"Aaron will be gathered to his peoples, for he will not come to the land that I have given to the sons of Israel, because you rebelled against my mouth at the waters of Meribah"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Aaron will be gathered to his peoples because he will not come to the land that I have given to the sons of Israel, since you rebelled against my mouth at the waters of Meribah]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 20:24 (#2)
content:
יֵאָסֵ֤ף אַהֲרֹן֙ אֶל־עַמָּ֔י⁠ו

"Aaron will be gathered to his peoples"

The expression will be gathered is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Aaron will join his ancestors]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 20:24 (#3)
content:
יֵאָסֵ֤ף אַהֲרֹן֙ אֶל־עַמָּ֔י⁠ו

"Aaron will be gathered to his peoples"

Yahweh is referring to Aaron’s death in a polite way by using the phrase will be gathered to his peoples. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [Aaron will die and join his ancestors]

See: Euphemism

title: Numbers 20:24 (#4)
content:
מְרִיתֶ֥ם אֶת־פִּ֖⁠י

"you rebelled against my mouth"

Yahweh is using my mouth to represent the commands that he spoke. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you disobeyed my commands]

See: Synecdoche

title: Numbers 20:24 (#5)
content:
מְרִיתֶ֥ם

"you rebelled against"

The pronoun you refers to Moses and Aaron. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Moses and Aaron rebelled against]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:26 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אַהֲרֹ֥ן יֵאָסֵ֖ף וּ⁠מֵ֥ת שָֽׁם

"And Aaron will be gathered and will die there"

The expression will be gathered is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Aaron will join his ancestors and die there]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 20:26 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אַהֲרֹ֥ן יֵאָסֵ֖ף וּ⁠מֵ֥ת שָֽׁם

"And Aaron will be gathered and will die there"

Yahweh is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase will be gathered. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [And Aaron will die there]

See: Euphemism

title: Numbers 20:27 (#1)
content:
וַֽ⁠יַּעֲלוּ֙

"And they went up"

The pronoun they refers to Moses, Aaron, and Eleazar. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Moses, Aaron, and Eleazar went up]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:27 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠עֵינֵ֖י כָּל־הָ⁠עֵדָֽה

"to the eyes of all the congregation"

The author is using to the eyes of all the congregation as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the sight of all the congregation.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while all the congregation watched]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 20:29 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּרְאוּ֙ כָּל־הָ֣⁠עֵדָ֔ה כִּ֥י גָוַ֖ע אַהֲרֹ֑ן

"And all the congregation saw that Aaron expired"

The phrase all the congregation refers to all the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And all the people of Israel saw that Aaron expired]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 20:29 (#2)
content:
גָוַ֖ע אַהֲרֹ֑ן

"Aaron expired"

Moses is referring to death in a polite way by using the word expired. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [Aaron died]

See: Euphemism

title: Numbers 20:29 (#3)
content:
כֹּ֖ל בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"all the house of Israel"

Here, all the house of Israel represents the entire people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the Israelites]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 20:29 (#4)
content:
כֹּ֖ל בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"all the house of Israel"

The author is using the possessive form to describe a house that is characterized by belonging to Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the Israelites]

See: Possession

title: Numbers - Chapter 21 Introduction
content:
Numbers 21 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes Israel’s journey toward Moab and victories over enemy kings. When the people complain, Yahweh sends poisonous snakes. He then provides a way for those who are bitten to live.

  1. Yahweh helps Israel defeat the king of Arad at the Battle of Hormah (1–3)
  2. Yahweh sends poisonous snakes and tells Moses to make a bronze snake (4–9)
  3. Israel continues the journey toward Moab (10–20)
  4. Israel defeats Sihon and takes his land (21–32)
  5. Israel defeats Og and takes his land (33–35)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The bronze serpent

In 21:4–9, the author narrates how the Israelites complained, and God punished them by sending venomous snakes that bit them. When the Israelites ask for forgiveness and help, Yahweh has Moses create a model of a serpent made from bronze. When any Israelite had been bitten by a snake, he or she could look at the model and would recover. The author does not explain how this works, so your translation also should not state that explicitly.

Citations of poetry

In this chapter, the author cites parts of three different pieces of poetry. Each citation supports a claim that the author has made. In 21:14–15, the citation proves that the Arnon River is the border for Moab. In 21:17–18, the citation identifies which story about a well the author is speaking about. In 21:27–30, the citation proves that Sihon captured Heshbon and its territory from the Moabites. It may also prove that the Israelites defeated Sihon. Consider how you might naturally introduce and format citations of poetry that support claims the author is making.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

The Book of the Wars of Yahweh

In 21:14–15, the author cites a small section of “The Book of the Wars of Yahweh.” This quotation is mostly names of places, and it does not include a main verb. The author probably cites it because it identifies the Arnon River as the border of Moab. Consider how you might naturally quote a small, incomplete section of a larger piece of poetry.

The song of the well

In 21:17–18, the author quotes a song (or part of a song) that the Israelites sang when God provided water for them at a well. The song must have been well-known enough that it helped the readers identify which well this was. Consider how you might introduce a quote from a well-known song.

The Song of Heshbon

In 21:27–30, the author quotes from a song that is sometimes called The Song of Heshbon. It is not clear if this is the whole song. Scholars debate whether this song was sung to celebrate the Amorites defeating the Moabites or the Israelites defeating the Amorites. It is also possible that verses 27–29 celebrated the Amorites defeating the Moabites, and verse 30 celebrated the Israelites defeating the Amorites. In any of these cases, the song proves that Sihon took over the territory of the Moabites, including Heshbon. So, when the Israelites defeated Sihon, they gained all this territory. See the notes on these verses for specific translation issues.

title: Numbers 21:1 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֞ע הַ⁠כְּנַעֲנִ֤י מֶֽלֶךְ־עֲרָד֙ יֹשֵׁ֣ב הַ⁠נֶּ֔גֶב כִּ֚י בָּ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל דֶּ֖רֶךְ הָ⁠אֲתָרִ֑ים

"And the Canaanite, the king of Arad, the one dwelling in the Negeb, heard that Israel had come the way of the Atharim"

The event narrated in 21:1–3 may have happened before or after Aaron died, which was narrated in 20:23–29. The Hebrew word translated as “and” at the beginning of this verse does not necessarily mean that this event happened after the previous event. If it would be helpful in your language, you could introduce this event in a way that does not indicate whether it came before or after the previous event. Alternate translation: [Now it also happened that the Canaanite, the king of Arad, the one dwelling in the Negeb, heard that Israel had come the way of the Atharim]

See: Order of Events

title: Numbers 21:1 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠כְּנַעֲנִ֤י מֶֽלֶךְ־עֲרָד֙ יֹשֵׁ֣ב הַ⁠נֶּ֔גֶב

"the Canaanite, the king of Arad, the one dwelling in the Negeb"

Here the author is introducing the Canaanite, the king of Arad, the one dwelling in the Negeb as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [the Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Numbers 21:1 (#3)
content:
דֶּ֖רֶךְ הָ⁠אֲתָרִ֑ים

"the way of the Atharim"

Here, the word Atharim could be: (1) a proper name for a city. In this case, the road probably led to Atharim. Alternate translation: [the road to Atharim]; or (2) a word that means “spies.” In this case, this is probably the road that the Israelite men traveled on when they explored the land (see Numbers 13–14). Alternate translation: [the way the Israelite spies had traveled]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 21:1 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יִּלָּ֨חֶם֙ בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַ⁠יִּ֥שְׁבְּ ׀ מִמֶּ֖⁠נּוּ שֶֽׁבִי

"and he fought against Israel, and he took captive from him a captive"

The pronoun him refers to the nation of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he fought against Israel, and he took captive from Israel a captive]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:1 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠יִּ֥שְׁבְּ ׀ מִמֶּ֖⁠נּוּ שֶֽׁבִי

"and he took captive from him a captive"

This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 21:2 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּדַּ֨ר יִשְׂרָאֵ֥ל נֶ֛דֶר לַֽ⁠יהוָ֖ה וַ⁠יֹּאמַ֑ר

"And Israel vowed a vow to Yahweh, and they said"

The term said introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 21:2 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּדַּ֨ר & נֶ֛דֶר

"And & vowed a vow"

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root: vowed a vow. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [solemnly vowed]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 21:2 (#3)
content:
אִם־נָתֹ֨ן תִּתֵּ֜ן

"If giving, you give"

The Israelites are repeating forms of the verb give in order to intensify their expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [If you give, give]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 21:2 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠יָדִ֔⁠י

"into my hand"

Here, hand represents the control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into my power]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 21:2 (#5)
content:
בְּ⁠יָדִ֔⁠י

"into my hand"

The pronoun my refers to the people of Israel, who speak of themselves here as a single person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [into the hands of our people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:2 (#6)
content:
אִם־נָתֹ֨ן תִּתֵּ֜ן אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֤ם הַ⁠זֶּה֙ בְּ⁠יָדִ֔⁠י וְ⁠הַֽחֲרַמְתִּ֖י אֶת־עָרֵי⁠הֶֽם

"If giving, you give this people into my hand, then I will devote their cities to destruction"

Israel is presenting a possible condition, that they will devote the cities of the Canaanites to destruction if Yahweh gives this people into their hand. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Suppose you give this people into my hand. In that case, I will devote their cities to destruction]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 21:3 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֨ע יְהוָ֜ה בְּ⁠ק֣וֹל יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל

"And Yahweh listened to the voice of Israel"

Here, voice represents what the people of Israel said. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh listened to what Israel said]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 21:3 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּתֵּן֙ אֶת־הַֽ⁠כְּנַעֲנִ֔י

"and he gave the Canaanite"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he gave the Canaanite into their hand]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 21:3 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יַּחֲרֵ֥ם אֶתְ⁠הֶ֖ם וְ⁠אֶת־עָרֵי⁠הֶ֑ם וַ⁠יִּקְרָ֥א

"and he devoted them and their cities to destruction. And he called"

The pronoun he refers to the people of Israel, even though Yahweh was the subject earlier in the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and they devoted them and their cities to destruction. And they called]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:3 (#4)
content:
חָרְמָֽה

"Hormah"

The word Hormah is the name of a place.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 21:4 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסְע֞וּ מֵ⁠הֹ֤ר הָ⁠הָר֙

"And they set out from Mount Hor"

The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 21:4 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסְע֞וּ

"And they set out"

The pronoun they refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites set out]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:4 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠תִּקְצַ֥ר נֶֽפֶשׁ־הָ⁠עָ֖ם

"And the soul of the people was short"

The author is using the soul of the people was short as a common expression of the culture to mean “the people became impatient.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the people became impatient]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 21:4 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסְע֞וּ מֵ⁠הֹ֤ר הָ⁠הָר֙ דֶּ֣רֶךְ יַם־ס֔וּף לִ⁠סְבֹ֖ב אֶת־אֶ֣רֶץ אֱד֑וֹם

"And they set out from Mount Hor by the way of the Sea of Reeds to go around the land of Edom"

Here, to marks go around the land of Edom as the goal or purpose of they set out from Mount Hor by the way of the Sea of Reeds. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Numbers 21:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֣ר הָ⁠עָ֗ם בֵּֽ⁠אלֹהִים֮ וּ⁠בְ⁠מֹשֶׁה֒

"and the people spoke against God and against Moses"

The term spoke introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 21:5 (#2)
content:
לָ⁠מָ֤ה הֶֽעֱלִיתֻ֨⁠נוּ֙ מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֔יִם לָ⁠מ֖וּת בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֑ר

"Why have you brought us up from Egypt to die in the wilderness"

The people are using the question form to complain against God and Moses. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You brought us up from Egypt only to die in the wilderness!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 21:5 (#3)
content:
לָ⁠מָ֤ה הֶֽעֱלִיתֻ֨⁠נוּ֙

"Why have you brought us up"

The pronoun you refers to God and Moses together. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Why have you two brought us up]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:5 (#4)
content:
לָ⁠מָ֤ה הֶֽעֱלִיתֻ֨⁠נוּ֙ מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֔יִם לָ⁠מ֖וּת בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֑ר

"Why have you brought us up from Egypt to die in the wilderness"

Here, to marks die in the wilderness as the goal or purpose of brought us up from Egypt. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Numbers 21:5 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠נַפְשֵׁ֣⁠נוּ קָ֔צָה

"and our soul loathes"

Here, soul represents the appetite of the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and we loathe]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 21:6 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠שְּׂרָפִ֔ים

"the fiery ones"

Here, the phrase fiery ones identifies what kind of serpents these were. Most likely, they were called “fiery” because of how their venom affected people, probably making people swell and have fevers. If your readers would not be familiar with what a fiery serpent is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the venomous serpents]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 21:6 (#2)
content:
וַֽ⁠יְנַשְּׁכ֖וּ אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֑ם

"and they bit the people"

The pronoun they refers to the serpents. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the serpents bit the people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:7 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּבֹא֩ הָ⁠עָ֨ם אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֜ה וַ⁠יֹּאמְר֣וּ

"And the people came to Moses and said"

The term said introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 21:7 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יָּבֹא֩ הָ⁠עָ֨ם אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֜ה וַ⁠יֹּאמְר֣וּ חָטָ֗אנוּ כִּֽי־דִבַּ֤רְנוּ בַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ וָ⁠בָ֔⁠ךְ

"And the people came to Moses and said, “We have sinned, for we spoke against Yahweh and against you"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And the people came to Moses and said, “We have sinned because we spoke against Yahweh and against you.]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 21:7 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יָסֵ֥ר

"and let him remove"

The pronoun him refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and let Yahweh remove]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:7 (#4)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠נָּחָ֑שׁ

"the serpent"

The people are using the serpent to represent all of the serpents that Yahweh had sent among them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the serpents]

See: Synecdoche

title: Numbers 21:8 (#1)
content:
שָׂרָ֔ף

"a fiery one"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [a fiery serpent]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 21:8 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָה֙ כָּל־הַ⁠נָּשׁ֔וּךְ וְ⁠רָאָ֥ה אֹת֖⁠וֹ וָ⁠חָֽי

"and it will be {that} all the bitten ones will see it, and he will live"

Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that anyone who has been bitten will live if he looks at the image on the banner. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [that whoever is bitten will live if he looks at it]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 21:8 (#3)
content:
כָּל־הַ⁠נָּשׁ֔וּךְ

"all the bitten ones"

The expression all the bitten ones is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [everyone whom a serpent has bitten]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 21:9 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְשִׂמֵ֖⁠הוּ עַל־הַ⁠נֵּ֑ס

"and he put it on the banner"

The pronoun it refers to the bronze serpent that Moses made. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he put the bronze serpent on the banner]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:9 (#2)
content:
אִם־נָשַׁ֤ךְ הַ⁠נָּחָשׁ֙ אֶת־אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠הִבִּ֛יט אֶל־נְחַ֥שׁ הַ⁠נְּחֹ֖שֶׁת וָ⁠חָֽי

"if the serpent bit a man and he looked to the serpent of the bronze, then he lived"

The author is presenting a possible condition, that a man who had been bitten would live if he looked at the bronze serpent. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [a man who had been bitten by a serpent and looked at the bronze serpent would live]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 21:9 (#3)
content:
אֶת־אִ֔ישׁ

"a man"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [anyone]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 21:10 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסְע֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"And the sons of Israel set out"

The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 21:11 (#1)
content:
עַל־פְּנֵ֣י מוֹאָ֔ב

"is} upon the face of Moab"

The author is using upon the face of as a common expression of the culture to mean “opposite” or “facing.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [{is} across from Moab]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 21:11 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠מִּזְרַ֖ח הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

"from the rising of the sun"

The author is using from the rising of the sun as a common expression of the culture to mean “to the east.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on the east side]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 21:13 (#1)
content:
כִּ֤י אַרְנוֹן֙ גְּב֣וּל מוֹאָ֔ב בֵּ֥ין מוֹאָ֖ב וּ⁠בֵ֥ין הָ⁠אֱמֹרִֽי

"For Arnon {is} the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorite"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 21:14 (#1)
content:
עַל־כֵּן֙ יֵֽאָמַ֔ר בְּ⁠סֵ֖פֶר מִלְחֲמֹ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה

"Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of Yahweh"

The phrase it is said introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 21:14 (#2)
content:
יֵֽאָמַ֔ר

"it is said"

The expression it is said is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people say]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 21:14 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠סֵ֖פֶר מִלְחֲמֹ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה

"in the Book of the Wars of Yahweh"

The Book of the Wars of Yahweh is the name of an ancient written record. If your readers would not be familiar with what this is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in the ancient written account called the Wars of Yahweh]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 21:14 (#4)
content:
מִלְחֲמֹ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה

"the Wars of Yahweh"

The author is using the possessive form to describe the Wars as ones characterized by belonging to Yahweh, that is, wars that Yahweh fought. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wars that Yahweh fought]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 21:14 (#5)
content:
עַל־כֵּן֙ יֵֽאָמַ֔ר בְּ⁠סֵ֖פֶר מִלְחֲמֹ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה

"Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of Yahweh"

The word translated as Therefore indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [As a result, it is said in the Book of the Wars of Yahweh]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 21:14 (#6)
content:
אֶת־וָהֵ֣ב בְּ⁠סוּפָ֔ה וְ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠נְּחָלִ֖ים אַרְנֽוֹן

"Waheb in Suphah and the wadis of Arnon"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [There is Waheb in Suphah, and there are the wadis of Arnon]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 21:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֶ֨שֶׁד֙ הַ⁠נְּחָלִ֔ים

"and the slope of the wadis"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and there is the slope of the wadis]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 21:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אֶ֨שֶׁד֙ הַ⁠נְּחָלִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָטָ֖ה לְ⁠שֶׁ֣בֶת עָ֑ר וְ⁠נִשְׁעַ֖ן לִ⁠גְב֥וּל מוֹאָֽב

"and the slope of the wadis that stretches out to the seat of Ar and leans to the border of Moab"

The author is speaking of the slope of the wadis as if it were a living thing that could stretch out and lean against something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [goes as far as the seat of Ar … and is at the border of Moab]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 21:16 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מִ⁠שָּׁ֖ם בְּאֵ֑רָ⁠ה

"And from there to Beer"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And from there they went to Beer]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 21:16 (#2)
content:
הִ֣וא הַ⁠בְּאֵ֗ר אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ לְ⁠מֹשֶׁ֔ה

"It {is} the well where Yahweh said to Moses"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 21:16 (#3)
content:
אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ לְ⁠מֹשֶׁ֔ה אֱסֹף֙ אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֔ם וְ⁠אֶתְּנָ֥ה לָ⁠הֶ֖ם מָֽיִם

"Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather the people, and I will give water to them"

The term said introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 21:17 (#1)
content:
אָ֚ז יָשִׁ֣יר יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת־הַ⁠שִּׁירָ֖ה הַ⁠זֹּ֑את

"Then Israel sang this song"

The author is using the word translated as Then to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 21:17 (#2)
content:
אָ֚ז יָשִׁ֣יר יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת־הַ⁠שִּׁירָ֖ה הַ⁠זֹּ֑את

"Then Israel sang this song"

The term sang introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 21:17 (#3)
content:
עֲלִ֥י בְאֵ֖ר

"Go up, well"

The Israelites are speaking to the well, which they know cannot hear them. They are doing this to communicate to the people listening to them that they feel very strongly about the well. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if they were speaking directly to the people about the well. Alternate translation: [May water flow up from the well]

See: Apostrophe

title: Numbers 21:18 (#1)
content:
חֲפָר֣וּ⁠הָ שָׂרִ֗ים כָּר֨וּ⁠הָ֙ נְדִיבֵ֣י הָ⁠עָ֔ם

"princes excavated it, the nobles of the people dug it"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [the princes and nobles of the people dug it]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 21:18 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מִ⁠מִּדְבָּ֖ר מַתָּנָֽה

"And from the wilderness {to} Mattanah"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And from the wilderness they traveled to Mattanah]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 21:18 (#3)
content:
בְּאֵ֞ר חֲפָר֣וּ⁠הָ שָׂרִ֗ים כָּר֨וּ⁠הָ֙ נְדִיבֵ֣י הָ⁠עָ֔ם בִּ⁠מְחֹקֵ֖ק בְּ⁠מִשְׁעֲנֹתָ֑⁠ם

"A well, princes excavated it, the nobles of the people dug it, with a scepter, with their staffs"

Here, the poet could mean that: (1) the princes and nobles authorized the digging of the well using their scepters and staffs. In this case, they do not dig the well themselves. Alternate translation: [A well, princes authorized its excavation, the nobles of the people authorized its construction; they authorized it with a scepter, with their staffs]; or (2) the princes and nobles dig at least part of the well themselves, using scepter and staffs. Alternate translation: [A well, princes excavated it themselves, the nobles of the people dug it themselves, using a scepter, using their staffs]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 21:19 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מִ⁠מַּתָּנָ֖ה נַחֲלִיאֵ֑ל וּ⁠מִ⁠נַּחֲלִיאֵ֖ל בָּמֽוֹת

"to} Nahaliel"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and from Mattanah they traveled to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel they traveled to Bamoth]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 21:20 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מִ⁠בָּמ֗וֹת הַ⁠גַּיְא֙

"and from Bamoth {to} the valley"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and from Bamoth they traveled to the valley]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 21:20 (#2)
content:
רֹ֖אשׁ הַ⁠פִּסְגָּ֑ה

"the head of the Pisgah"

The author is speaking of the top of the Pisgah as if it were a living thing that could have a head. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the top of the Pisgah]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 21:20 (#3)
content:
פְּנֵ֥י הַ⁠יְשִׁימֹֽן

"the face of the wasteland"

Here, the face of represents the surface of the wasteland that could be seen from the mountain peak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the surface of the wasteland]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 21:20 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠יְשִׁימֹֽן

"the wasteland"

Here, the word translated as wasteland could be: (1) a description of the area. Alternate translation: [the deserted area]; or (2) a name. Alternate translation: [Jeshimon]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 21:21 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֤ח יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מַלְאָכִ֔ים אֶל־סִיחֹ֥ן

"messengers to Sihon"

The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 21:21 (#2)
content:
אֶל־סִיחֹ֥ן מֶֽלֶךְ־הָ⁠אֱמֹרִ֖י לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"to Sihon, the king of the Amorites, saying"

The term saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 21:22 (#1)
content:
אֶעְבְּרָ֣ה בְ⁠אַרְצֶ֗⁠ךָ לֹ֤א נִטֶּה֙

"Let me pass over in your land. We will not turn aside"

The pronoun me refers to the people of Israel, even though it is singular and the following pronoun We is plural. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Let us pass over in your land. We will not turn aside]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:22 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠דֶ֤רֶךְ הַ⁠מֶּ֨לֶךְ֙

"On the way of the king"

Israel is using the possessive form to describe a way that is characterized by belonging to the king. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [On the main road used by the king]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 21:23 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא־נָתַ֨ן סִיחֹ֣ן אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל֮ עֲבֹ֣ר בִּ⁠גְבֻל⁠וֹ֒

"And Sihon did not give Israel to pass over in his border"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And Sihon did not give Israel permission to pass over in his border]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 21:23 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יָּבֹ֖א יָ֑הְצָ⁠ה וַ⁠יִּלָּ֖חֶם בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"And he came to Jahaz, and he fought against Israel"

The pronoun he refers to Sihon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Sihon came to Jahaz, and he fought against Israel]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:24 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּכֵּ֥⁠הוּ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְ⁠פִי־חָ֑רֶב

"to the mouth of the sword"

The author is using the phrase struck him to the mouth of the sword as a common expression of the culture to mean “killed him and his army with swords.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Israel put him to the edge of the sword] or [And Israel killed him and his people with swords]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 21:24 (#2)
content:
כִּ֣י עַ֔ז גְּב֖וּל בְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן

"For & the sons of Ammon {was} strong"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 21:25 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠כָל־עָרֵ֣י הָֽ⁠אֱמֹרִ֔י

"in all the cities of the Amorite"

The author says all the cities of the Amorite as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [in every city of the Amorite]

See: Hyperbole

title: Numbers 21:25 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠כָל־בְּנֹתֶֽי⁠הָ

"and in all its daughters"

The author is using its daughters as a common expression of the culture to mean “its surrounding villages.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in all its nearby villages]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 21:26 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י חֶשְׁבּ֔וֹן עִ֗יר סִיחֹ֛ן מֶ֥לֶךְ הָ⁠אֱמֹרִ֖י הִ֑וא

"For Heshbon, it {was} the city of Sihon, the king of the Amorite"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 21:26 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠ה֣וּא נִלְחַ֗ם בְּ⁠מֶ֤לֶךְ מוֹאָב֙ הָֽ⁠רִאשׁ֔וֹן וַ⁠יִּקַּ֧ח אֶת־כָּל־אַרְצ֛⁠וֹ

"and he had fought against the former king of Moab, and he had taken all his land"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 21:26 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠ה֣וּא נִלְחַ֗ם & וַ⁠יִּקַּ֧ח אֶת־כָּל־אַרְצ֛⁠וֹ מִ⁠יָּד֖⁠וֹ

"and he had fought & and he had taken all his land from his hand"

The pronoun his refers to the former king of Moab, not to Sihon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he had fought … and he had taken all the former king of Moab’s land from him]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:26 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠יָּד֖⁠וֹ

"from his hand"

Here, hand represents the control of the former king of Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from his control]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 21:27 (#1)
content:
עַל־כֵּ֛ן יֹאמְר֥וּ הַ⁠מֹּשְׁלִ֖ים בֹּ֣אוּ חֶשְׁבּ֑וֹן תִּבָּנֶ֥ה וְ⁠תִכּוֹנֵ֖ן עִ֥יר סִיחֽוֹן

"Therefore the ones speaking in parables say, “Come to Heshbon! Let it be built and be established, the city of Sihon"

The word translated as Therefore indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [As a result, the ones speaking in parables say]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 21:27 (#2)
content:
עַל־כֵּ֛ן יֹאמְר֥וּ הַ⁠מֹּשְׁלִ֖ים

"Therefore the ones speaking in parables say"

The term say introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 21:27 (#3)
content:
תִּבָּנֶ֥ה וְ⁠תִכּוֹנֵ֖ן

"Let it be built and be established"

The expression be built and be established is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let them build and establish it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 21:28 (#1)
content:
אֵשׁ֙ יָֽצְאָ֣ה מֵֽ⁠חֶשְׁבּ֔וֹן לֶהָבָ֖ה מִ⁠קִּרְיַ֣ת סִיחֹ֑ן

"a fire went out from Heshbon, a flame from the city of Sihon"

Here the poets are speaking as if Sihon’s conquering army were a fire and a flame that went out from Heshbon. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [an army went out from Heshbon, a destroying force from the city of Sihon]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 21:28 (#2)
content:
אָֽכְלָה֙ עָ֣ר מוֹאָ֔ב

"It consumed Ar of Moab"

Here the poets are speaking of the fire as if it were a living thing that could consume Ar of Moab the way a person eats food. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It destroyed Ar of Moab]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 21:28 (#3)
content:
בַּעֲלֵ֖י בָּמ֥וֹת אַרְנֹֽן

"the lords of the high places of Arnon"

The phrase the lords of is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [it swallowed the high places of Arnon]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Numbers 21:29 (#1)
content:
אוֹי־לְ⁠ךָ֣ מוֹאָ֔ב אָבַ֖דְתָּ עַם־כְּמ֑וֹשׁ

"Woe to you, Moab! You have perished, people of Chemosh"

The poets are speaking to Moab, which they know cannot hear them. They are doing this to communicate to the people listening to them that they feel very strongly about the destruction of Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if they were speaking directly to the people about Moab. Alternate translation: [How terrible it is for Moab! The people of Chemosh have perished!]

See: Apostrophe

title: Numbers 21:29 (#2)
content:
אוֹי־לְ⁠ךָ֣ מוֹאָ֔ב

"Woe to you, Moab"

The poets are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, dismay over the destruction that has come on Moab. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Terrible things have happened to you, Moab]

See: Exclamations

title: Numbers 21:29 (#3)
content:
עַם־כְּמ֑וֹשׁ

"people of Chemosh"

The poets are using the possessive form to describe a people who are characterized by their worship of Chemosh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [worshipers of Chemosh]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 21:29 (#4)
content:
כְּמ֑וֹשׁ

"Chemosh"

The word Chemosh is the name of the god whom the people of Moab worshiped. If your readers would not be familiar with who this is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [their god]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 21:29 (#5)
content:
נָתַ֨ן בָּנָ֤י⁠ו פְּלֵיטִם֙ וּ⁠בְנֹתָ֣י⁠ו

"He has given his sons {as} fugitives and his daughters"

The pronoun He refers to Chemosh, the god of Moab. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Chemosh has given his sons as fugitives and his daughters]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:29 (#6)
content:
בַּ⁠שְּׁבִ֔ית

"in the captivity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of captivity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as captives]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 21:30 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠נִּירָ֛⁠ם & וַ⁠נַּשִּׁ֣ים

"And we shot them & And we made desolate"

The pronoun we refers to the Amorites who composed and recited this song. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And we, the Amorites, shot them … And we, the Amorites, made desolate]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:30 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠נִּירָ֛⁠ם & וַ⁠נַּשִּׁ֣ים

"And we shot them & And we made desolate"

Here, the pronoun we could refer to: (1) the Amorites who were ruled by Sihon. In this case, the pronoun them refers to the Moabites whom they defeated. Alternate translation: [And we, the Amorites, shot them, the Moabites … And we made desolate]; or (2) the Israelites who defeated Sihon. In this case, the pronoun them refers to the Amorites who were ruled by Sihon, whom the Israelites defeated. Alternate translation: [And we Israelites shot those Amorites … And we made desolate]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:30 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠נִּירָ֛⁠ם אָבַ֥ד חֶשְׁבּ֖וֹן עַד־דִּיב֑וֹן

"And we shot them. Heshbon has perished as far as Dibon"

The words And we shot them. Heshbon has perished as far as Dibon are a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [And their descendants perished, Heshbon as far as Dibon]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Numbers 21:30 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֖רׄ עַד־מֵֽידְבָֽא

"which {is} as far as Medeba"

The phrase which is is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [fire as far as Medeba]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Numbers 21:32 (#1)
content:
וַֽ⁠יִּלְכְּד֖וּ בְּנֹתֶ֑י⁠הָ

"and they captured its daughters"

The pronoun they refers to the Israelites whom Moses sent. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the Israelites captured its daughters]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:32 (#2)
content:
בְּנֹתֶ֑י⁠הָ

"its daughters"

The author is using its daughters as a common expression of the culture to mean “its surrounding villages.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [its nearby villages]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 21:33 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּפְנוּ֙ וַֽ⁠יַּעֲל֔וּ דֶּ֖רֶךְ הַ⁠בָּשָׁ֑ן

"And they turned and went up the way of the Bashan"

The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 21:33 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּצֵ֣א עוֹג֩ מֶֽלֶךְ־הַ⁠בָּשָׁ֨ן

"And Og, the king of the Bashan, went out"

Here the author is introducing Og, the king of the Bashan as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Now there was a king named Og who ruled the Bashan, and he went out]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Numbers 21:33 (#3)
content:
לַ⁠מִּלְחָמָ֖ה אֶדְרֶֽעִי

"to the battle {at} Edrei"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of battle, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to wage war at Edrei]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 21:34 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֤ה אֶל־מֹשֶׁה֙ אַל־תִּירָ֣א אֹת֔⁠וֹ כִּ֣י בְ⁠יָדְ⁠ךָ֞ נָתַ֧תִּי אֹת֛⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־כָּל־עַמּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־אַרְצ֑⁠וֹ

"And Yahweh said to Moses, “Do not fear him, for into your hand I have given him and all his people and his land"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh said to Moses, “Do not fear him, because I have given him and all his people and his land into your hand.]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 21:34 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֤ה אֶל־מֹשֶׁה֙

"And Yahweh said to Moses"

The term said introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 21:34 (#3)
content:
אַל־תִּירָ֣א אֹת֔⁠וֹ

"Do not fear him"

The words translated as Do not fear are an imperative, but they communicate a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [Since you have no need to fear him]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

title: Numbers 21:34 (#4)
content:
בְ⁠יָדְ⁠ךָ֞ נָתַ֧תִּי אֹת֛⁠וֹ

"into your hand I have given him"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Yahweh giving Og before the phrase into your hand. Alternate translation: [I have given him into your hand]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 21:34 (#5)
content:
בְ⁠יָדְ⁠ךָ֞

"into your hand"

Here, hand represents the control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into your control]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 21:35 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּכּ֨וּ אֹת֤⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־בָּנָי⁠ו֙ וְ⁠אֶת־כָּל־עַמּ֔⁠וֹ

"And they struck him and his sons and all his people"

The pronoun they refers to the Israelites, while the pronoun him refers to Og. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites struck Og and his sons and all his people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 21:35 (#2)
content:
עַד־בִּלְתִּ֥י הִשְׁאִֽיר־ל֖⁠וֹ שָׂרִ֑יד

"until not a survivor remained for him"

The author says not a survivor remained for him as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [until no one was left alive]

See: Hyperbole

title: Numbers 21:35 (#3)
content:
בִּלְתִּ֥י הִשְׁאִֽיר־ל֖⁠וֹ שָׂרִ֑יד

"not a survivor remained for him"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [until not a survivor remained alive for him]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers - Chapter 22 Introduction
content:
Numbers 22 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting
