This chapter introduces Balak, the king of Moab, and Balaam. Balak hires Balaam to curse Israel. On Balaam’s journey, Yahweh uses a donkey and an angel to warn him to speak only what Yahweh tells him.

  1. Israel camps in Moab, and Balak sends for Balaam (1–20)
  2. Balaam’s donkey sees Yahweh’s angel, and the angel warns Balaam (21–35)
  3. Balak welcomes Balaam and takes him to see part of Israel’s camp (36–41)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Cursing

In Balak and Balaam’s culture, people believed that certain people made more effective curses than others. Balaam was a person who could make an effective curse. Balak wants Balaam to say, with words, bad things that would happen to the Israelites. Then, these bad things would actually happen. People in this culture believed that this kind of curse would work because one of the gods would make the bad things happen. Consider how you might refer to spoken words that cause bad things to happen to people.

Balaam’s profession

Numbers 22:7 indicates that Balak’s messengers brought “divinations” with them to Balaam. This indicates that Balaam’s profession was “diviner,” and Joshua 13:22 confirms this by calling Balaam a “diviner.” Divination included several different ways of receiving messages from gods. That included prophecy (speaking directly for a god or gods), receiving and interpreting dreams, and examining events (like the flight of birds) or animal entrails. Balaam encounters God in dreams, speaks for God, and participates in offering sacrifices. All these actions fit with his profession of diviner. Consider how you might refer to this kind of person in your translation.

Why was God angry with Balaam?

God permits Balaam to go with the messengers from Balak. However, once Balaam leaves, God is angry with him for going (22:22). The author does not indicate why God is angry. Some have speculated that Balaam’s intentions are wrong (he only wants money, or he intends to say something contrary to what God wants). Others guess that Balaam is unable to understand what God wants, and so God has to open his eyes. It is recommended that you leave the tension in your translation without explaining it. This best represents what the author of the narrator chose to include.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Introducing Balak

The author first introduces Balak in 22:2. However, the verse does not identify him as a king of Moab. In 22:4, the author again introduces Balak. This time, the verse does identify him as king of Moab. The author probably does this to build suspense. If in your language it would be helpful to introduce more information about Balak earlier, you could include some of the information from verse 4 in verse 2, as the UST does. Alternatively, you could move the information about Balak from verse 4 to verse 2.

Elders of Midian

In 22:4 and 22:7, the author mentions the elders of Midian, who are involved with asking Balaam to curse the Israelites. However, after verse 7, the author never mentions them again. Instead, the focus is on the leaders of Moab. The author may possibly imply that the elders of Midian are still involved. However, it is recommended that you do not include the elders of Midian as implied characters. The author of the passage clearly wanted to focus on the Moabite leaders only from verse 8 onwards.

title: Numbers 22:1 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסְע֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"And the sons of Israel set out"

Based on the previous chapter, the Israelites might have set out from Bashan. However, Numbers 33:48 indicates that the Israelites traveled to the plains of Moab from the mountains of Abarim. It is possible that the previous chapter describes the movements of the army, not the rest of the Israelites. It is also possible that Numbers 33 does not include all the places where the Israelites stopped. So, it is recommended that you do not explicitly indicate where the Israelites set out from in this verse. Alternate translation: [And the sons of Israel moved on] or [The Israelites continued to walk]

title: Numbers 22:1 (#2)
content:
בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"the sons of Israel"

Here the masculine term sons has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Israel]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 22:1 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסְע֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַֽ⁠יַּחֲנוּ֙

"And the sons of Israel set out, and they camped"

The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 22:2 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֥רְא בָּלָ֖ק בֶּן־צִפּ֑וֹר

"And Balak the son of Zippor saw"

Here the author is introducing Balak the son of Zippor as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [There was a man named Balak the son of Zippor, and he]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Numbers 22:3 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֨גָר מוֹאָ֜ב מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠עָ֛ם מְאֹ֖ד כִּ֣י רַב־ה֑וּא

"And Moab was very afraid from the face of the people, because it {was} many"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because the people were many, Moab was very afraid from the face of the people.]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 22:3 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֨גָר מוֹאָ֜ב & מְאֹ֖ד

"And Moab was very afraid"

Here, Moab represents the people of Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the people of Moab were very afraid]

See: Synecdoche

title: Numbers 22:3 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠עָ֛ם

"from the face of the people"

The author is using from the face of as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on account of the people]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 22:3 (#4)
content:
בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"the sons of Israel"

See how you translated the similar expression in 22:1.

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 22:4 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֨אמֶר מוֹאָ֜ב אֶל־זִקְנֵ֣י מִדְיָ֗ן

"And Moab said to the elders of Midian"

The author is using Moab to represent the king and leaders of Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the leaders of Moab said to the elders of Midian]

See: Synecdoche

title: Numbers 22:4 (#2)
content:
יְלַחֲכ֤וּ & אֶת־כָּל־סְבִ֣יבֹתֵ֔י⁠נוּ

"will lick up all around us"

Moab is using will lick up all around us as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [will consume everything around us]

See: Hyperbole

title: Numbers 22:4 (#3)
content:
כִּ⁠לְחֹ֣ךְ הַ⁠שּׁ֔וֹר אֵ֖ת יֶ֣רֶק הַ⁠שָּׂדֶ֑ה

"as the ox licks up the greenery of the field"

The point of this comparison is that just as the ox licks up the greenery of the field, consuming it entirely, so the assembly of Israel will consume everything around Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [leaving nothing, just as an ox eats up all the greenery of a field]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 22:4 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠בָלָ֧ק בֶּן־צִפּ֛וֹר מֶ֥לֶךְ לְ⁠מוֹאָ֖ב בָּ⁠עֵ֥ת הַ⁠הִֽוא

"And Balak the son of Zippor {was} the king of Moab at that time"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 22:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֨ח מַלְאָכִ֜ים אֶל־בִּלְעָ֣ם & לִ⁠קְרֹא־ל֑⁠וֹ

"And he sent messengers to Balaam & to call for him"

Here, the phrase to call for him marks the purpose for which Balak sent the messengers to Balaam. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Numbers 22:5 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֨ח מַלְאָכִ֜ים

"And he sent messengers"

The pronoun he refers to Balak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Balak sent messengers]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 22:5 (#3)
content:
אֶל־בִּלְעָ֣ם בֶּן־בְּע֗וֹר

"to Balaam the son of Beor"

Here the author is introducing Balaam the son of Beor as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [to a man named Balaam, the son of Beor]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Numbers 22:5 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠נָּהָ֛ר

"the River"

The implication is that the River here refers to the Euphrates River. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the great Euphrates River]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 22:5 (#5)
content:
בְּנֵי־עַמּ֖⁠וֹ

"the sons of his people"

Here the masculine term sons has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [the people of his own descent]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 22:5 (#6)
content:
בְּנֵי־עַמּ֖⁠וֹ

"the sons of his people"

The phrase his people is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading that some scholars have suggested. Alternate translation: [the sons of Amaw]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Numbers 22:5 (#7)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר

"saying"

The term saying introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 22:5 (#8)
content:
כִסָּה֙ אֶת־עֵ֣ין הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ

"it has covered the eye of the land"

Here Balak is speaking as if the surface of the land were an eye. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it has covered the surface of the land]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 22:5 (#9)
content:
כִסָּה֙ אֶת־עֵ֣ין הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וְ⁠ה֥וּא יֹשֵׁ֖ב מִ⁠מֻּלִֽ⁠י

"it has covered the eye of the land, and it is dwelling in front of me"

The pronoun it refers to the people who had come out from Egypt. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that people has covered the eye of the land, and that people is dwelling in front of me]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 22:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עַתָּה֩ לְכָ⁠ה־נָּ֨א אָֽרָ⁠ה־לִּ֜⁠י אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֗ה כִּֽי־עָצ֥וּם הוּא֙ מִמֶּ֔⁠נִּי

"And now, please come, curse this people for me, for it {is} mightier than I"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And now, because this people is mightier than I, please come, curse it for me]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 22:6 (#2)
content:
לְכָ⁠ה־נָּ֨א אָֽרָ⁠ה־לִּ֜⁠י אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֗ה

"please come, curse this people for me"

The words translated as come and curse are imperatives, but they communicate a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [I ask that you come and curse this people for me]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

title: Numbers 22:6 (#3)
content:
מְבֹרָ֔ךְ

"is} blessed"

The expression blessed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God blesses]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 22:6 (#4)
content:
יוּאָֽר

"is cursed"

The expression cursed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God curses]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 22:7 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠קְסָמִ֖ים בְּ⁠יָדָ֑⁠ם

"and divinations {were} in their hand"

Here, their hand represents what they were carrying with them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [carrying divinations with them]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 22:7 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠קְסָמִ֖ים בְּ⁠יָדָ֑⁠ם

"and divinations {were} in their hand"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 22:7 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠קְסָמִ֖ים

"and divinations"

The term divinations refers to payments given to someone in exchange for practicing divination, the attempt to gain hidden knowledge through magical or occult means. If your readers would not be familiar with what divinations are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [payments for divining]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 22:8 (#1)
content:
שָׂרֵֽי־מוֹאָ֖ב

"the princes of Moab"

The phrase the princes of Moab refers to the same men whom the author called “the elders of Moab” in the previous verse. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could make this clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [these same leaders of Moab]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Numbers 22:9 (#1)
content:
מִ֛י הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֥ים הָ⁠אֵ֖לֶּה עִמָּֽ⁠ךְ

"Who {are} these men with you"

God is using the question form to prompt Balaam to tell him about his visitors, not because he does not know. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Tell me about these men who are with you.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 22:10 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֥אמֶר בִּלְעָ֖ם אֶל־הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֑ים בָּלָ֧ק בֶּן־צִפֹּ֛ר מֶ֥לֶךְ מוֹאָ֖ב שָׁלַ֥ח אֵלָֽ⁠י

"And Balaam said to God, “Balak the son of Zippor, the king of Moab, sent to me"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. It may be more natural to express this whole statement as an indirect quotation, as modeled by the UST. Alternate translation: [And Balaam told God that Balak the son of Zippor, the king of Moab, had sent to him]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 22:10–11 (#1)
content:
בָּלָ֧ק בֶּן־צִפֹּ֛ר מֶ֥לֶךְ מוֹאָ֖ב שָׁלַ֥ח אֵלָֽ⁠י׃ הִנֵּ֤ה הָ⁠עָם֙ הַ⁠יֹּצֵ֣א מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֔יִם וַ⁠יְכַ֖ס אֶת־עֵ֣ין הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ עַתָּ֗ה לְכָ֤⁠ה קָֽבָ⁠ה־לִּ⁠י֙ אֹת֔⁠וֹ אוּלַ֥י אוּכַ֛ל לְ⁠הִלָּ֥חֶם בּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠גֵרַשְׁתִּֽי⁠ו

"Balak the son of Zippor, the king of Moab, sent to me, ‘Behold, the people coming out from Egypt, and it has covered the eye of the land. Now come, curse it for me. Perhaps I will be able to fight against it and drive it out"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Balak the son of Zippor, the king of Moab, sent word to me that the people coming out from Egypt have covered the eye of the land. He asked me to come and curse that people for him so that he may perhaps be able to fight against that people and drive it out.]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 22:11 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְכַ֖ס אֶת־עֵ֣ין הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ

"and it has covered the eye of the land"

See how you translated these same phrases in Numbers 22:5. Alternate translation: [it has covered the surface of the land]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 22:11 (#2)
content:
לְכָ֤⁠ה קָֽבָ⁠ה־לִּ⁠י֙ אֹת֔⁠וֹ

"come, curse it for me"

See how you translated these same phrases in Numbers 22:6. Alternate translation: [I ask that you come and curse it for me]

title: Numbers 22:11 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יְכַ֖ס אֶת־עֵ֣ין הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ עַתָּ֗ה לְכָ֤⁠ה קָֽבָ⁠ה־לִּ⁠י֙ אֹת֔⁠וֹ אוּלַ֥י אוּכַ֛ל לְ⁠הִלָּ֥חֶם בּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠גֵרַשְׁתִּֽי⁠ו

"and it has covered the eye of the land. Now come, curse it for me. Perhaps I will be able to fight against it and drive it out"

The pronoun it refers to the people coming out from Egypt. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and they have covered the eye of the land. Now come, curse them for me. Perhaps I will be able to fight against them and drive them out]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 22:12 (#1)
content:
בָר֖וּךְ

"is} blessed"

The expression blessed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [I have blessed it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 22:13 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֤קָם בִּלְעָם֙ בַּ⁠בֹּ֔קֶר וַ⁠יֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־שָׂרֵ֣י בָלָ֔ק לְכ֖וּ אֶֽל־אַרְצְ⁠כֶ֑ם כִּ֚י מֵאֵ֣ן יְהוָ֔ה לְ⁠תִתִּ֖⁠י לַ⁠הֲלֹ֥ךְ עִמָּ⁠כֶֽם

"And Balaam rose in the morning and said to the princes of Balak, “Go to your land, for Yahweh has refused to give me to go with you"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And Balaam rose in the morning and said to the princes of Balak, “Because Yahweh has refused to give me to go with you, go to your land.”]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 22:15 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֥סֶף ע֖וֹד בָּלָ֑ק שְׁלֹ֣חַ

"And Balak added again to send"

Balak is using added again as a common expression of the culture to mean “did something again.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Balak again sent princes] or [Balak sent more princes]

See: Idiom

acai.preferred_label: Bring Honor and Glory on Oneself

title: Numbers 22:15 (#2)
content:
מֵ⁠אֵֽלֶּה

"than these"

The pronoun these refers to the princes whom Balak sent the first time. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [than the princes he had sent the first time]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

acai.preferred_label: Bring Honor and Glory on Oneself

title: Numbers 22:16 (#1)
content:
כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ בָּלָ֣ק בֶּן־צִפּ֔וֹר אַל־נָ֥א תִמָּנַ֖ע מֵ⁠הֲלֹ֥ךְ אֵלָֽ⁠י

"Thus says Balak the son of Zippor, ‘Please, do not be withheld from coming to me"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Balak the son of Zippor says that you should not let anything keep you from coming to him]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 22:16 (#2)
content:
אַל & תִמָּנַ֖ע

"do not be withheld"

The expression be withheld is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [do not allow anything to hold you back]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 22:17 (#1)
content:
כִּֽי־כַבֵּ֤ד אֲכַבֶּדְ⁠ךָ֙

"for honoring, I will honor you"

Balak is repeating forms of the verb honor in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I will surely honor you]

See: Reduplication

acai.preferred_label: Bring Honor and Glory on Oneself

title: Numbers 22:17 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠לְכָ⁠ה־נָּא֙ קָֽבָ⁠ה־לִּ֔⁠י אֵ֖ת הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּֽה

"And please come, curse this people for me"

See how you translated these same phrases in Numbers 22:6. Alternate translation: [I ask that you come and curse this people for me]

acai.preferred_label: Bring Honor and Glory on Oneself

title: Numbers 22:18 (#1)
content:
מְלֹ֥א בֵית֖⁠וֹ

"the fullness of his house"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of fullness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [everything that fills his house]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 22:18 (#2)
content:
אֶת־פִּי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהָ֔⁠י

"the mouth of Yahweh my God"

Balaam is using the mouth of Yahweh my God to represent what Yahweh commands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the command of Yahweh my God]

See: Synecdoche

title: Numbers 22:18 (#3)
content:
לַ⁠עֲשׂ֥וֹת קְטַנָּ֖ה א֥וֹ גְדוֹלָֽה

"to do small or great"

Balaam is referring to any action at all by naming two extremes, small and great. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to do anything at all]

See: Merism

title: Numbers 22:18 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠עֲשׂ֥וֹת קְטַנָּ֖ה א֥וֹ גְדוֹלָֽה

"to do small or great"

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to do anything, whether small or great]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 22:19 (#1)
content:
שְׁב֨וּ & בָ⁠זֶ֛ה & הַ⁠לָּ֑יְלָה

"dwell in this tonight"

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [dwell in this place tonight]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 22:20 (#1)
content:
אִם־לִ⁠קְרֹ֤א לְ⁠ךָ֙ בָּ֣אוּ הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֔ים

"If the men have come to call for you"

God is speaking as if this were a hypothetical possibility, but he means that it is actually true. If your language does not state something as a condition if it is certain or true, or if your readers might think that what God is saying is uncertain, then you could translate this as a confident statement. Alternate translation: [Since the men have come to call for you]

See: Connect — Factual Conditions

title: Numbers 22:20 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אַ֗ךְ אֶת־הַ⁠דָּבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁר־אֲדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ אֹת֥⁠וֹ תַעֲשֶֽׂה

"But only the word that I speak to you, it you shall do"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the phrase it you shall do with or before the phrase the word that I speak to you. Alternate translation: [But you shall do only the word that I speak to you]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 22:21 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֤קָם בִּלְעָם֙ בַּ⁠בֹּ֔קֶר

"And Balaam rose in the morning"

The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 22:22 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּֽחַר־אַ֣ף אֱלֹהִים֮

"And the nose of God burned"

The author is using the phrase the nose of God burned as a common expression of the culture to mean that God is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God became angry]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 22:22 (#2)
content:
כִּֽי־הוֹלֵ֣ךְ הוּא֒

"because he was going"

The pronoun he refers to Balaam. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [because Balaam was going]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 22:22 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּתְיַצֵּ֞ב מַלְאַ֧ךְ יְהוָ֛ה

"And the angel of Yahweh stationed himself"

The author is introducing the angel of Yahweh as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Now there was an angel of Yahweh who stationed himself]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Numbers 22:22 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הוּא֙ רֹכֵ֣ב עַל־אֲתֹנ֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁנֵ֥י נְעָרָ֖י⁠ו עִמּֽ⁠וֹ

"And he was riding on his female donkey, and two of his young men {were} with him"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Numbers 22:22 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠שְׁנֵ֥י נְעָרָ֖י⁠ו

"and two of his young men"

Here, the phrase two of his young men could imply: (1) that Balaam had more than these two servants, but these two went with him. Alternate translation: [two young men from his household]; or (2) that Balaam had only these two servants. Alternate translation: [and his two young men]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 22:23 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠חַרְבּ֤⁠וֹ שְׁלוּפָה֙ בְּ⁠יָד֔⁠וֹ

"and his sword being drawn in his hand"

The expression being drawn is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he had drawn his sword in his hand]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 22:23 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֤ךְ בִּלְעָם֙ אֶת־הָ֣⁠אָת֔וֹן לְ⁠הַטֹּתָ֖⁠הּ הַ⁠דָּֽרֶךְ

"And Balaam struck the female donkey to turn her aside to the way"

Here, the phrase to turn her aside to the way marks the purpose for which Balaam struck the donkey. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Numbers 22:24 (#1)
content:
גָּדֵ֥ר מִ⁠זֶּ֖ה וְ⁠גָדֵ֥ר מִ⁠זֶּֽה

"a wall from this and a wall from that"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [with a wall on this side and a wall on that side]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 22:25 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תִּלָּחֵץ֙

"and she pressed herself"

The pronoun she refers to the female donkey. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the donkey pressed herself]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 22:25 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֖סֶף לְ⁠הַכֹּתָֽ⁠הּ

"and he added to strike her"

The author is using added to strike as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam struck the donkey again, that is, an additional time. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he hit her once more] or [he hit her again]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 22:26 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יּ֥וֹסֶף מַלְאַךְ־יְהוָ֖ה עֲב֑וֹר

"And the angel of Yahweh added to pass over"

The author is using added to pass over as a common expression of the culture to mean “continued traveling onward.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [continued on ahead] or [kept going]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 22:27 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּֽחַר־אַ֣ף בִּלְעָ֔ם

"And the nose of Balaam burned"

The author is using the phrase the nose of Balaam burned as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Balaam became furious]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 22:28 (#1)
content:
מֶה־עָשִׂ֣יתִֽי לְ⁠ךָ֔ כִּ֣י הִכִּיתַ֔⁠נִי זֶ֖ה שָׁלֹ֥שׁ רְגָלִֽים

"What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times"

The donkey is using the question form to protest what Balaam has done, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I have done nothing to you that should make you strike me these three times!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 22:29 (#1)
content:
ל֤וּ יֶשׁ־חֶ֨רֶב֙ בְּ⁠יָדִ֔⁠י כִּ֥י עַתָּ֖ה הֲרַגְתִּֽי⁠ךְ

"If only there were a sword in my hand, for I would kill you now"

Balaam is making a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. He is stating it as a condition to show that killing the donkey is not possible for him. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [I wish I had a sword in my hand, because then I would kill you now]

See: Connect — Contrary to Fact Conditions

title: Numbers 22:30 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠לוֹא֩ אָנֹכִ֨י אֲתֹֽנְ⁠ךָ֜ אֲשֶׁר־רָכַ֣בְתָּ עָלַ֗⁠י מֵ⁠עֽוֹדְ⁠ךָ֙ עַד־הַ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה

"Am I not your female donkey on which you have ridden from since you {were} until this day"

The donkey is using the question form to remind Balaam of their long relationship, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I am your female donkey on which you have ridden from since you were until this day.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 22:30 (#2)
content:
מֵ⁠עֽוֹדְ⁠ךָ֙

"from since you {were"

The donkey is using from since you as a common expression of the culture to mean “from the time you first owned me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the time you first owned me]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 22:30 (#3)
content:
הַֽ⁠הַסְכֵּ֣ן הִסְכַּ֔נְתִּי לַ⁠עֲשׂ֥וֹת לְ⁠ךָ֖ כֹּ֑ה

"Being accustomed, have I been accustomed to do thus to you"

The donkey is using the question form to insist that it has never behaved this way before, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I have never been accustomed to do thus to you!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 22:31 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְגַ֣ל יְהוָה֮ אֶת־עֵינֵ֣י בִלְעָם֒

"And Yahweh uncovered the eyes of Balaam"

Here the author is speaking as if Balaam’s inability to see the angel had been a covering over his eyes that Yahweh removed. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh enabled Balaam to see]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 22:31 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקֹּ֥ד וַ⁠יִּשְׁתַּ֖חוּ

"And he bowed and prostrated himself"

The terms bowed and prostrated himself mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [And he bowed low]

See: Doublet

title: Numbers 22:31 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁתַּ֖חוּ לְ⁠אַפָּֽי⁠ו

"and prostrated himself to his nostrils"

The author is using the phrase prostrated himself to his nostrils as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam lay face-down on the ground. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and lay face-down on the ground]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 22:32 (#1)
content:
עַל־מָ֗ה הִכִּ֨יתָ֙ אֶת־אֲתֹ֣נְ⁠ךָ֔ זֶ֖ה שָׁל֣וֹשׁ רְגָלִ֑ים

"Why have you struck your female donkey these three times"

The angel of Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke Balaam, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not have struck your female donkey these three times]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 22:32 (#2)
content:
יָרַ֥ט הַ⁠דֶּ֖רֶךְ לְ⁠נֶגְדִּֽ⁠י

"the way is precipitous in front of me"

Here the angel is speaking of Balaam’s course of action as if it were a way or road that is steep and dangerous. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your course of action is reckless before me]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 22:33 (#1)
content:
אוּלַי֙ נָטְתָ֣ה מִ⁠פָּנַ֔⁠י כִּ֥י עַתָּ֛ה גַּם־אֹתְ⁠כָ֥ה הָרַ֖גְתִּי וְ⁠אוֹתָ֥⁠הּ הֶחֱיֵֽיתִי

"Unless she turned aside from my face, then now I would have killed also you and kept her alive"

The angel says Unless she turned aside from my face to introduce an imaginary situation, describing what would have happened if the donkey had not turned away. Use a natural method in your language for introducing an imaginary situation. Alternate translation: [If she had not turned away from my face, then by now I would have killed you and let her live]

See: Hypothetical Situations

title: Numbers 22:33 (#2)
content:
נָטְתָ֣ה מִ⁠פָּנַ֔⁠י

"she turned aside from my face"

Here, my face represents the angel’s presence, that is, being in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [she turned aside from my presence]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 22:34 (#1)
content:
חָטָ֔אתִי כִּ֚י לֹ֣א יָדַ֔עְתִּי כִּ֥י אַתָּ֛ה נִצָּ֥ב לִ⁠קְרָאתִ֖⁠י בַּ⁠דָּ֑רֶךְ

"I have sinned, for I did not know that you {were} being stationed to meet me in the way"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [“Because I did not know that you were being stationed to meet me in the way, I have sinned.”]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 22:34 (#2)
content:
אִם־רַ֥ע בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֖י⁠ךָ

"if {it is} evil in your eyes"

Balaam is using in your eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean “in your judgment” or “in your opinion.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [if in your judgment {it is} evil]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 22:34 (#3)
content:
אִם־רַ֥ע בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֖י⁠ךָ אָשׁ֥וּבָה לִּֽ⁠י

"if {it is} evil in your eyes, let me return for myself"

Balaam is describing a possible situation in which he would return home if his going on this journey displeases the angel of Yahweh. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Suppose my going is evil in your eyes. Then let me return for myself]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 22:35 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֶ֗פֶס אֶת־הַ⁠דָּבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁר־אֲדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ אֹת֣⁠וֹ תְדַבֵּ֑ר

"but only the word that I speak to you, it you shall speak"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the phrase it you shall speak with or before the phrase the word that I speak to you. Alternate translation: [but you shall speak only the word that I speak to you]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 22:36 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁמַ֥ע בָּלָ֖ק כִּ֣י בָ֣א בִלְעָ֑ם

"And Balak heard that Balaam came"

The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 22:36 (#2)
content:
עִ֣יר מוֹאָ֗ב

"the city of Moab"

Here, the phrase the city of Moab could be: (1) a reference to a specific city in Moab, which is identified by the following phrases. Alternate translation: [a specific city in Moab]; or (2) the name “Ir Moab.” Alternate translation: [Ir Moab]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 22:36 (#3)
content:
אַרְנֹ֔ן

"Arnon"

The word Arnon is the name of a river.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 22:37 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠לֹא֩ שָׁלֹ֨חַ שָׁלַ֤חְתִּי אֵלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לִ⁠קְרֹא־לָ֔⁠ךְ לָ֥⁠מָּה לֹא־הָלַ֖כְתָּ אֵלָ֑⁠י הַֽ⁠אֻמְנָ֔ם לֹ֥א אוּכַ֖ל כַּבְּדֶֽ⁠ךָ

"Sending, did I not send to you to call for you? Why did you not come to me? Am I truly not able to honor you"

Balak is using the question form three times for emphasis, not to ask for information. In the first question, he stresses that he had indeed summoned Balaam; in the second, he rebukes Balaam for not coming sooner; and in the third, he asserts that he is certainly able to reward Balaam. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for those purposes, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [I certainly sent to you to call for you! You should have come to me immediately! I am truly able to honor you!]

See: Rhetorical Question

acai.preferred_label: Bring Honor and Glory on Oneself

title: Numbers 22:38 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠יָכ֥וֹל אוּכַ֖ל דַּבֵּ֣ר מְא֑וּמָה

"being able, am I able to speak anything"

Balaam is using the question form to stress that he cannot say whatever he wants, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I am certainly not able to say anything on my own!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 22:38 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠דָּבָ֗ר אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָשִׂ֧ים אֱלֹהִ֛ים בְּ⁠פִ֖⁠י

"The word that God puts in my mouth"

Here Balaam is speaking as if the message that God wants him to speak were an object that God puts into his mouth. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The message that God gives me to say] or [The words that God wants me to say]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 22:38 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠דָּבָ֗ר אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָשִׂ֧ים אֱלֹהִ֛ים בְּ⁠פִ֖⁠י אֹת֥⁠וֹ אֲדַבֵּֽר

"The word that God puts in my mouth, it I will speak"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the phrase it I will speak with or before the phrase The word that God puts in my mouth. Alternate translation: [I will speak only the word that God puts in my mouth]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 22:39 (#1)
content:
קִרְיַ֥ת חֻצֽוֹת

"to Kiriath Huzoth"

The word Kiriath Huzoth is the name of a town.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 22:40 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְשַׁלַּ֣ח לְ⁠בִלְעָ֔ם

"and sent to Balaam"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and sent some of the meat to Balaam]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 22:41 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְהִ֣י בַ⁠בֹּ֔קֶר

"And it happened in the morning"

The author is using the phrase translated as And it happened to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 22:41 (#2)
content:
בָּמ֣וֹת בָּ֑עַל

"to} Bamoth Baal"

Here, the words translated as Bamoth Baal could be: (1) a name for a place. Alternate translation: [to Bamoth Baal city]; or (2) a reference to the high places where people worshiped Baal. Alternate translation: [to the high places of Baal]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 22:41 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֥רְא מִ⁠שָּׁ֖ם קְצֵ֥ה הָ⁠עָֽם

"and he saw from there the end of the people"

The pronoun he refers to Balaam. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Balaam saw from there the end of the people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 22:41 (#4)
content:
קְצֵ֥ה הָ⁠עָֽם

"the end of the people"

Here, the phrase the end of the people could refer to: (1) the nearest group of Israelites. In this case, Balaam saw only a few of the Israelites, the ones who were closest to him. Alternate translation: [the nearest edge of the people]; or (2) the farthest group of Israelites. In this case, Balaam saw all the Israelites, including the ones who were farthest from him. Alternate translation: [all the people, to their farthest edge]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers - Chapter 23 Introduction
content:
Numbers 23 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Balaam pronounces two separate oracles that bless Israel. The first oracle focuses on how God has blessed Israel when Balak wants Balaam to curse Israel. The second oracle focuses on how God has acted for the Israelites and how strong the Israelites are.

  1. Balaam gives his first message and blesses Israel (1–12)
  2. Balaam gives his second message and explains that God’s blessing cannot be reversed (13–26)
  3. Balak takes Balaam to another place to try again (27–30)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Oracles

The word translated “oracle” in verses 7 and 18 is often translated “proverb” or “parable” in other places. Balaam’s speeches are too long to be considered proverbs. In this case, the word “oracle” may indicate that Balaam is speaking in paired lines (see the paragraph on “Parallelism” below) or perhaps that he has put together multiple statements that are like proverbs. Either way, it is clear that Balaam is speaking as a prophet when he delivers these oracles. Consider what word you might use to refer to poetic, prophetic speech.

Blessing and cursing

See the chapter introduction to Numbers 22 for more information on cursing. People in this culture believed that specific words, spoken by specific people, would have either good or bad effects. The words that led to good effects were blessings, and the words that led to bad effects were curses. In this chapter, Balak asks Balaam to curse the Israelites, but Balaam actually blesses them, as Yahweh commands him to do.

Different locations

After each of Balaam’s oracles in this chapter, Balak requests that they move to a different location and try again. The author does not state why Balak thinks that a change in location will help Balaam curse the Israelites instead of bless them. He may have thought that a different perspective would change Balaam’s mind. He may have thought that God only had power to control Balaam in certain places. Or he may have thought something else. In your translation, it should be clear that Balaam thinks that a change in location will be helpful, but it is recommended that you do not make explicit why Balak thinks the change in location will help.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Parallelism

Hebrew poetry often expresses ideas through parallelism, where two or more lines say similar things using different words. This repetition creates emphasis and helps the reader understand the meaning more fully. Balaam’s poetic oracles in this and the next chapter use parallelism frequently. When translating parallel lines, you may choose to combine them into a single statement, as the UST often does. Or, you may preserve both lines to reflect the poetic style of the original, connecting them with a word that shows repetition rather than addition. Your translation team should decide how to handle parallelism consistently throughout this chapter.

title: Numbers 23:1 (#1)
content:
בָּלָ֔ק

"Balak"

Balak is the king of Moab. See how you translated this in Numbers 22:2.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 23:1 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָכֵ֥ן לִ⁠י֙ בָּ⁠זֶ֔ה שִׁבְעָ֥ה פָרִ֖ים וְ⁠שִׁבְעָ֥ה אֵילִֽים

"and prepare for me in this {place} seven bulls and seven rams"

The implication is that Balaam wants these bulls and rams sacrificed as burnt offerings on the altars he just asked Balak to build. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [kill seven bulls and seven rams as a sacrifice]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 23:3 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠דְבַ֥ר מַה־יַּרְאֵ֖⁠נִי וְ⁠הִגַּ֣דְתִּי לָ֑⁠ךְ

"and the word of what he makes me see, I will declare to you"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about I will declare to you before the information about the word of what he makes me see. Alternate translation: [I will declare to you the word of what he shows me]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 23:4 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֗י⁠ו

"and he said to him"

The pronoun he refers to Balaam, not to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Balaam said to God]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֧שֶׂם יְהוָ֛ה דָּבָ֖ר בְּ⁠פִ֣י בִלְעָ֑ם

"And Yahweh put a word in the mouth of Balaam"

Here, the mouth of Balaam represents Balaam’s ability to speak, and putting a word there means that Yahweh told Balaam what to say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh gave Balaam a message to speak]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 23:6 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֣שָׁב אֵלָ֔י⁠ו

"And he returned to him"

The pronoun he refers to Balaam, and the pronoun him refers to Balak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Balaam returned to Balak]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:6 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֥ה

"and behold"

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [and there he saw]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 23:6 (#3)
content:
נִצָּ֖ב עַל־עֹלָת֑⁠וֹ

"being stationed beside his burnt offering"

The pronoun his refers to Balak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [being stationed beside Balak’s burnt offering]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:7 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשָּׂ֥א מְשָׁל֖⁠וֹ

"And he lifted up his oracle"

The author is using lifted up his oracle as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam began to speak a prophetic message. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he began to declare his prophecy]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 23:7 (#2)
content:
לְכָ⁠ה֙ אָֽרָ⁠ה־לִּ֣⁠י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וּ⁠לְכָ֖⁠ה זֹעֲמָ֥⁠ה יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"Come, curse Jacob for me, and come, denounce Israel"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Telling me to come and curse Jacob for him and to come and denounce Israel]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 23:7 (#3)
content:
לְכָ⁠ה֙ אָֽרָ⁠ה־לִּ֣⁠י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וּ⁠לְכָ֖⁠ה זֹעֲמָ֥⁠ה יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"Come, curse Jacob for me, and come, denounce Israel"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Come and utterly curse the people of Israel for me!]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 23:7 (#4)
content:
יַעֲקֹ֔ב וּ⁠לְכָ֖⁠ה זֹעֲמָ֥⁠ה יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"Jacob & and come, denounce Israel"

The names Jacob and Israel represent the people who are descended from the man Jacob, who was also named Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Jacob … the people of Israel]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 23:8 (#1)
content:
מָ֣ה אֶקֹּ֔ב לֹ֥א קַבֹּ֖⁠ה אֵ֑ל

"What will I curse? God has not cursed"

Balaam is using the question form to emphasize that he cannot curse a people whom God has not cursed. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I will not curse anyone, for God has not cursed]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 23:9 (#1)
content:
כִּֽי

"For"

The word translated as For indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 23:9 (#2)
content:
הֶן־עָם֙ לְ⁠בָדָ֣ד יִשְׁכֹּ֔ן

"Behold, a people dwells alone"

Balaam is speaking of Israel’s life as a distinct nation as if the people dwells alone, living apart from all other peoples. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, a people lives as a nation set apart]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 23:9 (#3)
content:
הֶן

"Behold"

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Indeed]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 23:9 (#4)
content:
לֹ֥א יִתְחַשָּֽׁב

"it does not reckon itself"

Here, the word translated as it does not reckon itself could indicate: (1) what the Israelites think about themselves. Alternate translation: [it does not consider itself]; or (2) what other people think about the Israelites. Alternate translation: [it is reckoned] or [people do not reckon it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 23:10 (#1)
content:
מִ֤י מָנָה֙ עֲפַ֣ר יַעֲקֹ֔ב וּ⁠מִסְפָּ֖ר אֶת־רֹ֣בַע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"Who has counted the dust of Jacob, or a number, the fourth of Israel"

Balaam is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to count the people of Israel, because they are so numerous. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one can count the dust of Jacob, or number even a fourth of Israel!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 23:10 (#2)
content:
עֲפַ֣ר יַעֲקֹ֔ב

"the dust of Jacob"

Balaam is speaking of the descendants of Jacob as if they were the dust of Jacob, which is too plentiful to count. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Jacob, as numerous as dust]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 23:10 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠מִסְפָּ֖ר אֶת־רֹ֣בַע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"or a number, the fourth of Israel"

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [or who has counted a number, the fourth of Israel]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 23:10 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠מִסְפָּ֖ר אֶת־רֹ֣בַע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"or a number, the fourth of Israel"

The word translated as a number is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, which uses the verbal form “has numbered.” Alternate translation: [or who has numbered the fourth of Israel]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Numbers 23:10 (#5)
content:
אֶת־רֹ֣בַע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"the fourth of Israel"

Balaam is using this possessive form to mean a fourth part of the people of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a fourth of the people of Israel]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 23:10 (#6)
content:
אֶת־רֹ֣בַע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"the fourth of Israel"

The phrase the fourth of Israel is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading that some scholars have suggested. Alternate translation: [the dust clouds of Israel]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Numbers 23:10 (#7)
content:
תָּמֹ֤ת נַפְשִׁ⁠י֙ מ֣וֹת יְשָׁרִ֔ים

"May my soul die a death of upright ones"

Balaam is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [May I die the same death that upright people die]

See: Poetry

title: Numbers 23:10 (#8)
content:
יְשָׁרִ֔ים

"upright ones"

Balaam is using the adjective upright as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are upright]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Numbers 23:10 (#9)
content:
וּ⁠תְהִ֥י אַחֲרִיתִ֖⁠י כָּמֹֽ⁠הוּ

"and may my end be like his"

The point of this comparison is that just as the upright come to a peaceful and blessed end, so Balaam wishes his own end to be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and may my end be as peaceful and blessed as theirs]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 23:10 (#10)
content:
אַחֲרִיתִ֖⁠י

"my end"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of end, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way I finish my life]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 23:11 (#1)
content:
מֶ֥ה עָשִׂ֖יתָ לִ֑⁠י

"What have you done to me"

Balak is using the question form to rebuke Balaam and to express his frustration, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Look what you have done to me!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 23:11 (#2)
content:
לָ⁠קֹ֤ב אֹיְבַ⁠י֙ לְקַחְתִּ֔י⁠ךָ

"I brought you to curse my enemies"

The word to marks curse my enemies as the purpose for which Balak brought Balaam. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Numbers 23:11 (#3)
content:
בֵּרַ֥כְתָּ בָרֵֽךְ

"blessing, you have blessed"

Balak is repeating forms of the verb blessed in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you have completely blessed them]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 23:12 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֖עַן וַ⁠יֹּאמַ֑ר

"And he answered and said"

The terms answered and said introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 23:12 (#2)
content:
הֲ⁠לֹ֗א אֵת֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָשִׂ֤ים יְהוָה֙ בְּ⁠פִ֔⁠י אֹת֥⁠וֹ אֶשְׁמֹ֖ר לְ⁠דַבֵּֽר

"Is it} not what Yahweh puts in my mouth, it I shall keep to speak"

Balaam is using the question form to emphasize that he must say only what Yahweh tells him to say. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I must be sure to speak only what Yahweh puts in my mouth!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 23:12 (#3)
content:
יָשִׂ֤ים יְהוָה֙ בְּ⁠פִ֔⁠י

"Yahweh puts in my mouth"

The phrase puts in my mouth represents what Yahweh tells Balaam to say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh commands me to speak]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 23:12 (#4)
content:
אֹת֥⁠וֹ אֶשְׁמֹ֖ר לְ⁠דַבֵּֽר

"it I shall keep to speak"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Balaam speaking before the information about it. Alternate translation: [Shall I not be careful to speak what Yahweh puts in my mouth?]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 23:13 (#1)
content:
תִּרְאֶ֣⁠נּוּ & אֶ֚פֶס קָצֵ֣⁠הוּ תִרְאֶ֔ה וְ⁠כֻלּ֖⁠וֹ לֹ֣א תִרְאֶ֑ה וְ⁠קָבְ⁠נוֹ־לִ֖⁠י

"you will see him. Only his end you will see, and all of him you will not see. And curse him for me"

The pronoun him refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you will see the people of Israel. Only their edge you will see, and all of them you will not see. And curse them for me]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:13 (#2)
content:
אֶ֚פֶס קָצֵ֣⁠הוּ תִרְאֶ֔ה וְ⁠כֻלּ֖⁠וֹ לֹ֣א תִרְאֶ֑ה

"Only his end you will see, and all of him you will not see"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about all of him you will not see before the information about Only his end you will see. Alternate translation: [All of him you will not see, and only his end you will see]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 23:14 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקָּחֵ֨⁠הוּ֙

"And he took him"

The pronoun he refers to Balak, and the pronoun him refers to Balaam. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Balak took Balaam]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:14 (#2)
content:
רֹ֖אשׁ הַ⁠פִּסְגָּ֑ה

"the head of the Pisgah"

The author is speaking of the top of the Pisgah as if it were a living thing that could have a head. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the top of the Pisgah]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 23:14 (#3)
content:
שְׂדֵ֣ה צֹפִ֔ים

"to the field of Zophim"

The word translated as Zophim could be: (1) a proper name. Alternate translation: [to Zophim field]; or (2) the word for “watchmen.” In this case, the field was used for guarding or watching something. Alternate translation: [to the field of watchmen] or [to Watchmen Field]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 23:16 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֥שֶׂם דָּבָ֖ר בְּ⁠פִ֑י⁠ו

"and put a word in his mouth"

Putting a word in his mouth represents Yahweh telling Balaam what to say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and told him what he should say]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 23:16 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֛אמֶר

"and he said"

The pronoun he refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh said]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:17 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּבֹ֣א אֵלָ֗י⁠ו

"And he came to him"

The pronoun he refers to Balaam, and the pronoun him refers to Balak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Balaam came to Balak]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:17 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִנּ֤⁠וֹ

"and behold him"

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [where he was]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 23:17 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִנּ֤⁠וֹ נִצָּב֙ עַל־עֹ֣לָת֔⁠וֹ

"and behold him being stationed beside his burnt offering"

The pronouns him and his refer to Balak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and behold Balak being stationed beside his burnt offering]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:18 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשָּׂ֥א מְשָׁל֖⁠וֹ

"And he lifted up his oracle"

The author is using lifted up his oracle as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam began to speak a prophetic message. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he began his prophecy]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 23:19 (#1)
content:
לֹ֣א אִ֥ישׁ אֵל֙ וִֽ⁠יכַזֵּ֔ב וּ⁠בֶן־אָדָ֖ם

"God {is} not a man that he lies, or a son of a man"

Here the masculine terms man and son of a man have a generic sense that includes any human being, both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [God is not a human being, that he should lie, or a mortal]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 23:19 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠בֶן־אָדָ֖ם וְ⁠יִתְנֶחָ֑ם

"or a son of a man that he changes his mind"

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and God is not a son of a man, that he should change his mind]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 23:19 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠ה֤וּא אָמַר֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יַעֲשֶׂ֔ה

"Has he said and will not do"

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Has he said he would do something and then not done it]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 23:19 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠ה֤וּא אָמַר֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יַעֲשֶׂ֔ה וְ⁠דִבֶּ֖ר וְ⁠לֹ֥א יְקִימֶֽ⁠נָּה

"Has he said and will not do? And has he spoken and will not raise up"

Balaam is using the question form to emphasize that God always does what he says he will do. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [He has said, and he will surely do it; he has spoken, and he will surely fulfill it!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 23:20 (#1)
content:
הִנֵּ֥ה בָרֵ֖ךְ לָקָ֑חְתִּי

"Behold, to bless I have taken"

Balaam is speaking of receiving a command to bless Israel as if it were an object that he had physically taken. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, I have received a command to bless]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 23:20 (#2)
content:
בָרֵ֖ךְ לָקָ֑חְתִּי

"to bless I have taken"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Balaam’s receiving the command before the information about blessing. Alternate translation: [I have received the command to bless]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 23:20 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בֵרֵ֖ךְ וְ⁠לֹ֥א אֲשִׁיבֶֽ⁠נָּה

"and he has blessed, and I cannot return it"

The pronoun he refers to God, and the pronoun it refers to the blessing. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and God has blessed, and I cannot return the blessing]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:21 (#1)
content:
לֹֽא־הִבִּ֥יט אָ֨וֶן֙ בְּ⁠יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְ⁠לֹא־רָאָ֥ה עָמָ֖ל בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"He has not looked at iniquity in Jacob, and he has not seen trouble in Israel"

Here, Balaam might mean that: (1) there will not be any of the results that come from iniquity and trouble. Alternate translation: [He has not looked at the results of iniquity in Jacob, and he has not seen the outcome of trouble in Israel]; or (2) the Israelites have not done any iniquity or trouble. Alternate translation: [He has not looked at Jacob doing iniquity, and he has not seen Israel making trouble]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 23:21 (#2)
content:
לֹֽא־הִבִּ֥יט & וְ⁠לֹא־רָאָ֥ה

"He has not looked at & and he has not seen"

Here, the pronouns He and he could refer to: (1) any person who observes the Israelites. Alternate translation: [No one has looked at … and no one has seen]; or (2) God. Alternate translation: [God has not looked at … and he has not seen]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:21 (#3)
content:
לֹֽא־הִבִּ֥יט אָ֨וֶן֙ בְּ⁠יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְ⁠לֹא־רָאָ֥ה עָמָ֖ל בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"He has not looked at iniquity in Jacob, and he has not seen trouble in Israel"

Here, looked at and seen represent God noticing wrongdoing in order to act against it, so Balaam means that God finds no fault to punish among the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He has found no fault to punish in Jacob, and he has found no wrong to act against in Israel]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 23:21 (#4)
content:
אָ֨וֶן֙

"iniquity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of iniquity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [anything wicked]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 23:21 (#5)
content:
עָמָ֖ל

"trouble"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of trouble, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [anything troubling]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 23:21 (#6)
content:
יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהָי⁠ו֙

"Yahweh his God"

The possessive form his God describes the relationship between Yahweh and the people of Israel: Yahweh is the God whom they worship and who watches over them. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom they worship]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 23:21 (#7)
content:
וּ⁠תְרוּעַ֥ת מֶ֖לֶךְ

"and the shout of a king"

Here, the word shout could refer to: (1) a shout of joy for the king. Alternate translation: [and the shout of joy for a king]; or (2) a battle-cry uttered by the king, indicating the king’s victory. Alternate translation: [and the battle-cry of a king in victory]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 23:22 (#1)
content:
כְּ⁠תוֹעֲפֹ֥ת רְאֵ֖ם לֽ⁠וֹ

"as the horns of a wild ox for him"

The point of this comparison is that just as the horns of a wild ox give it great power, so God gives the people of Israel great strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [giving them strength like the powerful horns of a wild ox]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 23:22 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠תוֹעֲפֹ֥ת רְאֵ֖ם לֽ⁠וֹ

"as the horns of a wild ox for him"

Here, the pronoun him could refer to: (1) God. In this case, it means God is like the ox. Alternate translation: [he is like the horns of a wild ox]; or (2) the Israelites. In this case, it means the Israelites are like the ox. Alternate translation: [they are like the horns of a wild ox]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 23:23 (#1)
content:
לֹא־נַ֨חַשׁ֙ בְּ⁠יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְ⁠לֹא־קֶ֖סֶם בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"there is} no omen against Jacob, and no divination against Israel"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [there is certainly no divination of any kind against Israel]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 23:23 (#2)
content:
לֹא־נַ֨חַשׁ֙ בְּ⁠יַעֲקֹ֔ב

"there is} no omen against Jacob"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of omen, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [no one can look for signs to predict harm against Jacob]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 23:23 (#3)
content:
קֶ֖סֶם

"divination"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of divination, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [words spoken by diviners]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 23:23 (#4)
content:
יֵאָמֵ֤ר לְ⁠יַעֲקֹב֙ וּ⁠לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"it will be said to Jacob and to Israel"

The expression it will be said is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will say to Jacob and to Israel]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 23:23 (#5)
content:
יֵאָמֵ֤ר לְ⁠יַעֲקֹב֙ וּ⁠לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל מַה־פָּ֖עַל אֵֽל

"it will be said to Jacob and to Israel, ‘What has God done"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [it will be said to Jacob and Israel that God has done amazing things]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 23:23 (#6)
content:
מַה־פָּ֖עַל אֵֽל

"What has God done"

The people are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of wonder at what God has done for the people of Israel. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Look at the great things that God has accomplished]

See: Exclamations

title: Numbers 23:24 (#1)
content:
עָם֙ כְּ⁠לָבִ֣יא יָק֔וּם וְ⁠כַ⁠אֲרִ֖י יִתְנַשָּׂ֑א

"a people rises up like a lioness, and like a lion it lifts itself up"

The point of this comparison is that just as a lioness and a lion rise up with great power, so the people of Israel rise up in strength against their enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [a people rises up as powerfully as a lioness, and lifts itself up in strength like a lion]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 23:24 (#2)
content:
לֹ֤א יִשְׁכַּב֙ עַד־יֹ֣אכַל טֶ֔רֶף וְ⁠דַם־חֲלָלִ֖ים יִשְׁתֶּֽה

"It will not lie down until it eats prey and drinks blood of slain {ones"

Balaam speaks of the people of Israel as if they were a lion that will not lie down until it eats prey and drinks blood of slain ones, meaning that Israel will not stop fighting until it has completely defeated its enemies. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The people of Israel will not rest until they have completely defeated their enemies]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 23:25 (#1)
content:
גַּם־קֹ֖ב לֹ֣א תִקֳּבֶ֑⁠נּוּ גַּם־בָּרֵ֖ךְ לֹ֥א תְבָרֲכֶֽ⁠נּוּ

"Both cursing, you shall not curse him, and blessing, you shall not bless him"

Balak is repeating forms of the verbs curse and bless in order to intensify his expression of the ideas that they convey. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [You shall certainly not curse him, and you shall certainly not bless him]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 23:26 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֣עַן בִּלְעָ֔ם וַ⁠יֹּ֖אמֶר אֶל־בָּלָ֑ק

"And Balaam answered and said to Balak"

Balaam answered and said to Balak using two speech verbs together, which was a natural way to introduce direct speech in the original language. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 23:26 (#2)
content:
הֲ⁠לֹ֗א דִּבַּ֤רְתִּי אֵלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר כֹּ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֹת֥⁠וֹ אֶֽעֱשֶֽׂה

"Did I not speak to you, saying, ‘All that Yahweh speaks, it I must do"

Balaam is using the question form to remind Balak that he had already warned him about this. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I certainly spoke to you, saying, ‘All that Yahweh speaks, it I must do.’]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 23:26 (#3)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר כֹּ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֹת֥⁠וֹ אֶֽעֱשֶֽׂה

"saying, ‘All that Yahweh speaks, it I must do"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Did I not speak to you that all that Yahweh speaks, it I must do]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 23:26 (#4)
content:
כֹּ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֹת֥⁠וֹ אֶֽעֱשֶֽׂה

"All that Yahweh speaks, it I must do"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what Balaam must do before the information about who determines it. Alternate translation: [I must do everything that Yahweh speaks]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 23:27 (#1)
content:
לְכָ⁠ה־נָּא֙

"Come, please"

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Even so, please come]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Numbers 23:27 (#2)
content:
יִישַׁר֙ בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֣י הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים

"it will be right in the eyes of God"

Balak is using the phrase in the eyes of God as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the judgment of God” or “according to what pleases God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it will please God] or [God will judge it to be right]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 23:28 (#1)
content:
רֹ֣אשׁ הַ⁠פְּע֔וֹר

"to the head of the Peor"

The author is speaking of the Peor as if it were a living thing that could have a head. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the top of the Peor]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 23:28 (#2)
content:
פְּנֵ֥י הַ⁠יְשִׁימֹֽן

"the face of the wasteland"

Here, the face of represents the surface of the wasteland that could be seen from the mountain peak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the surface of the wasteland]

See: Personification

title: Numbers - Chapter 24 Introduction
content:
Numbers 24 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Balaam pronounces two more oracles that bless Israel. The first oracle focuses on how prosperous and powerful Israel will be. The second oracle focuses on a future leader of the Israelites. Finally, Balaam gives three short oracles about other nearby nations.

  1. Balaam gives his third oracle, describing Israel’s future prosperity and strength (1–14)
  2. Balaam gives his fourth oracle, announcing a future ruler who will defeat Israel’s enemies (15–19)
  3. Balaam gives three short oracles about other nations and then leaves (20–25)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Oracles

The word translated “oracle” in verses 3, 15, 20, 21, and 23 is often translated “proverb” or “parable” in other places. Balaam’s speeches are usually too long to be considered proverbs. In this case, the word “oracle” may indicate that Balaam is speaking in paired lines (see the paragraph on “Parallelism” below) or perhaps that he has put together multiple statements that are like proverbs. Either way, it is clear that Balaam is speaking as a prophet when he delivers these oracles. Consider what word you might use to refer to poetic, prophetic speech.

Blessing and cursing

See the chapter introduction to Numbers 21 for more information on cursing. People in this culture believed that specific words, spoken by specific people, would have either good or bad effects. The words that led to good effects were blessings, and the words that led to bad effects were curses. In this chapter, Balak wants Balaam to curse the Israelites, but Balaam actually blesses them, as Yahweh commands him to do.

A prophecy about the Messiah?

Balaam’s final oracle (24:15–19) seems to refer to a specific person who will be a special ruler of Israel. Scholars debate whether this specific person is David, a future Messiah, or both. The oracle itself is not totally clear about who this person will be and what this person will do. It is recommended that your translation does not make explicit whether some earlier ruler, the Messiah, or both are the subject of the oracle.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Parallelism

Hebrew poetry often expresses ideas through parallelism, where two or more lines say similar things using different words. This repetition creates emphasis and helps the reader understand the meaning more fully. Balaam’s poetic oracles in this and the previous chapter use parallelism frequently. When translating parallel lines, you may choose to combine them into a single statement, as the UST often does. Or, you may preserve both lines to reflect the poetic style of the original, connecting them with a word that shows repetition rather than addition. Your translation team should decide how to handle parallelism consistently throughout this chapter.

Quotes in quotes

In 24:11, 13, there are quotes inside quotes. Consider how your language indicates that a quote contains a quote. The UST models how to express the idea with only one level of quotations.

title: Numbers 24:1 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֣רְא בִּלְעָ֗ם

"And Balaam saw"
