The author is using the word translated as And to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Numbers 24:1 (#2)
content:
ט֞וֹב בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֤י יְהוָה֙

"it was good in the eyes of Yahweh"

The author is using in the eyes of Yahweh as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the judgment of Yahweh” or “according to what Yahweh approved.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh was pleased]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 24:1 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠פַֽעַם־בְּ⁠פַ֖עַם

"as time by time"

The author is using as time by time as a common expression of the culture to mean “as he had done on previous occasions.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as he had done on previous occasions]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 24:1 (#4)
content:
נְחָשִׁ֑ים

"omens"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of omens, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the signs would tell him]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 24:1 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֥שֶׁת אֶל־הַ⁠מִּדְבָּ֖ר פָּנָֽי⁠ו

"and he set his face to the wilderness"

The author is using he set his face to the wilderness as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam turned and looked toward the wilderness. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he turned and looked toward the wilderness]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 24:2 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשָּׂ֨א בִלְעָ֜ם אֶת־עֵינָ֗י⁠ו

"And Balaam lifted up his eyes"

The author is using lifted up his eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam looked up and gazed ahead of himself. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Balaam looked up]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 24:2 (#2)
content:
עָלָ֖י⁠ו

"upon him"

The pronoun him refers to Balaam. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [upon Balaam]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 24:3 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשָּׂ֥א מְשָׁל֖⁠וֹ וַ⁠יֹּאמַ֑ר

"And he lifted up his oracle and said"

The author is using the phrase And he lifted up his oracle and said to introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 24:3 (#2)
content:
נְאֻ֤ם בִּלְעָם֙

"The declaration of Balaam"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the message that he himself is declaring. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Balaam declares this]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:3 (#3)
content:
בְּנ֣⁠וֹ בְעֹ֔ר

"the son of him, Beor"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean that he is the son whose father is Beor. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the son whose father is Beor]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:3 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠נְאֻ֥ם הַ⁠גֶּ֖בֶר שְׁתֻ֥ם הָ⁠עָֽיִן

"and the declaration of the man, opened of the eye"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the message spoken by the man, that is, by Balaam himself. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the message that the man whose eye is opened speaks]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:3 (#5)
content:
שְׁתֻ֥ם הָ⁠עָֽיִן

"opened of the eye"

The word translated as opened represents the written Hebrew text. However, some scholars have proposed that by changing the vowels of this word it would say “closed.” In this case, the meaning would be that Balaam’s eyes had previously been closed. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [having been closed of the eye]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Numbers 24:3 (#6)
content:
שְׁתֻ֥ם הָ⁠עָֽיִן

"opened of the eye"

Here Balaam is speaking of his ability to perceive what God reveals as if it were physical sight, describing himself as opened of the eye. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who perceives clearly]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 24:3 (#7)
content:
שְׁתֻ֥ם הָ⁠עָֽיִן

"opened of the eye"

The expression opened of the eye is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whose eye God has opened]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 24:3 (#8)
content:
נְאֻ֤ם בִּלְעָם֙ בְּנ֣⁠וֹ בְעֹ֔ר וּ⁠נְאֻ֥ם הַ⁠גֶּ֖בֶר שְׁתֻ֥ם הָ⁠עָֽיִן

"The declaration of Balaam, the son of him, Beor, and the declaration of the man, opened of the eye"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [This is the solemn declaration of Balaam son of Beor, the man whose eye is opened] or [The declaration of Balaam, the son of him, Beor, indeed, the declaration of the man, opened of eye]

See: Parallelism

title: Numbers 24:4 (#1)
content:
אִמְרֵי־אֵ֑ל

"the words of God"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the words that God speaks. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the words that God speaks]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:4 (#2)
content:
מַחֲזֵ֤ה שַׁדַּי֙

"the vision of the Almighty"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the vision that the Almighty reveals. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the vision that the Almighty shows him]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:4 (#3)
content:
נֹפֵ֖ל

"falling down"

This could mean: (1) Balaam bows down before God in worship. Alternate translation: [prostrating himself]; or (2) Balaam has fallen into a trance or dream state. Alternate translation: [falling into a trance]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 24:4 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠גְל֥וּי עֵינָֽיִם

"and uncovered of eyes"

Here Balaam speaks of himself as one whose eyes have been uncovered, as if a covering that prevented him from perceiving had been removed. He means that God has enabled him to perceive what God reveals to him. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and clearly perceiving what God shows him]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 24:4 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠גְל֥וּי עֵינָֽיִם

"and uncovered of eyes"

The expression uncovered of eyes is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God uncovered his eyes]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 24:5 (#1)
content:
מַה־טֹּ֥בוּ אֹהָלֶ֖י⁠ךָ

"How good are your tents"

Balaam is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of admiration. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Your tents are so good]

See: Exclamations

title: Numbers 24:5 (#2)
content:
אֹהָלֶ֖י⁠ךָ

"your tents"

The pronoun your refers to the people of Israel, whom Balaam addresses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the tents of your people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 24:5 (#3)
content:
מִשְׁכְּנֹתֶ֖י⁠ךָ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"your dwellings, Israel"

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [how good are your dwellings, Israel]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 24:6 (#1)
content:
כִּ⁠נְחָלִ֣ים נִטָּ֔יוּ

"Like wadis they are stretched out"

The expression are stretched out is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They spread out like wadis]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 24:6 (#2)
content:
כִּ⁠נְחָלִ֣ים נִטָּ֔יוּ

"Like wadis they are stretched out"

The point of this comparison is that just as wadis are stretched out and green with growth, so the settlements of Israel are widespread and flourishing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They spread out and flourish, widespread and green like river valleys]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 24:6 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠גַנֹּ֖ת עֲלֵ֣י נָהָ֑ר

"like gardens upon a river"

The point of this comparison is that just as gardens upon a river are lush and well-watered, so the people of Israel are prosperous and thriving. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like well-watered gardens that grow beside a river]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 24:6 (#4)
content:
כַּ⁠אֲהָלִים֙ נָטַ֣ע יְהוָ֔ה

"like aloes Yahweh has planted"

The point of this comparison is that just as aloes that Yahweh has planted are fragrant and pleasing, so the people of Israel are delightful and firmly established by God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [delightful and firmly established, like aloes that Yahweh has planted]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 24:6 (#5)
content:
כַּ⁠אֲרָזִ֖ים עֲלֵי־מָֽיִם

"like cedars upon water"

The point of this comparison is that just as cedars upon water are tall, strong, and enduring, so the people of Israel are strong and firmly established. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like cedars growing by the water, they are strong and enduring]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 24:7 (#1)
content:
יִֽזַּל־מַ֨יִם֙ מִ⁠דָּ֣לְיָ֔⁠ו

"Water will flow from his buckets"

Here Balaam is speaking of the future prosperity and abundance of Israel as if it were water that would flow from his buckets. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will have abundant prosperity]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 24:7 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠דָּ֣לְיָ֔⁠ו

"from his buckets"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the buckets that belong to Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the buckets that belong to Israel]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:7 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠זַרְע֖⁠וֹ

"and his seed"

Here, the phrase his seed could refer to: (1) seeds from plants that will produce food. Alternate translation: [and his seeds]; or (2) descendants of the Israelites described as if they were seeds. Alternate translation: [and his offspring]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 24:7 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠דָּ֣לְיָ֔⁠ו

"from his buckets"

The pronoun his refers to Israel as a nation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from Israel’s buckets]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 24:7 (#5)
content:
מַלְכּ֔⁠וֹ

"his king"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the king who will rule Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the king who rules Israel]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:7 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠תִנַּשֵּׂ֖א מַלְכֻתֽ⁠וֹ

"and his kingdom will be lifted up"

The expression will be lifted up is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God will exalt his kingdom]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 24:7 (#7)
content:
מַלְכֻתֽ⁠וֹ

"his kingdom"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of kingdom, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the land he rules]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 24:8 (#1)
content:
כְּ⁠תוֹעֲפֹ֥ת רְאֵ֖ם ל֑⁠וֹ

"as the horns of a wild ox for him"

See how you translated this same phrase in Numbers 23:22. Here, the pronoun him could refer to: (1) God. In this case, it means God is like the ox. Alternate translation: [he is like the horns of a wild ox]; or (2) the Israelites. In this case, it means the Israelites are like the ox. Alternate translation: [they are like the horns of a wild ox]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 24:8 (#2)
content:
יֹאכַ֞ל גּוֹיִ֣ם צָרָ֗י⁠ו

"He will devour nations, his adversaries"

Here Balaam is speaking of Israel conquering enemy nations as if Israel would devour them like an animal eating its prey. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will completely conquer nations, his adversaries]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 24:8 (#3)
content:
מוֹצִיא֣⁠וֹ

"is bringing him out"

The pronoun him refers to Israel as a nation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is bringing Israel out]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 24:8 (#4)
content:
כְּ⁠תוֹעֲפֹ֥ת רְאֵ֖ם ל֑⁠וֹ

"as the horns of a wild ox for him"

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he has strength like the horns of a wild ox for him]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 24:8 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠עַצְמֹתֵי⁠הֶ֛ם יְגָרֵ֖ם וְ⁠חִצָּ֥י⁠ו יִמְחָֽץ

"and their bones he will crush, and {with} his arrows he will shatter"

Here Balaam is speaking of Israel utterly destroying its enemies as if it would crush their bones and shatter them with arrows. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will completely destroy them]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 24:8 (#6)
content:
צָרָ֗י⁠ו

"his adversaries"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the nations that oppose Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the nations that oppose him]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:8 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠עַצְמֹתֵי⁠הֶ֛ם

"and their bones"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the bones that belong to the enemy nations. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the bones of those nations]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:8 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠חִצָּ֥י⁠ו

"and {with} his arrows"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the arrows that belong to Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and with the arrows that belong to him]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:9 (#1)
content:
כָּרַ֨ע שָׁכַ֧ב כַּ⁠אֲרִ֛י וּ⁠כְ⁠לָבִ֖יא

"He bowed down, he lay down like a lion, and like a lioness"

The point of this comparison is that just as a lion and a lioness lie down securely and are dangerous to disturb, so the people of Israel are secure and formidable. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [He lies down securely, as dangerous to disturb as a lion or a lioness]

See: Simile

title: Numbers 24:9 (#2)
content:
כָּרַ֨ע שָׁכַ֧ב

"He bowed down, he lay down"

The terms bowed down and lay down mean similar things. Balaam is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [He crouched down]

See: Doublet

title: Numbers 24:9 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠כְ⁠לָבִ֖יא

"and like a lioness"

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he lay down like a lioness]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 24:9 (#4)
content:
מִ֣י יְקִימֶ֑⁠נּוּ

"who will raise him up"

Balaam is using the question form to emphasize that no one dares to rouse or challenge Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one would dare to rouse him!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 24:9 (#5)
content:
מְבָרֲכֶ֣י⁠ךָ בָר֔וּךְ

"Ones blessing you {are} blessed"

The expression blessed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Ones blessing you receive blessing]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 24:9 (#6)
content:
מְבָרֲכֶ֣י⁠ךָ

"Ones blessing you"

The pronoun you refers to Israel, whom Balaam now addresses directly. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Ones blessing you Israelites]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 24:9 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠אֹרְרֶ֖י⁠ךָ אָרֽוּר

"and ones cursing you {are} cursed"

The expression cursed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and ones cursing you receive cursing]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 24:10 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּֽחַר־אַ֤ף בָּלָק֙ אֶל־בִּלְעָ֔ם

"And the nose of Balak burned toward Balaam"

The author is using the nose of Balak burned as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balak became very angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Balak became very angry with Balaam]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 24:10 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּסְפֹּ֖ק אֶת־כַּפָּ֑י⁠ו

"and he clapped his palms"

Clapping the palms together was a symbolic action by which Balak showed his anger and indignation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he clapped his palms together to show his anger]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Numbers 24:10 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֨אמֶר בָּלָ֜ק אֶל־בִּלְעָ֗ם

"And Balak said to Balaam"

The author is using the phrase And Balak said to Balaam to introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 24:10 (#4)
content:
אֹֽיְבַ⁠י֙

"my enemies"

Balak is using the possessive form to mean the people who oppose him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those hostile to me]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:10 (#5)
content:
בֵּרַ֣כְתָּ בָרֵ֔ךְ

"blessing, you have blessed"

Balak is using blessing, you have blessed as a common expression of the culture to emphasize the certainty and completeness of the action. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have surely blessed them]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 24:11 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עַתָּ֖ה בְּרַח־לְ⁠ךָ֣ אֶל־מְקוֹמֶ֑⁠ךָ אָמַ֨רְתִּי֙ כַּבֵּ֣ד אֲכַבֶּדְ⁠ךָ֔ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֛ה מְנָעֲ⁠ךָ֥ יְהוָ֖ה מִ⁠כָּבֽוֹד

"And now, flee for yourself to your place. I said, ‘Honoring, I will honor you,’ and behold, Yahweh has withheld you from honor"

Balak states a result first and then gives the reason for it. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [I said, ‘Honoring, I will honor you,’ but behold, Yahweh has withheld you from honor. So now, flee for yourself to your place]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

acai.preferred_label: Bring Honor and Glory on Oneself

title: Numbers 24:11 (#2)
content:
בְּרַח־לְ⁠ךָ֣ אֶל־מְקוֹמֶ֑⁠ךָ

"flee for yourself to your place"

Balak is using flee for yourself to your place as a common expression of the culture to mean “go back home at once.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [hurry back home right away]

See: Idiom

"your place"

"I said, ‘Honoring, I will honor you"

This includes a second-level quotation, something that Balak had said earlier quoted within his present speech. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [I said that I would honor you greatly,]

If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. title: Numbers 24:12 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠לֹ֗א גַּ֧ם אֶל־מַלְאָכֶ֛י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁר־שָׁלַ֥חְתָּ אֵלַ֖⁠י דִּבַּ֥רְתִּי לֵ⁠אמֹֽר

"Did I not also speak to your messengers whom you sent to me, saying"

What follows is a second-level quotation, the words that Balaam spoke to the messengers. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Did I not also speak to your messengers whom you sent to me and tell them that]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 24:12 (#2)
content:
הֲ⁠לֹ֗א גַּ֧ם אֶל־מַלְאָכֶ֛י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁר־שָׁלַ֥חְתָּ אֵלַ֖⁠י דִּבַּ֥רְתִּי

"Did I not also speak to your messengers whom you sent to me"

Balaam is using the question form to remind Balak that he had already told this to Balak’s messengers. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I also spoke to your messengers]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Numbers 24:13 (#1)
content:
אִם־יִתֶּן־לִ֨⁠י בָלָ֜ק

"If Balak gives to me"

This continues a quotation within a quotation. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [That if Balak gave to me]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 24:13 (#2)
content:
מְלֹ֣א בֵית⁠וֹ֮ כֶּ֣סֶף וְ⁠זָהָב֒

"the fullness of his house, silver and gold"

Balaam says the fullness of his house, silver and gold as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [even all the silver and gold that fills his house]

See: Hyperbole

title: Numbers 24:13 (#3)
content:
אֶת־פִּ֣י יְהוָ֔ה

"the mouth of Yahweh"

Here, the mouth of Yahweh represents “what Yahweh commands.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh commands]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 24:13 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠עֲשׂ֥וֹת טוֹבָ֛ה א֥וֹ רָעָ֖ה

"to do good or evil"

Balaam is referring to anything he might do by naming two opposite extremes, good and evil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to do anything at all]

See: Merism

title: Numbers 24:13 (#5)
content:
טוֹבָ֛ה א֥וֹ רָעָ֖ה

"good or evil"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of good and evil, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what is good or what is bad]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 24:13 (#6)
content:
מִ⁠לִּבִּ֑⁠י

"from my own heart"

Here, my own heart represents “my own will” or “my own initiative.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from my own will]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 24:13 (#7)
content:
מִ⁠לִּבִּ֑⁠י

"from my own heart"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the will that belongs to himself. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to my own will]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 24:14 (#1)
content:
לְכָ⁠ה֙

"Come"

Balaam is using the word Come to get Balak’s attention before telling him something important, not to tell him to move to a different place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen to me]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 24:14 (#2)
content:
יַעֲשֶׂ֜ה הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּ֛ה לְ⁠עַמְּ⁠ךָ֖

"this people will do to your people"

Here, this people refers to the Israelites, while your people refers to the Moabites, Balak’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Israelites will do to your people the Moabites]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 24:14 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠אַחֲרִ֥ית הַ⁠יָּמִֽים

"in the end of the days"

Balaam is using in the end of the days as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the future” or “in days to come.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the future]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 24:15 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשָּׂ֥א מְשָׁל֖⁠וֹ וַ⁠יֹּאמַ֑ר

"And he lifted up his oracle and said"

See how you translated the similar expression in 24:3.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 24:15 (#2)
content:
שְׁתֻ֥ם הָ⁠עָֽיִן

"opened of the eye"

See how you translated the similar expression in 24:3.

content:
אִמְרֵי־אֵ֔ל

"the words of God"

content:
דַּ֣עַת עֶלְי֑וֹן

"the knowledge of the Most High"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of knowledge, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the Most High reveals]

content:

"the vision of the Almighty"

title: Numbers 24:17 (#1)
content:
אֶרְאֶ֨⁠נּוּ֙

"I see him"

The pronoun him refers to a future ruler who will come from Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I see the future ruler]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 24:17 (#2)
content:
דָּרַ֨ךְ כּוֹכָ֜ב מִֽ⁠יַּעֲקֹ֗ב

"A star has trodden from Jacob"

Here Balaam is speaking of a future ruler who will come from Israel as if he were a star. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A great ruler has come from Jacob]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 24:17 (#3)
content:
דָּרַ֨ךְ כּוֹכָ֜ב מִֽ⁠יַּעֲקֹ֗ב וְ⁠קָ֥ם שֵׁ֨בֶט֙ מִ⁠יִּשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"A star has trodden from Jacob, and a scepter has risen from Israel"

Balaam is describing a future event as if it had already happened. He speaks this way to show that the event will certainly take place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the future tense to express this.

See: Predictive Past

title: Numbers 24:17 (#4)
content:
פַּאֲתֵ֣י מוֹאָ֔ב

"the edges of Moab"

The word translated as edges could refer to: (1) the edges of a face, or the forehead. The forehead of Moab is a figurative description of the leaders of Moab. Alternate translation: [the forehead of Moab] or [the leaders of Moab]; or (2) the borders of the territory of Moab. In this case, the phrase refers to all the territory of Moab, from one edge to another. Alternate translation: [all the borders of Moab]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 24:17 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠קָ֥ם שֵׁ֨בֶט֙ מִ⁠יִּשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"and a scepter has risen from Israel"

Here Balaam is speaking of a future ruler who will come from Israel as if he were a scepter. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a ruler has risen from Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 24:17 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠קַרְקַ֖ר

"and destroyed"

The phrase and destroyed is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, is rare and difficult. You may want to follow an alternative reading that scholars have proposed, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and the skull of]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Numbers 24:17 (#7)
content:
פַּאֲתֵ֣י מוֹאָ֔ב

"the edges of Moab"

Here, the edges of Moab represents “all the territory of Moab.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the territory of Moab]

content:
בְּנֵי־שֵֽׁת

"the sons of Seth"

Balaam is speaking as if the people descended from Seth were actually his sons. Alternate translation: [Seth’s descendants]

title: Numbers 24:18 (#1)
content:
יְרֵשָׁ֗ה

"a possession"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of a possession, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [owned by him]

אֹיְבָ֑י⁠ו

"his enemies"

Here, the pronoun his could refer to: (1) the star or scepter from the previous verse. In this case, his refers to a specific ruler. Alternate translation: [that person’s enemies]; or (2) the Israelites in general. Alternate translation: [their enemies] or [Israel’s enemies]

content:
וְ⁠יֵ֖רְדְּ

"And he will rule"

The pronoun he refers to the future ruler who will come from Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And a ruler will rule]

title: Numbers 24:19 (#2)
content:
שָׂרִ֖יד

"a survivor"

Here, a survivor does not refer to a specific person. Balaam means anyone who survives in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [every survivor]

title: Numbers 24:19 (#3)
content:
מֵ⁠עִֽיר

"from a city"

This phrase a city could refer to: (1) any city that this person conquers. Alternate translation: [from every conquered city]; or (2) a specific city, perhaps one named “Ir” or “Ar.” Alternate translation: [from the city] or [from Ar] or [from Ir]

title: Numbers 24:20 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יַּרְא֙ אֶת־עֲמָלֵ֔ק

"And he saw Amalek"

This could mean: (1) that Balaam looked toward the are where the region of Amalek was. Alternate translation: [And he looked in the direction of Amalek]; or (2) that Balaam saw the people of Amalek in a vision. Alternate translation: [And he had a vision of Amalek]

content:
רֵאשִׁ֤ית גּוֹיִם֙

"First of nations"

Here, the word first could refer to: (1) being the most important or powerful. Alternate translation: [First in power of nations]; or (2) being the first nation to live in that area. Alternate translation: [First of nations to arrive here]; or (3) being the first to attack the Israelites. Alternate translation: [First of nations to attack Israel]

title: Numbers 24:20 (#5)
content:
רֵאשִׁ֤ית גּוֹיִם֙

"First of nations"

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the nation that is foremost among the nations. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The foremost among the nations]

title: Numbers 24:21 (#4)

וְ⁠שִׂ֥ים בַּ⁠סֶּ֖לַע קִנֶּֽ⁠ךָ

"and set in the rock {is} your nest"

Here Balaam is speaking of the secure dwelling place of the Kenites as if it were a bird’s nest set in the rock. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your home is secure among the rocks]

title: Numbers 24:21 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠שִׂ֥ים בַּ⁠סֶּ֖לַע קִנֶּֽ⁠ךָ

"and set in the rock {is} your nest"

The expression set in the rock is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and you have built your nest in the rock]

title: Numbers 24:22 (#1)
content:
קָ֑יִן

"Kain"

The word translated as Kain could refer to: (1) an ancestor of the Kenites. See Judges 4:11, where this person may be mentioned. Alternate translation: [you descendants of Kain]; or (2) Cain, the son of Adam. Alternate translation: [Cain]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 24:22 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠בָ֣עֵֽר & עַד־מָ֖ה אַשּׁ֥וּר תִּשְׁבֶּֽ⁠ךָּ

"to burn until when Asshur takes you captive"

Here, the clause until when Asshur takes you captive could be: (1) a statement about when the burning takes place. Alternate translation: [to burn until Asshur takes you captive]; or (2) a rhetorical question about how long Asshur will keep them as captives. Alternate translation: [to burn; until when will Asshur hold you captive?] or [to burn; Asshur will hold you captive for a long time!]

title: Numbers 24:22 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠בָ֣עֵֽר

"to burn"

The verb that the ULT translates as burn often has this meaning in the Hebrew Bible. However, there is another verb with the same consonants that means “destroy” or “devastate,” and the author may have been using that verb here. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [to destroy] or [to devastate]

title: Numbers 24:22 (#4)

title: Numbers - Chapter 25 Introduction
content:
Numbers 25 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the Israelites worship Baal of Peor with the Moabites, and God punishes them. Then Phinehas kills an Israelite man and a Midianite woman who are involved in the worship, and this atones for the Israelites. God then blesses Phinehas. He also tells the Israelites to attack the Midianites.

  1. Israel worships Baal of Peor, and Yahweh commands punishment (1–5)
  2. Phinehas kills an Israelite man and a Midianite woman, and the plague stops (6–9)
  3. Yahweh promises Phinehas and his descendants a lasting priesthood (10–13)
  4. The man and woman are identified, and Yahweh commands Israel to attack Midian (14–18)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

What were the Israelites doing wrong?

Scholars debate what the Israelites were doing with the Midianite and Moabite women in this chapter. Some think that the Israelites were participating in cultic sexual acts with the women as part of their worship of Baal. Others think that the Israelites were marrying the women and then participating with their wives in the worship of Baal. Either way, it is clear that Israelite men were interacting with the Moabite and Midianite women, and these interactions led to the Israelites worshiping Baal. It is recommended that your translation does not indicate explicitly whether cultic sexual activity or marriage was happening.

Midianites and Moabites

In 25:1, the author indicates that the Moabites are the ones who convinced the Israelites to worship Baal. However, the woman whom Phinehas kills for doing this is a Midianite (see 25:6). Further, when Yahweh tells the Israelites to attack the people who convinced them to worship Baal, he identifies those people as the Midianites. Most likely, this area was populated by both Midianites and Moabites, and both groups of people were probably involved. So, you should leave references to both Moabites and Midianites in this chapter.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Events narrated out of sequence

When the Israelites worship Baal, God punishes them by sending a plague. However, the author does not mention the plague until the plague is stopped (see 25:8–9). The author implies that the plague was already happening when the Israelites were mourning near the sacred tent (see 25:6). The author may do this to keep the narration concise or to build suspense. Consider how you might indicate that the plague had already started before verses 8–9.

title: Numbers 25:1 (#3)
content:
בְּנ֥וֹת מוֹאָֽב

"Moab"

title: Numbers 25:2 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תִּקְרֶ֣אןָ לָ⁠עָ֔ם

"to the people"

The pronoun they refers to the daughters of Moab. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the daughters of Moab called to the people]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 25:2 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠זִבְחֵ֖י אֱלֹהֵי⁠הֶ֑ן

"for the sacrifices of their gods"

The author is using the possessive form to describe sacrifices that these people offered to their gods. If this is not clear in your language, you could express the meaning explicitly. Alternate translation: [for the sacrifices that they offered to their gods]

title: Numbers 25:2 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוּ֖וּ לֵֽ⁠אלֹהֵי⁠הֶֽן

"to their gods"

Prostrating themselves was a symbolic action by which the Israelites showed worship and submission to their gods. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [bowed down to the ground before their gods to show that they worshiped them]

title: Numbers 25:3 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּצָּ֥מֶד יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְ⁠בַ֣עַל פְּע֑וֹר

"And Israel was yoked to Baal of Peor"

Here the author is speaking as if the Israelites were animals that had been yoked to Baal of Peor. He means that the people bound themselves to the worship of that god. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [bound itself to the worship of Baal of Peor]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 25:3 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּצָּ֥מֶד יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל

"And Israel was yoked"

The expression was yoked is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Israel yoked itself]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 25:3 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠יִּֽחַר־אַ֥ף יְהוָ֖ה בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"and the nose of Yahweh burned against Israel"

The author is using the phrase the nose of Yahweh burned against Israel as a common expression of the culture to mean that Yahweh became very angry with the Israelites. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh became very angry with Israel]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 25:4 (#1)
content:
אֶת־כָּל־רָאשֵׁ֣י הָ⁠עָ֔ם

"all of the heads of the people"

This could mean: (1) that Moses was supposed to seize and execute all the Israelite leaders, even those who had not worshiped Baal. Alternate translation: [every one of the heads of the people]; or (2) that Moses was supposed to seize and execute only the Israelite leaders who had worshiped Baal. Alternate translation: [all of the heads of the people who worshiped Baal]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 25:4 (#2)
content:
רָאשֵׁ֣י הָ⁠עָ֔ם

"the heads of the people"

Here Yahweh is speaking of the leaders of the people as if they were the heads of the people. In this culture, the head was thought of as the leading part of the body. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the leaders of the people]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 25:4 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הוֹקַ֥ע אוֹתָ֛⁠ם

"and hang them"

Here, the word translated hang could mean: (1) that the leaders would be executed and their bodies hung up. Alternate translation: [and kill them and hang their bodies]; or (2) that the leaders would be impaled and their bodies left there. Alternate translation: [and impale them]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 25:4 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠יהוָ֖ה

"to Yahweh"

This could mean: (1) that the leaders were hung in Yahweh’s presence. Alternate translation: [in Yahweh’s presence]; or (2) that leaders were hung for the sake of or as a sacrifice to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [for Yahweh’s sake] or [as a sacrifice to Yahweh]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 25:4 (#5)
content:
נֶ֣גֶד הַ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶשׁ

"in front of the sun"

Here, the sun represents the open daylight, where everyone could see. Yahweh means that this should be done publicly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in open daylight where everyone can see]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 25:4 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠יָשֹׁ֛ב חֲר֥וֹן אַף־יְהוָ֖ה

"and let the burning of the nose of Yahweh return"

Yahweh is using the burning of the nose of Yahweh as a common expression of the culture to refer to his anger, and for it to return means that his anger will stop. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let the fierce anger of Yahweh turn away]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 25:5 (#1)
content:
הִרְגוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֲנָשָׁ֔י⁠ו

"Kill, a man, his men"

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Let each one of you kill the men under his authority]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 25:5 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠נִּצְמָדִ֖ים לְ⁠בַ֥עַל פְּעֽוֹר

"the ones being yoked to Baal of Peor"

Here Moses is speaking as if these people were animals that had been yoked to Baal of Peor. He means the people who bound themselves to the worship of that god. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones who have joined themselves to the worship of Baal of Peor]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 25:5 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠נִּצְמָדִ֖ים

"the ones being yoked"

The expression being yoked is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones who have yoked themselves]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 25:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֡ה

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: וְ⁠הִנֵּ֡ה"

title: Numbers 25:6 (#2)
content:
אִישׁ֩ מִ⁠בְּנֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל

"a man"

Here the author is introducing a man from the sons of Israel as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a certain man who was an Israelite]

אֶת־הַ⁠מִּדְיָנִ֔ית

"the Midianites"

Here the author is introducing the Midianitess, a woman from Midian, as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a certain woman from Midian]

title: Numbers 25:6 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠עֵינֵ֣י מֹשֶׁ֔ה וּ⁠לְ⁠עֵינֵ֖י כָּל־עֲדַ֣ת

"to the eyes of & and to the eyes of & the congregation of"

The author is using to the eyes of as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the sight of” or “in the presence of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. וְ⁠הֵ֣מָּה בֹכִ֔ים

title: Numbers 25:7 (#1)
content:
פִּֽינְחָס֙ בֶּן־אֶלְעָזָ֔ר בֶּֽן־אַהֲרֹ֖ן הַ⁠כֹּהֵ֑ן

"Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, the priest"

Here the author is introducing Phinehas, a priest, as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a certain priest named Phinehas, who was the son of Eleazar and the grandson of Aaron]

title: Numbers 25:7 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֗רְא

"And & saw"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [saw what the man had done]

title: Numbers 25:8 (#1)
content:
אֶל־קֳבָתָ֑⁠הּ

"to her stomach"

The pronoun her refers to the Midianite woman whom the man of Israel had brought near. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to the Midianite woman’s stomach]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 25:8 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠תֵּֽעָצַר֙ הַ⁠מַּגֵּפָ֔ה

"And the plague was restrained"

The expression was restrained is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God held back the plague]

title: Numbers 25:9 (#1)
content:
אַרְבָּעָ֥ה וְ⁠עֶשְׂרִ֖ים אָֽלֶף

"24,000"

You could translate the number 24,000 according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [twenty-four thousand]

title: Numbers 25:10 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֥ה לֵּ⁠אמֹֽר

"Yahweh & to"

The author is using the word saying to introduce a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

title: Numbers 25:11 (#1)
content:
הֵשִׁ֤יב אֶת־חֲמָתִ⁠י֙

"has returned my heat"

Here Yahweh is speaking of his anger as if it were heat that could be turned back. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has turned away my anger]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 25:11 (#2)
content:
אֶת־קִנְאָתִ֖⁠י

"with} my jealousy"

Here, Yahweh could be using the possessive form to refer to: (1) the jealousy that he himself feels. Alternate translation: [with the jealousy that I have]; or (2) jealousy for the sake of him, Yahweh. Alternate translation: [with jealousy for me]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 25:11 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠קַנְא֥⁠וֹ אֶת־קִנְאָתִ֖⁠י

"by him being jealous {with} my jealousy"

Yahweh is repeating words with related meanings, jealous and jealousy, as a common expression of the culture to emphasize how strongly Phinehas was jealous for Yahweh. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by him being intensely zealous for my honor]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 25:11 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא־כִלִּ֥יתִי אֶת־בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בְּ⁠קִנְאָתִֽ⁠י

"and I did not finish the sons of Israel in my jealousy"

The words and I did not finish introduce the result of Phinehas being jealous with Yahweh’s jealousy. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and so I did not destroy the sons of Israel in my jealousy]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 25:11 (#5)
content:
בְּ⁠קִנְאָתִֽ⁠י

"in my jealousy"

Yahweh is using in my jealousy as a common expression of the culture to refer to his zeal that his people worship him alone. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in my zeal that they worship me alone]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 25:12 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠כֵ֖ן

"Therefore"

The word translated as Therefore indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Because he did that, say, ‘Behold me, giving to him my covenant of peace.]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 25:12 (#2)
content:
הִנְנִ֨⁠י נֹתֵ֥ן ל֛⁠וֹ אֶת־בְּרִיתִ֖⁠י שָׁלֽוֹם

"Behold me, giving to him my covenant of"

The words that Moses is to speak contain a quotation within a quotation. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is giving to him his covenant of peace]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 25:12 (#3)
content:
הִנְנִ֨⁠י נֹתֵ֥ן ל֛⁠וֹ

"Behold me, giving to him"

Yahweh is using Behold me, giving as a common expression of the culture to indicate that he is about to do something, in this case, that he is now giving Phinehas his covenant. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to give to him]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 25:12 (#4)
content:
אֶת־בְּרִיתִ֖⁠י שָׁלֽוֹם

"my covenant of"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of peace, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my covenant that he will prosper peacefully]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 25:13 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠זַרְע֣⁠וֹ אַחֲרָ֔י⁠ו

"and for his seed after him"

Here Yahweh is speaking of Phinehas’s descendants as if they were his seed. Just as a plant grows from seed, so descendants come from a person. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and for his offspring who come after him]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 25:13 (#2)
content:
כְּהֻנַּ֣ת עוֹלָ֑ם

"a priesthood of eternity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of priesthood, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [serving as priests forever]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 25:13 (#3)
content:
תַּ֗חַת אֲשֶׁ֤ר קִנֵּא֙ לֵֽ⁠אלֹהָ֔י⁠ו

"because he was jealous for his God"

The word because indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before.

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 25:14 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠מֻּכֶּ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֤ר הֻכָּה֙

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: הַ⁠מֻּכֶּ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֤ר הֻכָּה֙"

The expressions being struck and was struck are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the one whom Phinehas struck, whom he struck]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 25:14 (#2)
content:
זִמְרִ֖י בֶּן־סָל֑וּא

"was} Zimri & Salu"

The words Zimri and Salu are the names of men.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 25:14 (#3)
content:
בֵֽית־אָ֖ב

"a house of a father"

The author is using a house of a father as a common expression of the culture to mean “clan” or “extended family.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [an ancestral clan]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 25:14 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠שִּׁמְעֹנִֽי

"QUOTE_NOT_FOUND: לַ⁠שִּׁמְעֹנִֽי"

The author is not referring to a specific Simeonite. He means the Simeonites in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for the Simeonites]

title: Numbers 25:15 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠מֻּכָּ֛ה הַ⁠מִּדְיָנִ֖ית

"the one being struck, the Midianitess"

The expression being struck is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Midianite woman whom Phinehas struck]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 25:15 (#2)
content:
כָּזְבִּ֣י בַת־צ֑וּר

"was Cozbi the daughter of Zur"

The word Cozbi is the name of a woman, and the word Zur is the name of a man.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 25:15 (#3)
content:
הֽוּא

"He"

The pronoun He refers to Zur, the father of Cozbi, not to Cozbi herself. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Cozbi’s father Zur]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 25:15 (#4)
content:
רֹ֣אשׁ אֻמּ֥וֹת בֵּֽית־אָ֛ב בְּ⁠מִדְיָ֖ן

"was} a head of peoples, a house of a father in Midian"

Here, the word translated as peoples could refer to: (1) a division of a people group that is the same size as a house of a father. The phrase a house of a father explains for readers what peoples means. Alternate translation: [was a head of peoples, that is, a head of a house of a father in Midian]; or (2) a division of a people group that is made up of several individual “houses of a father.” Zur would be the leader of several houses of a father. Alternate translation: [was a head of peoples, over several houses of a father in Midian]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 25:15 (#5)
content:
רֹ֣אשׁ אֻמּ֥וֹת

"was} a head of peoples"

Here the author is speaking of Zur as if he were the head of these people. In this culture, the head was thought of as the leading part of the body. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ruler over peoples]

title: Numbers 25:16 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֥ה לֵּ⁠אמֹֽר

"Yahweh & to"

The author is using the word saying to introduce a direct quotation. See how you translated saying in 1:1.

title: Numbers 25:18 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י

"for"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is the reason for the command that Yahweh gave. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before.

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers 25:18 (#2)
content:
לָ⁠כֶ֔ם בְּ⁠נִכְלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם אֲשֶׁר־נִכְּל֥וּ

If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by thoroughly deceiving you]

title: Numbers 25:18 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠נִכְלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם

"by their deceptions"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of deceptions, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by their deceitful acts]

title: Numbers 25:18 (#4)
content:
עַל־דְּבַר־פְּע֑וֹר וְ⁠עַל־דְּבַ֞ר כָּזְבִּ֨י

"on the matter of Peor and on the matter of Cozbi"

Yahweh is using on the matter of as a common expression of the culture to mean “concerning” or “in connection with” something. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [concerning Peor and concerning Cozbi … concerning Peor]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 25:18 (#5)
content:
אֲחֹתָ֔⁠ם

"their sister"

The pronoun their refers to the Midianites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the sister of the Midianites]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 25:18 (#6)
content:
הַ⁠מֻּכָּ֥ה

"the one being struck"

title: Numbers - Chapter 26 Introduction
content:
Numbers 26 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Moses and Eleazar take a census of the Israelite men who are at least 20 years old and who can be soldiers. They count the Levites separately. This census shows that none of the men counted in the first census are still alive except for Moses, Caleb, and Joshua.

  1. Moses and Eleazar count Israel’s fighting men by tribe (1–51)
  2. Yahweh explains how the land is to be divided (52–56)
  3. The Levites are counted separately (57–62)
  4. The count confirms that the earlier generation has died, except for Caleb and Joshua (63–65)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Census

In this census, Moses and Eleazar list all the Israelite men who are able to fight or, in the case of the Levites, to serve at the sacred tent. They list the men by their clans, which are subgroups within tribes. While the author uses different words in this chapter, the general format is similar to chapter 1. See how you translated the census record there.

Subclans

For every tribe, the author lists major clans that make up that tribe. In some cases, the author also lists smaller groups within those clans. These smaller groups are sometimes called subclans. Consider what terminology you might use for major groups within a tribe and the smaller groups that make up those major groups.

Dividing the land

In 26:53–56, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide the land up among the tribes. He indicates that larger groups should receive more land than smaller groups. He also indicates that the Israelites should cast lots to see who gets what land. Scholars debate how these two strategies work together. It seems most probable that the Israelites cast lots to see where their land would be, and then they decided on the size of the area based on the size of the tribal group. The author does not directly state whether the lots were cast for each tribe, for each clan, or for each individual. Because the census earlier in the chapter focuses on individual clans, the UST indicates that these instructions are about clans.

Lots

In 26:53–56, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide up the land among the Israelites. These instructions include using lots. Using lots was a way to randomize decisions. Lots could be cast, which would mean rolling or throwing marked stones or pieces of wood to see which side would land upright. Lots could be drawn, which would mean picking marked items without looking at the marks. In this culture, people believed that the decisions, although random from a human perspective, were directed by God. Consider how you might refer to this way of making decisions, which removes human choice but leaves open divine choice.

The Levites

In 26:57–62. Moses and Eleazar count the Levites. The author states why the Levites are counted separately. They do not receive land, so they are not counted among the rest of the Israelites in this census. Additionally, every male who is at least one month old is counted, unlike the rest of the Israelites, who are counted if they are at least 20 years old. The placement of the Levites after the list of the rest of the Israelites shows that the Levites are set apart for God.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Repetition and variation

Many of the entries in this list use the exact same wording. However, in some cases the wording is slightly different, with some words omitted or other words chosen instead. See the ULT for a representation of the differences. Unless the differences are significant, the UST generally models how to keep the entries similar.

Large numbers

The numbers in this chapter are all over 10,000. Consider how you would express large numbers in your language and use that form consistently in this chapter. See how you translated the large numbers in chapter 1.

Breaks in the list

In 26:8–11 and 26:19, the author interrupts the census list to give some details about specific people or groups within a tribe. Consider how you might introduce and format these breaks in the list.

title: Numbers 26:1 (#4)

"Eleazar & Aaron"

The author is not distinguishing this Eleazar from another Eleazar who is not the son of Aaron the priest. The author is reminding his readers that this Eleazar was the son of Aaron who had succeeded him as priest. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [Eleazar, who was the son of Aaron and who had become the priest]

See: Distinguishing Versus Informing or Reminding

title: Numbers 26:2 (#1)
content:
שְׂא֞וּ אֶת־רֹ֣אשׁ ׀ כָּל־עֲדַ֣ת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל

"Lift up the head of all the congregation of the sons of Israel"

Yahweh is using Lift up the head of all the congregation as a common expression of the culture to mean “take a census of all the congregation.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Count the total number of all the congregation of the sons of Israel]
