וַ⁠יָּנִ֕יאוּ אֶת־לֵ֖ב בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"and they forbade the heart of the sons of Israel"

Here Moses is speaking as if the will and courage of the Israelites were their heart. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they weakened the resolve of the sons of Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 32:9 (#2)
content:
נַ֣חַל אֶשְׁכּ֗וֹל

"Wadi Eshcol"

See how you translated this name in 13:23.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 32:9 (#3)
content:
בֹא֙ אֶל

"go to"

See how you translated the similar expression in 23:17. This also occurs in verses 17 and 19.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 32:10 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּֽחַר־אַ֥ף יְהוָ֖ה

"And the nose of Yahweh burned"

Moses is using the nose of Yahweh burned as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh became very angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 13. Alternate translation: [Yahweh became furious]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:10 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠ה֑וּא

"on that day"

By on that day, Moses means the time when the spies gave their report to the people, not necessarily a specific 24-hour period. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [when that happened]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 32:11 (#1)
content:
אִם־יִרְא֨וּ הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֜ים הָ⁠עֹלִ֣ים מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֗יִם מִ⁠בֶּ֨ן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ וָ⁠מַ֔עְלָ⁠ה אֵ֚ת הָ⁠אֲדָמָ֔ה

"If the men, the ones going up from Egypt, from a son of 20 years and upward, see the ground"

Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [The men, the ones going up from Egypt, from a son of 20 years and upward, will certainly not see the ground]

See: Oath Formulas

title: Numbers 32:11 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠בֶּ֨ן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ וָ⁠מַ֔עְלָ⁠ה

"from a son of 20 years and upward"

See how you translated from a son of 20 years and upward in 1:3.

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:11 (#3)
content:
לֹא־מִלְא֖וּ אַחֲרָֽ⁠י

"they did not fill after me"

Yahweh is using they did not fill after me as a common expression of the culture to mean “they were not completely loyal to me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they were not wholeheartedly devoted to me]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:12 (#1)
content:
בִּלְתִּ֞י כָּלֵ֤ב בֶּן־יְפֻנֶּה֙ הַ⁠קְּנִזִּ֔י וִ⁠יהוֹשֻׁ֖עַ בִּן־נ֑וּן

"except Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and Joshua the son of Nun"

If it would appear in your language that Yahweh was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [Only Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and Joshua the son of Nun will see it, because they followed Yahweh completely]

See: Connect — Exception Clauses

title: Numbers 32:12 (#2)
content:
מִלְא֖וּ אַחֲרֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"they filled after Yahweh"

Even though Yahweh is the one speaking, he is referring to himself in the third person as Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [they filled after me]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 32:12 (#3)
content:
נ֑וּן

"Nun"

See how you translated this name in 11:28. This also occurs in verse 28.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 32:13 (#1)
content:
כָּל־הַ⁠דּ֔וֹר הָ⁠עֹשֶׂ֥ה הָ⁠רַ֖ע בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"all the generation, the ones doing the evil in the eyes of Yahweh"

Moses is not distinguishing this generation from another generation that was not doing the evil in the eyes of Yahweh. Moses is reminding his listeners that every adult of that generation had done evil. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [all that generation, who had all done what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh]

See: Distinguishing Versus Informing or Reminding

title: Numbers 32:13 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠עֹשֶׂ֥ה הָ⁠רַ֖ע בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"the ones doing the evil in the eyes of Yahweh"

Moses is using doing the evil in the eyes of Yahweh as a common expression of the culture to mean “doing what Yahweh considers to be evil.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones doing what Yahweh considers to be evil]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:13 (#3)
content:
תֹּם֙

"the finishing of"

See how you translated the similar expression in 14:35.

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:14 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠סְפּ֣וֹת

"to sweep away"

The phrase to sweep away is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [to add]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Numbers 32:14 (#2)
content:
תַּרְבּ֖וּת אֲנָשִׁ֣ים חַטָּאִ֑ים

"a brood of sinful men"

Here Moses is speaking of these men as if they were a brood produced by sinful men. He means that they are behaving sinfully as their fathers did. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [men who sin just as your fathers did]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 32:15 (#1)
content:
תְשׁוּבֻ⁠ן֙ מֵֽ⁠אַחֲרָ֔י⁠ו

"you will return from after him"

Moses is using you will return from after him as a common expression of the culture to mean “you will stop following Yahweh.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will turn away from following him]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יָסַ֣ף ע֔וֹד לְ⁠הַנִּיח֖⁠וֹ בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֑ר וְ⁠שִֽׁחַתֶּ֖ם לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּֽה

"and he will add still to make him rest in the wilderness, and you will destroy all this people"

In this verse, the word him is singular in form, but it refers to all the Israelites as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “him.” Alternate translation: [and he will add still to make them rest in the wilderness, and you will destroy all this people]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 32:16 (#1)
content:
גִּדְרֹ֥ת צֹ֛אן

"pens of a flock"

The term pens of a flock describes enclosures, often built of stone, in which people kept their sheep and goats safe. If your readers would not be familiar with what pens of a flock are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. This also occurs in verse 36. Alternate translation: [walled enclosures]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 32:17 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנַ֜חְנוּ נֵחָלֵ֣ץ

"And we, we will be equipped"

The sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are stating the pronoun we twice for emphasis. They are doing this to stress that they themselves will fight along with the other Israelites. If a speaker of your language would use a repeated pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 32:17 (#2)
content:
חֻשִׁ֗ים

"being hurried"

This could mean: (1) that the people will act quickly. Alternate translation: [as fast as possible]; or (2) that the people will be ready to fight. Alternate translation: [ready to fight]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 32:17 (#3)
content:
נֵחָלֵ֣ץ חֻשִׁ֗ים

"we will be equipped, being hurried"

The expressions be equipped and being hurried are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [we will arm ourselves and hurry]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 32:17 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠פְּנֵ֖י יֹשְׁבֵ֥י הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

"from the face of the dwellers of the land"

The sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are using from the face of the dwellers of the land as a common expression of the culture to mean that their children would be “safe from the people who lived in the land.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [protected from the people who live in the land]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:19 (#1)
content:
בָ֤אָה נַחֲלָתֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ אֵלֵ֔י⁠נוּ

"our inheritance has come to us"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of inheritance, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [we have already received what we will inherit]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 32:19 (#2)
content:
וָ⁠הָ֑לְאָה

"and beyond"

See how you translated the similar expression in 15:23.

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:19 (#3)
content:
מִזְרָֽחָ⁠ה

"toward the sunrise"

The sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are using toward the sunrise as a common expression of the culture to mean “toward the east.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [toward the east]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:20 (#1)
content:
אִֽם־תַּעֲשׂ֖וּ⁠ן אֶת־הַ⁠דָּבָ֣ר הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה אִם־תֵּחָֽלְצ֛וּ לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה לַ⁠מִּלְחָמָֽה

"If you do this word, if you are equipped to the face of Yahweh for the battle"

Moses is presenting a possible condition: the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben will receive this land only if they arm themselves and fight along with the other Israelites. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Suppose you do what you have said, and suppose you arm yourselves for battle in the presence of Yahweh]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 32:20 (#2)
content:
אִם־תֵּחָֽלְצ֛וּ לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה

"if you are equipped to the face of Yahweh"

The expression are equipped is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [if you arm yourselves before Yahweh]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 32:20 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה

"to the face of Yahweh"

See how you translated the similar expression in 5:16. This also occurs in verses 21, 22, 27, 29, and 32.

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 32:21 (#1)
content:
כָּל־חָל֛וּץ

"every equipped one"

Moses is using the adjective equipped as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. This also occurs in verses 27 and 29. Alternate translation: [every man who is equipped for battle]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Numbers 32:21 (#2)
content:
עַ֧ד הוֹרִישׁ֛⁠וֹ אֶת־אֹיְבָ֖י⁠ו מִ⁠פָּנָֽי⁠ו

"until he has dispossessed his enemies from his face"

The pronouns he and his refer to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [until Yahweh has driven out the enemies of Yahweh from before him]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 32:22 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נִכְבְּשָׁ֨ה הָ⁠אָ֜רֶץ לִ⁠פְנֵ֤י יְהוָה֙

"and the land is subdued to the face of Yahweh"

The expression is subdued is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and you subdue the land in the presence of Yahweh]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 32:22 (#2)
content:
וִ⁠הְיִיתֶ֧ם נְקִיִּ֛ים מֵ⁠יְהוָ֖ה וּ⁠מִ⁠יִּשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"and you will be innocent from Yahweh and from Israel"

Moses is using you will be innocent from Yahweh and from Israel as a common expression of the culture to mean “you will have no further obligation to Yahweh or to the rest of the Israelites.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will have no further obligation to Yahweh or to the rest of the Israelites]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:23 (#1)
content:
חַטַּאתְ⁠כֶ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּמְצָ֖א אֶתְ⁠כֶֽם

"your sin, that it will find you"

Moses is speaking of your sin as if it were a living thing that could find the person who committed it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that Yahweh will hold you accountable for your sin]

See: Personification

title: Numbers 32:24 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠יֹּצֵ֥א מִ⁠פִּי⁠כֶ֖ם תַּעֲשֽׂוּ

"and the thing going out from your mouth you shall do"

Moses is using the thing going out from your mouth as a common expression of the culture to mean “what you have promised.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you shall do what you have promised]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:25 (#1)
content:
אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י מְצַוֶּֽה

"my master is commanding"

Even though the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are addressing Moses directly, they are speaking of him in the third person as my master to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [you, sir, are commanding]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 32:26 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־בְּהֶמְתֵּ֑⁠נוּ

"and all our animal"

See how you translated the similar expression in 31:9.

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 32:28 (#1)
content:
רָאשֵׁ֛י

"the heads of"

The author is using the heads of as a common expression of the culture to mean “the leaders of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the chiefs of] or [the leaders of]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 32:30 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אִם־לֹ֧א יַֽעַבְר֛וּ חֲלוּצִ֖ים אִתְּ⁠כֶ֑ם

"But if they do not pass over, being equipped, with you"

The expression being equipped is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But if they do not equip themselves for battle and pass over with you]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 32:32 (#1)
content:
נַ֣חְנוּ נַעֲבֹ֧ר

"We, we will pass over"

The sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are stating the pronoun We twice for emphasis. They are doing this to stress that they themselves will cross the Jordan with the other Israelites. If a speaker of your language would use a repeated pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 32:32 (#2)
content:
נַ֣חְנוּ נַעֲבֹ֧ר חֲלוּצִ֛ים

"We, we will pass over, being equipped"

See how you translated these similar phrases in Numbers 32:30.

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 32:32 (#3)
content:
אֲחֻזַּ֣ת נַחֲלָתֵ֔⁠נוּ

"will be} the possession of our inheritance"

See how you translated the similar expression in 27:7.

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 32:33 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠חֲצִ֣י ׀ שֵׁ֣בֶט ׀ מְנַשֶּׁ֣ה בֶן־יוֹסֵ֗ף

"and to the half of the tribe of Manasseh the son of Joseph"

Here the author is introducing the half of the tribe of Manasseh as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and to another group as well, the half of the tribe of Manasseh, who descended from Joseph]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Numbers 32:33 (#2)
content:
הָֽ⁠אֱמֹרִ֔י

"the Amorite"

The author is not referring to a specific Amorite person. He means the Amorite people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Amorites]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 32:38 (#1)
content:
מֽוּסַבֹּ֥ת שֵׁ֖ם

"being changed of name"

The phrase being changed of name could apply to: (1) just Nebo and Baal Meon. Alternate translation: [the names of these two towns were changed]; or (2) some of the previous town names. Alternate translation: [the names of some of these towns were changed]; or (3) just Baal Meon. Alternate translation: [the name of this town was changed]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 32:38 (#2)
content:
מֽוּסַבֹּ֥ת שֵׁ֖ם

"being changed of name"

The expression being changed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, it could be: (1) Israelites at some later time. Alternate translation: [the Israelites later changed the names]; or (2) the people of Reuben when they fortified the cities. Alternate translation: [the Reubenites changed their names]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 32:39 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֵּ֨לְכ֜וּ בְּנֵ֨י מָכִ֧יר בֶּן־מְנַשֶּׁ֛ה גִּלְעָ֖דָ⁠ה וַֽ⁠יִּלְכְּדֻ֑⁠הָ וַ⁠יּ֖וֹרֶשׁ אֶת־הָ⁠אֱמֹרִ֥י

"And the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead and captured it, and he dispossessed the Amorite"

In this verse, the word he is singular in form, but it refers to all the descendants of Machir as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “he.” Alternate translation: [And the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead and captured it, and they dispossessed the Amorite]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Numbers 32:39 (#2)
content:
אֶת־הָ⁠אֱמֹרִ֥י

"the Amorite"

The author is not referring to a specific Amorite. He means the Amorite people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Amorites]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 32:39 (#3)
content:
בֶּן־מְנַשֶּׁ֛ה

"the son of Manasseh"

See how you translated the similar expression in 1:34. This also occurs in verses 40 and 41.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 32:41 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּלְכֹּ֖ד אֶת־חַוֺּתֵי⁠הֶ֑ם

"and captured their villages"

The pronoun their refers to the Amorites who lived in the region of Gilead. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and captured the villages of the Amorites]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 32:41 (#2)
content:
חַוֺּ֥ת יָאִֽיר

"Havvoth Jair"

The words Havvoth Jair are the name of a group of villages. The name means “the tent villages of Jair.”

See: How to Translate Names

title: Numbers 32:42 (#1)
content:
אֶת־קְנָ֖ת וְ⁠אֶת־בְּנֹתֶ֑י⁠הָ

"Kenath and its daughters"

Here the author is speaking as if the villages surrounding Kenath were its daughters. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Kenath and the villages around it]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers - Chapter 33 Introduction
content:
Numbers 33 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the narrator records places where the Israelites camped on the way from Egypt to the plains of Moab. At the end of the chapter, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how the Israelites should conquer and divide the land.

  1. Moses records the stages of Israel’s journey (1–2)
  2. Israel’s journey from Egypt to the plains of Moab is listed (3–49)
  3. Yahweh commands Israel to drive out Canaan’s inhabitants, destroy their places of worship, and divide the land (50–56)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Dividing the land

In 33:54, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide the land up among the tribes. He indicates that larger groups should receive more land than smaller groups. He also indicates that the Israelites should cast lots to see who gets what land. Scholars debate how these two strategies work together. It seems most probable that the Israelites cast lots to see where their land would be, and then they decided on the size of the area based on the size of the tribal group. See how you translated the similar instructions in 26:53–56.

Lots

In 33:54, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide up the land among the Israelites. These instructions include using lots. Using lots was a way to randomize decisions. Lots could be cast, which would mean rolling or throwing marked stones or pieces of wood to see which side would land upright. Lots could be drawn, which would mean picking marked items without looking at the marks. In this culture, people believed that the decisions, although random from a human perspective, were directed by God. Consider how you might refer to this way of making decisions, which removes human choice but leaves open divine choice. See how you translated the instructions concerning lots in 26:53–56.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Unknown locations

Many of the places named in this chapter are unknown to contemporary scholars. Not only is it uncertain where the places were, but it is also uncertain what kind of places they were. Each of the place names could be a town, a wadi, a hill, an oasis, or something else. Because of this uncertainty, it is recommended that you refer to these places as generically as you can.

title: Numbers 33:1 (#1)
content:
אֵ֜לֶּה מַסְעֵ֣י בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל

title: Numbers - Chapter 34 Introduction
content:
Numbers 34 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter describes the borders of the land Israel will receive in Canaan. Yahweh also names the leaders who will divide the land among the tribes.

  1. Yahweh describes Canaan’s southern, western, northern, and eastern borders (1–12)
  2. Moses explains which tribes will receive land west of the Jordan (13–15)
  3. Yahweh names the leaders who will divide the land (16–29)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The borders of Canaan

In the first part of this chapter, Yahweh outlines the borders of Canaan. He describes a shape that is almost a rectangle. He starts at the southeast corner, which is the bottom of the Sea of Salt. The south side is a curved line from there to the Mediterranean Sea. The west side simply follows the Mediterranean Sea. The north side begins in the west at the Mediterranean Sea and goes east, somewhere above the Sea of Chinnereth. The east side begins somewhere above the Sea of Chinnereth and goes south to the southern part of the Sea of Salt. While the Israelites did not succeed in conquering all this territory, this is the area that Yahweh instructed them to conquer.

Inheriting the land

In the second half of this chapter, Yahweh speaks of leaders “inheriting the land.” This phrase refers to the process of dividing the land up into sections. The leaders would then assign each section to a tribal group or family. They would do this using lots (see the chapter introduction to Numbers 33 for more information on lots). Yahweh ensures that at least one leader from each tribe was involved in this process.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Unknown locations

Much like in chapter 33, many of the place names in the first half of this chapter are unknown. Not only is it uncertain where the places were, but it is also uncertain what kind of places they were. Each of the place names could be a town, a wadi, a hill, an oasis, or something else. Because of this uncertainty, it is recommended that you refer to most of these places as generically as you can.

Yahweh is using who will inherit the land for you as a common expression of the culture to mean “who will divide the land among you as your inheritance.” These men will not receive the land for themselves. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who will distribute the land to you as your inheritance]

See: Idiom

Alternate translation: [to divide the land among the Israelites as their inheritance]

אֵ֕לֶּה אֲשֶׁ֖ר

"These {are} whom"

content:
לְ⁠נַחֵ֥ל אֶת־בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל

"to make the sons of Israel inherit"

The author is using to make the sons of Israel inherit as a common expression of the culture to mean “to divide the land among the Israelites as their inheritance.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to distribute to the sons of Israel their portions as an inheritance]

title: Numbers - Chapter 35 Introduction
content:
Numbers 35 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter gives instructions for towns and pastureland for the Levites. Six towns will be places of refuge for people who kill someone by accident. The chapter explains how to distinguish murder (intentional killing) from manslaughter (unintentional killing) and how each case must be handled.

  1. Yahweh commands Israel to give towns and pastureland to the Levites (1–8)
  2. Yahweh commands Israel to set apart six cities of refuge (9–15)
  3. Yahweh gives laws about murder, manslaughter, and protection in cities of refuge (16–29)
  4. Yahweh requires witnesses for a murder conviction and forbids payments that would cancel the required punishment (30–34)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Cities of refuge

Six of the cities that the Israelites were supposed to give to the Levites functioned as cities of refuge. When a person killed someone, he or she normally deserved to be killed by the dead person’s close relative. However, if the person killed someone by accident, the person could flee to one of the six cities. If he or she stayed in that city, the dead person’s close relative was not allowed to kill him or her. In this way, the city provided refuge, or safety, for someone who unintentionally killed someone else. Eventually, that person would stand trial to confirm whether they killed someone unintentionally or intentionally.

One redeeming the blood

This chapter describes a close relative of a person who was killed as “one redeeming the blood.” This phrase fits with what Yahweh says in 35:33–34. When a person kills someone (sheds their blood), redemption or atonement needs to be accomplished. The close relative could accomplish this redemption by killing the murderer. In this way, they “redeemed the blood” of their relative and made things right before God.

Intentional and unintentional killing

This chapter distinguishes carefully between intentional killing (murder) and unintentional killing (manslaughter). The criteria for deciding between murder and manslaughter include the weapon used, the way the person died, the relationship between the people, and whether the action was intentional or accidental. Consider what words you might use to distinguish between murder (intentional killing) and manslaughter (unintentional killing).

The death of the high priest

Yahweh indicates that a person who killed someone unintentionally would have to stay in a city of refuge until the high priest died. What the high priest’s death accomplishes is not directly stated. Most likely, the high priest’s death atoned for all the unintentional killings during his time as high priest. This is like the sacrifices offered on the Day of the Atonement, which atoned for many sins committed throughout the year. However, since Yahweh does not make the function of the high priest’s death explicit, it is recommended that you also do not make it explicit in your translation.

Polluting the land

In 35:33–34, Yahweh explains that whenever someone is killed, it pollutes or defiles the land where the Israelites live. This is not good, since Yahweh was present with the Israelites in the land. Because Yahweh was present, both the Israelites and their land needed to be pure. So, it was very important for the Israelites to deal with murder and manslaughter properly. Only executing a murderer and keeping a manslayer in a city of refuge would keep the land pure. These verses provide the motivation for following the commands earlier in the chapter.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Metonymy with blood

Yahweh refers to “blood” ten times in this chapter. Blood can refer to death, or even more specifically to murder. It can also refer to the guilt from killing someone. See the UST for the meaning in each case. Blood is an important figure of speech in the Bible, so if possible include references to blood in your translation.

Singular and plural “you”

Most instances of “you” in this chapter are plural. The only exceptions are when Yahweh is speaking directly to Moses in 35:2 and 35:10 and when Yahweh addresses each individual Israelite at the beginning of 35:34.

title: Numbers 35:1 (#1)
content:
עַל־יַרְדֵּ֥ן יְרֵח֖וֹ

"beside the Jordan {at} Jericho"

See how you translated the similar expression in 26:3.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 35:2 (#1)
content:
צַו֮ אֶת־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵל֒ וְ⁠נָתְנ֣וּ לַ⁠לְוִיִּ֗ם מִֽ⁠נַּחֲלַ֛ת אֲחֻזָּתָ֖⁠ם עָרִ֣ים לָ⁠שָׁ֑בֶת

"Command the sons of Israel, and they shall give to the Levites from the inheritance of their possession cities to dwell"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [Command the sons of Israel, ‘You shall give to the Levites from the inheritance of your possession cities to dwell in’]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Numbers 35:2 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נָתְנ֣וּ לַ⁠לְוִיִּ֗ם מִֽ⁠נַּחֲלַ֛ת אֲחֻזָּתָ֖⁠ם עָרִ֣ים לָ⁠שָׁ֑בֶת

"and they shall give to the Levites from the inheritance of their possession cities to dwell"

The implication is that the Levites would not receive a territory of their own, as the other tribes would, so the other tribes needed to give them cities to live in. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and since the Levites will not receive a territory of their own, they shall give to the Levites from the inheritance of their possession cities to dwell in]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 35:2 (#3)
content:
מִֽ⁠נַּחֲלַ֛ת אֲחֻזָּתָ֖⁠ם

"from the inheritance of their possession"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe an inheritance that is characterized by being the possession of the tribes of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the inheritance that they will possess]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 35:2 (#4)
content:
תִּתְּנ֖וּ לַ⁠לְוִיִּֽם

"you shall give to the Levites"

The pronoun you refers to the Israelites, not to Moses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. This also occurs in verses 4, 6, and 7. Alternate translation: [you Israelites shall give to the Levites]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 35:2 (#5)
content:
אֶת־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵל֒

"the sons of Israel"

See how you translated the similar expression in 1:2. This also occurs in verses 8, 10, 15, and 34.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 35:3 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לִ⁠רְכֻשָׁ֔⁠ם

"and for their property"

This could mean: (1) items that they would use for farming or tending animals. Alternate translation: [and for their farming equipment]; or (2) sheep and goats. Alternate translation: [and for their flock]

title: Numbers 35:4 (#1)
content:
אֶ֥לֶף אַמָּ֖ה

"1,000 cubits"

These cubits were a unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or 18 inches. So 1,000 cubits would be about 460 meters or 1,500 feet. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this distance in modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [about 1,500 feet]

See: Biblical Distance

title: Numbers 35:4–5 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מִגְרְשֵׁי֙ הֶֽ⁠עָרִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּתְּנ֖וּ לַ⁠לְוִיִּ֑ם מִ⁠קִּ֤יר הָ⁠עִיר֙ וָ⁠ח֔וּצָ⁠ה אֶ֥לֶף אַמָּ֖ה סָבִֽיב׃ וּ⁠מַדֹּתֶ֞ם מִ⁠ח֣וּץ לָ⁠עִ֗יר אֶת־פְּאַת־קֵ֣דְמָ⁠ה אַלְפַּ֪יִם בָּֽ⁠אַמָּ֟ה וְ⁠אֶת־פְּאַת־נֶגֶב֩ אַלְפַּ֨יִם בָּ⁠אַמָּ֜ה וְ⁠אֶת־פְּאַת־יָ֣ם ׀ אַלְפַּ֣יִם בָּֽ⁠אַמָּ֗ה וְ⁠אֵ֨ת פְּאַ֥ת צָפ֛וֹן אַלְפַּ֥יִם בָּ⁠אַמָּ֖ה וְ⁠הָ⁠עִ֣יר בַּ⁠תָּ֑וֶךְ

"And the pasturelands of the cities that you shall give to the Levites {shall be} from the wall of the city and outside 1,000 cubits all around. And you shall measure from outside to the city the edge to the east 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the south 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the west 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the north 2,000 by the cubit, and the city in the midst"

This could mean: (1) that there was a block of land along each side of the city that was 1,000 cubits deep and 2,000 cubits long. Alternate translation: [And the pasturelands of the cities that you shall give to the Levites shall be 1,000 cubits, measured directly away from the wall of the city all around. And you shall measure the width of the land on each side: the edge to the east 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the south 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the west 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the north 2,000 by the cubit, and the city in the midst]; or (2) that the land on each side of the city was 1,000 cubits deep. Ignoring the size of the city itself, that would create a square that measured 2,000 cubits on each side. Alternate translation: [And the pasturelands of the cities that you shall give to the Levites shall be from the wall of the city and outside 1,000 cubits all around. So, you shall measure the total land outside the city: the edge to the east 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the south 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the west 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the north 2,000 by the cubit. Adjust the shape of this area to include the city in the middle]; or (3) that the city had sides that were 2,000 cubits long. So, when the land was measured from the center of the town, the edge of the land was 2,000 cubits away. When the land was measured from the edge of the town, the edge of the land was 1,000 cubits away. Alternate translation: [And the pasturelands of the cities that you shall give to the Levites shall be 1,000 cubits all around when you measure from the wall outward. When you measure from the center of the city to each edge: the edge to the east 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the south 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the west 2,000 by the cubit, and the edge of the north 2,000 by the cubit]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 35:5 (#1)
content:
אֶת־פְּאַת־קֵ֣דְמָ⁠ה אַלְפַּ֪יִם בָּֽ⁠אַמָּ֟ה

"the edge to the east 2,000 by the cubit"

A cubit was a unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or 18 inches. So 2,000 cubits would be about 920 meters or 3,000 feet. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this distance in modern measurements, either in the text or a footnote. The same distance is given for each of the other three sides in this verse. Alternate translation: [the edge to the east about 3,000 feet]

See: Biblical Distance

title: Numbers 35:6 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠נֻ֥ס שָׁ֖מָּ⁠ה הָ⁠רֹצֵ֑חַ

"for the fleeing there of the one having killed"

The implication is that the one having killed is someone who has killed another person and is fleeing to one of these cities to be safe from anyone who wants to kill him in revenge. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. This also occurs in verse 11. Alternate translation: [for the fleeing there of the one having killed another person, so that he may be safe from anyone seeking revenge]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 35:7 (#1)
content:
אֶתְ⁠הֶ֖ן וְ⁠אֶת־מִגְרְשֵׁי⁠הֶֽן

"them and their pasturelands"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [you shall give them together with their pasturelands]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 35:8 (#1)
content:
מֵ⁠אֵ֤ת הָ⁠רַב֙ תַּרְבּ֔וּ וּ⁠מֵ⁠אֵ֥ת הַ⁠מְעַ֖ט תַּמְעִ֑יטוּ

"from with the many you shall increase, and from with the few you shall decrease"

Yahweh is using the adjectives many and few as nouns to mean tribes that have much land and tribes that have little land. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [from with the tribes that have much land you shall increase, and from with the tribes that have little land you shall decrease]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Numbers 35:8 (#2)
content:
אִ֗ישׁ

"A man"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [Each one]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Numbers 35:8 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠פִ֤י נַחֲלָת⁠וֹ֙

"according to the mouth of his inheritance"

Yahweh is using according to the mouth of his inheritance as a common expression of the culture to mean “in proportion to the size of the land that he inherits.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in proportion to the size of his inheritance]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 35:9 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֥ה לֵּ⁠אמֹֽר

"And Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying"

See how you translated the similar expression in 18:25.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Numbers 35:10 (#1)
content:
דַּבֵּר֙ אֶל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֖ אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֑ם

"Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them"

See how you translated this expression in 33:51.

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 35:11 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִקְרִיתֶ֤ם לָ⁠כֶם֙ עָרִ֔ים

"then you shall make happen for you cities"

Yahweh is using make happen for you cities as a common expression of the culture to mean “select cities for this purpose.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then you shall designate cities for yourselves]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 35:11 (#2)
content:
מַכֵּה־נֶ֖פֶשׁ בִּ⁠שְׁגָגָֽה

"one having struck a person by mistake"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of mistake, you could express the same idea in another way. This also occurs in verse 15. Alternate translation: [one having struck a person without meaning to]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 35:12 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠מִקְלָ֖ט מִ⁠גֹּאֵ֑ל

"for refuge from one redeeming"

The one redeeming is a kind of close relative who has the responsibility to avenge the death of a family member by killing the person who killed him. If your readers would not be familiar with what this is, you could use the name of a similar role that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [for refuge from the relative seeking revenge]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 35:12 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הָ⁠עֵדָ֖ה

"to the face of the congregation"

See how you translated this expression in 16:9.

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 35:12 (#3)
content:
לַ⁠מִּשְׁפָּֽט

"for the judgment"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of judgment, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [so that they may judge him]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 35:14 (#1)
content:
מֵ⁠עֵ֣בֶר לַ⁠יַּרְדֵּ֔ן

"from across to the Jordan"

See how you translated the similar expression in 34:15.

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 35:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠גֵּ֤ר וְ⁠לַ⁠תּוֹשָׁב֙

"and for the sojourner and for the temporary resident"

A sojourner is a kind of foreigner who lived among the Israelites for a long time, and a temporary resident is a kind of foreigner who stayed among them for a shorter time. If your readers would not be familiar with these kinds of people, you could use the names of similar kinds of people that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [and for the long-term foreigner and for the short-term foreigner]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 35:16 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אִם־בִּ⁠כְלִ֨י בַרְזֶ֧ל ׀ הִכָּ֛ה⁠וּ וַ⁠יָּמֹ֖ת

"But if he struck him with a vessel of iron and he died"

Yahweh is presenting a possible condition: that a person might strike someone with an object made of iron and cause that person to die. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [But suppose he struck him with a vessel of iron and he died]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Numbers 35:16 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠כְלִ֨י בַרְזֶ֧ל ׀ הִכָּ֛ה⁠וּ וַ⁠יָּמֹ֖ת רֹצֵ֣חַֽ ה֑וּא

"he struck him with a vessel of iron and he died, he {is} one having killed"

The pronouns he and him refer to different people in this verse. The first he and the last he refer to the person who struck someone, while him and the second he refer to the person who was struck. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the attacker struck the other person with a vessel of iron and that person died, the attacker is one having killed]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 35:16 (#3)
content:
בִּ⁠כְלִ֨י בַרְזֶ֧ל

"with a vessel of iron"

The implication is that the word vessel refers here to any tool or object, not only to a container. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with an object made of iron]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 35:16 (#4)
content:
מ֥וֹת יוּמַ֖ת הָ⁠רֹצֵֽחַ

"Dying, the one having killed shall be put to death"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb translated as Dying and put to death in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. This also occurs in verses 17, 18, 21, and 31. Alternate translation: [The one having killed must certainly be put to death]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 35:16 (#5)
content:
יוּמַ֖ת הָ⁠רֹצֵֽחַ

"the one having killed shall be put to death"

The expression shall be put to death is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to state who would do the action, the context indicates that it would be the close relative who avenges the dead person. This also occurs in verses 17, 18, 21, and 31. Alternate translation: [the avenger shall put the one having killed to death]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 35:17 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠אֶ֣בֶן יָד֩

"with a stone of a hand"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a stone that is characterized by being small enough to hold in a hand. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with a stone small enough to hold in his hand]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 35:19 (#1)
content:
גֹּאֵ֣ל הַ⁠דָּ֔ם

"The one redeeming the blood"

Here, the blood represents “the death of a relative whom someone killed.” The person redeeming the blood is the close relative who had the responsibility to avenge that death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. This also occurs in verses 21, 24, 25, and 27. Alternate translation: [The one avenging the death of his relative]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 35:19 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠פִגְע⁠וֹ־ב֖⁠וֹ

"In his meeting with him"

Yahweh is using In his meeting with him as a common expression of the culture to mean “whenever he finds him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 21. Alternate translation: [As soon as he finds him]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 35:21 (#1)
content:
הִכָּ֤ה⁠וּ בְ⁠יָד⁠וֹ֙

"he struck him with his hand"

The implication is that the person struck the other person with his bare hand without using any weapon, and yet he killed him intentionally. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he struck him with just his fist, without using any weapon]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 35:22 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אִם

"But if"

Yahweh uses the word But here to indicate a contrast between the cases in which a person kills someone on purpose, which the previous verses describe, and the cases in which a person kills someone by accident, which this verse and the next verse describe. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [On the other hand, if]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Numbers 35:22 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠פֶ֥תַע

"in suddenness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of suddenness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [unexpectedly]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 35:23 (#1)
content:
א֣וֹ בְ⁠כָל־אֶ֜בֶן אֲשֶׁר־יָמ֥וּת בָּ⁠הּ֙ בְּ⁠לֹ֣א רְא֔וֹת

"or with any stone, by which he dies, while not seeing"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [or if with any stone by which a person could die, while he did not see the other person]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 35:24 (#1)
content:
גֹּאֵ֣ל הַ⁠דָּ֑ם

"the one redeeming the blood"

Here the word “blood” is a metonym for the murder. See how you translated this phrase in Numbers 35:19. Alternate translation: [the one who avenges the murder] or [the relative seeking vengeance]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 35:25 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠יַּד֮ גֹּאֵ֣ל הַ⁠דָּם֒

"from the hand of the one redeeming the blood"

Here, hand represents “power” or “control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the power of the one redeeming the blood]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 35:25 (#2)
content:
עַד־מוֹת֙ הַ⁠כֹּהֵ֣ן הַ⁠גָּדֹ֔ל

"until the death of the great priest"

The implication is that the death of the great priest, that is, the high priest, would end the time that the person who killed someone had to stay in the city of refuge. After that, he could safely return home. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. This also occurs in verse 28. Alternate translation: [only until he may safely return home at the death of the high priest]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 35:25 (#3)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־מָשַׁ֥ח אֹת֖⁠וֹ

"whom he anointed"

The pronoun he does not refer to the person who killed someone. It refers to an unspecified person who anointed the priest. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [whom another person anointed]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 35:25 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠שֶׁ֥מֶן הַ⁠קֹּֽדֶשׁ

"with the oil of the holy place"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe oil that is characterized by being set apart for use in the holy place. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with the oil that is set apart for use in the holy place]

See: Possession

title: Numbers 35:26 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אִם־יָצֹ֥א יֵצֵ֖א הָ⁠רֹצֵ֑חַ

"But if going out, the one having killed goes out"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb translated as going out and goes out in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [But if the one having killed actually goes out]

See: Reduplication

title: Numbers 35:27 (#1)
content:
אֵ֥ין ל֖⁠וֹ דָּֽם

"there is not to him blood"

Yahweh is using there is not to him blood as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one redeeming the blood is not guilty of murder.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he is not guilty of murder]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 35:29 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠חֻקַּ֥ת מִשְׁפָּ֖ט

"for a statute of judgment"

See how you translated the similar expression in 27:11.

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 35:30 (#1)
content:
כָּל־מַ֨כֵּה־נֶ֔פֶשׁ לְ⁠פִ֣י עֵדִ֔ים יִרְצַ֖ח אֶת־הָ⁠רֹצֵ֑חַ

"Everyone having struck a person, to the mouth of witnesses he shall kill the one having killed"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Everyone having struck a person with the information about the one having killed, since both phrases refer to the same person. Alternate translation: [To the mouth of witnesses he shall kill everyone who has struck and killed a person]

See: Information Structure

title: Numbers 35:30 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠פִ֣י עֵדִ֔ים

"to the mouth of witnesses"

Here, mouth represents “testimony,” what the witnesses say about what happened. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [on the testimony of witnesses]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 35:30 (#3)
content:
יִרְצַ֖ח אֶת־הָ⁠רֹצֵ֑חַ

"he shall kill the one having killed"

The pronoun he does not refer to the person who killed someone. It refers to whoever carries out the execution, such as the close relative who avenges the dead person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the one redeeming the blood shall kill the one having killed]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Numbers 35:30 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠עֵ֣ד אֶחָ֔ד לֹא־יַעֲנֶ֥ה בְ⁠נֶ֖פֶשׁ

"And one witness shall not answer against a person"

Yahweh is using answer against a person as a common expression of the culture to mean “testify against a person.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And one witness shall not testify against a person]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 35:31 (#1)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־ה֥וּא רָשָׁ֖ע לָ⁠מ֑וּת

"who is wicked to die"

Yahweh is using who is wicked to die as a common expression of the culture to mean “who is guilty and deserves to die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who is guilty and deserves to be executed]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 35:32 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא־תִקְח֣וּ כֹ֔פֶר לָ⁠נ֖וּס אֶל־עִ֣יר מִקְלָט֑⁠וֹ לָ⁠שׁוּב֙ לָ⁠שֶׁ֣בֶת בָּ⁠אָ֔רֶץ

"And you shall not take a ransom to flee to the city of his refuge, to return to dwell in the land"

The implication is that someone could offer a ransom payment in order to be allowed to leave the city of refuge before the death of the high priest. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And you shall not accept payment from someone in exchange for allowing him to leave the city of his refuge and return to live in his own land before the death of the priest]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 35:33 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י הַ⁠דָּ֔ם ה֥וּא יַחֲנִ֖יף אֶת־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ

"for the blood, it pollutes the land"

Here, the blood represents “the killing of a person.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for murder pollutes the land]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 35:33 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ לֹֽא־יְכֻפַּ֗ר לַ⁠דָּם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שֻׁפַּךְ־בָּ֔⁠הּ כִּי־אִ֖ם בְּ⁠דַ֥ם שֹׁפְכֽ⁠וֹ

"and atonement for the land shall not be made for the blood that was poured out in it, except by the blood of the one pouring it out"

If it would appear in your language that Yahweh was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [and atonement for the land can be made for the blood that was poured out in it only by the blood of the one pouring it out]

See: Connect — Exception Clauses

title: Numbers 35:33 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ לֹֽא־יְכֻפַּ֗ר

"and atonement for the land shall not be made"

The expression shall not be made is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and you cannot make atonement for the land]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 35:33 (#4)
content:
לַ⁠דָּם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שֻׁפַּךְ־בָּ֔⁠הּ

"for the blood that was poured out in it"

The expression was poured out is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for the blood that someone poured out in it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 35:33 (#5)
content:
בְּ⁠דַ֥ם שֹׁפְכֽ⁠וֹ

"by the blood of the one pouring it out"

Yahweh is using the blood of the one pouring it out as a common expression of the culture to mean “the death of the person who killed someone.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by the death of the person who killed someone]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 35:34 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֧א תְטַמֵּ֣א אֶת־הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֤ר אַתֶּם֙ יֹשְׁבִ֣ים בָּ֔⁠הּ

"And you shall not make unclean the land in which you are dwelling"

The word you in the phrase you shall not make unclean is singular here because Yahweh is speaking to each individual Israelite. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. The word you in the phrase you are dwelling is plural because Yahweh is speaking to all the Israelites. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Numbers 35:34 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֧א תְטַמֵּ֣א אֶת־הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֤ר אַתֶּם֙ יֹשְׁבִ֣ים בָּ֔⁠הּ אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲנִ֖י שֹׁכֵ֣ן בְּ⁠תוֹכָ֑⁠הּ כִּ֚י אֲנִ֣י יְהוָ֔ה שֹׁכֵ֕ן בְּ⁠ת֖וֹךְ בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"And you shall not make unclean the land in which you are dwelling, in the midst of which I am dwelling, for I, Yahweh, am dwelling in the midst of the sons of Israel"

The word translated as for indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And because I, Yahweh, am dwelling in the midst of the sons of Israel, you shall not make unclean the land in which you are dwelling, in the midst of which I am dwelling]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Numbers - Chapter 36 Introduction
content:
Numbers 36 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Moses gives Yahweh’s instructions concerning keeping ancestral land within a tribe when daughters inherit that land. He gives specific instructions for Zelophehad’s daughters, which continue from 27:1–11, and then more general instructions. Daughters that inherit land must marry someone from the same tribe to keep ancestral land within that tribe. The chapter ends with a brief conclusion to this section of Numbers.

  1. Manasseh’s clan leaders raise a concern about land passing to another tribe through marriage (1–4)
  2. Yahweh commands women who inherit land to marry within their father’s tribe (5–9)
  3. Zelophehad’s daughters obey and marry within their tribe (10–12)
  4. Closing summary of the commands given on the plains of Moab (13)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Property, marriage, and inheritance

In this culture, when a woman married a man, the man would be in charge of any property or possessions that the woman had. If the woman had inherited land from her father, that land would now belong to her husband. If the husband was from a different tribe than the wife, the land would permanently belong to a different tribe than the tribe of the wife’s father. This situation is what the leaders of Manasseh wish to avoid. Yahweh tells Moses to agree with them and require women who have inherited land to marry within their tribe. That way, the property would continue to belong to their father’s tribe.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Marriage within the tribe or the clan?

In 36:6 and 36:8, Moses indicates whom daughters who inherit may marry. It is possible that he means that they must marry someone from the same tribe and clan as their father. It is possible that he means only that they must marry someone from the same tribe as their father. The UST follows that interpretation. See the notes on these verses for alternate translations.

title: Numbers 36:1 (#1)
content:
רָאשֵׁ֣י הָֽ⁠אָב֗וֹת

"the heads of the fathers"

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the heads of the fathers’ families]

See: Ellipsis

title: Numbers 36:1 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֤י מֹשֶׁה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י הַ⁠נְּשִׂאִ֔ים

"to the face of Moses and to the face of the leaders"

Here, to the face of represents “into the presence of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to Moses and to the leaders]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 36:1 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"for the sons of Israel"

See how you translated the similar expression in 1:2. This also occurs in verses 2–5, 7–9, and 13.

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 36:1 (#4)
content:
בֶּן־מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה

"the son of Manasseh"

See how you translated the similar expression in 1:34. This also occurs in verse 12.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 36:2 (#1)
content:
אֶת־אֲדֹנִ⁠י֙ צִוָּ֣ה יְהוָ֔ה לָ⁠תֵ֨ת אֶת־הָ⁠אָ֧רֶץ

"Yahweh commanded my lord to give the land"

Even though the leaders of the clan of Gilead are addressing Moses directly, they are speaking of him in the third person as my lord to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [Yahweh commanded you, sir, to give the land]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Numbers 36:2 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠נַחֲלָ֛ה

"in inheritance"

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of inheritance, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be inherited]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Numbers 36:2 (#3)
content:
וַֽ⁠אדֹנִ⁠י֙ צֻוָּ֣ה בַֽ⁠יהוָ֔ה

"and my lord was commanded by Yahweh"

The expression was commanded is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh also commanded my lord]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 36:2 (#4)
content:
אֶֽת־נַחֲלַ֛ת צְלָפְחָ֥ד אָחִ֖י⁠נוּ

"the inheritance of Zelophehad our brother"

The leaders are using the term brother to describe Zelophehad as someone who was descended from the same ancestor as they were, that is, a member of their own clan. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the inheritance of Zelophehad our fellow clansman]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 36:3 (#1)
content:
וְ֠⁠הָיוּ לְ⁠אֶחָ֞ד מִ⁠בְּנֵ֨י שִׁבְטֵ֥י בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל֮ לְ⁠נָשִׁים֒

"And they will be for wives to one from the sons of the tribes of the sons of Israel"

The leaders are using they will be for wives to as a common expression of the culture to mean “they will marry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they will marry men from the sons of the tribes of the sons of Israel]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 36:3 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נִגְרְעָ֤ה נַחֲלָתָ⁠ן֙ מִ⁠נַּחֲלַ֣ת אֲבֹתֵ֔י⁠נוּ וְ⁠נוֹסַ֕ף עַ֚ל נַחֲלַ֣ת הַ⁠מַּטֶּ֔ה

"and their inheritance will be taken away from the inheritance of our fathers, and it will be added upon the inheritance of the tribe"

The expressions will be taken away and will be added are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and their husbands will take their inheritance away from the inheritance of our fathers, and they will add it to the inheritance of the tribe]

See: Active or Passive

title: Numbers 36:3 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠נַּחֲלַ֣ת אֲבֹתֵ֔י⁠נוּ

"from the inheritance of our fathers"

The leaders are using the term fathers to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 8. Alternate translation: [from the inheritance of our ancestors]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 36:3 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠מַּטֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּהְיֶ֖ינָה לָ⁠הֶ֑ם

"the tribe that they will be for them"

The leaders are using that they will be for them as a common expression of the culture to mean “into which they will marry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 4. Alternate translation: [the tribe into which they will marry]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 36:3 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠מִ⁠גֹּרַ֥ל נַחֲלָתֵ֖⁠נוּ

"And from the lot of our inheritance"

Here, lot represents “the portion of land that was assigned by lot.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And from the portion of land that was assigned to us by lot as our inheritance]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 36:4 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אִם־יִהְיֶ֣ה הַ⁠יֹּבֵל֮ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵל֒ וְ⁠נֽוֹסְפָה֙ נַחֲלָתָ֔⁠ן עַ֚ל נַחֲלַ֣ת הַ⁠מַּטֶּ֔ה

"And if the Jubilee is for the sons of Israel, then their inheritance will be added upon the inheritance of the tribe"

The leaders are speaking as if this were a hypothetical possibility, but they mean that it is actually true. The Jubilee would certainly come. If your language does not state something as a condition if it is certain or true, or if your readers might think that what the leaders are saying is uncertain, then you could translate this as a confident statement. Alternate translation: [And when the Jubilee comes for the sons of Israel, their inheritance will be added upon the inheritance of the tribe]

See: Connect — Factual Conditions

title: Numbers 36:4 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠יֹּבֵל֮

"the Jubilee"

The Jubilee was a kind of special year that occurred every fiftieth year, when land that had been sold was returned to the family that originally owned it. If your readers would not be familiar with what the Jubilee was, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the special fiftieth year for giving land back to its original owners]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Numbers 36:4 (#3)
content:
מַטֵּ֣ה אֲבֹתֵ֔י⁠נוּ

"the tribe of our fathers"

See how you translated the similar expression in 26:55. This also occurs in verse 7. This also occurs in verses 6–8.

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 36:5 (#1)
content:
כֵּ֛ן מַטֵּ֥ה בְנֵֽי־יוֹסֵ֖ף דֹּבְרִֽים

"The tribe of the sons of Joseph is speaking rightly"

Here, tribe represents “the leaders of the tribe” who spoke to Moses. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The leaders from the tribe of the sons of Joseph are speaking rightly]

See: Metonymy

title: Numbers 36:5 (#2)
content:
עַל־פִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה

"upon the mouth of Yahweh"

See how you translated the similar expression in 3:16.

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 36:6 (#1)
content:
אַ֗ךְ לְ⁠מִשְׁפַּ֛חַת מַטֵּ֥ה אֲבִי⁠הֶ֖ם

"only to the clan of the tribe of their father"

This could mean: (1) that they can marry into any clan within the tribe of their father. Alternate translation: [only to any clan of the tribe of their father]; or (2) that they can marry only someone from the same clan as their father. Alternate translation: [only to the same tribe and clan as their father]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 36:6 (#2)
content:
לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר לַ⁠טּ֥וֹב בְּ⁠עֵינֵי⁠הֶ֖ם תִּהְיֶ֣ינָה לְ⁠נָשִׁ֑ים אַ֗ךְ לְ⁠מִשְׁפַּ֛חַת מַטֵּ֥ה אֲבִי⁠הֶ֖ם תִּהְיֶ֥ינָה לְ⁠נָשִֽׁים

"saying, ‘To the good in their eyes they will be for wives, only to the clan of the tribe of their father they will be for wives"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that to the good in their eyes they will be for wives, only to the clan of the tribe of their father they will be for wives]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Numbers 36:6 (#3)
content:
לַ⁠טּ֥וֹב בְּ⁠עֵינֵי⁠הֶ֖ם

"To the good in their eyes"

Moses is using To the good in their eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean “to whomever they think is best.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [To whomever they consider best]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 36:7 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־תִסֹּ֤ב נַחֲלָה֙ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל מִ⁠מַּטֶּ֖ה אֶל־מַטֶּ֑ה

"And an inheritance for the sons of Israel shall not go around from tribe to tribe"

Here Moses is speaking as if an inheritance were able to go around from one tribe to another. It means that land must not pass from the ownership of one tribe to another tribe. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the ownership of an inheritance for the sons of Israel shall not pass from one tribe to another tribe]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 36:7 (#2)
content:
אִ֗ישׁ בְּ⁠נַחֲלַת֙ מַטֵּ֣ה אֲבֹתָ֔י⁠ו

"a man in the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers"

Moses is not referring to a specific man. He means men in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [each person in the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 36:7 (#3)
content:
יִדְבְּק֖וּ

"shall cling"

Here Moses is speaking as if each Israelite would cling to the inheritance of his ancestral tribe. It means that each Israelite would keep the land that belonged to his ancestral tribe. If this meaning would not be clear in your language, you could use a comparable expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [shall remain]

See: Metaphor

title: Numbers 36:8 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠מִּשְׁפַּ֛חַת מַטֵּ֥ה אָבִ֖י⁠הָ

"from the clan of the tribe of her father"

As in verse 6, his could mean: (1) that the woman can marry into any clan within the tribe of her father. Alternate translation: [from any clan of the tribe of her father]; or (2) that the woman can marry only someone from the same clan as her father. Alternate translation: [from the same tribe and clan as her father]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Numbers 36:9 (#1)
content:
אִישׁ֙

"a man"

Moses is not referring to a specific man. He means each person among the tribes of the sons of Israel. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [each person]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

title: Numbers 36:11 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י דֹדֵי⁠הֶ֖ן

"to the sons of their uncles"

Your language may have its own term or expression for this relationship. The phrase the sons of their uncles refers to the sons of their father’s brothers. Alternate translation: [to their cousins on their father’s side]

See: Kinship

title: Numbers 36:12 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תְּהִי֙ נַחֲלָתָ֔⁠ן עַל־מַטֵּ֖ה מִשְׁפַּ֥חַת אֲבִי⁠הֶֽן

"and their inheritance was upon the tribe of the clan of their father"

The author is using their inheritance was upon as a common expression of the culture to mean “their inheritance remained with.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their inheritance stayed with the tribe of the clan of their father]

See: Idiom

title: Numbers 36:13 (#1)
content:
אֵ֣לֶּה הַ⁠מִּצְוֺ֞ת וְ⁠הַ⁠מִּשְׁפָּטִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה

"These {are} the commandments and the ordinances that Yahweh commanded"

This verse is a comment that summarizes the commandments and the ordinances that Yahweh gave in the preceding chapters. This signals the end of the book of Numbers. Use the natural form in your language for expressing the conclusion of a story. Alternate translation: [In conclusion, these are the commandments and the ordinances that Yahweh commanded]

See: End of Story

title: Numbers 36:13 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠מִּצְוֺ֞ת וְ⁠הַ⁠מִּשְׁפָּטִ֗ים

"are} the commandments and the ordinances"

The terms commandments and ordinances mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all the commands]

See: Doublet
